text: This place is the very defintion of over-promise and under-performance. The atmosphere is cute and comfortable. They did a great job with the space. The menu was tempting; we couldn't decide which tasty-sounding dish to try first. The four of us split the breakfast pizza which was okay save the runny, undercooked egg. Basically, everything we got was undercooked. We were not in a rush, we would've happily waited for thoroughly cooked food. One of us got the breakfast salad. She enjoyed it, but didn't understand why they didn't chop up the huge undercooked "pork belly" lard cubes (called bacon on the menu) before serving it. Another friend ordered the Monte Christo (although they called it something else) which was a delicious combo of flavors on unfortunately soggy bread. I got the steak and eggs. What was I thinking? The meat tasted horrible. We couldn't exactly define what was wrong with it, but we all agreed. The manager removed it from the check, but felt the need to argue that it was fresh. The freshness wasn't in question, it simply did not taste good at all. My hot date had an omelet which contained, I kid you not, raw bacon. They took that off the check as well. Our server, who like all of the waitstaff showed a sultry amount of skin, was sweet and attentive but did forget to bring us the ketchup, hollandaise, cappuccino and tea refill we asked for. She did throw in a free stickybun. Thanks, toots. Unfortunately, we will probably not return, unless it is just for the wonderful cinnamon-sprinkled cappucino.
label: NEG

text: The stuff stated earlier by Mark is SO TRUE and I wish I had read it before my visit to Matoi. My experience tonight was very similar to his. First of all, when everyone arrives we head to the tables and they send us three waitresses (not that there is a problem with that) and the waitresses take forever to get peoples drinks and FORGET to get certain peoples orders. Order was an issue as the waitresses scrambled to get our meals correct. The waitresses often stuck around to converse in a foreign language what was happening when all they had to do was go to the back to deal with the issue. My sisters friend was allergic to avocados and clearly asked the lady for none on her sushi (even going as far as to write it on the order slip) and the lady STILL delivered the sushi with avocados much to the dismay of my sisters friend. My Aunt and Step-Sister asked for a fork and the waitress was RUDE and DELAYED in getting the forks. If a place serves Chinese and Korean food, I see no reason why utensils should not be given to paying customers. The sushi I had (Rainbow Rolls and California Rolls) was decent, but I can think of at least 5 sushi places I have already reviewed on here that would have the same quality sushi with better service than that of Matoi. The younger waitresses, I must say, were actually very good. One girl named MULAN, helped us pretty well and tried to keep my family from blowing up at the restaurant staff when things continued to go wrong. We also brought a cake for my sisters birthday, and the waitresses waited, IN THEIR INTELLECTUAL MOMENT, to come out with the cake ready when 2/3 of the table was outside smoking or in the bathroom, SPOILING the surprise element of my sisters birthday. Throughout the whole dinner the waitresses continued to pester us if we were done or if our drinks needed to be refilled, even when our drinks were 4/5 full. So basically they were useful when it wasn't necessary, and useless when it was necessary. The last notable thing is that when we finally received our checks the waitresses pestered my parents for the money for the bill as my Mom analyzed the check and my Mom was about five seconds from telling everyone in the whole place off because of how rude they had been. Long store short: AVOID AT ALL COSTS Where to go instead: Jo-To's (Which is right up the street and has a pretty cashier =])

text: An open letter to Cavanaugh's River Deck. Dear Cavanaugh's River Deck, I hate you. I LOATH you. I came to you for a quick bite to eat before a concert at Penn's Landing, and you managed to turn my, what was to be enjoyable evening into an anger filled nightmare. We got to your establishment over an hour before our concert started, plenty of time to grab a sandwich or burger...or so I thought. After seating us, our server gave us about 20 minutes to decide on what we wanted to eat. I say gave us, but I think I mean she forgot about us. In fact, I think everyone in your restaurant forgot that they were open, because if it were not for me going to find someone, I'm not sure if I would have ever ordered. I'll skip past the part about the terrible food and messing up our order, because I can deal with that, it happens. What I can not deal with is rudeness to your customers. We were finished our meal and now begin to hear the very concert we have tickets to. Once, again, not a soul is to be found to get a bill from. It is at this point where I decide I am going to walk towards the exit, and unless I see an employee I am not stopping. I somehow managed to see someone who appeared to be employed by Cavanaugh's so I went over to them and asked for our bill...she said, "you'll have to talk to your server." I replied with something like, "Our server has gone missing, can I speak to your manager." Another woman walked out who introduced herself as the manager. After explaining my situation and horrible experience, I expected an apology or something. What I got was unprovoked attitude. She printed out my bill, and I paid. I regret paying to this day. Thanks for nothing, Russ C. It is said that if one person has a bad experience in a restaurant, he or she will tell at least nine people about it, those nine people will tell at least five, who will tell at least 3 and so on. I'm trying to tell as many people as possible. Cavanaugh's sucks, I would fish for my meal in the Delaware before I visit Cavanaugh's again. Spread the word.
label: NEG

text: Beware that this place charges $18 per day for parking and a "resort fee" of $15 for internet access, 2 bottles of water a day and on line access to a newspaper site. I called and spoke to a manager on duty about these fees and she refused to refund the fees since I checked the terms and conditions box on the reservations page. I informed the MOD that I had neglected to read all of the terms and conditions, therefore she refused to help. After returning home I looked at the terms and conditions on the reservations page, where the check box appears and indeed it does tell of the $15 resort fee, but fails to mention the $18 parking fee. This room was $250 per night before taxes. The room was nothing special. I've stayed in La Quinta Inns and other places that were just as nice, if not better, for far less. I also was left wondering what happened to the southern hospitality that us southerners are supposed to be so well known for. When I pay $250 a night for a room, I don't expect to be charged exorbitant fees for things I get for free at far less expensive hotels.

text: Tool central. Whether they're making up new rules in order to charge you more or glaring at your "I-don't-feel-the-need-to-try-that-hard" handbag, the staff here is neither friendly nor helpful in any way. Though I have given up in recent months, each of the last three times I attempted to patronize Byblos my group was faced with some new ridiculous and awkward stipulation. First, all of a sudden, parties of 5 or more had to purchase at least two hookahs, then tables were reserved for parties ordering food, and then it was a minimum charge per head at the table. text: I reserved a car from Budget St. Louis on-line, through Southwest Airlines web site. Something in the back of my mind told me I had not liked my prior experience with them, but that was a few years ago and I travel frequently. The shuttle was reasonably timely, and the staff polite. However, they had none of the information I had already given through the web site and tried to up-sell me. Being in a hurry, I declined the up-selling efforts and got my car. The car was fine. Upon return late that same night, I was the only person in the place. The young man behind the counter was pleasant and efficient. I did notice however, that not having been on top of things earlier, I had without being asked, purchased a full tank of gas. I returned it 3/4 tank full because it was late and I didn't want to fool with a gas station. They would have gotten to me either way, but they really should have asked me which option I preferred. I asked for a ride to the airport Holiday Inn. The young man smiled and called the van. As we were leaving the parking lot the driver told me there would be a $5 charge. I said WHAT? No one mentioned that inside. The driver then said he was going to charge me because the hotel was "not on his route." Being tired, I agreed to the $5 shakedown. He then demanded cash in advance, saying that if he just took my word for it, I could just get off without paying. At that point, I demanded to be returned to the car lot. He took me back with many a poisonous glance. When I told the young man at the desk what had happened, he apologized and called the hotel van for me. SO, my review is mixed: 1) Processing in was not efficient and wasted my time trying to up-sell 2) They sold me a tank of gas without asking me first; 3) Staff at the desk were polite and helpful; 4) The car itself was fine; 5) The van driver was operating a petty shake-down racket in the middle of the night.

text: Bottom line: I'd definitely stay here again. While looking around for a hotel room near New Orleans' French Quarter, we came across a unique special offered by the Pere Marquette that pretty much had us sold: a "super small room at a super small rate," which came out to about $100 (including tax) per night. Even though the hotel decision-making was pretty much predicated on that low rate and the hotel's boutique status, we were very pleased by all aspects of the hotel. The "super small room" ended up being just right, perfectly spacious for a couple that didn't mind being in closer quarters. The queen bed was cozy, the bathroom was marvelous, and the television was even attached to the ceiling to afford maximum space. The hotel was also very generous in making an early check-in available at least three or four hours before our scheduled check-in. The decor and overall feel of the hotel was pleasant, too, and certainly provided a comfortable "home base" and contrast to the chaos of the New Orleans streets. Our floor paid homage to famous king of swing Benny Goodman, much to the delight of the clarinetist of our party. Although we didn't use the hotel's restaurant or bar services, the entire bar and lounge area was gorgeous (although the miss called it "cheesy"). It sounds from the other reviews that the restaurant is uniquely good among New Orleans hotel restaurants, too. Staff was friendly, especially the information concierge stationed to the left of the entrance, who helped hook us up with cab rides, travel recommendations, maps, and more. Locationwise, the Pere Marquette can't be beat, either -- who knew the street it's on basically turns into Bourbon Street? Despite the convenient location, though, the room was extraordinarily quiet and definitely seemed safe enough. Final verdict: the Renaissance Pere Marquette fit nicely into the budget and ended up being an excellent choice. I'd particularly recommend it for the "super small room," fun boutique feel, and excellent tactical location from which to launch your Bourbon Street at

text: Of all of the noodle houses I frequent, including the ones in Chinatown, this location of Hoang Long is one of my favourite Vietnamese restaurants. The bowls of pho are enormous - probably the biggest I have ever had without ordering a large size. And it tastes great. I also really like anything with lemongrass grilled chicken or beef. As an appetizer, I order skewers of the chicken and beef, which are long and loaded with meat and covered in a spicy peanut sauce. They take a while to prepare but are worth the wait. To drink I often order tea, iced coffee over condensed milk, or a "sunrise" - a combination of orange juice, pineapple juice, and grenadine, served in a tall glass. The drink is as great to look at as it is to drink. A family owned establishment with other Edmonton locations, Hoang Long has great food, good prices (slightly higher than other Vietnamese restaurants by a dollar or two for most dishes), and good service.

text: Spectacular. Went for dinner the other night, and have been back repeatedly since. What the restaurant lacks in atmosphere, it more than makes up for in terms of food quality and immaculate service. The Achari Lamb sang with the perfect sour bite of freshly-made pickle chutney, while the Boti Kababs were soft, succulent, and rich with savory spice. The Garlic Naan was fresh, yeasty, and pillow soft. Dishes were brought to our tables on a cart in proper metalware, and the proprietor himself served us rice and saw to our every need during the evening. Glazed ceramic plates and silverware were clean and of good quality. Oh, and I did I mention it's a no-corkage-fee BYOB? Yeah, it is. I'm not entirely sure the other reviewers went to the same restaurant that I did. I'm going to be a devoted regular here, eating my way up and down the menu. A truly superior operation, and one obviously conducted with copious love and pride. We in West Philly should count ourselves lucky to have restaurants like this.

To Elle's credit, both of our vegetables were perfectly cooked: mine a ratatouille and her's a haricots verts. We both also had potato dishes--her's mashed, mine gratin--that were very good. Desert was the bread pudding. The bourbon sauce was very good, but the bread pudding itself was laughably made from whole slices of grocery store sandwich bread. I suggested they use the day old bread they served us to begin our meal next time. I ordered a bottle of wine with my meal which was $48 and excellent (Dunham Trutina 2006) and the balance of the $123 bill was the disappointing food. We don't mind spending for a truly great meal but this was a long ways away from that. It bordered on us feeling ripped off. Sad to say this place has passed it's hey day and will soon see its demise if it continues down the road of mediocrity at $$$ prices.

text: Ahh, the reservation system. The arbitrary, cronyistic institution of harassment used by conductors to bully unsuspecting passengers. Its use has diminished the otherwise admirable Amtrak Keystone Service. On the Keystone Service, you may board a train without a ticket and purchase one on board unless the train is "Reservation Required" or is sold out. The website clearly shows which trains are Reservation Required when searching train schedules. We attempted to catch a 6:10 p.m. train back to Philadelphia the other night. Despite the train being half-empty, the conductor would not let us on-board without a reservation and simply drove off, leaving us in the cold with the lone option of making a reservation for the 8:10 train. I called Amtrak's line, which stated that all trains during Thanksgiving week required a reservation. This is stated nowhere on the website when checking train schedules. I made a reservation for the 8:10 train. Two hours later we went back to the train station. The train pulled up and the conductor let us on board without needing the reservation. He did not ask for my reservation number, he did not ask for my boarding code, and he did not ask for our IDs. He simply sold us two tickets. I described what happened at 6:10. The 8:10 pm train conductor asked me for a description of the conductor who wouldn't let us on, and confirmed that he has done this to other passengers. He intimated that the guy was simply being mean and that he himself wouldn't have done that. The issue is not about a policy, it's about choice. The reservation requirement is arbitrary; that conductor could have chosen to let us on the train, especially since we bought tickets on an even more crowded train without a reservation. He could have let us on. He didn't. This is what makes him a jerk, and this is why the otherwise excellent Amtrak Keystone Service gets two stars.

text: In the past I've used capital grille as a jumping off point for other restaurants. Come here, have a decent cocktail, then head out. For a change, my guest and I decided to have lunch here yesterday. The host was not to be found, but Ralph, the pleasant bartender, waved us in and had our drink orders in process in no time. We glanced at the menu, but decided to stay when he described the scallop special. This was three large 'lion's paw' scallops, served of a toasted brioche bun, lightly sauced and complimented with fresh grape and mini heirloom tomatoes. My guest and I exchanged glances knowing one of us was going to order this. I blinked first, so he won out. I had the Wagyu carpaccio as a consolation prize. At $15, the carpaccio was nice. It was served with a huge mountain of endive, large curls of aged provolone, and 1/2 a lemon to squeeze as desired. I shoveled a mouthful of greens in only to find yowza! they were dressed with a pepper/horseradish dressing that really had a kick. Now, had this been prime Kobe, I would have been very unhappy to have this much intensity taking away from the base taste of my beef. No worries there. The 'Wagyu' beef was far from top notch. In fact, as we looked at the beef we could see that what had happen was the usual poor prep. The beef had been frozen so the could cut it paper thin. This breaks down the meat a bit and causes it to rip to shreds (or simply turn to mush) when you disturb it. Worse, after this was cut the plate was left out, sans salad, waiting for little ole me to order it. While it waited, the beef air dried to literal dried beef. Luckily the dressing and a liberal squirt of lemon reconstituted it well. Overall, I did really like this dish, but don't be passing off JRZY heffer as Kobe. Call it what it is, a lovely beef carpaccio, and move along. Yes, I would order it again, for $15 it was a well priced dish, and it tasted good. The scallops were a knockout. One of the few places where the scallops were perfectly cooked, they were then lightly seasoned with garlic and a light drizzle of olive oil. Hardly the size of a Lion paw, they were good size nonetheless. The brioche went perfectly, it's roasted eggy richness soaking up all the juices of the scallops and tomatoes as you munched along. The tomatoes were a lovely mix of small grape, tiny yellow pear, and quartered purple russians. A bit heavy on the garlic, the dish overall was exceptional and for $17, a win in our book. A side note on our bartender. He was polite, meticulous, there when you needed him and not when you didn't. He also understood that if you enjoy a dirty martini on the very dirty side, you tend to have an 'overage' after you pour, and rather than shoot it down the sink like some places do, he didn't. He got an extra bump in his tip for that. Seems basic, but some places are so bad for this you almost want to order the olive juice on the side! The house made potato chips served in late afternoon are also devilishly good, and seem to evaporate quickly from the bowl. Guard your bowl closely. We look forward to dinner here soon, perhaps at the new Cherry Hill facility!

text: I hate to see this place crash and burn, given how much I loved it these last few months, but these last few visits have had their bumps and glitches, and today's visit sealed their fate, in my eyes. We were informed of a 45 minute wait when we arrived--not a big deal nor a surprise on a busy Sunday morning. But while the others waiting ahead of us had coffee and other beverages, we were offered nothing. And, an hour later, when we finally were offered coffee, it never came to us. So, we wandered around towards the back of the store, browsing the beer selection, and then made our way back towards the front as the crowd started to thin out. But as the tables turned over, we couldn't figure out why we were still not being seated. Turns out, there was a large private party coming in, but I wish we'd been told of this. Hawthornes revealed themselves to be really ill-equipped for such a large crowd, in addition to full service for their other patrons. The service we received once we were seated was incredibly poor, and completely unapologetic. Our waiter's response to a request for a side of toast while we waited to order was "I have 3 other tables. This is an uncharacteristic day. I'll get your coffee..." and then left. We should have, too. Once our orders were taken, it was still a challenge to get the attention of our server, for basics: water; cream and sugar for the coffee; and some butter and jelly for the toast that accompanied our breakfast. 3 of the 4 of us were supposed to have cheese in our omelettes, but it was completely undetectable. And then, the bill: You charged us for a side of jelly?! We had waited, patiently, for over an hour; received "service" that made us feel like we weren't supposed to even be there; and had several errors in our collective orders that were never acknowledged. I hope that surcharge, for a measly ramekin was worth losing the several hundreds of dollars we've been spending there, in food & beer. Not to mention the fact that this is no longer the "must try" word-of-mouth reference I've been telling everyone I can, up until now. When asked at the register how everything was, my father's response was "disappointing," to which the person at the register shrugged it off with a pat "sorry about that." If you're not interested in the feedback from your repeat customers, because you're busy enough where you don't think each party matters, you'll find yourselves with an empty restaurant, wondering why. Sh!t happens. But it's how you handle the sh!t that really matters. And this morning's experience left me feeling frustrated with a cafe that used to be a go-to fave. I won't be back.

Flying for years visiting relatives, although fun when I get there, is almost always torture. Squished together, the lines, check in, re-check in, security check, and now pat down/shoes off/power up laptop, take off jewelery etc.. ad nauseam... Amtrak has none of that nonsense. Advice: I always recommend the business class as it is only 20 bucks more, with the same lousy food naturally (hehe) but the seating is more spacious and comfortable with a lower noise volume which makes the comfort level goes up the scale to 100% in comparing to just regular fare. I have tried coach (LOUD and sometimes Greyhound-sque) & I have tried the lowest level of 2 person suite for travel (less leg room,) and I still prefer the business class. Perks: Business class you have 2 foot rests... one in front of you that you can rest your feet on and a leg/foot rest that props up like a lazyboy chair. You can lean back in your chair without disturbing who is behind you. There are 120V electrical plugs (for coach also) for every seat pairing. Pros/Cons: It is a longer way to travel, by train, but not that much longer if you are going to Chicago or Michigan. Sleeping our way to Michigan, rather then driving through the ice and snow is a blessing. Your luggage does not get searched, you can pack liquids and breakables as you choose, you don't have to take off your shoes, in business class you sit in a different (A LOT less crowded) waiting room. For $20 it is beyond worth the cost. Pros: Your luggage is always with you. You don't have to pack like someone might go through your stuff and you don't have to worry about your lip gloss causing an international incident etc.. If you pack something your big suitcase that is your favorite item, you don't have to worry about a luggage handler/sorter/etc.. lifting it off your hands. Carry that hair gel and in your carry on with no worries. This part is a big deal for me. Through many years of flying and the last few years of having to pack everything trying to keep in mind where to pack valuables (on me,) liquids of any sort (sealed in something and pray it doesn't burst in the suitcase.. oh the horrible memory of ruining a beautiful dress from Hair conditioner. :( etc....) .. THANK GOODNESS all I have to do is pack it up and go to take the train! Cons: Your luggage is always with you. Make sure ALL your luggage rolls or your shoulder bag is VERY light. Trust me. Your shoulders/back will NOT like you if you lug your heavy (or soon to feel that way) luggage around everywhere (thinking of Union Station and trading off to go to another hub.) The station itself: I like the location, as it seems a bit removed from the immediate area's traffic. The people who are working the ticket counter have 10 shades of attitude but they get 10 flavors of crazy going through there and not just mine. ;) (Good crazy is ok :p :D ) The fastfood joint is dirty and I couldn't bring myself to eat there. The chairs are horrible and there are no good places to put your luggage nor yourself for that matter. All sorts of characters walking in and out of there. I feel safe enough but I wouldn't have anyone I care about stay there too long waiting for me to pick them up. Always room for improvement. What's up: Take luggage that has wheels. Your shoulders/back/neck will scream at you if you try to carry bags everywhere. Pay the extra 20 bucks for business class for a much better experience. I love trains now. So stress free compared to driving/flying. Don't tarry at the station. Time your rides to be close to pick up time. I have heard many stories of VERY long waits for taxicabs, be warned. As you can call while you are on the train there is no reason to make people wait at the station for you or vise versa. Have fun! :)

They brought out our tea (and brought milk in a little cow dish as well as lumps of sugar). Then, they brought our first course of scones and muffins. The scones were OK... just OK, but darn those muffins were GOOD!!! The 2nd course, we chose the type of soup we want. My mom and I had the potato soup, while my sister had the chicken mushroom noodle. BOTH of the soups were YUMMY! Course 3 was a savory torte... they called it a quiche, but i wouldn't say that as it really wasn't egg-y enough. We all had the spinach and artichoke one, but the other option was a broccoli one. This course was just okay. I wasn't so impressed with it. After this they brought our a tiered tray. The first tier was of fruit... kiwi, orange, and pineapple. (BOO!!! I LOVE MANGO AND OTHER THINGS... i thought the fruit could've been more fun). The second tier was the little snacky sandwiches-- a curried chicken salad in phyllo, cucumbers with some basil, and a tomato- bacon one. SUPER YUMMY!!!! The bottom tier was of desserts! Each of us had a chocolate covered strawberry, a little pineapple upside down cake and another crisp of some sort that tasted citrus-y. YUM!!! Finally, they brought out sherbet... which I could hardly eat because i was STUFFED! The bill itself was about 84 bucks and with tip, I spent 102. TOTALLY YUMMY THOUGH and a great experience! Only thing i would change is the fruit options, and maybe make that torte actually more of a quiche! YUM!!! We left the tea room happily cracked out from all that caffeine and VERY full!!!

We asked if they still had time for us and they gladly took us in, I never knew everything shutdown at 9 in this town. We were greeted by Robert Miranda, who was also our server for the night. He and the rest of the Elements staff made us feel very comfortable and welcome. First things first, get a table outside. It's worth it. The restuarant is really nice but the combination of good food and nice weather make the experience that much better. We began with a cheese appetizer which was well chosen and a great start. It was served with dates, pinenuts and perfectly toasted bread. Next us was a salad for each of us, I had a Caesar's Salad and my wife a Root Salad. Both were perfectly put together showcasing the local produce available in the area. We were very happy so far but then came the mail courses, I had the Tuna and my wife the Swordfish. Both in my opinion were equally excellent. Both of our dishes were cooked, seasoned and presented perfectly. I don't think it could have been done any better. When fish is that good you don't need too much nor do you want anything more to hide it. We tried Enterprise Fish Co. the night before and they put so much in thier fish it felt like they were hiding something. None of that here. We finished off with Molten Chocolate Cake and an Apple Fritter type dessert. Icing on the cake. This is a legit place for good food, good service, and good company. You won't be disappointed at Elements. No need to think about it, its Good, really GOOD. Give Robert and crew a visit you'll be happy at the end of your meal.

text: I will NEVER go back to Cliff's, after experiencing the most unprofessional service ever. I wouldn't even give it one star. I recently brought in a sandal for repair. The thong of the sandal had come loose, and although I've had the same repair done before successfully at another place, I thought I'd bring it to Cliff's, which was closer. The man working there was very friendly and promised the repair would be done within 3 days. I paid the cost of the repair upfront, faithful that the repair would be done in a timely manner. I also left the other shoe, which was in perfect condition, with him, as he had asked to use it for reference on the shoe's construction. When I returned to pick up on the date he had promised, I arrived to find he was not there. Someone else carelessly told me to come back after the weekend. When I returned on Monday, I was informed that it was not ready and to come back tomorrow. When I came a third time, I was told it was, again, not ready, and the man complained about being swamped with work over the weekend and lamented about how he had so much to do and was there by himself. If I returned at 5 pm, he'd have it. I came back at 5 pm, the 4th time I'd come to pick it up, and he said that the shoes were not there, but at another location. If I came the next day, he'd have it. When I went FOR THE FIFTH TIME to pick up my shoes, he looked at me woefully and told me "that there was a problem." He had fixed my shoe, finally, BUT HAD LOST THE OTHER ONE. The situation was beyond ludicrous. Instead of completely owning up to his mistake and incompetence, he said that "no one was perfect" and blamed the shoe itself, saying that it was a little shoe and easy to lose track of. I am livid. Not only was my repair not done in a timely fashion, but he lost the match to the shoe, making the repair to the one shoe useless. It doesn't matter if I have the shoe fixed if I don't have the other one to match it. He gave me a refund on the repair, but it doesn't come close to amounting to the cost of the shoes. He's been "looking" for the shoe for a few days now, and he hasn't found it. It's only fair that he refund me the cost of the pair, since I've gone through all this extra trouble on a simple repair. So far, nothing. I'm disappointed that such a long-standing business could be so unprofessional and inconsiderate about the needs and priorities of its consumers. Even if they do find the shoe, I will never go back, and I would HIGHLY DISCOURAGE anyone considering going there. Customers are a privilege, and if a shoe repair place is going to be so careless with both shoes and business, they don't deserve patronage.

text: I ate there last night for restaurant week as a party of 7. The only reservation I could get was for 9:30 PM. At 9:25 we checked in and were told that it would be a few more minutes. We dropped off a few bottles of wine and asked that the white be chilled. We returned at about 9:35 to check the status of the table and were told the table was still not ready. They asked us to wait in their cramped hall with no ETA on the table. At 9:55 I asked the hostess the status of the table and she could not give a straight answer - all she said was that she couldn't rush the other table and they couldn't say how long. We were finally seated a little after 10. Then we were made to wait for bread, water, and menus. When they brought the bottles of wine - the white and champagne were warm (we would have been better leaving them on the cold sidewalk). The meal was OK - and very welcomed as we were starving. When the bill arrived we were a little shocked to find that 20% gratuity had already been added -service was nowhere near deserving of that. Each person at the table put credit cards in to pay and the waiter came back and said they only took 2 credit cards per table. We told them that that information is not written anywhere and they argued that it was restaurant policy. The hostess came over to explain the same thing - however she said that they don't accept more than 2 cards per table because the credit card fees are so high. We went back and forth with her for a bit and then the manager came out - apparently he never heard the term 'the customer is always right." We asked him to split the bill into 'separate' tables so we could each pay on the card; he said he wouldn't do it that one person can charge on their card and get money from the rest or that we could go down to the ATM to get money. We asked him why he takes large reservations but doesn't tell customers the policy. He didn't waiver and we weren't going to either. He finally took the bill with all the cards-we assumed he gave up and was going to divide it. But No, rather he charged everything to my debit card - he said "You made the reservation, so I charged it to you - they can pay you." I refused to sign the slip - which didn't matter because it's a debit card and the money was already withdrawn. The manager threatened to call the cops - which I still don't understand because we PAID the bill through his fraudulent and deceiving manner. We argued and I took the bill and left the unauthorized slip on the table. He followed us out with a bunch of busboys-still not sure why. Almost to hold us there until the cops arrived - still not aware that he'd already stolen the $$$ from us. He continued to argue with us on the sidewalk but we got in cabs and left - before the police arrived. All I can say is that I've worked in the service industry and concessions can always be made - no matter how hard it is. I have dined in a plethora of Italian BYOs in the city, as well as many upscale restaurants, and have NEVER in my life been treated in such a way. Don't waste your TIME and MONEY on this place - we live in such a great city for restaurants - the mediocre food isn't worth the terrible treatment. I can say I will NEVER be back - even if they give the food for FREE!!

She poured us drinks right away, took our order, and the food was out quickly. Things were looking great and I was happy to be proved wrong. Then we started eating... I ordered the Cajun Tilapia and Zack ordered the Meatloaf. They both sounded awesome on the menu. Meatloaf stuffed with pepperoni, roast beef and cheese..... how can you go wrong!?! Zack and I both agreed that their meatloaf was very bland. It almost tasted like a calzone since you could only taste the pepperoni and cheese. My tilapia was cooked perfectly, but it was not cajun what so ever. It came with a dollop of cajun butter (that wasn't spicy or flavorful) and obviously once frozen mixed veggies. The tomato-artichoke orzo was the highlight of my dish. I would suggest waiting for them to work the kinks out before visiting. If we go back it will only be for breakfast or a wrap for lunch.

text: This could be my favorite place on earth. It uniquely creates an artistic and fun environment that feels like a giant playground for adults. Luckily, i went there on a wednesday in november when there wasn't that many kids - i hear they overrun the place on the weekends and during the summer. In order to appreciate this fully, you have to be able to act like a kid - get down on all fours and crawl through holes to secret rooms and passageways. Once you do, it becomes an exciting and adventurous place. There's 3 major areas to explore on all fours, 2 inside, one outside. There's also tons to do for people who don't want to crawl around - they have a bar (a real cool one, too, with crazy tables and seats), they have an area that feels like a penny arcade from 1906, they have an arts and crafts section next to mini-skate park where you can slide on your socks instead of rollerblades or skateboards. And almost the entire place is filled with stuff found within st. louis. Talk about recycling. Check out the website or my pics - http://www.citymuseum.org/about.html - http://flickr.com/photos/chadn/tags/citymuseum/

text: I stopped in a few weeks ago for a bikini wax before I made the trip to OBX for the 4th of July. My friend and I walked in, and took our seats in the semi-crowded waiting area. We waited for about 40 minutes - there were like 5 people ahead of us when we got there, but they also let people who've waited earlier in the day, but have to leave, come back and get in front of the line. The wait didn't really bother me, because I didn't have anything to do for a few hours. Plus, Emma kept us entertained - she's funny! She stopped at the nail station next to me to get something, and I told her that I wanted her to do my wax, as my friend had told me to ask for her. Emma said ok. So fast forward to my turn. I walk in and Emma tells me to lift up my skirt, then to get on the table. *gulp* "Ok," I replied. I made sure to tell her that I only wanted a bikini wax and NOT a Brazilian. Now I'd be lying if I said this wax was completely quick and painless. However, it was as close to quick and painless as you can get when somebody is waxing near your "girly place." The entire thing took her about 10 minutes, and after a frenzy of waxing and ripping, I was all done and as smooth as ever. And it LASTED! My friend had a slightly different experience. She didn't tell Emma that she just wanted a basic bikini wax - so she got the works. When she came out from the back she looked completely horrified. When I asked what was wrong, she said that she thought she'd just gotten a Brazilian. Between my laughing and patting her back for moral support, she told me that she didn't explain what she wanted beforehand, and that's why she got the works. I never thought I'd want to frequent a place like this, because I've always said that when you're working down there, you need to speak nothing but "sweetness and love" to me. Emma and her daughter aren't the most friendly, but I wouldn't call them mean either. However, they are completely focused and skilled at their craft. Oh, and their prices are nice, too! text: A little over a year ago, my boyfriend and I took in a kitten that was dropped off on our roof by her mother. While The Cat Doctor wasn't the cheapest, it was pretty close -- and after I saw their website, I couldn't possibly choose anyone else because I knew they'd care for Madeline like she was their own. The lovely people at this vet have taken in several cats that were either abandoned by their previous owners or, in some cases, were too sick for their owners to afford to help them. All of the office cats are now in wonderful health and have made the office of The Cat Doctor their home. You usually just see them wandering around in the background -- they're very well behaved, and the atmosphere is a very serene one. I've never had anything but attentive service from these people, and they've taken good care of our very skittish Madeline the two times they've had her [the second time for more vaccinations and to rid her of fleas she'd developed]. They're very friendly and you can feel free to ask them anything at all and they'll help you out. Also, they have a sort of daycare service, where they'll house your cat for a day or so if needed. This, of course, is a bit pricey, but if you're like me and can't get out of work to pick your kitty up right after her appointment is over, it's a huge help.

Just slap some pate on there along with some chili peppers, cilantro, pork products you have a masterpiece. What kind of creole fusion cuisine is this? It's the taste of two great culinary cultures in a mash-up. I've never been to the Vietnamese markets in California so it was a treat to have this place open up in Boise. The bread is baked at the Orient Market and it is excellent. I'm hooked on the house special with the pate and the jalapenos. Kids might want to skip the hot peppers. My daughter wanted to know why the menu said the sandwiches come with "egg mayo". Cuz dat's what mayo is, kido - an egg and lemon juice colloid. The BBQ pork is tasty. The chicken is so so. I have got to try the Cajun shrimp. Speaking of Cajun - the last time I had a beignet like they serve here I was in New Orleans at Cafe du Monde. ;-) actually these are kind of leathery and oily. Kind of reminds me of the Fusion Asian Grill / Krispy Kreme combo out in Meridian. So raise a glass of boba tea (the thai tea is my fav) and celebrate mixing things up.

text: A rule of thumb when hubby and I try to do something major is that it works out in the end, but there will always be something crazy stress inducing on the way. So when we showed up at Uhaul with our movers to be reunited with our worldly possessions, only to find that the elevator was broken, we actually managed to stay pretty calm. Enough people, including our movers as we stood around waiting for it to work, had mentioned how the elevator breaks at this facility regularly. The very pleasant surprise this time, however, was that the staff was helpful, quite the opposite demeanor from when we'd moved in. They ran around trying different techniques that had worked in the past, including climbing to the roof to reset it. After an hour of standing around we shrugged, figured this was our stressful moment, and agreed that the movers should just start using the stairs. And then the elevator started working! And by working I mean one of the cleaning staff volunteered herself to stand in the elevator while they loaded and unloaded jiggling whatever combination of buttons she'd found to work for her. The front desk guy also made a call to his manager for us to ask for a refund of our last month, which they gave without a lot of hassle! So, I probably wouldn't use it again (hopefully will never need to), but I'm grateful for the staff we had on the day, and for the lesson in staying calm and not getting belligerent. As for the stuff that had been in storage for 4 months, it was surprisingly clean. Definitely cover at least your cloth furniture with plastic, and check for spiders that may have taken up shop in corners of tables and whatnot.
label: NEG

text: I ate at Crabby Bill's many years ago when we went to visit some family. Finally made it back. They all warned me that it wasn't the same as I remembered when I went there the first time. You leave still hungry with a much lighter wallet. My sister-in-law got the "all-you-can-eat" crab. Don't order this unless you aren't very hungry or you have a few hours to kill. They wont cook you next plate until you've finished you previous one. So once your ready for another one you have to sit there with nothing to eat for ten or more minutes till they bring out your next batch. By that time everyone else is done with their meal and ready to go. The wait staff aren't rude, they are just blah. The girl waiting our table had no business waiting tables, at least not without much more training. Their bartender is hit and miss. My first pina colada was great, my second one tasted horrible and was nothing but marble sized chunks of ice. I hate to see icons of an area do this to themselves. It has become completely commercialized. Sad to say but Crabby Bill's is just not good any more. Oh they'll survive off tourists lured in by nostalgia (and the open air bar they've added) but it will be a disappointment for most.

text: This is a great meat/seafood/specialty item market. Although I've never had the occasion to use their catering service, I'm sure it is top notch and would recommend trying it. Harr's seems to have the largest selection of quality meats in the immediate area. They are also one of the very few places to procure dry aged prime beef. Try their specialty kabobs for a treat. While there are several excellent seafood markets in Pinellas county, Harr's quality and selection make it a convenient stop, especially if meat is the primary reason for the trip. They will happily clean shrimp for $2/pound extra. Overall, their prices are extremely reasonable and comparable to the chain supermarkets. They also have a full selection of wines and specialty items as well as deli and both fresh and frozen prepared foods (made on site). This is definitely not a place to go when hungry. Open the door and the aromas will beckon you to step in a little further. On initial glance, it might appear to be any small market. Once past the check stand, a whole foodie haven awaits. Warning: at this point, unless you are only one of five people in the place, walk directly to the meat counter and grab a number - note the crowd gathered here - it takes a while! Note: if you call in your order ahead of time, there is a place to pick it up and you don't have to wait in line. It will be prepared to order, wrapped and ready for you. My only "beef" is that the produce selection is very limited and not quite as fresh as one would expect. For that reason alone I rated them a 4 versus a 5. I've yet to find anyone that can rival the Fresh Market's when it comes to produce. So, if you're in the neighborhood, drop in and check it out. As I said...don't go hungry (you could always run next door to Mecca for a nosh first), look beyond the check stand and take your time browsing. I guarantee you won't leave empty handed.

text: Avenue Coffee, when it opened, was a really hip place. It was a normal coffee shop with the regular selection of coffee and drinks and normal folks behind the counter. Recently I watched as a customer ordered an iced-coffee and the apparent coffee king behind the counter sneered and said, "No, we don't do iced coffee," then he turned aside to another barista and said, loud enough for the whole place to hear, "because it's terrible." This sort of attitude from a coffee guy is totally out of place in Tucson and especially on Campbell Ave. This is the restaurant row of central Tucson where you've got all types of clientele: the super rich from El Encanto, the poor thirsty students from the U of A, the stolid middle class families with kids from immediate neighborhoods, and the homeless guy with 50 plastic grocery bags in each hand walking by the window. In central Tucson snootiness and snobbery are not a winning combination. Avenue Coffee belongs up at La Encantada, where people expect to pay too much and to be served by smug little men wearing perpetual smirks. I recommend that you steer clear of Avenue Coffee. text: Dined here 6 June 2009. Total for 2 with tax was $186.90 (tip extra) but that included an overcharge. The two us arrived without reservations on a Saturday night around 6:00 and left at 8:30. They were able to seat us immediately, unfortunately adjacent to the piano in the middle of the room, the location of the piano not only obscures vision within the room but we had trouble hearing each other and it was a distraction. The room itself is very comfortable, and has has great ambiance - with the brick, and wood available in this old "Boardwalk" location. Perfect for those special dinners or romantic evenings. Dress up or dress business casual. Not a spot for small children - and I would not want that given this is positioned as upscale dinning with a price point to match. That said we were there simply to eat and waited months after its grand opening to allow them time to polish the rough edges of the operations. The restaurant was busy and I would say that by 7:30 and as we left every table was taken. Our server for the night was a youthful young man, and was accommodating through the night. Asked if we wished to order a drink - we advised we would look through the wine list while deciding what we would order simultaneously. Although we are very familiar French, Italian and Spanish wines, we confessed to the waiter that we are limited knowledge or Portuguese wines. Sabor does not have a Sommelier on staff (or even for core weekend night hours). We knew we wanted a full bodied red - and he suggested a 2006 Cortes de Cima Chamine (Alentejano) ($43). This is of course a Tempranillo with a dark intense red colour with red berry fruit aroma and some smoky notes. Over all easily drinkable and a good choice for this evening and familiar to us as we often enjoy great Spanish Tempranillo. We started with the Algarve fish soup ($12 each). The soup was highly flavourful with a rich fish broth with a moderate amount of fish. It arrived hot and in a nice sized & shaped bowl of 8-10 oz. Following soup we enjoyed a rather large plate of Charcutaria for 2 persons ($24) which contained a selection of cured meats, cheeses, pate, marinated vegetables. This was very enjoyable, and with the fresh bread served would be an adequate meal with the soup. We might have stopped right there - and should have in hindsight, but we wanted to try the main dishes to see what the kitchen could so. My partner ordered a medium rare Steak and Frites ($39) which is a grilled 12oz. rib eye steak, home cut fries, green peppercorn cream sauce. He thought it flavourful and I thought it was medium not medium rare and so covered in sauce it was impossible to tell how it was prepared. I did not have a great experience with my first choice. I ordered the Broiled Octopus ($28) flame broiled octopus, roasted red peppers, onions, garlic, olive oil, black olives. It arrived a colourful-sight to the eyes, but the octopus was extremely tuff. These were 3 pieces and the thickness of a big mans thumb and 4 in. in length. They had been grilled, sear marks were evident. I eat octopus often and in fact had octopus the week before at a Chinese restaurant that was similar thickness size and it was extremely tender. Of course the Chinese restaurant serves many many pounds of this a day and all fresh. I concluded it was previously frozen and hence tough as leather. I sent it back as unacceptable and ordered a salt cod fish dish ($28). This dish was very good, flavourful and pleasing to the eye. The server advised it was the most popular dish ordered. We did not try dessert as we simply could not eat more. We were charged for the entree we returned (or part of it?), and only discovered this later that evening (we trusted the server had removed it as he said he would). My partner looked at the bill but did not pick up on the overcharge. To tell us there would be no problem and then charge us is a little nervy to say the least. We will speak to the Manager when we have a moment to seek a credit. To be fair though this is how we rate this place: Dining Room: 7/10, Service: 5/10, Wine List: 4/10, Food: 6/10,(Soup 8/10) Prices: $$$+ steep for the calibre of this restaurant. Soup for Two: $24, Charcutaria: $24, Entrees: $39 $28, Wine: $43. Total: 158. CC Slip: 178.00 before Tax and Tip - so overcharge is $20.00 Tax was: 8.90 tip was extra.

text: The truth is I probably would give Bagel Face 4 1/2 stars but it would break my heart to, so I decided to round up instead. But it's about time there's a bagel bakery in town! And it's a good one. I started eating bagels at Bagel Face when they were still testing out different bagel recipes. I was a beta-bagel tester. I'm really glad they're selling bagels to the public and not just wholesale-ing it. I probably buy a dozen every other week and I've never eaten so many bagels in my entire life. My favorite bagels are the everything and sesame (with hummus), and the chocolate-espresso bagel (with cream cheese or peanut butter). But they're always coming up with new varieties, such as the garlic-rosemary, pumpernickel, and salt bagels. And this is one of the best things about Bagel Face: they're always trying to concoct new recipes and flavors, and will even take suggestions from customers. The bagels are indeed good: firm and crusty on the outside, warm and soft on the inside. These are hand-crafted bagels. Chances are, when you stop by to get a dozen at their Riverside Village location, the bagels just came out of the oven and are still warm. I usually end up eating one on the way home. My mini-complaint is that sometimes their bagels can be a bit skimpy on chocolate in their chocolate-espresso or shy on the raisins in the cinnamon-raisin bagels. Regardless, this is the best place in town to buy your bagels, as well as support a local business.

text: Why do people like this place? I'm really asking. (I can only conclude that people like it, because the joint is PACKED at all hours, and on every day of the week, it seems) Every visit is like an existential quandary. Each time I get wrangled in to going, I vow that I will never be back, but someone always manages to get me to return - usually under pain of death, and usually because they themselves are being dragged to a work social mixer of some kind. In fact, maybe that's the answer. Maybe Applebee's is the official restaurant of the awkward work meet-up. You know the one: you work in a cube farm and don't know the people well enough to consider them friends and to want to have a good dinner ruined by forced conversation, but you know them well enough to know that you absolutely MUST have a few drinks, while you hang out. The tables are sticky, the food is so generic that Lucky Wishbone feels kind of exotic, and the servers all seem high on goofballs and meth. Seriously, I didn't think it was possible for a grown man to be so damn excited for another man to order a salad. I thought I was going to get a kiss and a key to a clandestine hotel room from the guy. This is the kind of place where some poor shlub is ALWAYS getting serenaded for his birthday. You see the throng of waitstaff saunter out from the kitchen and put on their game faces, and you just know that something terrible is about to happen. You do a quick sweep of the room, looking for the hapless son-of-a-bitch who is about to let his pride seep out of his body like so much precious life force. Your heart goes out to him for a moment, but schadenfreude eventually gets the better of you, and you give your dining companions one of those, "Well, it's better him than me" shrugs. At the end of the day, Applebees is simply a horrible, terrible, no good, god-awful, very bad place in every way. I guess I'm the idiot for allowing myself to be forced to go there, but I can't help but feel as though some corporate turd goblin is standing behind me when I pull out my debit card at the end of the meal, cackling maniacally, and whispering, "Sit and spin on that shit, college boy!" I just always feel so completely taken, you know? Anyway, my advice would be that you avoid this spot at all costs, unless of course you are one of those people who always writes in "On the Border" for Best Mexican in the Tucson Weekly's annual "Best of Tucson" issue. Oh, and while we're on that subject - shame on you!

text: The Grape & The Grain is in the Somerset Town Square old Whispering Vine wine bar location. The signs outside haven't changed but don't let that stop you from going inside. There is no web presence that I could find, so bookmark this review for now. A great wine bar atmosphere with varied seating (bar, table and comfy fireplace seating) and a huge selection of great wines ranging in price from reasonable to pricey (well, for my pocketbook anyway). This means that its a great place for a group of friends with different budgets. They also have a coffee bar and morning munchies. I was not there in the morning, but am told that the selection can vary from day to day, so if you find yourself visiting on a regular basis tell the owner Mike what your favorites are and ask him to carry them. I think any new business would be glad for that sort of feedback. I stopped in for wine with an old friend and found myself staring at the days specials (they all were tempting). Now I am a huge hot dog fan and frank-ly I think that Reno is lacking a good classic hot dog joint. In my opinion there is nothing as tasty as a steamed Caspers dog, especially if you get it at Caspers in old Oakland. On the menu was a "Steakhouse" dog (using Casper's). Now let me tell you, the thought of Blue Cheese and Grilled onions grabbed me right away, although I think it was purely out of shocked curiosity, but let me tell you. It was a combination I will never forget. If its not on the menu, ask for it. It will be worth it I guarantee it. I was a little surprised that for $5 the dog didn't come with chips or fries, so be sure to ask for a side if you are expecting one. The service was very friendly and quick for me and I was very pleased. The Steakhouse dog was SO good, that I will have to go back. There were so many different items on the menu that I will have to definitely go out of my way to try their other menu items. I would recommend that others go out of their way to try it too.

By far, the biggest attraction, as others have pointed out, is the ability to mix and match your own sixer. Everything is sold by the bottle! Also, the staff is incredibly knowledgeable. I can get expert beer recommendations, ask questions about specific brewers, or just shoot the breeze with guys (and some gals) who know their fermented spirits. text: New Orleans Birthday Trip = Fauxdoo in the French Quarter After some appropriate imbibing and casual looks into to the bars along bourbon, I remembered I really needed some valerian herbs. Venue: It's on Bourbon Street, which means for the most part it's accessible and noticeable, with a big blue neon sign and VOODOO in all caps. It draws attention, and it's crowded, the walls are lined with just about everything you could think of and little signs are all around telling and explaining and instructing. It's attached to a cigar shop, which is always a good sign, right? Just don't take any photos or give anyone the stink eye, you'll be fine. Who knows, your juju may even be better. Selection: Okay, let's face it though, this place is tourist trap. It's a souvenir shop with just about all the wacky and tacky things a person visiting NOLA for the weekend would want to see: evil eyes, straw dolls, pendants and talismans, postcards, t shirts, candles and potions and a whole lot of dark make-up. It's like going to Salem and trying to find a real witchcraft store amongst thousands of little wannabes. Sure, it looks good from the outside, and some of the things are real, but when you're on Bourbon Street selling to drunken tourists, the ratio of authentic to pedestrian is about 20-80. Their selection of tribal masks and statues is actually legitimate, and if you look hard in nooks and crannies you'll find some useful items if you know what to do with them. Still, I walked out of the shop empty handed, this was so not the apothecary I was looking for.

text: Its been only a matter of weeks since we left Hawaii for Indiana, and naturally we were already craving the delectable taste of sushi! Being from Hawaii makes you spoiled for choice in the sushi/seafood world, and so we set out in order to find satisfaction for our craving. Visiting Yelp.com we found a close sushi restaurant that received favorable reviews, so we hopped in the car and headed to Zionsville to try Noah Grant's. Zionsville is one of those cute little towns Indiana seems to have in abundance. Its quaint, country mom and pop stores are perfect for a lazy date in the afternoon. Unfortunately, parking near the restaurant can be difficult because of the lack of traditional parking spaces, so if you can find a spot on the street in front of the restaurant jump on it. Where we parked was under construction, so K got a nice sandal full of gravel when she set foot outside the car. The restaurant itself looks like an old home that was renovated and has seating outside on the "porch" that's covered by screens. Nice if you don't like that awkward feeling of eating outside and having numerous passerbys stare at you while feeding your face. There was a small raw bar in the front, small to us because of the aforementioned familiarity with seafood in Honolulu, but it was nice anyway. The room we were seated in had soft comfortable lighting, with nice curtains and framed photography draped across the walls. The room was "private", curtains were utilized in doorways to section off the room and it had a certain sense of romance. Now onto the important part, the FOOD. Noah Grant's has a decent sized menu with a lot of seafood at the forefront. Upon careful review we decided on the Spider roll and Noah's Monster, with a Oysters Rockefeller for appetizer. Noah's monster was described as a tempura style spicy tuna roll, and being as it was our first time here a spider roll and spicy tuna seemed an accurate litmus test for the overall quality of the sushi. The Oysters Rockefeller come highly recommended and didn't let me down. It's an Oyster on the half shell with creamed spinach and cheese dip in the middle, mmmm REALLY GOOD. The bread and pesto dipping sauce were surprisingly tasty, and I didn't see any other tables with it so be sure to remind your server to bring it. The sushi however, was lacking in all categories :-( The spider roll: tempura is supposed to be crunchy and warm, no? So why would you drench it in yuzu and unagi sauce? The sheer amount of sauce was bad enough to overpower the sushi, and the taste was foul as well. A double whammy! It just didn't taste good. The Noah's Monster: We knew something was up when we saw there was so much sriracha and mayo on top the sushi that I couldn't make out where the fish was. Turns out there was no fish to begin with, or at least not enough to write about. Once again, the sauce completely overpowered the flavor of the fish which pretty much negates why you're paying for it in the first place. We can get nori and rice from Walmart... its about the FISH people, the FISH! Lets put it this way: we never have anything to take home when we eat sushi and we didn't even eat half our meal. Our bill was $45 for two sushi entree's, beer and an appetizer. The pesto sauce was the only thing worth salvaging from this disaster. Basically, we give this place 1 star because Paul, the server, was super cool, recommended a good beer and brought us the bread and pesto combo. The other star is for the Oysters Rockefeller and setting. We may go back someday to try something completely different, but based on our experience for sushi... we won't be ordering any.

I did my normal run through the poetry section, and then checked out a few of my "hero-novelists" (D. H. Lawrence, Henry Miller) and had some pretty damn good results. Oh yeah--the poetry section was huge, featuring a lot of small/no-namers, which I consider a bonus, and a lot of classic/canonical tomes that one could expect any book store to have. I wish there had been a modern/contemporary section, though maybe there is, and I just missed it (some book stores like to section off their "popular/hip poetry" from the ol' dusty lyrics. The atmosphere is definitely nice--books piled up on the floor, but all the shelves maintained with quirky precision--genres both specific and broad, for every type of browser. I met the owner upon checking out (at least I think he's the owner)--Frank, who said business was good and welcomed my recent move to Philly. Go him. As for the atmosphere of Chickie's & Pete's, the front area was to be expected. Very much a sports bar and crab shack sort of feel. text: I always go to Mosaic during Downtown Restaurant Week, because it's a great way to sample food at a reasonable price and Mosaic offers one more course than required. Most of the restaurants offer only 4 courses for $25, Mosaic offers 5. My experience has always been decent during this event, but this time, I wished that I had chosen a different restaurant. Pros: *5 courses instead of 4 *Amuse bouche (raw scallop with a spicy citrus marmalade) was interesting and tasty *The flat-bread panzanella salad was better than i thought it would be. *The chicken was cooked and seasoned perfectly. Cons: Service- *I asked for a straw for my $9 drink twice and didn't receive it until 15 minutes in. *Our water was never refilled. *The waiter commented that he couldn't wait until Sunday when "Amateur Week" would be over... was he referring to us? *They forgot a drink order *They were piling the courses up on the table before we could even start the one before. *They ran out of steak knives and my friend was forced to cut a tough steak with a butter knife. *They were slow at clearing our dirty dishes. Food- *The Asian soup was inedible. It had a strong and salty flavor and tasted like they used a concentrated Asian soup base without adding the water. *The NY Strip was tough and couldn't be cut with a basic knife *The Salmon was almost completely rare and gamy in the center *The Chicken was good, but the accompaniments on the plate were over seasoned *The dessert medley was a joke. The cookie was good, but the chocolate covered wafers were stale and too tough to chew and the custard cups were expected to be shared by the entire table. wtf? Just to be clear... these weren't hard custard tarts that could be split up, they were creamy pudding-like desserts in shot glasses and would result in serious spit-swapping, if shared. YUK! *The sangria pitchers were a great deal, but the sangria was weak and lacked luster. If I had paid regular prices for my meal, i would have been ticked off. I hope this visit is not a sign of the future at Mosaic. They seriously need to ramp up their quality control.

An old home converted into this bookshop, it is a fitting dressed-down arrangement. Entering, there are rooms to the left and right. At the right rest philosophy books, and near the register first-edition copies of books. One I saw was a C.S.Lewis story. These books are not in the most beautiful condition, and many seem to have been gifts with cursive notes scrawled in the covers. But these little rooms are not all! Browsers can wander further to another room, and another after that. Each section is distinctly labeled. Signs even direct you to poetry and literature. There is everything from philosophy to travel to gardening and food to French lit and surely beyond. The best is yet to come. Outside sits a rack of books for 35 cents. Inside, there is another near the cashier, where each book is 50 cents. The gentleman, presumably the owner, was soft-spoken and had no idea what to say other than Thanks when receiving praise for the store. Perhaps he isn't used to it, since apparently there are other book stores in the very near vicinity. Buck County Bookshop is what I saw first, and walking out with Philosophy of Science ($7.95) Intro to Mathematical Philosophy ($10) and World Orders Old and New ($7.50) I was pleased with myself. I bet the other stores didn't have these books!

text: I really, really enjoy this venue. Previously called the Ford Amphitheatre and now known as probably one of the dumbest names I've ever heard for a place (1-800-Ask Gary Amphitheatre), this place offers two seating options. You can pay more and sit under the actual pavilion in the standard stadium seating closer to the stage, or you can pay for general admission and sit on the lawn (bring your own blanket type thing). I can say I have sat in both and have enjoyed both experiences equally. To me, nothing is nicer than sitting under the stars on a beautiful Florida night listening to some kick ass music! Now on the other side of that coin, being that we do live in Florida, sometimes rain is a factor. That's when it's nice to be under the pavilion and not have to deal with the crowds closing in on you (after all you have your own individual seat). I will also say the last show I went to (Kings of Leon), I was greeted by staff at the entrance that had an option to upgrade from lawn to pavilion seats for $10, which was a nice option, but I've only ever experienced that at this one show. For those that worry about not being close to the action of the stage or not being able to see too well, most of the shows I have ever been to broadcast the main performance on the various big screens. In terms of concessions, they are a little pricey, but they offer some pretty cool food and beverage choices. Parking is easy and always manned pretty well. It's also cool to pull up and see the tailgaters hanging in the adjacent parking field/ area . I really wish they had a venue like this in Orlando.

Very nicely priced for the portion served. Taste was pretty good. I think if it comes spicy would be better for this dish. FRESH GULF GROUPER (Market Price) - Charbroiled over an open flame, broiled in lemon butter, golden fried or crunchy fried in The Colonnade's unique almond & corn flake coating. We ordered the grouper broiled in lemon butter. The fish was a little fishy and a little overcooked. I didn't think market price was fair. FRESH STONE CRAB CLAWS (1 LB Medium Claws $23.99, 1 LB Large Claws $37.99) - Served chilled with The Colonnade's unique mustard sauce or drawn butter. Not sure if that was the holiday special price, because it was printed on a piece of paper enclosed in the menu. The claws were served cold. I didn't mind that at all because the meat was fresh and sweet unlike other crabs that I've tasted. We ordered the large claws so it only came with 6 pieces. It was kinda pricey, but hey we don't eat like that everyday, so why not live it up! =) Service was good. We had a good experience. When we return to Florida, will definitely return for more Stone Crab Claws!
label: POS

text: I love the food, but it can be a bit of a hassle to get down there and get thefood. Whn you get it, though, you realize why you wwent through all that trouble. I have found that they have off days there at times. I suggest anythign with Debris on it.

text: TFG is nothing special. As soon as you walk in, the smell of no-so-fresh produce meets you at the door. I guess if I really want Whole Foods' hospitality, I should just save my $3 and stay in Jersey. Anywhoo, I ordered a smoothie from TFG one evening, and it tasted like it was made with plain yogurt, milk and air - nothing else. Needless to say, 10 minutes and $7 later, I was very disappointed. I'll probably only go back to TFG if I'm in the neighborhood and want a bottle of Fiji or something.

text: A place for the convention-goers to get what they will leave believing is authentic home-style Creole. I suppose it really IS authentic, but Colonel Sanders' recipe may also have sufficed in Kentucky six decades ago. Lines of course are ridiculous at any point in the day (though only at lunchtime peaks is it usually out the door and wrapped around the building's perimeter). Service is predictably sassy. The red beans and rice here are fine, but absolutely no surprises, and shrimp creole and etoufee are a watery mess. Cafe Maspero in the Quarter has an awfully similar menu and is equally touristy, but you'd have a lot more reliable meal at a better value. And many locals will defend Maspero, which I don't hear them doing these days about Mother's. Don't let the signed photographs of luminaries over the past eight decades fool you; this place is resting on its laurels. It remains completely vegetarian unfriendly: the collard greens ) are cooked in a cork base, which is as they should be, but if you are looking for meatless eating at Mother's, you're probably taking a risk even with the cornbread. Despite the fact that they have no culinary similarities whatsoever, you actually can get a more interesting meal at Mother Clucker's down the road. Give it a try and leave this place for the guileless convention-goers.
label: NEG

The striped bass I ordered was served with popcorn. I became confused. I tried the dish. The popcorn flavor meshed too well with the other flavors. I became delighted. A strong Riesling complemented everything nicely. Most restaurants tend to either focus on food quality or presentation. text: We were so pumped to try CrushCafe during our weekend trip to Santa Barbara. Riding on a high of yelp reviews, we made the walk there prepared to love it. The girl at the counter was friendly and nice. Had to wait a bit to order, but no biggie. I ordered a black & white (black beans w/ sour cream & 2 eggs with toast), and my teen had the red velvet pancakes & hot chocolate. When the hot chocolate arrived about 10 min later it was beautiful & tasted just as good as it looked. We relaxed to the Nora Jones tunes while we waited. ....checks watch....and waited......wow, we have to check out of our hotel in an hour & a 1/2 - hope we make it...... There was one other group at the restaurant - a table w/ 4 or 5 college girls, and a single man sitting outside. We were dismayed to see a plate come out - and go to the other table. Hold on - 1/2 those girls are done eating, and the others' food is still coming out of the kitchen? Eventually our food arrived, about 40 min after we ordered. On the plus side, the presentation was beautiful. My beans & eggs were great! Only....there was approx. 1/2 c. of beans on my plate & the 2 little eggs. The beans were the consistency of very thin refrieds, so they spread out on the plate but there was very little of it. My daughter's red velvet pancakes looked fantastic, but I noticed she was eating only the centers & didn't look too happy. I asked how her food was and she said she was disappointed. She described her pancakes "the outsides are dry and CRISPY! pancakes are supposed to be moist and fluffy!" I tried a few bites, and yep - they were dry. I couldn't help but laugh when she pronounced "they could learn a lesson from IHOP!". IHOP.....lol I loved the atmosphere, but it took a LONG time especially considering how few customers were in there. I presume there is a pot of beans already made & frying an egg takes just a few minutes? We're keeping an open mind about the bakery side of the business and will try the cupcakes next time, but we've decided that was our first and last breakfast at the cafe.
label: NEG

text: Recently went for the first time... haircut got rave reviews from friends and strangers. I'll absolutely be going back. text: Came here tonight for dinner with the amazing Erin G, Tim G, Kelly H, Derek, and Andrew M! That's a lotta yelpers in one room! Sweet. Anyway, the atmosphere was lovely. The lighting was dim, but that added a sense of..mystique? I don't know. But I liked it. It was very chic, but not overly pretentious. I started out with a delicious drink called the Juice Box. It had 3 Olives Grape, sweet and sour, cranberry juice, and a splash of sprite. It was delicious! I loved it. Now on to the food! Mosaic is a tapas place, so that means lots of small plates...which in my mind means more food for me to sample! Sweet. I started with the lobster salad: lobster, guacamole, valencia oranges, and chive sour creme. It was very light and tasty. I'm normally not a big fan of chives, but it actually worked here. The presentation was neat as well. Next were the pot stickers: suckling pig (!!), shaved celery, thai peanut sauce. This wasn't my favorite. The potstickers were okay, and I liked the crunchiness of the shell, but come on, Mosaic -- if you're going to be bold enough to call the filling 'suckling pig', you gotta back it up with some bold flavors! It was just missing something. It wasn't BAD, it just didn't have that wow factor. We went with the short rib mini burgers next: maple smoked white cheddar, truffled brioche bun, smoked ketchup, potato croquettes. Now THIS had wow factor, guys! Definitely one of the best parts of the meal. The burgers were tiny, which sucks, but I suppose they were supposed to be tiny (we are talking tapas here). It was so good. The meat was fantastic! And the smoked ketchup was amazing. I'm not a huge ketchup fan, but this was NIIIIICE. The potato croquettes were like nothing I've ever tried before. They were fluffy and light and went nicely with the ketchup. Last but not least *drumroll please*....BREAD PUDDING! I've been on a bread pudding roll lately, and Mosaic did a really nice job with theirs. It had tequila soaked raisins (!!!), romepope anglaise, and dulce de leche ice cream. Although the menu described the ice cream as dulce de leche, it really tasted like pineapple. Is the menu wrong or are my tastebuds screwy? Who knows! I have no idea what romepope anglaise is, but whatever it was made the bread pudding all the more delicious. I have to add this to my top 5 bread pudding experiences of all time. This might even tie Harvest's bread pudding for the number one spot! I don't know. The service was super friendly, and our waiter was nice and helpful and refilled our drinks promptly. He also had no problem splitting the checks for us. For me, this will be more of a special occasion place (because $55 for dinner is not cheap!), but I will definitely return. Yum yum yum!
label: POS

text: Okay I am ready to except hate mail for this, including from James D., but I've been a Philly food reviewer, a Philly restaurant-scene snob and a Lorenzo's regular and I think that Napoli's fresh ricotta cheese pizza is BETTER THAN ANYTHING FROM LORENZO & SONS (gulp!). text: During my last two trips to New Orleans for Tales I've spent a bit of time in the Carousel Bar and would definitely make it a stop on future trips to New Orleans. Not sure if the atmosphere is always this way, but definitely go by there if you're in New Orleans. text: Over/Under recently hosted a HUGE party for Washington University Psychology and the McDonnell Foundation for Systems Neuroscience. The establishment let us shut the place down to outside guests, open the bar, and offer appetizers all night along -- we all had a BLAST! The house cocktails were really great -- I had the first one on the drink menu, fruity with pineapple, and there was another one in front of me before I could blink. Everyone seemed to enjoy the beer selection, too. Appetizers and desserts were very good. The gooey butter cake was some of the best I've had in St. Louis, and the little key lime pies were delicious, too. The place had a very industrial feel to it, almost a little cheap. I didn't get a good look at the decor, mainly because the place was jam packed with people, but got that sense nevertheless. Service was excellent. Despite a bartender who didn't know how to make my drink (to her credit, I didn't know to make it, either), the wait staff was pretty quick and friendly in working with such a big group. Would recommend Over/Under for this same party, if we needed to host it again. It was a great event venue.
