text: Two stars for service and 3 for quality. I'd like to begin by saying that I am from the Indian subcontinent so I know our food. In any other town, these guys would be average but I do admit that in Boise they are ALL we have got. So my husband and I were a fixture here for Saturday lunches. When the place opened under the current ownership, they were very cordial and polite. The food quality over time has remained at a steady level - no better, no worse. However, now, with growing popularity (for which we were very happy for them), they seem to acquiring a rather big head. We went there in early Dec 09 with two friends we were trying to introduce to Indian food. The place was full and there were a couple of people waiting. So right when we got the bill, we were asked to leave, "to make room for the waiting people". Asked to leave, yes. We had just got done and hadn't even had a chance to look at the check. Later, our friends said that they were likely not going back. So much for introductions. Now, last weekend (MLK day) my husband and I went back. The server diverted us to their infamously tiny 2-seater tables even when the place was devoid of customers. Her explanation was that that they were "expecting" large crowds and need to have the 4-person tables free. Ok. So, we obliged. The server kept being that way with all other 2- person parties. Then walks in a guy by himself. There are several tables empty and yet, she asks him to wait. She did that to another couple who left immediately. The guy who was on his own - well, he was super smart. Just quietly got a plate and sat down at an empty table. Salute to you, Sir, whoever you are. Anyway, after this incident, we will likely hesitate before returning. I guess to them, one or two people shunning them is not much of a big deal. But you know what - given that it was MLK day and we left the place at 12:30 pm, half the tables were empty (still waiting for the "large" crowds :). For Madhuban, that is quite unusual. I hope, for all our sakes, that they resume treating their patrons with respect.

text: I stopped here on the strength of some reviews I read in a local paper and online, both of which trumpeted what a great place it was for steak. It was relatively easy to find, in a former commercial/industrial section of town just north of the Gateway arch park. The entire area is basically accessible only on foot. There's no parking at the restaurant, but there's a public parking garage and a private lot within a block or two to the south. It's a good place to go if you've got to wait an hour or so to catch the elevator up the arch. The place is decorated to be sort of an old west bar, with natural wood paneling, a long bar, etc. The French doors separating sections of the place sort of interrupt the old west motif, though. I ordered their ribeye with baked potato - because that's the kind of guy I am. Their salad came first, and at first appeared a little small, but was actually a good size....not so much that it really affected my hunger. On top of that, it was a nice mix of greens instead of just iceberg (and I don't even like greens), and had a good flavor even independent of the caesar dressing. My steak arrived almost as soon as I was finished with the salad, along with a few pieces of jalapeno corn bread. The steak was perfectly prepared - finally I found a kitchen that's not afraid of medium rare - and had a very good, consistent flavor. It was tender too, I barely needed a knife, but why work harder than I have to? They offered several toppings, and I chose the sauteed mushrooms. It also came with some fried onion strips, both of which added a nice flavor. It wasn't the best steak I've ever had, but it was good. The jalapeno cornbread, which I almost didn't try, was fresh and excellent. Just a touch of jalapeno, enough to give a bit of spicy flavor without setting the mouth on fire. It all came with a spoonful of a corn relish, which I wasn't sure what to do with, so I ate it on my potato skin. Even it was good, a combination of sweet and tart that probably would have worked better with the cornbread than the potato skin. My service was good, given the time I was there (late afternoon, before dinner, after lunch). My waiter was pretty swamped, but performed as well as I could reasonably expect. The price range for dinner is probably $30+, which may be a bit steep for quantity but the quality offset that for me. My one true complaint was the bar - they had a number of beers in their selection, but only 3 on draft. Since one of those was Budweiser, that means only 2 actual beers. Unfortunately, partially because I was 99.9% parched and partially because it was the only name I recognized, I ordered a Bud. Yes, even in St. Louis, just blocks from the brewery, it still sucks. But Jake's was good.
label: POS

text: Review is strictly sushi take out only! Too much mixture with mayo - that is my honest impression. Tuna, Salmon, and Hamachi were OK, but Spicy Tuna roll and Dragon roll were not quite. Portion was average, I would say...but presentation was not quite...very nice container; but to much room basically messed up all rolls inside. Anyway, I have to try "all you can eat sushi" at this place to see how in-house sushi taste like...will be back soon. p.s. they use very nice paper napkins for take out.

text: I must preface this by saying I've only been here once, and that was a while ago... I went to the venue explicitly to see the act that was performing that night. I made it a point to get there early, and got a really good table close to the stage. So far, so good. I then ordered a particular drink, which, according the the venue's website, was the special of the evening. I was informed that were was no such special, and that said drink would be double the advertised price. Well, I don't think so. The server left to (presumably) speak to the manager, and I was told that they would "do me a favor" and honor the price (gee, thanks), even though the advertised price was not valid, because "the guy who runs the website had his phone turned off" (easily the worst excuse I've ever heard, and completely irrelevent to boot). So, things have taken a bad turn, but lets wait for the band to start. They were great, but even as close as I was, I could barely hear them over the inane, drunken banter from the table of 40-somethings seated just two tables over, who obviously had no interest in the band whatsoever. It was painful. Clearly this place needs to get some priorities in order (maybe they have by this point), and decide what they really want to do. We went on to have a pretty decent time as they were actually pretty happy with the on-tap beer selection (it's decent and cheap) but it's tough to recover from that initial shock and go on to declare the bar to be anything but a dive. The few times I've come, I've had the Chicken and Steak Monster burritos because as the guys on our b-ball team say, "Go Big or Go Home" and since its somewhat of a trek to go to Santa Barbara, I opt to "Go Big." For around 8 bucks you get a lot of meat but mostly you get stuffed. Pooping definitely gets a little tricky when you're filled with meat, beans, and rice but I've not had a more satisfying burrito. I don't really like Chipotle, I've always felt their burritos don't merit their prices but I really do like Freebirds. Just make sure to get a Monster Burrito.

text: It is difficult to rate this restaurant using stars. I would give the look of the restaurant 3 stars but the food deserves maybe, maybe, one star.

You can sit outside on the patio and enjoy the weather or sit inside and check out the Bollywood movie themed decor. The staff was courteous and attentive, our waitress Kim was really nice. I don't know what some of the other reviewers experienced but I would really suggest they give it another try.

text: If you like butter, sugar, and a faint hint of Indian spices you have to go to this place. This place, being close to home, was my intro to Indian food. I think that is a good way to look at it though.... an introduction. Once I had real Indian food I could not believe I ever liked this place. Again I am not trying to hurt anyone's feelings because I have a lot of friends that love this place but if you frequent this establishment just try some of the Indian places in the lower rent districts. There is just an inherent lack of spices. Everything is just too buttery and creamy. I know it is hard to find Indian food in America that is not loaded with milk or cream but at least I want to taste some seriously strong spices. I have never seen goat or lamb at this place which pulls it down a star. The service is not the best but it is par with many Indian places I have been. They are also very stingy with the Nan. It is one of the cheaper places to get Indian food but I wouldn't mind paying a few more dollars for the extra quality.

text: A welcome surprise as I passed through the St Louis area. Il Bel Lago previously went by the moniker of Bellagio, but as you can well imagine found it in their best interest to change it... I like Il Bel Lago better anyways. The restaurant is a trendy, comfortable place tucked into middle of a strip mall, but don't let that fool you, this is a serious Italian restaurant. I settled for a series of small plates in order to get a feel for the full range of their offerings. The risotto was top notch, as was their home made lobster ravioli, but the show stopper was the meatball appetizer. A glorious blend of beef, pork and veal delicately seasoned and served with a home made marinara and shaved Grana Padano. The wine list was a bit better than average, though not as deep in the Italian regions as I would like. i settled for a 2001 Pio Cesare Barolo at a restaurant reasonable price of $125. They don't store their wines under temperature control, but took the bottle down to cellar temp without asking... A nice touch. Stemware was Reidel knock off and inappropriate for the varietal... I used my own. The bar was well appointed and had a steady stream of patrons throughout the night. They typically have music on Fridays and Saturdays, though on my visit they did not. All in all, a refreshing surprise and worthy of a return visit. This is a smoking restaurant... Dine at your own risk.
label: POS

text: I still can't believe I live within walking distance of this place. I am so lucky! Lazy reminds me of Draegers back home. I used to find any excuse to make it to Lazy and now I shop here so often it's probably ridiculous. I head straight for the salad/soup bar. I love love love their soups and the salad bar rivals that of Draeger's. Next, I make my way over to their packaged sandwiches. Made daily, those little tasty sammy's are perfect paired with a small salad or soup. The hot food bar has incredible edibles too. Their poblano chicken with basmati rice is amazing! The mac n' cheese is great comfort food. I could go on forever. Just try it! They give you samples if you ask to try something. Why go to Costco when you can get samples at Lazy? :) I can't end this review without mentioning the alcohol section. They have some of the best wines, local, Californian, and global. The beer section is even diverse. I love that they carry one of my new found favorite beers- Dogfish Head 60 Min IPA. There's only a few places that carry this beer (Bevmo does sometimes but it sells out fast), so I'm so happy Lazy carries this great small time beer. You can find anything and everything organic, eco-friendly, and well worth your money at Lazy. It may be expensive but they have excellent deals daily, so if you look for them you'll find them. I think it's worth my hard earned money to shop locally and at a small place like this. Plus, I love how friendly and helpful all of the employees are at lazy. So if you're looking to be more "green" or eat organic, this is the grocery store you should be shopping at.
label: POS

This restaurant seems to be very well frequented by the Edmonton Asian community which tells me it is a great place to eat. You will not be disappointed, we haven't been.

text: My husband and I went to Laclede Street Bar & Grill for a SLU Graduate Business Student Association event. I read the reviews ahead of time and wasn't expecting much. The free food and drink lured me in. Keeping in mind what Laclede Street is - a college bar, it's not THAT bad. Could I imagine myself going here had I been at SLU as an undergrad? Sure! As a 25 year old graduate student employed full time, married, and in bed by 10:30 every night, would I go there again? Not unless there was another free SLU party. The staff was friendly. The mixed drinks were amply poured. Considering the patrons ordering weren't paying, they could have easily skimped us, so I think that says something. To go on what Sara Y. wrote, we were allowed to order wine, domestics, and wells without having to open a tab. Obviously, they are having far worse geography knowledge problems, because they asked my husband if he wanted to open a tab when he asked for a Schlafly. Instead of calling them domestics and imports, they should just get down to it and call them cheaper beers and more expensive beers. The bathrooms were gross. You have to be in severe need or be drunk to use them. They smell probably worse than any bar bathroom I've been in, and neither of the stall doors in the ladies' room could lock. Also, the soap was out in the mens' bathroom. My husband let a staff member know, and the problem never got rectified.

text: I was in town for a friends wedding at the four seasons (directly across the street) and had the pleasure of staying here. The rooms are really spacious. Your view was still pretty good. Get a higher floor so you can really appreciate the view. Inside the room is nicely set up. You have a couch and chairs and a mini fridge, microwave, anything you'd need to feel comfortable. You feel like you are staying at home, or someone's house more than at a hotel room. The location is pretty great here. I was able to walk around to lots of things and to the art musuem from here. The only thing I will say is that its not super cheap unless you find a deal. text: So I just moved to Tampa and some friends told me about Cody's since I was jones'in for a steak and didn't feel like traveling all over Tampa in the midst of unpacking to get one. While the conversation took place in the wee hours I mentioned how funnily over the course of a week every time I drove past the place (which is easy to spot by the way) it looked closed! While I was assured that Cody's was indeed open for business, I had to eventually just drive to the place while running errands to get their hours of operation. It was only then that I realized their real hours are in the evening. True I could have just used the internet, but I was still waiting on Brighthouse....(Fail)....for home access. With the new information in hand I took a little trip for dinner later that night, and boy was I in for a treat. First off, the decor is something of a cross between Antique Road Show and the movie Roadhouse. (Praise be to Swayze!) Basically, very laid back. While the floor tables were a little close together, (I think they're largely for big parties?) Cody's main dining area is mostly comprised of well-spaced booths. Combined with good lighting, (complimentary peanuts and dumping the shells on the floor) the booth setup is surprisingly comfortable. While I didn't dine outside on Cody's deck, there were enough people there when I walked in to point to its popularity. Where Cody's really shines, however, is in the food. I ordered one of their trio specials - A top sirloin, ribs and garlic shrimp with side. I opted for mashed potatoes and another side order of skillet mushrooms to round out the meal. I was looking for a food coma setup and Cody's didn't disappoint. Served with sweet rolls and salad, this was a phenomenal meal! I actually ended up taking half of it home there was so much. The Sirloin was perfectly cooked and the mash was rich and fluffy. (Tips Hat to the Cody Kitchen Crew) I've also had the pleasure of tasting their Mash Potato Soup (very, very good.) So if you're in the Westchase/Oldsmar area, or just driving down Hillsboro towards the Gulf head over to Cody's. If the sun's setting you won't be disappointed.
label: POS

text: Hot Yoga Nashville is not for those who dislike sweat or being confined to a room for up to 90 minutes for a class. I have been told in the past (maybe from an ex-boyfriend or two?) that I may have "control" issues but I couldn't admit it until I first started taking classes here. When you walk into a room that is hovering around 103 degrees while holding onto yoga poses but asked not to leave the room unless you absolutely have to....you give up ALL control. Not easy. The classes put your mind and body into a trance of concentration while extending your limbs and muscles during the course of the class. Due to the intensity, it is advised that you don't eat 2 hours before the class. (I had a friend who didn't oblige and vomited - not very Zen) Bring a large supply of water because you will need to sip throughout the class and guzzle it down right after. If you happen to forget your water supply, you will be charged dearly at the studio. I believe that I paid $5 for a Powerade on one of my visits! Bring 2 towels along as well. You will need one to lay on your yoga mat to soak up your sweat and prevent a slip. The other towel can be smaller in size because you will use it to wipe the sweat from your body throughout and after the class. It will smell like a hockey team locker room when you are done so don't forget to leave them in your car! The workout itself is intense and satisfying for both mind and body. The instructors basically stick with the same routine so once you attend a few classes, you will be able to follow along quite nicely. The classes can get quite crowded, so I would suggest getting there 15- 20 minutes before class time. Avoid the back of the class if you don't want to be in the hottest part of the room. Classes are not inexpensive but they offer promotions for newbies and there is quite the price break if you pay for a package upfront. Right now there is a deal where you can purchase 7 months of unlimited classes for $777. This is a chunk of money but considering that each class is normally $15-$18 each, if you plan to practice more than twice a week, you will get quite the deal. You can also have an automatic credit/bank debit each month for unlimited classes at around $100 a month. The key is to get your tush to class! When I practiced 3 -4 times a week, my body and mind were at it's best but I have to admit that it is sometimes tough to get motivated especially when you know that you are going to literally turn into liquid. TIP: Sign up for their email list and you will get promotion and event information. I also received an email for a free class on my birthday. It's much healthier than birthday cake, right?

text: Great prices, great food, great people. That said, lets break it down... Food on buffet line: Ranging from reasonably good to amazing, her prepared dishes are full of flavor, very approachable, and very well priced. They have really added their own flare to many of these dishes with some delicious variations on things you may find elsewhere. The shining stars for me: the curried tofu and the seaweed salad. The tofu is bursting with flavor and just enough heat. The seaweed salad is the best I have ever had because i so beautifully balances the sweet, sour, and heat. Food to order: This place reminds me of my grandmother's house, if my grandmother were Thai. If they have the ingredients, they can make it. That said, there is not a specific menu with all of the things people like to order. From soups to noodle dishes, they do it all. My recommendation? Keep a very close eye on other people in line. They may be ordering the dish that will rock your world, but unless you watch, you won't know it exists. I could live in their Tom Yum soup. Try the veggie dumplings. I think the Beatles put it best when they said, "..had I looked the other way I might have never been aware, but as it is I'll dream of her tonight" Patty's House Salad: Did you catch the article about it in the Scene? If not, allow me to blow your mind. Start the process by getting together a group of at least 4 to 6 people (the minimum and suggested maximum). Then call at least 2 days in advance and choose your meat, tofu, seafood, or whatever you want. Start preparing for an interactive feast. Patty comes out with somewhere in the neighborhood of 27 different ingredients. She then instructs you on how to fill a lettuce leaf appropriately some of every single ingredient and eat it in one bite. This was not a suggestion, but a requirement. You have to be willing to put absolutely everything into your wrap and stuff this gargantuan piece of loveliness into your mouth all at once. You will be glad of the challenge though, as each time you chew you get a different burst of flavor. This is genuine Thai family style. You spend most of your time walking around the table, stuffing food in your hand, then your mouth. You are strongly encouraged to go outside and walk around the block for fresh air from time to time. This allows things to settle a little so you can go back in for another round. Even though you will eat until you explode, it is SUPER FRESH and very light. Not that same old soul food coma afterward. The only downside is that it costs $30 per person. But with the amount of prep work and love that goes into this dish, it is totally worth it when you want to splurge a little and have one of the most incredible food experiences of your life. Market: A small but nice selection of Asian market items. The Gen Mai Cha (Green Tea with toasted rice) is a low grade, but super yummy and very cheap. Try the peanuts, coated in-house with honey, sesame seeds, and apparently something very addictive. There is a very nice assortment of curry pastes to play with and some very attractive Sake and tea sets. Don't forget to pick up a bottle of Sriracha while you're there. Everything is Miscellanea: The decor is a ton of fun. Super casual, but laced with Thai treasures. Each table has an amazing set of condiments to customize your dish to perfection. They definitely take care of their regulars, so loyalty pays off here. There are some amazing seasonal treats. Fall brings coconut custard in baby pumpkins. You eat the pumpkin with the custard and it is both adorable and delicious. This place is not quite a 5 star for me because of several small imperfections, but I would still eat here almost every day if I still lived close enough. An unequivocal gem.

text: Described as the Queen of the Missions, established on December, 4th,1786 during the Feast of St. Barbara, MIssion Santa Barabara sits up the Santa Barbara hills with a gracious and serene charm. It is the tenth of the 21 missions founded by the Spanish Franciscans. Padre Junipero Serra established the first 9, but died two years prior to Mission Santa Barbara. It was his successor, Padre Fermin Franicisco de Lasuen who first rasied the cross, and appointed Padre Antonio Paterna to run and manage the mission, Paterna had the buildings built. The current church, preceded by 3 smaller ones, was dedicated in 1820. Prior to the Spanish, the area was home to the Chumash Indians, who were hunter/gatherers, but also skilled artisans in basket weaving and stone work. The Museum in the mission has a lot of antique items and period pieces, including Chumash, Mexican and Spanish artifacts. The self guided museum tour can take you through 14 areas of interest, from a missionary's bedroom to the Chapel, garden and kitchen. It is one of the more majestic of the California missions in architecture, with a bell tower and fountains, and its museum is one of the better ones. The donation to tour is only $5 and it is a worthwhile stop on your central coast tour. There is a nice large lawn in front for you to picnic or enjoy the great weather..

text: Honestly, the food is no better or worst than any of the other upscale NO restaurants - but I've always had a soft spot for the Sunday brunch here. Brunch is a 3-course affair - picking among the appetizers with Eggs Sardou (poached egg on top of artichoke heart, surrounded by creamed spinach) a favorite; a range of entrees, including their classic pecan-crusted fish in a pool of creamed corn - skip the beef entree; and desserts (including a fan favorite, the $3 extra bread pudding souffle - which really seems to be bread pudding in a ramekin, topped with a still gooey meringue). Commander's reminds me of the bygone days in NO, without completely falling into the wilted-salad, stained tuxedo trap of other, classic restaurants in the French Quarter. Cocktails are highly encourage, and their bloody mary is a hand-crafted affair, served with pickled okra and peppers, as well as a bit of pomp and circumstance. However, it's just as likely diners will be working on their second or third martini before the noon bell strikes. Every local will tell you this place is overrated - agreed - but if you had to pick one of this ilk, Commander's Palace would be it. Yes, it's a jazz brunch, with strolling musicians - but chances are you'll only see them once, playing 2-3 songs, and then disappear to another room in this large restaurant. All told, with one cocktail, brunch will set each of you back about $50-70 total, depending if you opt for cocktails and the scattered $3 supplemental charges on some of the dishes.

text: I went on this tour a few years back and I hope it has changed since I experienced it. I don't share the mostly bubbly assessments of the plantation and tour, and found nothing "quaint and romantic" about it. I was turned off by the cover up and/or diminishing of the sad "other" story. The tour and preservation efforts focused almost completely on the wealthy owners of the mansion. The slaves were a footnote. Yet it was the blood, toil and misery of the slaves that allowed the grand lifestyle of these spoiled confederate slave owners. Let's not forget, slavery was an evil institution. The historic presentation at Belle Meade should focus more on the plight of these enslaved people. Ask yourselves, weren't their lives at least as important as their blood sucking slave owners? Then why is their contribution minimized? At least when I took the tour, there was no presentation of slave quarters, no attempt to show how slaves lived and how integral their lives were to the running of the facilities. Merely halfhearted, cursory comments in passing of what slaves contributed. And no mention of how miserable their lives were, no attempt to balance the story by telling how these people were bought and sold, whipped and punished, how heroic their efforts to escape upon pain of death. One african american was singled out because of his contributions to maintaining the race horses, but the "less valuable" fieldhands and less skilled workers were hardly mentioned. My several questions regarding the lives of the slaves were largely unanswered. In light of the way the slaves on the plantation continue to be suppressed and treated as lesser beings by the superficial treatment given them at the Belle Meade Plantation, I found the tour completely creepy and depressing. The BMP does too little to educate about this equally important aspect of the BMP and southern life. The romanticizing of the south during slavery a la "gone with the wind" continues to this day, as evidenced by the BMP presentation. Where are the slave quarters? Why are they not maintained and shown in detail? How many of the tour guides are african american? Until they do more to honor the contribution and memory of these enslaved people and come clean with the plantation owner's complicity in furthering this evil institution, I cannot recommend this tour.

text: I finally had the opportunity to try out Robert Halpern's cooking and the positive buzz about the new Marigold Kitchen was fully confirmed by the array of beautifully cooked dishes I sampled. The vibrant beet risotto pleased by its intense "beetness" as well as the prefect risotto consistency (something few restaurants here achieve). The mixed green salad was well composed and the pieces of lush, ripe persimmon gave it a unique flavor combination. We liked the Champagne braised escargots on crispy polenta, a very generous dish that brought a good number of rich mollusks to be shared around the table. Of the entrees, the "Colorado" rack of lamb brought four succulent, glorious lamb chops, the "New World Paella" featured was studded with cockles, scallops and langoustine, its seafood accent balanced by pieces of chorizo. Of the desserts, the Tahitian vanilla burnt cream was an excellent version of the ubiquitous crème brûlée: a thin, crackling caramel crust covered an intensely rich cream, livened by chili pepper. The profiteroles with a seasonal ice cream of pumpkin were good, the apple tart serviceable. The seasonality of the desserts was, unfortunately, marred by the chef's insistence to garnish almost all of them with strawberries - certainly a great accompaniment in early summer when local fruit is available, less so when flown in from the southern hemisphere. The tasting menu looked intriguing and I have no doubt that it would provide a fuller appreciation of Halpern's considerable talent. At $85, it does not strike me as an easy ad-hoc decision for diners. It would be nice to have the option of ordering a less expensive (and extensive) tasting menu, let's say for $65. Given the quality and originality of the food, I am sure many patrons would come back for the larger menu. The service was friendly and accommodating but a good distance away from the professionalism of the kitchen. "Who ordered the snails?" and "you guys" as a form of address are two things that could easily be improved on. The restaurant had a very nice vibe later on in the evening, when many tables were filled with smartly dressed diners of various ages and nationalities. The new Marigold Kitchen is highly recommendable.

I made a comment to the gentleman who is the owner (and he waits on tables as well) in high praise of how good they looked, and said that I definitely wanted to order THAT the next time I was there... He explained that it was actually his own lunch, and that, for a variety of reasons (which he elucidated a few of) it's not on the menu and they don't generally offer that in the restaurant. A couple of minutes later though, just before he did sit down to eat (I and my friend were the last couple to still be there at the end of their busy lunch session and were about to leave), he walked over and, with a big sincere smile, set down a plate in front of me with five or six of those beautiful clams on it. Mmmmmm delicious! Gosh they were good. The point is, these people don't see their customers as strangers or as not mattering. Lots of places say that, and sometimes you run into the odd restaurant owner or host/hostess who does try to adopt that "service-with-a-smile, you're-our-friends" kind of attitude (some more sincerely than others), but these people are the real deal. They have live music on the weekends and NEVER ever is there a cover charge. This place seriously gets packed. People wake up early and line up just to eat, booze it up, and hang out here. text: A one and a half star experience for this location. A far cry from what we've experienced at other Crabby Bill's locations. We've been to one of the other Crabby Bill's locations a number of times and always had a great experience. The other diners we were with had been to this location before and had pleasant enough experiences. I don't know what happened tonight, but it wasn't good. We arrived at just before 8pm and got on the waiting list for a table of 5. Unfortunately, the restaurant only has two tables large enough to seat five without moving tables together, so we had to wait. And wait some more. After a while, we asked to make sure they hadn't forgotten about us. They reassured us that it would be just a few more minutes. Eventually, a couple of tables cleared and they could shuffle two tables next to each other. Without exaggerating, it actually took 3 people to do this. These aren't heavy tables, so I don't really know why it took 3 people, but ok. The first thing that struck us was that this place didn't feel like a Crabby Bill's. Normally, Crabby Bill's feels like a homey seafood restaurant. This location was built in what felt like a garage or storeroom. Looking up, you could see the ductwork. Everything felt very clinical, with some ocean themed decorations thrown on because it's a seafood restaurant. The waitress came by and let us know that they had some new margarita, which most of us ordered. It was a bit crowded and busy, but 15 minutes seemed like an awful long time to wait for our four margaritas. When they arrived, they tasted mostly of sour mix. Definitely not worth the $7 each. Upon looking at the menu, we were immediately surprised at how small it was. Maybe half the size of the St Pete location we normally visit. The others commented that it was smaller than the times they had been to this particular location before. We ordered a couple of appetizers: crabbyfeller oysters and some sort of shrimp (which I did not try). The crabbyfeller oysters were described on the menu as having a spinach dip, some cheese and then being baked. Our friends had ordered these at a different location before. When they came out, the first thing we noticed was that they were covered in bacon. Oysters - covered in bacon. Now, bacon may make most things better, but pescetarians don't eat bacon. The waitress noticed our horror and confusion on our faces and asked if something was wrong. "I guess I didn't realize there was bacon on these oysters. Are these the right ones?" "Yes, the crabbyfellers have bacon, it's the clevelanders that don't" "We wanted the ones with the spinach dip" "That's the crabbyfellers. They normally have bacon, but I can ask them to make them without it. Would you like that? It's no problem." And so, the bacon covered oysters went back to the kitchen. Meanwhile, I grabbed a menu. Lo and behold - none of the oyster options mentioned bacon -anywhere-. When the waitress returned, I pointed this fact out to her. "Oh, that's a typo. But we're trained that they have bacon on them. I'll tell the manager and the cooks that the menus don't mention it though." Eventually, the oysters came back without bacon. They were alright. The spinach dip flavor was nice, but the cheddar cheese was unnecessary. Apparently, other locations serve it as oysters, spinach dip and a bit of grated parmesan which sounds much more appetizing than what we got. The appetizer debacle aside, how were the entrees? Our friends found them acceptable, but not up to the quality level we've grown accustomed to from Crabby Bills. My wife ordered a rare grilled tuna steak which came out crusted in Old Bay spice and cooked medium. My clam strips were slightly undercooked and a little soft. By this point though, we knew we would be tempting fate sending anything else back to the kitchen. I grabbed some cocktail sauce from the squeeze bottle for my clams and immediately had to check to make sure it wasn't ketchup. It was super runny and watery. Tasting it, there was only the slightest hint of horseradish. We checked another bottle - and it was the same. When it came time to tip, I commented that "Food aside, the waitress was nice and really apologetic." My wife countered that when we were first seated, she overheard the waitress complaining about having to serve us to the manager. We only came to this location because it was the most convenient for a friend visiting town. Even he said he'd rather just drive the extra 20-30 minutes next time and avoid this location.
label: NEG

There was nothing 'fusion' about it, unless you say it's Asian food cooked western take-out style. The dishes there were the typical beef, chicken, pork, and seafood with a different sauce. You pay way too much for the food, and the service here was not that great either. The waitress came perhaps twice our entire meal. text: This place was really crowded when I went. Every booth was filled, and from the waiting area it seemed as if I wouldn't be able to hear my own thoughts, let alone the words of the person I was dining with. I also expected a long long wait. Luckily, the wait was only 5 minutes. They do an admirable job of getting the food out and bussing the table after people leave so even with a full house the waiting was short. And, after we got to the table the din of the crowd combined into white noise, so we could even hear the 50s hits over it all. I ordered a bacon cheese burger (healthy!) and french fries. My dining partner had a cheese burger with tomato and lettuce and onion rings. The burgers are small and inexpensive. If you decide you need more cow you can easily order a double burger. The bacon was crispy and delicious. They say they have a butcher on site and the meat is fresh, and that might be true, but I can't understand why they cook it so much with such fresh meat. It wasn't burnt, of course, but well done. Still in spite of that flaw it was a tasty burger. The fries were a little bit too potatoey for my tastes. I prefer my fried foods to lose any sense of naturalness, so that might be a personal quirk. There was a bunch of them, though! The onion rings were huge. I didn't taste them, but I heard they were quite good. Now, on to my favorite part. The sodas they have a huge list of flavored sodas you are allowed to try. From toasted marshmallow to boring old cola. I liked these sodas so much that I think I drank too much, and that might have affected any complaints I had about the food. I had two colas, one orange soda and one lime soda. Not a big fan of the lime but the cola and orange were very good. I think I could spend a day there just trying their different soda flavors. Of course this would cause me to quickly float away. I will be back for sure. Perhaps just to have a milkshake which looked really good on the tables all around me. And, much like the sodas, your are provided with a cornucopia of choices. The only thing I know is that my shake will involve chocolate. The ambiance was fun. The waitstaff draws their names on their hats, and if you ask they will give you a hat and some crayons so you can feel like you are part of the family. They have the 1950s thing going on, but it's not so strong that they come up to you and ask you to sit on it, or say that your hat is neato. So, it's not too pervasive. The staff was friendly and quick. It's a fun place to go. Good prices and good food.
label: POS

text: Husband, Toddler, and I stopped in here yesterday for a treat, and unfortunately we fall into the ranks of Yelpers that find this place vastly overrated. The atmosphere is pretty fancy for a bakery, which I guess is supposed to help justify the prices you are about to pay for cupcakes. Toddler was VERY excited to pick out her cupcake, a process made even more lengthy by the fact that they kept pulling trays out of the display to fill a large order in back. Not a huge deal, but something that made me feel like they don't much care about the customers in-store...I think they probably make most of their money on outside orders, which would explain a lot of the problems previous reviewers have had with the customer service. But this would all have been forgiven if the cupcakes had been good. I had the Dark Night, Husband had the Red Velvet, and Toddler had the "Bugs in Mud." Three very different cupcakes, and yet somehow they all managed to taste the same. The Dark Night had little chocolate flavor, and certainly not the deep, rich flavor of dark chocolate. The red velvet had no cocoa flavor. The "Bugs in Mud" was a white cupcake, so of the three, it tasted like it should--that is, bland. Like Justin says below, if you are going to do just one thing, it should be done extremely well. I was left feeling that I could easily make far superior cupcakes at home for a fraction of the price. Or, for that matter, I could go buy a dozen doughnuts for the price of three cupcakes at Batch.

text: Full disclosure, a relative of mine worked here, so I've eaten at Risky Business on numerous occasions, but I think I've had ample opportunity to fully assess this place... A relic of the recent fin-de-siècle, Risky's is an aptly named revamp of the failed "Ventana Grill," a midpriced American that never quite took flight after two attempts in the mid-90s. The new concept seems to have stuck: a family-oriented (in the daytime at least) sports bar, which embodies all of the hedonistic virtues of that prosperous era... a wide-ranging menu (salads to ribs to pizza to burgers to seafood to pasta to steak) that is wide in palate (asian, italian, southwest, mexican and cajun influences), carb heavy (the so-called "angry" mashed potates), and heaping in portion. Desserts are monstrous and unabashedly decadent. I was never truly impressed with the cooking; it seemed to try to please too many people at once, and never really scored well at anything in particular. Often they went a little haywire with the jerk seasoning, which always hurt on the way out. Particularly in these lean, recession hit days, where such extravagance seems out of fashion, it's surprising to note how little has changed at Risky's...even the loud fire-engine-red decor and staff attire (cargo shorts, ankle socks, running shoes) seems dated. The bar really seems to be the primary attraction here...well stocked, with TVs at every angle, and filled with regulars: Air Force types, guests from the resort up the road. But if you truly like that gluttonous, stone in your gut feeling after you eat, don't let me stop you from going here!

text: Pretty shabby for a place that aspires to "upscale." On the plus side, the bathroom was wonderful -- I had an "upgraded, 2 queen beds" room, although when I saw my colleague's regular 2 queen bed room, I was less impressed with my "upgraded" room. I will also say, the staff was very professional, and the view from my room (12th floor) and location were very good. Now, the facilities... Since the hotel was fully booked due to a conference in town, they could not change my room. The TV volume was fixed and could not be changed from its way-too-loud setting -- so the TV was essentially unusable. The bedspreads were stained and dirty looking, and the sheets were equally bad. The hotel changed the sheets for me, but the new set was no better. One of the pillowcases actually had what looked like a cigarette burn hole in it -- why would the housekeeper even use that one? There was half a bag of opened M&Ms left on the desk in the room in plain view, an indication that the housekeeper wasn't paying much attention. The carpet in the room looked dirty. The pool and fitness center are essentially a children's play area -- I realize there's nothing the hotel can do about that, but if you're a business traveler like me and really rely on using those facilities, you're going to be disappointed. This was true on both weekends and weekdays. "Family friendly" in this case means not adult friendly. The internet access was both horribly slow AND expensive ($12.95/day) -- not a good combination. There were two gaping holes in the wall where large light fixtures had been replaced with smaller ones and the hotel did not bother to patch or fill in the extra space -- obviously not critical, but yet another indication that things are not kept up. One more thing -- the on-site restaurant is too expensive for regular dining. As a business traveler, I just want a basic, moderately-priced restaurant that's within my expense limits, but Loews is explicitly trying to make this a "destination restaurant" (which makes no sense since New Orleans already has tons of great restaurants with which a hotel can not compete). I would never stay here again -- too much deferred maintenance and icky bed linens. The price-to-value ratio is off, and nasty linens are a deal-killer for me, regardless of price. PS: I almost forgot -- how could I forget? -- the prominently placed Gideon Bible. While I appreciate the retro factor, I don't think it's there for camp value. It's not even hidden in a drawer. Nope, sitting right out there in plain view. The Unitarian in me finds it offensive that a hotel is trying to convert me to its owners' religion. Tacky!

text: Zakes Cakes and Cafe opened as an outpost in the suburbs to serve "light fare" and continues to satisfy the community's collective sweet tooth today. Located in Fort Washington, Zakes (sometimes listed with an apostrophe) resides on the lower floor of a house at the bottom of a hill. To quote directly from another review: "Zakes' salads, sandwiches and soups are all outstanding, but save room for dessert! Many delicious specials to choose from, in addition to a great menu. The only problem here is making a decision. Be prepared to wait for a table around lunchtime..." Unless you arrive early, you'll have to wait at least 15 minutes to get a table. After noon, the place fills up! You'll get to wait on the patio's couch (!) and appreciate the garden outside at least. The main room can seat a reasonably large party. Look around and you'll see regulars from the surrounding area: residents of Ambler and Fort Washington and droves of worker bees from the nearby industrial parks. On a sunny day the place is cheery and well-lit. On cloudy days, the ceiling lighting is well-arranged and doesn't overwhelm. The walls are decorated with framed photographs thrown about. I can't remember any music playing in the background. The menu has Italian, Vietnamese, French, Chinese, and English highlights. Daily specials are available at Zakes. I had a bowl Mediterranean tomato soup with orzo. It was lightly flavored with tomato and herbs and had a light, pleasing taste. Chunky bits of orzo added substance to the dish. The portabello sandwich tasted like pizza and had the consistency of a tomato pie. It was topped with brussel sprouts... I looked forward to taking another bite as soon as I took the first! The mocha gatteau didn't live up to my expectations. I was disappointed that the mocha was not as strong as I would have liked. The level of the baker's expertise is evident in the clean presentation of the cake. Zakes is a comfortable place to go for lunch and a cup of coffee. Next time I go I think I'll get the Saigon salad, summer rolls (with chicken, shrimp) or the bourbon glazed salmon... so many choices...

text: Pulling into the parking lot, we noticed there was a $9.99 all you can eat sushi happy hour 3:30-6 p.m. We were informed that this includes all the long rolls and hand rolls, but no nigiri. I'd still consider this a screaming deal though. We opted instead for the unlimited all you can eat (a reasonable $17.95 each) which included the nigiri and dim sum. The only thing unavailable on the all you can eat is the spider (soft shell crab) roll. Very few a.y.c.e. sushi deals include this now, so I didn't consider that a huge drawback. I wonder if there was a staffing issue when Wan L. went, because the service was almost overwhelming when my buddy and I took the plunge. 3-4 workers gravitated immediately to us to get us sushi, offer dim sum, drinks, etc. Granted, there was only one other pair of diners there when we arrived, but even when it got busier later, they continued to be attentive. Literally seconds after we finished a sushi order, the chef raced over to offer another. I ate mostly hand rolls and nigiri. Too much rice fills the belly, especially with a beer or two, and I like to maximize my a.y.c.e. experience. Hard to choose a favorite, but the Eddie roll (salmon skin/octopus) was good, not too greasy which is saying a lot when you're dealing with deep-fried salmon skin. Nigiri-wise, the red snapper was one of the best I've had, and the unagi was as good as any competitor. My friend likes eel, and had about 3-4 orders. They also had one which I believe was called the "fireman" hand roll with spicy tuna & roasted jalapeno. For those who can take some real heat, check this one out. The habanero sauce used on the tuna didn't overwhelm the flavor of the meat. It takes some talent to pull off quality spicy food, so the chef definitely was paying attention. He told me he was using the sauce that the "old chef" made and that his version was going to include habanero and serrano peppers and would be even hotter. Use caution, because I got mine one level below spiciest and it still packed a good punch. With a hotter sauce I would call this one the "nuclear roll." The quail egg shooters were pretty decent but I like mine a little spicier, next time I'll ask for a extra dose of hot sauce in mine. Overall, all the sushi was pretty good. I'd say for purely sushi in Reno, Sushi Pier 2 and Sushi Teri still have the edge as far as quality. But what makes Yen Ching great is the inclusion of the dim sum. There are about 8-10 appetizer items that you can order by filling out a ticket, including skewered (teriyaki?) chicken, shrimp dumplings, pork buns, and paper-wrapped chicken. My favorite were the shrimp dumplings, which were probably frozen pre-made shu mai, but man were they insanely good. I could have probably eaten 20 of those damn things if there wasn't sushi there too. The pork buns were the best I've had since living in San Francisco, with a tasty filling incorporating ground pork and onions. That said, I haven't hit up Honey Bakery yet, which I've heard makes killer pork, chicken, beef, and dessert buns. These were mini-pork buns rather than the muffin-sized ones, which is fine by me since they're a.y.c.e. Being a filling (i.e. starchy) item, next time I'll probably save those for the final round. All in all a great experience. My buddy who's also a huge Asian food fan was also impressed. Both of us have lived in SF, which to me is the ultimate Chinese food mecca outside of China, so we're pretty experienced in this area. I'm usually leery of Asian restaurants that offer multiple ethnic cuisines like this one, because the overall quality tends to suffer, but not in this case. The only reason I didn't give this the full five stars was that the sushi wasn't quite at the level of the best a.y.c.e. sushi restaurants in Reno. But it was close, and given the value, the service, and the sheer variety of food available I'd give Yen Ching a solid 4 1/2 stars. For those who prefer cooked sushi, the happy hour would seem to be the best deal around. Like my buddy said about the scope of the Asian food available and the service: "Hey, if you asked for a bowl of Pho they'd probably whip that up for you in the sink!" Nicely put bro...

text: Maybe I am stuck in my ways with East Bay Area Vietnamese food but this place was an extreme disappointment. I usually go to Sunny's place for Viet food in Reno at 777, but we decided to gamble and try what the yelpers liked. This place had every intention of being right. Hole in the wall looking spot in a strip mall, really to-the-point restaurant name and a menu that screamed NOM NOM. My family ordered: 2 of the most famous soups Bun Bo Hue without thinking, and an Egg noodle soup with wontons. After much anticipation, the bad news started pouring in. Maybe its just me, and you can argue that, but the famous soup here was a huge disappointment. The noodle is basically spaghetti and I was expecting the traditional thinly cut, transparent and chewy pho. I got nothing of that sort. Secondly, if you are not as accustomed to hardcore Asian dining (as I am not), the soup features an array of ingredients that may make you uneasy: pig feet, blood cubes, etc. Lastly, although claiming to be hot, this soup was not spicy at all and lacked any interesting flavor. The egg noodle was also very overcooked and the wontons were nothing special. Broth was plain and didn't do much for me. I give this restaurant a one star for the food, and another for the service. Although there was one stern lady working at the register and tables, we didn't get here and instead got a very pleasant woman who was extremely nice and polite. After throwing in the towel on two full soups b/c we didn't like them, she smiled and didn't press the issue or make us feel terrible about it. I've had better.

text: From the second we walked into the park I was pleasantly surprised. It looks beautiful and inviting from the entrance gate. The first thing we did was head to the gift shop. It was huge. They had such a great selection, including infant products, which was perfect because I have a 7 month old who needed a hat. (about $6). I also picked up a stuffed white alligator in the Louisiana Swamp section, and it was only $3.99. The prices were great. Usually you go to a theme park gift shop, and the prices are outrageous that you can only afford to pick up one thing. Prices on the refreshments, that's another story. I paid almost $3 for a fountain drink, and $12 at the Haagen Dazs for a shake and cup of ice cream! Geeze. Talk about raping my wallet. I'd recommend taking your own beverages, and food because they don't check your bags and there is a large lawn area to have picnics on. We arrived at the Zoo at 11:00 AM and didn't leave until 3:30 PM. There was so much to do!!! You also felt like you could reach the animals they were so close. That was so great. Actually, we went to see the Giraffes, and I was only about 10 inches away from reaching the Giraffe when it tilted it's head over the railing towards us. The reptile section was amazing. It was an entire building dedicated towards all different types of reptiles. My husband really loved it. There were so many different types of snakes, I lost count! The Louisiana Swamp area was my favorite, and probably one of the largest exhibits. They had a huge swamp with green water, and filled with about 10 Alligators! There is a deck built above it all so you can just look down an observe all of it. They also had a Raccoon and Nutria exhibit. It was a lot of fun!!! It was such a great experience for my little girl. She really loved it all! It was entertaining for all of us, and I can't wait to go back! The only complaint I have is the parking situation. We got there early, only about an hour after the park was open and there was no where to park. They don't have a section that you pay for parking, or that is just excluded to the people who are visiting the zoo, so anyone who is visiting the area can park there. We actually had to park in one of the local soccer fields adjacent to the parking lot, but it wasn't a far walk so it wasn't too bad. So get there early if you can!

text: With a staunch, well-documented history of heterosexuality behind me, I feel proud to say that I am a huge fan of Tavern on Camac. In fact, although it may seem counterintuitive, the straighter you act, the more suitors you will attract. While we all know this isn't true, you should take advantage of this false belief. Instead of being offended when a tiny little man in a tight v-neck tee, True Religion jeans, an out of season tan, and an impeccable complexion approaches you to talk about football, embrace the opportunity. Live in the moment. Accept the drink that he has offered to buy you. If you can simply maintain conversation, that one drink may turn into two drinks which may turn into three drinks...all for free. Think straight dudes. How many dollars have you spent in your life buying drinks for girls at bars? How significant of a return on investment have you seen from those dollars? Generally speaking, I'd be willing to bet it's pretty low. So why not recoup some of those sunk costs? Why not get yours? Shed your antiquated inhibitions. It's your turn to feel pretty. It's your turn to feel special. It's your turn to feel wanted...sigh! At Tavern on Camac, for once in my life, I could keep my wallet in my pocket, sit back, and enjoy an evening of lively chatter and free booze. Take...Ad...Vantage. 2) Keep your head on a swivel. While it's fun to get free drinks, it gets a little old as the night draws closer to last call. At some point, you will have had your fill of dudes night out. And herein lies the magic of the gay club - a secret fact of life that most of my straight friends are hesitant to believe, but are quick to embrace once they bear witness to this amazing phenomenon. In Philadelphia, gay bars are the best place to pick up chicks. Now wait wait wait. Take it easy over there. Allow me to explain. Every weekend, girls get together with their pack and head out looking for fun. Invariably, they end up at the same old bars getting hit on by same old guys. It's gets tiresome. They need a change of pace. So what do they do? They call their gay friend and they set up the classic - GIRLS NIGHT OUT! "Whoooo...it's going to be great. You can literally see this switch flip in their brain as they start to frantically scan the dance floor for anything even slightly resembling a straight man. The fact is, you can't compete with these tools because they have no sense of shame, so why even try? Go gay bar and avoid the competition all together! Most guys don't realize this aspect of the Tavern. They shy away for no good reason at all. As a result, they are seriously missing out. To all my straight men out there, get on over to Tavern, drink for free, and meet some chicks. Doesn't get any more hetero than that. text: *this review is from a vegetarian perspective, for what it's worth* I was super ecstatic to hear of a place serving a Chicago-style veggie dog. The problem is not with the bun or condiments - these were all pretty good and I'd expect, based on that, that the meaty dogs are probably good. However, their veggie dog is house-made (I think, and a bonus), but they're not really franks. They are more like veggie burgers loosely shaped to fit a hot dog bun. Now, as a burger, they are good, but they don't have the taste and texture to really do a frank justice. If they just called it a veggie patty with Chicago-style accompaniments, maybe it would take some of the sting out of it. But, as a dog, it just doesn't work. I still eat one now and then and they are a fine sandwich, but not a substitute for a Chicago dog.

text: Very interesting Mexican food, right there on Locust near all the cool kids. Their margaritas and other drinks are decent, although I have seen a sort of disconnect between servers and bartenders on more than one occasion. text: Roaming in Reno, Nevada on a Friday late afternoon around 4ish, my mother who doesn't like eating anything except Vietnamese or Mexican food, insisted and then demanded that we find a Vietnamese restaurant to eat at. Without any regard to whether or not there's a Vietnamese community in Reno, I tell my mother, "Mom, there's no way that Vietnamese people live here. We haven't seen an Asian person since we got here! Plus, this place looks so dead! There's barely anyone here on a Friday evening. Don't we typically live in clusters of our kind? Ya know, enclaves?" As I finished my spiel, my mom, sister and I decided to cross the sidewalk and midway across the street, I noticed this janky-looking building with faded paint that's suppose to be yellow, green, and red (I think) with a flower logo. At first, I thought to myself, "This is a really ugly looking building. No wonder this town is dead. They place needs massive architectural redevelopment." As I continued my critique of physical disapproval of the building, to my surprise, I stumbled upon the the name on the building, "Golden Flower" and then the other phrase "Vietnamese Restaurant" in white italics! In awe of our discovery, we immediately agreed to eat here despite the lack of exterior appeal of the building. Why not, right? What were the chances of finding a Vietnamese restaurant immediately after such a conversation? :D We walked into the restaurant feeling hesitant and skeptical about what we'll find here. Surprisingly, there were several tables occupied, scattered throughout the restaurant--1/4 of the room--of various people of different ethnic backgrounds. The decor wasn't anything special, but it definitely gave off a family-run kind of vibe. The waitress was friendly--greeted us and showed us to a table. Once we sat down, it was sort of strange how I kind of felt at home. The ambiance of this place was laid back and kind of noisy but it was just because a lot of people were talking at once. Dress code was very casual. I am certain that if you walked in with your pjs from your hotel, I'm sure they'll serve you anyways. :) My sister got the bowl of pho Tai (steak), nam, gau and sach, with Tai on the side (about $5.50). [sorry folks. I don't know how to translate the rest] My mom got the rice dish with bbq pork (about $7-8) and I got the rice dish with broiled beef (about $7-8). We all shared an order of spring rolls ($4.99) and che ba mau (3 color dessert) ($2.50). The pho is okay here. I think it's missing an ingredient that gives it a certain kick/flavor at the end of each bite. I still think pho restaurants in San Diego kicks ass. Both rice dishes were pretty good. They gave us plenty of meat. I even forced myself to finish it because it was that good and filling. I hate wasting food and I don't prefer taking things to-go because some things just taste better when you eat it right away, so I forced myself to finish. :P The spring rolls were good too (similar to SD), but I think $4.99 is WAYYY overpriced!! It takes less than $0.50 to make and it doesn't even take that long to make it! The 3-colored-dessert was BOMB! This dish was definitely unique to me because they used two types of bean desserts in this one instead of just one. They didn't use the green string ingredient, so it threw my taste buds off but it was delicious nonetheless. So if you're ever in Reno and you're just sick and tired of casino and hotel food that typically charge you up the a** for food that is next to mediocre and you're feeling like exploring a new culture, I say, "Check this place out." My mom didn't want to pay more than $10 per person for food, so this place rocks in that arena! Plus, this place is my-mother-approved! If you're looking for pho, then this place is okay, but if you're looking for rice dishes with good meat and desserts, then I say, "Yay all the way!" So until next time, enjoy your food explorations as I will with mine. cheers!
label: POS

text: First Off, I love going to O'Connell's after the 1 a.m. bars close and hanging out by the bar and watching the show. However, I am reviewing the burger, which is, in my opinion, MASSIVELY OVERRATED! My last visit was March 16...the eve of St Patty's. We were directed to the table in the bar area closest to the kitchen. We had a bird-eye view of the massive softball-size scoops of ground beef that are subsequently molded into MASSIVE patties, then cooked with choice of Swiss or American cheese. Personally watched my burger grill for an appropriate time (ordered medium). Food arrived...looked awesome. At this point, I will flashback to my only previous burger experience here. Looked great. Mouth-watering anticipation. Guess what?... Flash Forward!!!!! The burger SUCKED! Raw to bleeding rare in the center. ABSOLUTELY 1000% FLAVORLESS! Not even a hint of seasoning or grease or pepper or FLAVOR! What the hell? How can you have a burger with that much meat and taste NOTHING????? I swear, even a little sprinkle of "Meat Magic" or Lawry's special seasoning or something would have been welcome. NADA, ZIP, NOTHING....'cept for a bloody hunk of tasteless, bloody flesh. I had to add Grey Poupon mustard just to give it any flavor at all (not a fan of drowning in ketchup...but I had to do this too to breath some semblance of flavor...although given the impossibly rare innards...it was practically still mooing). Now, I know that this burger sat on the grill for a good 25 minutes because I watched it cook and watched the cook flip it and watched him mash it down at least a couple times, so why didn't it cook? The griddle is obviously not hot enough. Plain and simple. Would it have rescued the flavor? Hell, even charred meat tastes better than unseasoned raw ground beef/chuck. Come on. Now I'm gonna rant on St Louis taste buds. You people do it to yourselves by accepting mediocre meat. Your steaks are bland and your burgers are bland, for the most part. So, in conclusion, if you are going to O'Connell's for the burger, you will get a lump of flavorless ground beef. It will make a turd (or worse), but as far a tasty burger. No. Note----I tried the rare roast beef a couple years ago based on glowing praise and found it to be absolutely flavorless. I'm talking, if you blindfolded me and asked me to identify the meat, I would have guessed wet paper towel. That bland...that flavorless. For all the folks that are going to pile on and tell me I don't know what I'm talking about...I say...Try eating sometime when you're not blind drunk. Flavor matters. This place needs a new recipe.

text: Diagonally across grid-locked Route 70 from Han-Ah-Reum (or H-Mart), set back in the Barclay Shopping Center, is the Chinese answer to the Korean mega-mart. I think the Koreans have won. Not that there's nothing to like at the Asian Mart, mind you. For one, it's big. Which means plenty of varieties of instant noodles, canned pickled vegetables, fermented sauces and snacks. They have a five star snack section. Pocky! dried Mango! Salty Prunes! Dried Squid! For the same prices as you would see at Philly's C-town, the deli offers up decent roast pork, duck, soy sauce chicken, curried octopus and porcine offal. The small buy-by-the-pound hot foods section offers mapo doufu and braised pork butt. Just remember to get there early since most of the deli and hot foods are gone by mid-afternoon. Coincidentally, these are items that for obvious reasons, cannot be found at the Han-Ah_reum. Chinese 3, Koreans 0 But what could be a vibrant Asian market experience, turns flat when you visit the fresh veggies and fruit section, and their meat and fish markets. Sure you can get the usual Chinese veggies like Shanghai bai cai and Chinese broccoli and bitter melon, but they like to wrap everything in plastic bags (so that you can't pick certain things and they control the portion you buy). That really irks me. The H-Mart, on the other hand, has that laissez faire thing where I can choose which ever green bean I please and only get 3 ounces if I that's all I need. And, the veggies look fresh, unencumbered by the plastic bags. Chinese 3, Koreans 1. Both places have small fish sections where you can pick a living fish which they will give last rites to and clean it as well. I do find that the H-Mart have somewhat fresher iced fish than the Asian MArt. You can tell by the clarity in the fish's eyes. That is, if you can get yourself to look it in the eye. CHinese 3, Koreans 2. In the meat sections, they both have butchers on hand as well as prepackaged meats. But it's hard to find basic meats, like chicken legs and pork chops at the Asian Mart and often the meats behind the case don't look appetizing. The only time I bought any meat there was when spare ribs were on sale. If I need ground pork for dumplings (jiao zi) or mandoo, I brave crossing Rt. 70 to get to H-Mart. The Koreans have tied it up. But the main reason why I wind up saying "Annyong ha shimnikka" to the missionaries in the parking lot and head into H-Mart is the crispy, demurely sweet store-made rice treats. The stoic rice-cake man pops them out like nobody's business and the free samples keep my whiny kids sedate. Pop! There goes another rice cake. Pure theater! Koreans 4, Chinese 3. So, Asian market, you need loosen up a little. Free the vegetables from their clear plastic straight jackets! Get rid of the rigor mortised, bleary eyed fish on ice! Play on your strengths! Have a Pocky themed event! Cooking classes with durian! Show us that you can partay and we'll come.

text: I was in St. Louis for a conference and went to Hannegan's (with 3 other people) simply because it had outside seating and the menu looked like it might be regional (read: had barbeque). There were about 10 outside tables, only a few of which were populated when we sat down. The tone of the meal was set quickly when a waiter dropped three big, thick pint glasses filled with beer on the sidewalk, shattering the glass all about the sidewalk and tables. We watched in astonishment as he half-heartedly kicked a few of the larger pieces towards the building, and walked away. This mess of beer and glass was left untouched during the ENTIRETY of our meal, which, as you will see, was virtually endless. I ordered some sort of bbq turkey sandwich whose description sounded fairly unique, and a beer. Two of the others ordered burgers and the third ordered the Irish Stew. Then we sat there to wait. And wait we did. We watched as the other tables filled up, peopled ordered, were served, and left. The time progressed like one of those old doomsday movies where people stare at the big clock on the wall and time seems to stand still. Occasionally, the waitress would race by, glance over her shoulder, and say "It's on the way". We began to wonder where it was on the way from. I finally called her over and she told us it was taking so long because the Irish Stew "takes a little longer", where "a little" apparently meant "a lot". Someone at our table suggested that the stew was being made in Ireland, and flown over. I immediately mentally docked our waitress big tip points for not having told us this right away, which is inexcusable. We were almost ready to get up and walk out when our meals finally came, only making me wish that I had followed my instincts and left first. My special turkey sandwich was comprised solely of two wafer-thin slices of processed turkey lodged along with a dessicated piece of lettuce and a sad little tomato slice between some dry, flavorless bread. I was so hungry that I just picked up the little pieces of meat and popped them in my mouth and was done with it. We were so late for the afternoon session of the conference that we had to flag down our waitress and race out of there, stepping carefully over a mess of beer and broken glass to do so. I gave this one star because it was a sunny day and we were sitting outside. Who says I'm not a generous reviewer?

text: So boyfriend booked the place and I must say, it was fairly nice. The shower door had a hole in the glass (to open and close) - which I thought was strange since water could easily splash out, but it worked out in the end. The hotel provides two free bottles of Fiji water and our room didn't come with a snack bar, so we didn't have to worry about getting late night cravings or moving the food. The TV quality was decent, though I don't believe that it was HD. Either that, or the channels weren't HD. Downstairs in the shopping area - well, there's not much to it. There are two clothing stores, but nothing that I could see myself, a 22-year-old female, wearing any time soon. For the most part, the stores seemed pretty dead, but considering that we were there during the middle of the week - perhaps it picks up during the weekends? There was one small gripe though - they advertised "The Beach" - which was supposed to be their nice pool and spa services. Well, I can't comment on the pool since it was closed, but their spa services? You have to go downstairs, again, in the dingy little shopping area, go through the gym, then into the massage rooms. The whirlpools are single sex - installed in the locker and shower rooms of each sex. However, they do provide steam and sauna rooms. They do offer free valet, but be aware that it might take them some time to get to your car if there's a few people waiting in line as well - which there will almost always be, considering it's free. However, if you do self-parking, you'll be relatively closer to the elevators, so this might be a better option after you've unloaded all of your belongings. Overall, I'm a fan of this place. text: Citygarden is just two blocks of happiness and a great argument for what can be done when public spaces are left in capable hands. I like the fact that the layout of the Citygarden gives a nod to St. Louis and Missouri geography while still managing to look modern. I always find something new with each visit here. An audio tour is available by calling a free number from your cell phone. The New York Times recently listed Citygarden as a 'must see' in their '36 Hours in St. Louis' article, and they are so right. text: Bullet Points: - so much heart and soul in the decor and food, I just fell in love straight away - they served me dairy on sandwich I requested vegan - slow credit card - they were out of the thing I ordered but didn't inform me until 15 min later - gave me a free vegan brownie for the wait - vegan brownie was so good I almost wept - food is pretty good, baked goods are outstanding - open early Sweet Art is so cute inside. I walked in on a week day morning and there was a line out the door. The place is bright and green with cutely mis-matched chairs and tables. The art on the walls is just so St. Louis and filled with so much passion and soul. There was a quote of the day that said "Don't tell god how big your problems are, tell your problems how big your god is." The menu is covered in "vegan friendly" options. There were 2 varieties of vegan cupcakes in the case. I ordered the Tofuallo sandwich and attempted to pay with a card. It took FOREVER to run my card and eventually it just didn't go through. I had money in my account, but it's a small out of state credit union so who knows. I paid cash. Then about 15 minutes later the guy comes out and tells me that they're out of Tofuallo. So I got a sweet burger instead. It took another 20-25 minutes for that to come out. I could see the girl making it, while bopping to the music and just smiling ear to ear. When it finally came out they gave me a free brownie for the wait. I took everything with me and ate it later (STL vegan survival, ya know?) I was alone in the car when I ate that brownie and cried out loud it was so good. Quite possibly the best I've ever had. The food was good too. The Sweet Burger is a hearty mix of lentils and such. The Caesar Salad was right on. I went back a second time and again had problems with my credit card. This time I ordered a bagel sandwich with veg bacon and I definitely asked for it to be made vegan. Unfortunately it had real cream cheese on it. : ( They apologized and made me another one. The bagel sandwich was fine. Nothing to write home about. It would be a lot better if they made their own fakin bacon (cough:: super-firm tofu sliced thin, dipped in soy with liquid smoke and olive oil and baked ::cough). My sister had the vegan frech toast which was puts any eggy toast to SHAME. It also puts Mokabe's sad little vegan french toast breakfast to shame. All in all, I love Sweet Art - and I hardly ever say that about a place that gives dairy to vegans. But really you can just feel the love that went into this place. The girls bouncing to the music behind the counter, the smiles, VEGAN CUPCAKES. Finally, there is a good place for a vegan breakfast in St. Louis.

They really fell down on the job with the complimentary van transfer service. Getting to our location (the Opryland Complex) was smooth and we were assured that the van would pick us up until 11pm. We called for 45 minutes and there was no answer. In a panic, we called a cab and paid $23 for the service. When we approached the night clerk, he smirked and said he was there and the phone didn't ring. I was still calling the hotel as I exited the cab and he did answer at that point so I had the correct number. HOWEVER! Carla, the manager, refunded my cab fare and even went so far as to offer me an extra bonus. She really stepped up to the plate to make up for the night clerk's failing. The free drinks and dinner Monday through Thursday is a nice plus. We didn't feel like going to the quaint charming restaurant next door (raining, cold, long day wandering Nashville) on our second night and went downstairs for the burgers and fries. The food was okay but the hot cookies ROCKED!!! The free wine and beer - nice! Note: get your cookies early - they are gone by the time the late shift (7pm) is done. Breakfast is the quality of the Hampton in the chain - okay but nothing special. I would go light on breakfast (though the coffee was very good) and eat a nice lunch at one of Nashville's many excellent restaurants (see The Tin Angel). Carla The Manager was very present at breakfast - greeting customers, picking up dirty dishes, bagging trash. I stay in a lot of hotels and NEVER see a manager much less one getting her hands dirty. So, my original 3 stars is being upgraded to 4 based on CTM. She seems young and very enthused. I think the staff problems will be gone shortly under her. The Homewood Suites is off Briley Parkway about 10 minutes from the Opryland complex and 20 minutes from downtown as well as 10 minutes from the airport. If you have a car and like the apartment atmosphere, give HS a try.

text: So to answer your first question: Yes, it is indeed an old Taco Bell converted into a Mexican Restaurant. Well, not quite, they took off the bell. Menu is on the wall, although there is a real menu and table service available as well. I think the wall is to reminisce to the Bell Years. On the menu are the usual suspects you would expect to see at a local Mexian place, including Tacos, Tortas, Burritos, Chimichangas etc. They also have some unadvertised dishes if you ask, and daily specials that rotate. Today it was fish tacos, but another group a couple of tables down ordered a whole fish which looked mighty tasty. The last time I was there they had some fresh flan - ask for it! I suggest trying the tacos and tortas here. They are excellent. If you have never had a torta before, it is basically a sandwich with meat, avocado, and many other vegetables. Very very good. My favorite meat is tongue, it may sound unappetizing but really it is just very tender beef. (Try it) The spicy pork is excellent as well. The tacos are the classic style, on a soft tortilla with your choice of meat, and then onion, cilantro and lime. Price: Not as cheap as The Bell, lunch of Torta + 2 Tacos + Mexican Coke came out to ~$12. If it was just the Torta + water it would have been about 1/2 that. For the quality of the food though, not bad. I have 3 favorite authentic Mexican joints in the STL, and this is one of them. Big note here though: This is NOT Hacienda or Casa Gallardo. Everything is not covered in cheese and taco seasoning. They have their place... but not here. Conclusion: Great food, good price, good to eat in or carry out an order of Tacos. Perfect.
