text: Like so many Nola eateries, you have gobs and gobs of fried food. And I'm not saying that's a bad thing, but it's a shame that Coop's poboys dominate the menu (last time I went in for lunch it seemed everyone was eating fried crawfish, shrimp and oysters). The real prize at Coop's is their jambalaya. So many places turn out crap jambalaya, but Coop's does it right: with great big chunks of pepper in a flavorful broth with super spicy tasso. They also do a great red beans and rice (slow cooked and peppery with plenty of stock meat). If you go out back you can see where they cook all the meals: under the open sky. They have a big smoker and huge stew pots back there. Most back allies in Nola smell like sewage, but this back alley smells like heaven! Anyway, skip the fried seafood and try something with real local flavor. Also, don't cross the waitresses because they WILL win in any bar brawl.

text: For those looking to enjoy a heaping mound of fresh New Orleans seafood, I highly recommend Bourbon House's Plateau de Fruits de Mer. Loose translation: big ass plate of seafood. My financee and I are big seafood eaters but we were definitely intimidated when we saw the size of the plate. Huge, huge, HUGE plate of seafood consisting of mussels, clams, oysters, shrimp, crawfish and seafood salad. It was literally a feast and the carnage we left behind in the form of shrimp and crawfish carcasses was both amazing and disgusting. As if that wasn't enough food, we also ordered the Trio of Baked Oysters, which consisted of Oysters Rockefeller (parsley, cheese, butter and bread crumbs), Oysters Bienville (bacon, shrimp, onions, cheese and other stuff) and Oysters Fonseca (tomatoes, peppers, chees). Not quite as good as as the chargrilled oysters at Acme but still pretty decent and a nice contrast to all the chilled seafood that was served on the big ass plate. One more thing I have to share: Bourbon House has this drink called the Frozen Bourbon Milk Punch. Think a creamy milkshake with some bourbon in it. Absolutely delicious -- I am totally going to steal the recipe and make some of my own the next time I have a BBQ at home. Service at Bourbon House was pretty good. They have three different servers that tend to you, depending on what you need: Server A for ordering and paying the bill, Server B for refilling drinks and bringing out the food, and Server C for clearing plates. It's an odd system but it works. Getting a window seat is nice because you get a sweet view of the drunken passerby's on Bourbon St. Bourbon House is definitely worth the trip the next time you're in the French Quarter.
label: POS

text: Steer clear of Roberta. I had the worst massage ever at Adolf Biecker today from Roberta. It had been a rough week, and I thought I would cut out of work early on Friday afternoon and get a massage. After striking out trying to get an appointment at Rescue (my usual massage spot), I tried Adolf Biecker, figuring that it was nearby and in a nice hotel, so it should be good. Um, not so fast. The facilities were ok, but the real problem was Roberta. Oh, Roberta. I am hesitant to trash someone's ability to practice her chosen profession, but I would hate for someone to waste $100 and an hour on this massage. The word that comes to mind in describing the massage is unskilled. It honestly felt like my husband (who is an attorney, not a massage therapist) rubbing cold sunscreen on me. It was weird when she started with my feet, and it just got worse. I was laying there thinking, "What is she doing? Is she a professional massage therapist? Was she trained? Can I stand this for a full hour?" At one point she had my hand pinned back to the middle of my back. It wasn't painful, just annoying. When I felt her pressing into my kidneys, a big massage no-no, I knew it was time to go. I decided that I would tell Roberta that I had to go to the bathroom. I came back and explained that it just wasn't working for me. Frankly, she did not seem surprised. I would guess this was not the first time it happened to Roberta. When I checked my watch back in the locker room, I realized that I had only been in the massage for about 20 minutes. I asked to speak with the manager. I told her that I have been to a lot of massage therapists at different spas in Philly, and I had never ever even considered walking out in the middle. I told her that Roberta's touch felt unskilled and amateurish. I asked whether they had confirmed that Roberta had formal training. The manager responded that Roberta had several years of experience, which is not the same as training. The manager swore that Roberta had regular repeat customers. Maybe it was just a bad match between me and Roberta, but, like I said, I have had a lot of massages and this is the first time I ever considered leaving. The only bright spot was that they did not even suggest that I should pay for the service.
label: NEG

text: Is it your first time? With ABSINTHE I mean! Well, this is like getting swimming lessons before dipping your toe into the pool under the watchful eye of a lifeguard rather than being thrown off the high dive into the cold, scary deep end with no warning. Or, to say it in fewer words, Pirate's Alley is great for beginner absinthe drinkers. They feature multiple brands and are patient and willing to explain the difference in flavors (licorice versus mint or a mixture of both) in order to help you pick your poison. Then, you get to watch as they light your sugar cube on fire, slowly drip water over the sugar cube on a fancy spoon, and then mix up a licorice and/or minty concotion. I hung around for a couple of days and noticed that one of the (off-duty) bartenders likes her absinthe mixed with cranberry juice. An interesting concotion that I have yet to try ... This bar is tucked away from the storm of bourbon street but still serves up the good stuff.

text: This is my first Yelp review, so bare with me. I am a vegan whose favorite Philadelphia restaurants include Rangoon, Mi Lah, and Horizons. I also like Blue Sage a good deal. As you may know, or may have gathered from these reviews, Thoreau is the new restaurant from the Blue Sage owners. First, the much discussed ambiance/space. It is a bit cramped. We (I went with a friend) were lucky enough to get the table in the back, near the server station and kitchen, which was far enough away from the general seating that it was a bit private. But, if the restaurant was packed, and I had to sit super close to another party, I'd be complaining about it right now, as that's a huuuge pet peeve of mine. The decor is very sparse. Sort of greyish walls with a couple pieces of abstract art. The decor is passable, if not a bit boring. First Impressions of the Menu: Pricey. Entrees average $22. This seems to put the price point a tad above Horizons, and way above Mi Lah, Rangoon, and most delicious Asian restaurants. But, if the food is good, then it would obviously be worth it. Soup: We ordered the soup of the day, which was some sort of Indonesian Peanut soup. It was good. It was pretty tasty with wholesome chunks of sweet potatoes, fresh herbs on top, and peanuts. It was very filling. We split it, and it served to fill us up a great deal. The soup could have been a bit spicier for my taste, but it was good just the same. I'd give it a B+. For me, the soup has always been the best part about Blue Sage. Well, that and the Paninis or Pubanos or whatever they call them. Entrees: Ouch. I'll say up front, neither of us enjoyed our entrees. My friend ordered the "Blue Plate: Rosette of purple Okinawa sweet potatoes atop sweet corn gravy, grilled avocado with edamame succotash, brochette of Szechwan carrot syrup-glazed shiitakes." The potatoes were lacking flavor big-time. Their lovely swirling presentation and texture was the best part, but they had no kick, no butteriness, no garlic flavor, nothing. The seared avocado was good and creamy, and the edamame was, well, edamame. The mushrooms were good. The tangy sauce that covered them was interesting enough, but they were completely slathered in this sauce, and it was a bit overwhelming in this way. I wanted to enjoy a bit more of the natural mushroom flavor, rather than only this tangy sauce. I ordered the "Tamarind Peanut Noodles soba noodles, grilled asparagus, chopped peanuts and many herbs in sweet-spicy tamarind-kaffir lime broth. topped with tatsoi-white asparagus salad." And I'm still regretting it. This dish was odd, ill-conceived, and terribly muddled. I kept picturing Gordon Ramsay going raving mad over this sorry dish. In short, it tasted like a strange mix of spaghetti and tomato sauce with asian flavor notes. The peanut noodles lay on the very bottom of the plate, in a wet, watery mess of sauce. There were about 2 asparagus stalks total, which were good. There were a few tiny red/purple potatoes that were ok. The greens on top of it all were really out of place. While they looked nice, they just did not seem to fit the dish at all. Additionally, there were whole cooked shallots throughout, that were a bit slimy as well. I ate about 1/5th of it, and threw in the towel. This dish sounded great on paper, but again, came off as a strange mix of a sort of sweet tomato sauce with faint hints of asian flavor. I could never picture eating it again. Dessert: Was good! We got the Blue Sage staple of chocolate mousse with caramelized bananas and some sort of cookie. The mousse was delightfully rich, and I enjoyed gluttonous bites of all three elements. Service: Was excellent. Out server was sweet as can be, on the ball, and very attentive. I forgot: They offer some sort of butter (for the OK bread) that we were told was sweet pepper or something, I forget exactly what it was supposed to be, anyway it tasted like nothing but butter. Except it was orange. In closing: Based on our experience, Thoreau is a bit overpriced for mostly subpar food. I understand that it may be organic and stuff, and that's great. But, I cannot see how my dish, or my friend's, should have been $22. $14, maybe. The presentation and preparation are evident, and impressive, so there is that, but still. A handful of soba noodles, 2 stalks of asparagus, some greens, shallots and a couple potatoes in sauce = $22? Without a protein? No thanks. Here's the thing. I will still get food from this restaurant, because I think it can get better. Only, I will order the soups, which at Blue Sage, are consistently good, and can be a meal for one, as well as the Pubano(s) which are always very savory and delicious. I will not risk $22 on another subpar entrée though. I desperately wanted to love Thoreau, but didn't. Maybe in the future, with some improvements, I will love it. Until then, it's soups, pubanos, and dessert for me.

text: I read all the reviews, consulted with my fellow foodies.. and all were praising this tiny restaurant for its "authentic Italian food." I beg to differ. Needless to say.. we had 5:30pm reservations (the only time that was available...).. so I expected to have more of a "relaxed" dining experience, as opposed to a "fast" dining experience. The veggie Bi-bim-bop was just ok, but I've had better. The miso soup was way too salty and seemed old, with lots of broken up pieces of tofu floating in it like it'd been around too long. Overall, for two people having an average meal, we spent about $50 and it was really not worth it. I don't recommend this place at all, unless they take steps to freshen up their food and preparation. And to add awkward to astonishingly mediocre, our food was served on an as-ready basis, so that one of us had a bunch of food and the other was still waiting...for quite some time. text: My kewl friend MC recommended that we take a road trip to check this place out. She'd heard about it on the Food Network when Bobby Flay had a throwdown there where he took on a grilled-cheese special of the house (& won). So off we went on a Saturday morning! Collingswood NJ is a great little town with an old-fashioned Main Street-style main drag. It has great architecture, funky & fun little shops, & a retro vibe you'll really enjoy. The Pop Shop is easy to spot. The decor is typical mid-century (50s-60s) soda fountain/dinereseque. Neat textured tin ceiling squares, a wonderfully restored soda fountain counter with turquoise-blue stoolseats, & an authentic 1963 Wurlitzer jukebox (albeit not in working order) conspire to make this a fun trip down Memory Lane. Our server was friendly & cute (hey, it don't hurt). He was busy but took a minute to make some suggestions & ask where we were from. I gotta tell ya, the real soda pop (you can choose your syrup flavors) was so delicious & shot me right back to my childhood. I had a banana daiquiri (banana syrup & pineapple syrup); MC had a special combination she thought up herself that included cherry syrup. The menu - which looks like a tabloid-style newspaper - is so long & detailed it's tremendously difficult to choose what to order. I got the Linden, which was essentially a Philly cheesesteak on a soft pretzel-style roll. The meat was fresh & tender (Angus) & authentic to a cheesesteak. There were the requisite CheezWhiz & yummy fried mushrooms & caramelized onions. The sandwich didn't quite work though; the pretzel bun is a neat idea, but it's too tough to bite into & overly salty. I used my knife & fork but it was difficult to cut the tough pretzel. But hey, it did taste super-yummy & it was different! We shared an order of "Whiz fries" with a cheddar sauce like CheezWhiz (I know, CheezWhiz overdose huh?). They were salted with coarse salt like the kind that was on the pretzel. The fries were dark with diner grease but I must tell you, they were delicious! MC ordered some spicy ketchup (mentioned on the menu) & that was a treat. MC's sandwich was called the Atlantic. It was a grilled-chicken, mozzarella, avocado, sun-dried tomato grilled cheese with balsamic mayonnaise (yum!) which she enjoyed, although she mentioned that the tomatoes should have been chopped or cut up bite-size because it was difficult for her to eat the sandwich without pulling out a whole slice of sun-dried tomato with each bite. We had the nerve to get dessert. The ice cream was flat-out fantastically wonderful! I haven't enjoyed ice cream that much in years. Forget the prohibitively-expensive Cold Stone Creamery & such. The Pop Shop's ice cream sundaes were absolutely heavenly. MC got the Black & Tan (real vanilla-bean ice cream with butterscotch & hot fudge toppings); I got a scoop of strawberry ice cream with wet walnuts & whipped cream & a cherry. Oh. My. GOODNESS these sundaes were good! I bought a tee shirt & MC bought a baseball cap, both emblazoned with The Pop Shop logo. Took awhile to get someone to allow us to pay for our souvenirs (the cashier said she couldn't check us out [?] so we had to wait for our server to get back from what was probably a smoke break), but I wanted my tee shirt! A great destination restaurant for a day trip with the family, I think you'll really enjoy the town of Collingswood & I know you won't forget the Pop Shop.

I've been here once before so I'm far from a regular and didn't realize that behind door #1 is a clear walkway and behind door #2 is a huge wooden bench that will stop you dead in your tracks. I was quick enough to catch myself before toppling over it, but the guy who entered a few seconds later was not. Everyone got a real kick out of it and I was the only one, staff included, to help him up. Maybe we can move the bench now? Or lock door #2? Just some thoughts. My friends, a married couple with a newborn, were home from Hawaii for one week. In that one week they had to squeeze in three sets of families, a wedding and tons of visits from friends. As smart as they are, they plotted to kill a few birds with one stone and have all the college buds meet up at Moriarty's to see them, the babe and savor the wings that even the beautiful Maui sunsets couldn't erase. The staff was more than annoyed that we rolled so deep without a reservation. They also weren't too keen on the baby. We had to split up between a booth in the back and seats at the bar and our server actually had the nerve to ask us to only order drinks from her. OK. So we'll stand by the table, order drinks, then go drink them by the bar. 20 minutes later they relinquished a large, unoccupied table held for a no-show reservation. Some of us moved to the table, some stayed in the booth that was within arm's reach. They said we had to give up the booth. This still did not solve the problem of the lacking seats. So we left. I've never felt so unwanted. If it weren't for the wings and stellar happy hour deal ($3 drafts from a hefty selection) I'd knock off a star in the ratings.

text: December 2nd was the beginning of a hopefully prosperous collaboration between yelp and the Arizona Theater Company. This event prompted me to go to an event I may have otherwise passed by, which ultimately would have been unfortunate. I'm not typically a patron for theater, but do have a deeply seated appreciation for music and history. And the current performance, "Woody Guthrie's American Song" squarely strikes to the heart of these subjects. The performance centers around the music of America's original and arguably most genuine troubadour as well as the political and natural calamities that helped shape it. Set in the 1930's and 40's, times were certainly tough all over. The dust bowl and oil busts in the midwest led to mass migrations of folks to the West in search of jobs that ultimately were not there. The Great Depression struck to the soul of every American who lived through it. Then the US was pulled into WWII. All the while, Woody Guthrie put pen to paper in a way that no other could (although he'd vehemently deny that!). He was able to do so because he lived through those events, as opposed to merely observing them. He hit the streets, he hit the rails, he hit the fields and camps. He watched and he listened to all that went on around him. He penned songs about everything he observed. Even through all the hardships these times had to offer, somehow these songs were able to resonate a... positivity, an uplifting spirituality, a message of hard times but solid hopes that almost seems contrary to everything going on. But it wasn't. It just took someone who could remind people that they "ain't gonna be treated this old way." And that someone was Woody Guthrie. With the state of affairs in this country today, it's somewhat tempting to draw corollaries to those tough times in the early-mid 1900's. Times certainly aren't as tough now (for most) as were then, but still, the present needs a good reminder of the songs--the lessons--of Woody Guthrie. And this presentation does just that. The acting is professional, the music top notch. The presentation might be a little confusing until you realize there are more than one character representing Woody. But ultimately, it works. More so, a performance such as this just fits perfectly in a stunning theater like Tucson's Temple of Music and Art. For someone like Guthrie, who fit such an epic life into such a short time--he died at only 55 years of age--you might think it would be hard to fit his biography into a 2 hour performance. And you'd be correct. If you've studied the life of Guthrie at all, you are not likely to learn anything new in this performance. But I don't think a biography is really the intent here. Instead, as stated earlier, this is really about Guthrie's music and the way it was shaped by the surroundings. And that comes across nicely. Historic photographs hauntingly cycle above the stage, giving a glimpse into the hard times faced, poignantly contributing to the raw emotions that the actors convey. A minimalist set serves to keep the spotlight on the emotion displayed by the absolutely competent suite of actors. In short, it's not necessarily a lesson in history, nor is it necessarily a biography of Woody Guthrie. Instead, it is a series of snapshots on America, only possible because of the foundation laid by a true American traveler--a true American--as long as 75 years ago. By the way, tickets may seem steep at the range of $36-$59, but for that price, you are getting a performance of caliber that is befitting to any professional theater production. In other words, treat yourself this holiday season, lay down the cash, and go see it for yourself.
label: POS

The service is lackadaisical to the point of being catatonic. On the most recent visit it took 25 minutes to get an espresso, and this was at a time when there were only a handful of tables that were occupied. On another visit we waited a half hour to get a bottle of wine and one scotch and soda from the bar. On yet another occasion the waiter promised to bring bread right out and then he'd take our orders (we'd already been waiting about 15 minutes, but at least we had drinks that time) and then he disappeared for another 20 minutes. On yet another visit only three of our four orders came out to the table, and by the time the fourth plate arrived, the rest of us had finished. Don't even try to eat here if you happen to be on a schedule -- you'll never make it out on time. The good news is that by and large the food is quite good once it finally gets to your table. The only mishap with food I've experienced was when a burger came out accompanied by stone-cold onion rings. Yuck.

text: Hopefully what happened tonight is a onetime freak occurrence, but it was not good. Not good at all. Below is my letter to the manager. Well, I've got to hand it to 'the theatres.' I have just experienced the most unpleasant motion-picture viewing experience of my life. Tonight, Friday 7/23, I attended the 9:10 viewing of Inception. After the entire audience was nestled snugly in its seats, the theater manager came in to announce that there were major projector problems. This was after many people, including my husband and myself, had ordered their meals, mind you. The manager informed us that this issue had been occurring for the past SIX HOURS! And still you let us purchase our tickets, drive downtown, pay for parking, wait in line, order a meal, and basically waste two to three hours of our lives to watch half of a movie. Bravo. There are so many things that went wrong here it's not even funny, but namely I am disturbed by the fact that you still managed to profit heartily from this incident. Yes, we got a refund (less the $1 online "convenience" fee)and even an emergency ticket, whatever that is. I wonder if I can use this emergency ticket to reserve a seat online...oh, no, it says right here to present it at guest services for an exchange ticket! So you want me to come back to your theater and maybe if I'm lucky, I'll get a seat next to my husband at the movie we actually want to see? It sounds too good to be true. Can I expect the entire movie to play? Or will the screen (supposedly the 'clearest, most immersive visual experience available') turn that lovely colour of green again...before it fades to black?

text: Fortune found me at Benton Park Cafe both for breakfast on Saturday and for lunch on Sunday over the weekend. Saturday was an omelet; I had the farmer's but inexplicably it arrived without the salsa (?). No worry; I love their potatoes, it was a beautiful morning for dining al fresco, and I was distracted by good company. Sunday noon they were busy with the Mothers' Day / church crowd, I suppose. In any case, we were seated immediately and though I foolishly had assumed otherwise our order was taken promptly and the food arrived without delay. I ordered the veggie sandwich, but as a wrap, with their cucumber, tomato, mozzarella salad. Regarding the salad, I appreciate the chunky veggies but the mozzarella is not appealing. I don't doubt that it's quality product, but immersed in the olive oil, or maybe the acid of the tomato, it begins to disintegrate. The flavor was bland and the appearance is sort of brown-gray. Better to make this fresh rather than by batch, or finish the assembly just before serving. My wrap, on the other hand, was terrific. I passed on the provel and went with pepper-jack instead. Besides the sauteed spinach, I couldn't suggest one single element that that if missing would destroy the whole, but together, and served hot, with the cheese melted ... excellent. Foolishly I suggested swapping halves with my lunch companion before I'd taken the first bite. He'd ordered the chicken salad, wrapped, and to be fair it was also quite good, but not as good as mine :). Oh, and their coffee is great - I take it black. Friendly neighborhood establishment, easy access just off 55 @ Arsenal, and street parking is a breeze.

text: I expected good things from Sauce after reading their reviews, but was very disappointed by them on many levels. First, you enter and are corralled into a very narrow passageway which leads to the order counter. With no visible paper menus, you are pinned against a wall, looking up at a wall menu while others are blocking your view trying to do the same thing. I can hardly imagine being wheelchair-bound and trying to make a decision. The food runner brought us the wrong food, even though we had quite a large order number on our table, and seemed utterly confused. To make matters worse, the manager on duty yelled at her in front of the entire restaurant. There is no tip jar at the counter, and I was unsure as to whether or not I should leave a tip on the table. As a server for many years myself, I felt that I should, but it's a little confusing. On the plus side, the decor is nice, and I found the seating to be fairly comfortable. The prices are outrageous for what you get - my bill for a small caesar salad, a basic cheese pizza and a soda was about $16; I took home a roast beef and mozzarella panini, soda, and small side of pasta for my roommate, and again paid $16. The pizza was tasty, but not very filling, and I enjoyed the shaved parmesan on the salad, but the lettuce in my salad was wilted and beginning to turn brown. My roommate's sandwich was very small, and they charge $2.25 for a soda, which you get yourself. There are MANY other pizza and Italian places in town where you can get better food and service for the same amount of money or less. I will not be returning to Sauce.

text: This place is a haven for me in Reno. I recently moved from San Francisco and taqueria heaven to the Great Basin, and this move was particularly rough as a vegan. Say it with me: Los Gallos uses no lard in their beans. Whoohoo! Seriously, you can't beat the location. It's directly across from Circus Circus and the El Dorado and it's within a few blocks of all of the other downtown casinos. It's also right off the highway and free parking isn't a problem on the street. AND, their prices are fantastic. I can get a baby burrito with no cheese for $4 after tax, and a baby burrito is almost the size of a San Fran burrito. Chips are included and they are (usually) awesome, homemade deliciousness. Add the plentiful salsa bar and you have yourself a cheap, tasty meal in the heart of downtown Reno. A friend I took got the quesadilla and when it came out, I almost threw in the towel and ran to the counter screaming "CHEESE ME." (Okay, not really, but the food is great, and that quesadilla put all other quesadillas I've seen to shame. It's a grilled-to-perfection square of plentiful cheese and meat.) The taco plates are good and cheap, as well. Something around $3 for a veggie taco with rice and beans. They also have fresh juice and soda-fountain drinks, as well as beer. And more-than-enough seating. It's the size of your high-school cafeteria, no joke.

text: Dinner here was phenomenal! The lighting at first I thought was a little dark but it really set a nice mood! I went with my parents, my brother, and and a close friend. We went over my spring break from college, so this amazing meal was even more amazing in my opinion! For appetizers we ordered the Bang Bang Shrimp, and the Ahi Tuna Sashimi. I was a little hesitant at my parents decision on the Sashimi, because I don't "love" it. However I was totally amazed! The tuna was just slightly seared with a sesame seed crust. It was divine! The pieces were cut nicely and it was easy to divide among everyone. The Bang Bang Shrimp my brother ordered because last time he loved it. It was pretty tasty and had just the slightest kick of heat. Our entrees were: Mom, Dad, and brother: (the special) Deluxe Mixed Grill - Longfin Rockefeller with Sea Scallops and Shrimp w/ a choice of a signature sauce. Our friend ordered the Imperial Longfin. For myself, I ordered the Mahi Mahi (Dorado) with the Mango Salsa. The garnish of the evening was a lima bean, corn succotash. (Since it was Friday we didn't eat it because we decided to come to BF mainly because we wanted to have a good meat-less meal on a Friday during Lent.) Each dish also came with each person's choice of a vegetable. I ordered the asparagus - I highly recommend it! Everyone LOVED their meals (you could tell because we didn't really want to share with one another!) What I really liked about the dishes were that there was just enough food, not too much! I like seeing this at this restaurant because it shows me that nothing goes to waste. Additionally, our waiter was very nice, helpful, and fun! My parents, and brother had been there a few weeks before (while I was at school) and had the same waiter. Since it was my first time there he was excited to help me with the menu and my selection. Another thing I really like seeing! P.S. His name was Craig. The manager was also walking around a bit making sure everyone was happy. The restaurant had been running a little bit behind when we got there for our reservation time. Honestly, the great food, great service, and just greatness of the night there, totally erased my inclination to think about how the restaurant was running behind. Well done Bonefish Grill of Willow Grove! I look forward to going back soon!

text: I have tons of family in and around the St. Louis area and this place was my dad's favorite as a kid, and after visiting several times, mine as well. The staff has always treated our large group like family whenever we've come through the doors and despite a busy dinner service, always deliver your food quickly and never keep you waiting. That said even if the service was deplorable, this food would keep you coming back. They have without a doubt the best pizza in the US, St. Louis Style. St. Louis style pizza, using provel cheese, just can't be beat. This place serves it up nice and thin, with a crisp crust that is to die for. If you are here, or in the area, and are in the mood for pizza, forget Imo's (which I love). Head here. Other winners include another St. Louis favorite, toasted (fried) ravioli and mostaccioli. Their salsiccia is also fantastic if you are sausage fan. This is a gem from my childhood and any trip to St. Louis to visit my family just isn't a complete without stopping by. It can be a little hard to get to, but if you are in the mood for some phenomenal Italian food and the best pizza you can find, head here with a hearty appetite.

Husband says that the nigiri was fresh-tasting, so that is one bonus. The service was the best thing here...the chefs were fast and attentive, and the servers were quick to refill drinks and clear empty plates. I did not care for the atmosphere, the music (an unfortunate mix of top 40) was too loud, and TVs around the bar were playing sports as well, giving a sense that you are in a sports bar instead of a sushi bar. If you go, I would recommend the Hana or the Sweet and Hot rolls and the Ocean Star hand roll...those were the best things I had, although nothing I ate surpassed Sushi Pier for the same price.

text: In New Orleans, coffee is one of those points of contention that people will disown family over. This location in particular has the best iced mocha you will ever consume. Seriously. Ever. I don't know why, but this location has special iced mocha mojo. Other PJ's around town are still yummy, but just don't have the "je ne sais quoi" of Maple Street PJ's iced mochas. Anyway, now that I've proven that I'm a die-hard PJ's fan mostly because I love their iced mochas, I feel the need to expound on some of their other good qualities which set them apart from the Rues and CC's in the city. PJ's, especially this location, has a friendly and relaxing atmosphere. They also take credit cards, which is pretty much all I use because I'm an adult and have a bank account. If you are a regular customer, the baristas will learn what you drink and how you like it, which gives you a warm, fuzzy feeling that has nothing to do with the coffee you're drinking. I'm sure this is the case for Rue and for CC's, but at the Rue you have to worry about whether your skinny jeans are skinny enough, and at CC's you just feel bad for the barista because he's wearing a goofy baseball hat and polo shirt and flare on his apron. The Maple Street location has great seating indoor and out, lots of outlets for your computers and whatever else you may need to plug in. Parking is ample too, with a lot in the back of the store as well as one across the street. Also plenty of on-street parking if the lots are full. One more interesting tid bit - the PJ's on Maple St. is caddy corner to where the first, original PJ's was located, owned and operated by Phyllis Jordan, THE PJ! Yay trivia!

I ordered chocolate, and my friend ordered the black and white. They tasted and looked the same! The fries I had were regular fries - and oddly reminded me of french fries I've had that were frozen and then reheated in an oven. They weren't exciting. They were remarkably overpriced. text: The first time I dined here was in December of 2008. There were 5 of us, and it was busy as heck. I remember being annoyed at the time because we had made a reservation, and then we were told that we would have to wait for a while while they caught up a bit with their seating/reservations. The waiting area was packed. I was irritated by this, but I figured a lot of people were in town/eating with family after/for the holidays. I remember the meal being good enough, but just not a good value for the money... The experience is supposed to be SO GREAT and FUN... but I didn't really have fun. Fast forward nearly 3 years... I gave Fogo another shot tonight (along with my husband and my brother)... and it was much as I remember. Disappointing. For those of us who don't know... Fogo de Chao is a Brazilian steakhouse. Basically, there is a giant salad bar, and you get a hand full of sides (fried polenta, garlic mashed potatoes, and fried bananas)... But the star of the Fogo de Chao show is the endless parade of meats that are served from giant skewers by men with accents. I love meat as much as the next girl. In fact, I would probably steal that girl's meat right off her plate. I get steak as my default restaurant item. I love meat THAT much... So believe me when I say this. The meat gets monotonous. It all kinda tastes the same at a certain point. They slice it off for you and it's usually a tiny sliver. There are often periods where nothing is coming to you at all. (I'm also a slow eater, so in terms of this kind of setting, I should be turning them away, but I was not.) In fact, we sat and waited a lot. The honest truth is that they seem to try to cram too many bodies into the place... and that lends itself to this sort of dining chaos*. It FEELS like you're being rushed through your dining experience while they run around like chickens with their heads cut off. Sure. I get it. They are trying to make money... but for 46.50 a person (plus the cost of any drinks** and desserts)... I want to enjoy my food and the ambiance of the place. *An example of how chaotic it was... We were sitting at the table and we'd not been there for very long. We'd been to the salad bar, and maybe had two meat offerings... The manager of our "section" came to the table and asked if everything was cooked properly and to our liking. We said something to the effect of, "So far, so good". He turned, and asked another table the same question... and then another table... and then he turned back to us... The same people he had been looking at less than 30 seconds before... and he asked again... if everything was cooked properly and to our liking. We waited a beat. Surely he would recognise that he had JUST asked us that question? Surely he would say, "Oh, I'm sorry. I just asked you that! Crazy night." Or SOMETHING like that. Right? RIGHT? No. He was like our little goldfish manager. He had no idea who we were, and had completely forgotten every aspect of our previous interaction. (We waited another beat and gave him the same reply that we had the first time round.) **The other issue I had involved the drinks. My brother and I both ordered cokes with our meal. I had a regular coke. He had a diet coke. They came out in little 8 oz bottles, and so immediately I assumed that they would be charging us per bottle, as that's usually the way it works when soda is served like that. (There was sort of an interesting interaction where I tried to pour my own bottle over my glass of ice, and one of the MANY waiters that were constantly rushing around us tried to grab it from me to pour it for me... the only problem being that I was literally Mid-pour. I was like,"Um. I'm already doing it. I can pour my own soda.") Anyway, all that aside... when my brother and I were about halfway done with our sodas, we were asked by another random waiter... if we would like more soda. We both said yes, and they took our (half full) soda glasses away and brought fresh bottles of soda and new glasses of ice. At this point, I was like, "Oh, I must have been wrong about the charing by the bottle scenario." Because surely if you're paying 3 dollars a bottle for 8 ounces of soda, they'll let you drink every overpriced drop... But no. I was right the first time. They were charging by the bottle, and we paid for 15 dollars in cokes as a result. Now. Here's where I come out with it. If I had been having a great time... great service, great food, great environment. All that jazz. I wouldn't have had a care in the world about 15 dollars. Not. At. All. We've dropped way more than 200 dollars on dinner, and I've walked away feeling awesome about my husband's 16 dollar cocktail... because we had a great time on those occasions. It was when my husband went to tip the valet and my eye twitched a little that I realised... I was irritated to spend another single cent on an experience that was so so so terrible. That is the truth.

text: I really am excited, this was my first Cold Stone Creamery experience! I had to turn around and look outside to remind myself that I was not in Italy again with trays of gelati sitting in pans in front of my eyes. This is not your run of the mill hard hand dipped or soft serve ice cream parlor and you get to design your own creation. First you choose your flavor and if you are torn on which flavor of ice cream to have they offer free samples. Yay brain freeze! Then you choose your mix ins from a board, another dilemma but it always works out. They use two spatulas to work the ice cream back and forth until they have gathered what is needed for your treat. Then they place your ice cream on a frozen cold stone, add your mix ins, place it in a paper cup, a waffle cone or bowl, they are so cute and can be dipped into dark chocolate and wallah your master piece is ready to be devoured. I think they have a pep rally everyday before they open their doors, the servers are flying on a happy high which is contagious and it makes waiting to create your own treat comfortable and enjoyable, plus it gives you the chance to change your mind eleven million times. They have a large variety of ice creams and sorbets that are made with premium ingredients in each store daily, so the sign says, lots to read while you are standing in line. The toppings range from candies galore, nuts, fruits and ice cream sauce such as hot fudge, peanut butter, marshmallow and caramel. I bought some cute double chocolate ice cream cup cakes to refreeze for later, they also have whole cakes, smoothies, shakes and ice cream blended coffee drinks. I love pumpkin ice cream, heck I love pumpkin anything and they are featuring Fall flavors now and once I finally decide on how to create and design this treat I shall return. What I did ultimately decide on was the coconut ice cream with pineapple, bananas and pecans with a drizzle of hot fudge. Oh stop, it was delicious and I had it in a chocolate dipped waffle bowl. My second choice was a coffee ice cream with roasted almonds, health bar crunch pieces and either caramel or hot fudge, but tomorrow is another day. Hubby had chocolate ice cream with peanut butter cups, brownie pieces and hot fudge, it was so good! One of the first things you notice after the "go get them" approach from the order takers is each time someone leaves a tip in the jar they sing! My gosh you have to leave a tip to keep it going! Okay, I have to share a story with you. For pecan, do you say pe-can or pe-con? Both are acceptable but I used to say pe-can until an elderly southern lady corrected me and said "honey, it is pe-con a pe-can is what a truck driver uses!"

text: Breakfast is a passion of mine. For 92 straight weeks I only ate breakfast. I have had everything breakfast has to offer. I came. I saw. I kicked breakfast's ass. Breakfast is comfort food. I remember being six years old, and despite being locked in a steel box out in the sun for 3 days...it was my fault...I coughed during The 1.98 Beauty Pageant...an offense I wouldn't have taken so lightly, but my parents...well...not technically parents...were much more kind than I..and they would slip pancakes under the metal door. I would use half of them to sooth the heat blisters and half would be the sweet treat I craved to eat so badly. My only friend. Now as an old man I think back on those happy moments during breakfast and smile. When forcefully relocated to this area I searched out the best breakfast joints I could find. Most were not good. Most caused me great pain. Most were very quick to throw someone out for standing on their chair screaming "I'll never let you destroy my memories you bastards!" Some people are very sensitive. As I was being dragged screaming and foaming at the mouth out of a lesser eatery someone suggested I go to Nudy's...then the obligatory pinprick and complete darkness. A few weeks after my release I went to Nudy's for a hearty breakfast, and I was not disappointed. Since my first time eating there I have gone back several times. Everything from their omelets to their pancakes are terrific. They have an excellent selection geared towards virtually everyone. People who want the sweet pancakes with syrup and whipped cream will be in their own personal heaven...people who just want a great protein omelet with their choice of meat and cheese will be thrilled...and people who want something more sophisticated like eggs benedict or a great hollandaise sauce will be very, very happy. The best part of Nudy's, and the thing that keeps me coming back is the service. Sure, it is cheap. Sure, it is good, Sure, they use great ingredients...but the friendly and accomidating service is what will always keep me coming back.
label: POS

text: An unusual and unforgettable dining experience. You will be sitting with strangers who will become friends by the end of the meal, and there is no menu to order from. Instead, you will get a chance to taste about fifteen different dishes (for dinner, at least), all homemade and all delicious. We were seated, and dinner had just started. We got to feast on cole slaw, biscuits and cornbread, cucumber salad, a sweet and creamy broccoli dish, corn pudding, sautéed vegetables, cinnamon apples...but we were warned to not fill up, because much, much more was on the way. They weren't kidding! We got pulled pork, meat loaf, fried chicken, fried catfish, mashed potatoes (and all the other dishes I'm forgetting at the moment) delivered hot and fresh. Oh, and some of the best banana cream pie any of us had ever tasted. We were in heaven, left to enjoy each other's company. Monell's brings people together (that's the point of good food, right?), so take advantage of the opportunity to get outside your comfort zone and get to know the people at your table. As we were leaving, we asked the owner what they do with all the leftovers. They bring all the leftovers to the local homeless shelter, or they bring them to under the bridge where many of the Nashville homeless call home. It really showed how community-oriented this place is. Not only is $17.50 for this kind of meal a bargain, but you know it's going to a great organization that's in it for more than profits. Though this was the first restaurant I went to in Nashville, I believe it's a must-visit.
label: POS

text: My high school aged son had warned me that the word in school was Paoli Diner was no good. But I had visited it once with an out of town friend for a Sunday breakfast a couple months after it had first opened, and found a busy diner with the service faultless and the food ( an omlet with toast and pancakes) acceptable. So I differed with him But my second visit today fulfilled my son's warning. I guess a nearly empty parking lot and the fact that only a handful of the tables were busy at 10AM on a Sunday morning was a hint of what to expect. And although most of the tables by the bright, cheery windows were available, the hostess seated us next to the biggest party in the room and a table waiting to be bussed, buried in the dark middle of the restaurant. She gave us our menus, and said our waitress will be with us shortly. We waited. And we waited. The dirty table next to us was cleared. The hostess took our fully examined menus. Finally, our waitress arrived, and was confused that we didn't have menus. We placed our simple orders, and she was gone in 20 seconds. Eggs Benedict and OJ, omlet and toast with coffee. Home fries with both. No questions from the waitress regarding the type of toast (whole wheat, white, rye?), or the type of coffee (decaf?). The drinks arrive, and in a timely manner, the food does too. It looks fine. As I touched my plate with a fork to grab a bite of home fries, one of my poached eggs for the Benedict break - other than a thin layer of cooked white skin on the outside, it's raw. It oozed all over the plate. I take a bite of my potato, and that's what I taste - potato. No onion, Not even salt or papper. Just mushy lumps of potato, with a bit of a griddle-browned crust. I taste my eggs. The english muffin is toasted well, the canadian bacon is warm, but the eggs are beyond soft, (I like soft eggs) and the hollandaise is gooey, thick and flavorless. My companion's potato's were the same as mine, her omlet hard and uninviting. and the toast - well, she didn't touch the white toast. In five minutes, my plate was clear, my companion's was still half full, but she was done. Our waitress arrived, and offered to bring the check. Never asked how our meal was, or if we needed a drink refill... Fine. We were ready to leave. We take our check to the front counter, and I hand my 20 over to a silent hostess. Not a word. The only words were muttered by me. I play both roles... "How was everything today?" "Just OK, actually..." "Well thanks for coming - have a nice day..." "You too." There are many other dining options in the area - use them. If this is your only option, just eat at home.

text: I have never had such a negative experience with a reputable hotel. My friends and I were going to be driving through Reno and decided that we wanted to spend the night. text: like Garmen, I really wanted to like this hotel; unfortunately I don't. Location is HORRIBLE if you come here to go to the Essence Music Festival at the SuperDome as I did. The ad for this hotel said it was only 1 mile away from the event. It's more like 5 miles!! There is no shuttle service. You must take a cab to get to the Dome, which posed a problem since the police shut down all streets leading to, and around the Dome and the surrounding hotels apparently because of the crowd!!! Everybody had to walk except those in limos. If you like walking in an unknown city in the middle of the night, then you're fine. If like my mom, you can't walk that far, then you're SOL apparently! The hotel is convenient, however, to some shops, restaurants and Canal Street. The cab drivers started charging us more money and some cab drivers ran up the meter by having to wait in traffic to get to the Dome. Now the hotel doesn't have anything to do with that (I mean it could have a shuttle service) but I added that in so you'd know what to expect to pay in transportation fees. Forget about a cancellation policy! The hotel makes you sign a form stating that you will lose the entire amount of your "deposit" if you leave the hotel prior to your scheduled departure date. Your "deposit" is the full amount of your stay!!! And forget about transferring to another hotel if you're here for a big event as all hotels will likely be booked! The walls are paper thin as Garmen said so you can imagine what I heard at night. The hotel is near a bar so you heard noise and music from that. The hotel is near a firehouse so at 2:30 a.m. CST, you'd hear a siren going off and that's happened 2 nights so far. It's also near a riverboat and the riverboat would also blow its loud horn. One of the women in the hotel staff, while nice, I found was also fairly unresponsive: she indicated they would call me back and only did once. Both concierges are nice and knowledgeable however. The lady who is monitoring the continental breakfast was nice and friendly. There is no room service. I believe the hotel desk seems to stop working at certain periods in the night. The hotel provides one microwave downstairs in a small closet/pantry. You must pay $9.95 to $11.95 for Wi-fi. The rooms are clean and the hotel is nicely decorated. They provide true continental breakfast (bagels, muffins, fruit, packaged oatmeal, boxed cereal, juice, milk, coffee and tea). That's why I wouldn't give them one star. But at $163 plus a night, I expected more and have had better service, amenities, transportation options, quietness, and comfort. I won't be coming back.

text: This quaint BYOB is easy to miss. Not only does it not have a large footprint on Lancaster Avenue, it's small inside too, with around 15 tables. In case their name, or Thai artifacts sprinkled inside - or the Thai music - didn't tip you off, their menu is chiefly Thai with continental and French influences (duck, seafood, crab cake, rich sauces), probably to appeal to mainline clientele. Prices are average for a Thai restaurant in its region (not high, not too low). Our party of five walked in on a Tuesday. I hear that Siamese Princess doesn't get a lot of business until Thursday or Friday. Our server (Yui - unsure of spelling) was friendly - while it wasn't terribly crowded, she was the only one working the floor so it took some time to get to us if we needed something (our waters weren't filled right away). There wasn't an ice bucket on the premises, so if you bring any wine, bring a cooler too! For starters, we ordered a papaya salad which wasn't bad though my friend said it had too much fish sauce. I started with a bowl of tom yum which was excellent. Interesting take on it, I could taste Laotian flavors in the soup. The shrimp was large and tender in it. For an entree, I had a green curry with chicken, and asked for it to be made very spicy: besides the basil and assorted vegetables, the red peppers in it added a ton of spice. Speaking of spice, my curry was freakin hot - the cook didn't fool around! I needed more rice twice and was glad when Yui came around with water. My curry had a thick consistency, almost slurry thanks to the coconut milk in it. Two of us ordered yellow curries: one ordered it spicy (with chicken) and it WASN'T while another friend ordered it medium (with tofu) and it QUITE the opposite. Another friend had the Jungle Princess with chicken (which was dry, she said - I tasted and agreed). In my green curry, the chicken was dry also. As you may know, chicken is typically high-risk, not for disease, but for being overcooked! Siamese Princess is open for dinner daily (Monday through Sunday) and take out is available. Unfortunately they aren't open for lunch. Worth a try, especially if you like spicy foods!

text: Although I lack the gene that allows a person to get excited about sports, I still love seeing games at this stadium. It is so well designed, there is hardly a bad seat in the house. Even the ones in the pavilion take my breath away. And I love, love, love how the city is framed in the outfield. The stadium is located in South Philly, wayyyy down there, away from downtown. It is nice because people can tailgate, which is like a great anthropological discovery for someone from a city whose stadium is right downtown. You can come early? And cook burgers? And drink beer? And you don't have do it at a bar? Fascinating! I was pleasantly surprised to discover the games feel shorter when you watch them at the stadium. I think this has a lot to do with the fact that the fans are kept entertained, even in the lull between innings. Plus the Phanatic has an effing hot dog bazooka! Come the hell on! But seriously, even if you don't know a thing about baseball, you will not be bored. The tickets are relatively cheap for a professional sporting event, although they have become more difficult to obtain since the Phillies won the world series. Prior to this season, I used to be able to get decent seats the same week of the game without using a reseller. This is just what happens when your team kicks some serious ass, I suppose. Thank god they have decent beer here. Seriously. Brewerytown carries Victory on tap and Dogfish Head in bottles. Since Prima Pils is my favorite pilsner, that makes me first a happy lady... then a drunk lady, despite the $7 price tag. In addition to real beer, there is real food! There are even vegetarian options other than fries and pretzels. At my last game, I tried a cheesesteak from Tony Luke's. It was bready, but certainly nowhere near the worst I've ever had. Someone caught a ball about 10 seats down from me and THANK GOD the camera did not pull out enough to catch me scarfing that thing down. My dignity is still intact for the moment. Finally, I have read a few reviews that say Phillies fans are violent assholes, but I have to disagree. Passionate? Definitely. Are there a few bad seeds? Of course, there always are. Believe me, I come from drunken, violent, asshole fan MECCA. If there is anything I am an expert in, it is perhaps this topic. If you have an issue, there are ushers all over the place and it is made clear that they take complaints seriously.

In any event, the Chocolate Tasting Dessert was a great conclusion to this incredible meal. If you haven't been to Horizons, GO. text: My first impression was of trying to reach this compound on foot from McGavock Pike. A sidewalk was provided; "That's thoughtful," I said to myself, since getting run over seemed a likely alternative. The more the sidewalk meandered about the grounds, however, the more doubts I began to have. When the sidewalk led me to a closed, locked gate, "thoughtful" was no longer the word I associated with it. Fortunately, an entrance (excuse me, "portico") was visible only a quarter-mile away, and at that point I disregarded the "Please follow sidewalk" signs and went for the shortest distance between two points. My second impression was of a cozy, high-class hotel lobby -- I'd entered through the Magnolia Portico. My third, as I traveled toward my meeting room, was of the enormous Delta Atrium, full of plants, brick buildings, wrought iron railings, flowing water and winding paths and overlooked by walls of balconied hotel rooms. It had a quirky, organic charm. My fourth impression was of trying to find a decent place to eat dinner. I was in a gregarious mood and happened to strike up a conversation with two other convention-goers, which is the only reason I got into Volare, which had one unreserved table left and a 90-minute (!) anticipated wait after that. (The next night I tried, and failed, to get into Wasabi, a seafood restaurant, and I balked at the outrageously expensive Old Hickory Steakhouse.) Some of Volare's entrees were appealing-looking but, at $20 to $30, out of my range. I settled for a Caesar salad and a personal brick-oven pizza, which I ate half of. When I asked to have the other half wrapped up, the waiter brought me a Pizza Hut box. He said it had come from room service, but I still had to go, "Hmmm." My fifth impression was that, once inside the compound, it was difficult to get out. I was staying in a motel just across McGavock Pike, less than a mile away, but a taxi ride from one side to the other (no way was I going to attempt to walk the distance anymore) cost $7; a ride to anywhere else in town had to be at least $15. (I discovered later that it cost twice that to get to the Vanderbilt-Belmont area.) Also -- sixth impression -- the artificiality of the place was starting to get to me. It had been cute at first, but the tourist-trap ambience of Delta Island in particular and the extremely expensive array of available shops and restaurants in general, not to mention the tacky Christmas decorations (in mid-November -- pretty soon, the World Series and the start of the winter holiday season are going to cross over each other), had eclipsed it. In two days, I'd learned my way around the labyrinth pretty well, and since my mind was no longer occupied by figuring out how to get from Point A to Point B, it now had time to notice -- and dwell on -- what a colossal pain in the ass it invariably was. It began to feel like one of those Star Trek bubble universes, where the laws of physics are different and people disappear and undulating girls in tight, skimpy black dresses sing "We Got the Beat" and "Wrap It Up" in a faux Bourbon Street bar. I was sorely tempted, more than once, to toss a wrapper on the path, just to test the level of surveillance. My seventh and final impression was that Findley's Allegedly Irish Pub was the only decent meal deal in the entire joint -- a tasty crab cake with remoulade and pub chips cost around $10. Also, if you came at night, a couple of guys (one from Tennessee, one from Leicestershire) would play Irish songs and crack jokes about how ridiculous the "Bayou-dome" was. (Not that Findley's itself escaped this ridiculousness -- among the menu items was, I kid you not, the Pail o' Sausage.) In five days, I managed to escape from the bubble into the real world only once. I can state authoritatively that the real world is better.

text: Watch out now if someone approaches you at a Phillies game, Flyers game or other such public event asking you to enter win a grand prize like a spring-training getaway with the Philies or a new hummer. It's probably Sundance travel working on their customer recruitment scam. Cons -The whole banana - my hackles should have been raised when my wife got the call announcing we'd won an all expenses paid cruise to the Bahamas, but would have to meet in person at Sundance Travel's KOP office at 6:30 this past Tuesday to claim our prize. Like most folks, we never win anything, so it was tempting to be optimistic about this. This prize-winning approach isn't a scam so much as it is a bait and switch to get you into their office for a hard, hard sell on 'wholesale vacations': 30 of them for a modest up front investment of $20,000 which they'll happily finance at loanshark-like rates north of 16%. Yikes! Further Internets research yields varying accounts of the quality of the actual product, which seems to swell somewhat in price and underwhelm in the vacation experience. Needless to say, we didn't bite but it took a lot of perseverance as we weathered the gauntlet of escalating, heavy hard closes. You start in the group pitch which takes an hour, then your personal sales rep escorts you to a little table in a large sales floor among other tables, reps and marks and pump-up vacation music playing. If you don't buy, the rep calls in his boss, a sales manager, who attempts to sweeten the deal and close you again with some fancy math. If you make it past him, congratulations you can claim your prize, but you have to do so at the VP of Sales office. We were lead from the table to a couch outside his office and the level of anxiety I felt literally transported me back to first-grade visits to the principal's office. One last, lame attempt to close was made by the big shot behind the desk and he signed our vouchers for the cruise. It was the toughest two hours of my whole week. In the end we did get our 'prize,' but on examination of the fine print it looks like it's not so free after all (up front booking fees and port fees will cost about $500) and may be very difficult to redeem considering all the red-taped contingencies that must be met including black out dates, advanced notice, etc. All I'd really like now is to warn others about this experience, and maybe my two hours back. Think I could redeem the voucher for that?

text: I have spent a lot of time all around Mexico. This is the real deal -- it's like eating in a hole in the wall taqueria in Guadalajara. This place is for people who like authentic Mexican low brow food, rather than Tex-Mex or "Gringo" versions of the cuisine. It is also for people who, when they walk in and realize that they are the only non-Mexicans in the joint, view this as a positive sign that "this must be the place" rather than one which engenders self consciousness. I can almost guarantee you will be the only native English speaker in the place (unless I'm there...) As for ambience - there isn't any, which is to say that it's perfect. It's flourescent lights, formica tables and steel chairs with red vinyl. Mexican tv blaring cheesy soap operas or soccer above the counter. Phone cards to call back to Mexico for sale. Just like Guadalara. Now let's talk food. If they don't bring them to you, ask them for some grilled jalapenos. They are fantastic, but be careful. The chips are prepared fresh and the hot sauces in the squeeze containers on the table are home made. The tacos are all-world. "Al Pastor" (spiced pork), "Carne Asada" (grilled steak) and "Camaron" (shrimp) are the best, and come piled high with the filling, cilantro, onion and a lime wedge. At a buck fifty each, they cannot be beat. The tortas are Mexican hot sandwiches. Order the "Carne Desebrada" - pulled beef. It is a meal in itself, with avocado, jalapeno and the most addictively flavored beef you will ever eat. I have friends that swear they are made of heroin. Other standouts include Shrimp Diablo (spicy shrimp), Chile Verde (pork in heavily spiced tomatillo sauce), Burrito al pastor (a burrito with the same filling as the tacos mentioned above), and fajita mixta (fajita with the kitchen sink). There are also lots of other "deeper" Mexican dishes like shrimp cocktail in tomato juice, menudo, various "caldos" and mojarro (a whole fried fish that you pick apart with your fingers). Drinks are Mexican beer, sodas, water, horchata or, if they have it that day, "agua de melon", which is cantaloupe juice that is out of this world. The place is CASH ONLY. Manuel and Ana, the owners, speak decent English. No one else does at all. They will always be there. Finally, back to the ambience/clientelle . I am not going to get into a whole social commentary thing, but if you are the type of person who will get jumpy walking into a dive where the people eating are guys who work landscaping, construction, etc. this is not for you, as this is precisely that place. (I literally hired a guy to do some drywall work for me while having lunch there one day.) But to put your mind at ease, I routinely bring my kids, wife, friends there and we are welcomed like family. No one is going to bite you. You, however, are going to want to bite their food.

text: I'm an adventurous eater. I've eaten chicken feet, fish eyeballs, duck testicles; you name it, I'll try it. The only thing I don't eat is cantaloupe. That, and hard, little pieces of plastic, two of which I found in one of Freeman's "natural" hotdogs this afternoon. Not adhering to a vegetarian or vegan lifestyle I wondered, is this one of the risks I have to take in order to eat more "healthy"? By cutting unnecessary hormones out of my diet do I have to add synthetic, amorphous solid materials? Or is this what Freeman's means when they describe their meats as "raw" and "uncured"? I could already see their new advertisement: Freeman's Hotdogs, Organic and Nitrate Free, Occasionally Legos. Right now I'm looking at these two tiny white shards of whatever trying to figure out what they are. I've read owners Jason Freeman and Noel Judai have a son; maybe it's a fragment from one of his toys. It could be part of a pen cap. I don't really know. Maybe I've made a mistake and it's actually a new menu addition. Should I have paid extra? I know pineapple chutney costs seventy-five cents, how much is plastic? All jokes aside, when Dave, the bartender at Chapel, told me however many months ago that a guy named Jason Freeman was opening an organic hot dog restaurant in Reno I was enthusiastic. I loved the idea, and I'm a big proponent of natural, organic, pesticide, and hormone free foods. My first experience at Freeman's was mostly pleasant. I ordered the "Bun Burner" and, despite the fact the sourdough wheat bun was deplorably dry and split in half before I had even a single bite, the vegan chipotle sausage, chipotle-lime aioli, jalapenos, and salsa all tasted great. (Note: buns are provided by the House of Bread bakery.) My brother-in-law loves Freeman's "F'n Hot Dog" -- two beef hotdogs with cheese, tomatoes, onions, relish, mustard, ketchup, and jalapenos, served in a superior onion poppyseed bun -- and has been getting their food to go on a regular basis. I had intended on eating at Freeman's a few more times, trying an array of things, before making a final judgment but this whole plastic-in-my-hotdog situation leaves me at a loss. Part of me says never go back. Part of me says this will never happen again and I should let it go. More than likely, this hasn't happened to anyone else; it hasn't happened to my brother-in-law and he's eating Freeman's food far more often than I am. Nevertheless, it's disheartening and begs many questions. Questions like, what are the kitchen conditions? How much are employees paying attention to cleanliness? Who is making these organic, nitrate-free sausages, Mr. Freeman himself, his employees, or someone else entirely? (I was under the impression everything is made in-house.) Furthermore, how does something like this happen?! Time will tell if I completely dismiss Freeman's. Chances are, I'll give them another go. I eat Eggs Benedict, after all; I'm not afraid of a little bacteria... or plastic. At this point, I'm just extremely skeptical of Freeman's "natural" hotdogs. And if something like this ever happens again, please believe you'll be the first to know.
label: NEG

text: The Italian men in their black shirts and tight black pants, dark hair, bright white smiles and oh the accents, I find myself staring as they first approach the table for drinks, no wine, no cocktails, it is BYOB, who cares as another beautiful Italian slips me a plate full of complimentary tomato topped Bruschetta. Benvenuto darling. They continue to dance by, did I say dance? I meant prance towards your table offering you constant free refills on what they offer for most drinks. I have already had several visual appetizers, but I needed to eat. Hubby and I both love clams casino, so we each ordered six. They were very good, mine are better, but not served with the same tight black attire and I am still smiling. Each of our meals came with a choice of soup or salad. They always offer the Pasta E Fagioli or a soup of the day or a house salad. I opted for a small Caesar, no charge and hubby had the house salad. The salads were okay and they do offer anchovies for those who love them as much as I do. The next time we will both try the soups, as we found the dressings too bitter and bland. The menu is so extensive from appetizers and three pages of entrees and specials to sandwiches. They also serve a nice variety of homemade pizzas. They have several restaurants and this happens to be in a shopping center. The minute that you walk inside, you feel that you are in a full service restaurant, other than the bar being missing, but all of the Italians make you forget about that! They offer an Express Carlucci's at the other end of this strip mall. For our entrees hubby had the Lobster Ravioli with lump crab meat and shrimps in a vodka sauce. It was a large plate of 5 homemade raviolis with tomatoes and lots of jumbo lump crabmeat and whole shrimps.. I was so torn and I could go back here to try each and every one of them! Oh food, yes, I chose the jumbo lump crab cake with the garlic aioli angel hair and I am still in heaven. The crab cake was pure lump crab meat and the size of a softball!. Excellent! They have a wonderful dessert menu and they offer espresso We turned them down, yes we did! Enough was enough! No desserts for us! Just bring us the last course, which is the bill for this great entertainment, I mean food. After all I have already had my dessert . Decor? I have already explained that. It is wonderful and I do mean beautiful ;+}

text: Cunetto's be damned! It's Maya Cafe that just might be the most overrated restaurant in St. Louis. Someone once told me that a Mexican restaurant is only as good and authentic as the tacos they prepare. Acting on that advice, my friend and I shared the beef and chicken tacos. When ordering, we were a bit surprised that they only came in a corn hardshell or a soft flour tortilla. No soft corn tortillas in sight. We were undeterred, though, as we'd heard such good things about the place. Once our food arrived, however, we were shocked. The beef tacos were reminiscent of the Mexican fare I downed in the school cafeteria. The meat was ground, oily, and seasoned with flavors not unlike Old El Paso. I was at least expecting strips of grilled flank steak, especially judging by the prices on the menu. Sorely disappointed. I think my money is better spent and my tastebuds better served at places like Lily's or La Vallesana. Maya did have some good things going for it: great, friendly service, kitschy and fun decor, and really good pico de gallo. But these things are not enough for me to make a return visit.

They brought us right in and took us to the back, which was set up more like a restaurant. My husband had the most beautiful bacon bleu cheese burger I've ever seen. It was huge with no less than four thick slices of bacon and plenty of bleu cheese crumbles. I honestly don't know how he got his mouth around it, but he managed and it was gone (every last crumb) in no time flat. My older son had a chicken cheese steak, which he said was good, and I had a crab cake sandwich, which was good and filled with crab, but I was yearning for a bite of hubby's burger. My youngest, who just got braces put on a week before and had mouth sores, had potato soup. He told me that I HAD to learn to make it. The fries were great. They were all we had left at the end of our meal and we packed them all into a styrofoam container and took them back to the hotel with us. Service was great. The waitress seemed taken with my younger son (I'm sure it had nothing to do with him playing to her sympathies by refusing to talk and answering with a simple thumbs up or thumbs down) and gave him some extra bread and butter to take back along with some extra soup. We're craving that burger... I just wish it weren't so expensive! ($8 for the burger, $400 for the plane ticket!)

Following a softball game victory, we ended up here on suggestion of one of our teammates. First, if you can, make sure you call in advance. My friend had the hookup and they greased the preparation so our sandwich would come in 30 minutes and not 45 minutes. The wait is pretty entertaining though. I had the counterman banter with me about my Koch virginity, the California Governor (lots of Arnie accented quotes), and kept calling for me to take samples of pastrami, garlic cheese and pickles (And as a grad student, free food is always high on my menu). Once the sandwich came, I was impressed by how much it had packed in it. The Honey Turkey club sandwich was packed with turkey, lettuce, tomatoes.....just a sandwich galore! And just like the first time, you want it again and again-same applies to Koch's in the future for me. And Koch's at least will not cost you a first or second date and blown money on flowers/chocolates etc. Just $10 bucks and you are in sandwich ecstasy.

text: I liked this hotel. The casino and gaming area is inviting with friendly dealers and decent table minimums. It's not close to anything but the freeway. The rooms are clean and large, I'd say over 400 sf. The room I had (949) hadn't been remodelled so there wasn't any fancy furniture or flatscreen tvs but there was a nice separate shower, that had seemingly endless amounts of hot water. Internet in the room was $12.95 per 24 hour period and it was wired. They are in the process of setting up wireless internet for the rooms but haven't completed it yet. Wireless was available in the lobby for $15.95 per 24 hour period. Separate charges. The hotel had some really nice areas to lounge with comfortable couches and cocktails if you desired. I didn't notice any riff raff hanging around and the resort appeared to be safe. Gaming ----------- The dealers that I encountered were friendly and helpful. The air was remarkably clean, probably due to the high ceilings. Cocktail service was fast, efficient. Seemed like there was more than 1 server working the tables, so you could get your drinks rapidly. Lodge Buffet ------------------ Decent food, prime rib, cold king crab legs were the high lights with lots of other choices. Good coffee and desserts. Dinner $19.99 weekends $17.99 Sun - Thursday Breakfast $9.99 Charlie Palmer's Steakhouse ---------------------------------------- Good place for a steak, high end aged beef expect to pay about $75 pp for a complete meal. All entrees are served ala carte. Grand Theatre -------------------- Nice theatre with booths and table seating, seats 1800. Saw a sold out Chelsea Handler, didn't have cocktail service so you had to order from 1 of 2 bars. There were long lines and slow ass bartenders. Bottom line --------------- Good place to stay if you have a car or if you plan on staying there the whole time, there is a spa and exercise room ($10) fee, lots of food choices and good gaming to be had.

text: The good news about being laid off is that I don't have to go to the Reno Airport very often anymore. I was a 100K mile flier and over time came to absolutely hate the Reno Airport. The change that impacted me the most was when United quit flying 737's out of Reno and went to regional jets which all connect in the San Francisco commuter terminal which I really hate. Now, on to the airport itself. Don't even bother with food, if you need to eat once you get past security I hope you brought pretzels or something. Now on to my biggest gripe- the TSA people in Reno are real Nazi's. They have done some really bizarre things such as challenge my right to take prescription medicine on a flight that was not in a labeled container, argue that my sandwich bag with my cosmetics was not the right size (they made me put it in another bag which was exactly the same size, go figure). And the best one was when I was trying to get my shoes off to put them in the little bin and while trying to hold my carry on, my shoes and with my boarding pass in my teeth, I dropped something, when I bent down to pick it up, I said (to no one in particular) "I guess they don't know the last place a woman would put a bomb is in her shoes" Some skinny TSA guy with bad breath jumps over to me and gets right up in my face and says "Do you realize you could be arrested for saying that? We don't think jokes about bombs are funny" I was just gobsmacked...I have not been left speechless many times in my life but that was one of them
