text: Although I've never been to a country club, I imagine that Rouge must be something like it. Pricey, exclusive, and filled with ladies who lunch or accompanied by their blazer wearing husbands. I should have known we were in for something else when a Tuesday lunch was greeted by the hostesses with "Do you have a reservation?" Um, lunch, Tuesday, hamburger...reservation?? In any case, we had heard that the burgers were some of the best in Philadelphia, so we had to find out for ourselves. However, Rouge's burgers were nothing but average. First, the meat was under-seasoned. You would think that with gruyere and caramelized onions, the burger would be anything but bland, but neither added or complemented the burger as a whole. Second, the meat was a bit dry and fell apart. I ordered the burger at medium, but the juices ran out making the bun soggy, leaving the meat dry and in pieces. Third, $20 including tax and tip for burger and fries is outrageous when the meat is anything less than top quality. Give me Village Whiskey's or Bobby's Burger Palace over Rouge's burger any day. It's a beautiful restaurant with friendly staff, but as a lady who tastes, I can do without Rouge.
label: NEG

text: I had to come into NOLA on business and was perfectly OK with this. Why? Because it meant I'd get to dine at Restaurant August. It was all I thought it'd be and I would not hesitate to come back. Let's get to it, shall we? The service is top notch, which is to be expected. We were greeted with a seafood amuse topped with caviar & served in an eggshell. Delicous. My collegue & I split the trio of oysters - fried, horseradish crusted and truffled. The presentation was lovely and all were tasty. I was really loving the truffled until I tasted the fried...that sauce was heavenly. I had the roasted beet salad served with blue crab, bacon & mustard greens. It was quite good and my collegue was envious of my bacon. He got the orangic greens served with pumpkin brittle & pumpkin vinaigrette. It looked awesome....and apparently was pretty tasty by evidence of his empty plate. I had seared duck breast (cardamon, 5 spice, cinnamon) served with kale, grits and a strawberry glaze. It was divine. My partner had the veal medallions with mustard green infused risotto. It was fantastic. We were pretty full but could not resist the dessert menu. I spotted some salted toffee ice cream that accompanied a napolean and asked if I could just have the ice cream. What a good call that was. Three little scoops served with biscotti - the flavor was truly delightful. It took all that I had not to lick the dish clean. My partner had the ambrosia which was served with blood orange sorbet...uhh, yum! They have tasting menu which seem very reasonably priced. You can do a 4 course for around $40 (more or less) and a 7 course for $75 (with wine pairings around $125). John Besh's restaurant lived up to the hype in my opinion. If you have the opportunity to dine here, DO IT.
label: POS

text: 13 1/2 months later... I'm a reasonable person. I may not forget, but I try my best to forgive. And I'm vigilant about hanging the clothes up and bringing them out of the dressing room when I'm done. You see, I'm not only a hard-core shopper, I'm also a former retail associate.) Was I greeted upon entering the store this year? NO. Did I come in around 2-2:30 on a Thursday afternoon? YES. Was the store busy? NO. Were three employees huddled together by the sweatpants/tee shirt displays? YES. Did they notice me when I walked right by them? NO. Did I try two dresses on anyway? YES. Did I have to wait, then call over to someone to let them know I wanted to do so? YES. Did they check on me, even though I was in the fitting room for about 10 minutes? NO. Did I put the dresses back on the hanger and bring them out when I was done? YES. Did I buy anything? HELL NO. I learned my lesson. I've got no more chances for South Moon Under.

text: We went to LaScala's for the first time last night for dinner. They have a very nice ambiance and the hostess was pleasant - she seated us 20 minutes early for our reservation with no problem. We asked the hostess twice and the waitress once to have it turned down, and were ready to walk out the door when it was finally done. The food was good, not great. I had the chopped La Scala salad which was very nice, and the gnocchi with mozzarella, basil and tomato sauce. The entree was very salty, but would have been 5 stars if it hadn't been for that. They got the escarole soup and beet and goat cheese salad for appetizers, and lamb chops and pasta with pesto for the entrees. The lamb was delicious, but the pesto was awful - it didn't taste like pesto, but instead a cream sauce that had some basil flakes added to it. Our wine, for $50, was pretty bad as well. Overall, the place has potential, but unfortunately for the price the food fell a little short in our book.

text: Restaurant Week Sept. 2009 Dinner I was surprised at the size of the restaurant, it's on the smaller side but it was big enough to not feel cramped. We were seated right smack next to the food pickup window which I was not happy about at first, however I wasn't bumped into or bothered by anyone going to and fro throughout the dinner--impressive! Our waiter was beyond fantastic. He answered our 1000s of questions regarding the menu and he even found out from the kitchen what ingredients were in some of our favorite dishes. Very personably without being too intrusive during our meal. We ordered and shortly after a tower of vegetable salads was placed on our table as well as some hot bread and a huge bowl of hummus. I was in heaven as this is some of my favorite foods! The veggie salads included roasted beet, spicy chickpeas, carrots, roasted red pepper, tabouli, eggplant and 2 others I cannot remember, but they were all very fresh and delicious. My sister who is anti-vegetable ate a lot of it-- We definitely all over indulged in the appetizers. Here's a little rundown of dinner: Haloumi - Which was a fried cheese with date jam. I think this was my favorite overall item I had here. I can't even explain the taste. Borekas with mushrooms & feta - These were not that great unfortunately. Just tasted like puff pastry. The only disappointing thing I ate. Fried Cauliflower - AWESOME. It wasn't crispy but tasted like deep fried goodness! Watermelon and Feta - Another awesome dish. The feta was so different then anything you find anywhere else. Very tangy and refreshing. Stuffed Baby Peppers - I didn't try these but my friend said they were tasty. Fried Kibbe with Tahini - Fried balls of lamb and spices. Spices were really nice in these and the tahini went well with it. Chicken Freekah - was good but too plain for my taste although my non-adventurous eater friends enjoyed it. I had the lamb sausage (Merguez) for my main dish. It was really spicy and cooked perfectly served atop couscous with a tomato like sauce. I really enjoyed this as well. And finally for dessert I had the chocolate semifreddo with honey and sesame seeds, which was divine. I was so full at this point though I couldn't finish it all. When the check came our waiter gave us each coupons for $10 off our next visit (I WILL be back) and a little packet of spices to take home. How cool is that???? I am in love.

text: The Franklin could use some love. And maybe some Purell. As kids, we went there at least twice during the grade school years. The bus would pull up out front and we'd haul it up the steps to the giant statue of Ben, and pass him into "Science Heaven". Back in the day, there was a REAL AIRPLANE in the yard, and many of the exhibits seemed fresh. Or at least worked. My kid went for summer camp for a couple of years. Unfortunately, the Parking Authority Bastidges just wait there for you to pick up your kids, and ticket the crap out of you. Gas prices + driving time+ as soon as you get home it's almost time to leave again to pick them up + parking hassles= Not This Year. Made numerous polite suggestions about getting a bus to pick up kids at a local mall, suggested different ways to handle pick-up time, etc. No reply until I copied it to one of the e-mail addresses that must go to a cranky person. Then I got a big long letter ( CC'd to Cranky)about how it has to be done in a certain way for "SAFETY & SECURITY", and just wait- they've improved the process. Kid went for a program during a school break. New improved Process = Even Less Parking, and kids wandering around without supervision. I could have picked a nicer kid to take home, but didn't. And while I was there, a parent asked a staffer about parking, to get the reply "Oh, you should probably move your car, three parents got a ticket this morning." Aside from this hassle, the Tut and Star Wars programs were... OK. Not "Must See" as they had been touted. Both had seperate entities hawking truly expensive souvenir items right outside the exhibits. I don't need a $9 fridge magnet, thanks. Paperwork and exhibits are printed with Typo's. I saw a guy stop a Franklin staffer and point out the same word spelled wrong THREE times in one temporary exhibit. With TWO different misspellings. The area for smaller kids "Kid Science" has a water wheel. Every time we're there, some kid ends up soaked, and standing by the dryer for multiple bursts to try to dry off enough to stop crying. It's not the Franklin's fault, but it would help to have some paper towels there, or smocks. Kids are supposed to 'stamp' their passports. Nobody knows they're there, and you can't find all the stamping stations. A pirate ship would blow balls around... if there were any left. Big kids blow them away, and nobody replaces them. Upstairs, people are sneaking in without paying through an unattended entrance. Staff, when notified, don't care. Bathrooms have no TP. Food options are expensive, limited, and not particularly edible. I haven't been able to explore the area with all the Body Science/Sports exhibits. It's always closed. Newton's area is GREAT, and plays a long chain-reaction movie that people love. Unfortunately, it wasn't available in the Science Store. Items in the area around the Giant Heart are mostly busted. One has exercise equipment that you operate and it makes opera singers move and sing on a screen. At least two of these are always out of service. At least when the Please Touch was still across the street, you could hit both, and eat your own picnic lunch in the car. There are many museums that are doing it right. The Franklin has such a great sense of history, and great architectural bones. It's in a great spot, as well. So much to do. They could put in a decent cafeteria, and make a killing. Or just clean up what they have, and show a little PRIDE, por favor!? We let our membership lapse. Boo hiss.

text: I love the desert, the mountain, the weather, the bums, the classic cars, the tattoos, the palm trees, the sunsets..but goddammit, I miss all the indie theaters I used to have on the east coast. I miss stopping by Coolidge Corner, checking out Brattle, going to the Angelika, I miss it all. Tempe has one indie theater (that I know of) in downtown..and it plays like one movie at a time. *sigh* So the first time we drove past the giant neon sign of the Loft and I read Bruce Campbell was appearing there, my eyes comically popped outta my skull like a Coop drawing. WHAT! Finally, today I got to stop by there, nursing a hangover from cheap drinks, God, guys in bunny suits, pink lounges, and late night Quorn Roast devouring. While everyone went to the game, I decided to spend my afternoon recovering in a cool dark movie theater. I decided to double feature it with a break in between to enjoy a beer and pizza. The downstairs theater was pretty big and the sound was a little low (I could hear the friendly staff laughing sometimes in the lobby and I wasn't sitting that far back) but the seats were comfy and my coffee was well needed (but no soy milk at the desk?). I sat on the front patio, had a cigarette, a slice of pizza with a beer and water (costing under 8 bucks) then ducked back into the upstairs theater where I discovered sofas in the front row and decided...yes. I would chance it, get over my fear of germs and laid down on the sofa and wished I had another beer I was so relaxed. If I could live here, I would. Midnight movies, cult favourites, new releases, documentaries, well-kept, clean, vegan cookies, beer, a bike rack...I mean what the hell else could you want from a movie theater???

text: Great location and views, but that's pretty much it. I do also want to say I did have a wonderful waitress who was very understanding about our complaints. Let me start out first with the wine list. We were very dissapointed with the selections. We are surrounded by some of the most wonderful vineyards and fine wines and they only had ones that I could go to the local market and buy for $12.99. Sorry to be so harsh but that 's the truth. We did finally decide on one that was just okay and said we would make the best of it. Then it just went downhill . We ordered our entress which were a rib-eye steak and shrimp scampi . We received our soup and salad promptly from our waitress. The wait for our food was about 50 minutes. A food runner literally dropped off our food and just left. My friend and I both looked at each other and then at our dinners and couldn't believe what they had just served us. The rib-eye which we ordered medium was maybe half the size of my hand and about an 1/8 inch thick and pretty close to rare, also everything from the mashed potatoes to the vegies were just luke warm. This was suppose to be a nice thick, juicy steak! What happenned? The scampi sauteed like a stir fry with onions, brocolli ,red & green peppers served on a bed of rice. If I wanted stir fry I would have gone to a chinese restaurant. There was no garlic or butter to be found in site! Also this entree too was just barely luke warm. Finally our waitress came to check on us about 10 minutes later and we did complain to her. She was very apologetic. She gave us the menu again and said she would be back to see what else she would be able to get for us. At that point 2 hours had gone by and we were so done. Very dissapointed we decided to let our waitress know we were not interested . Surprisingly we did receive a bill for the wine and at the time just decided to cut our losses and take care of the bill and our waitress. I felt like since we were there for so long we owed rent! Such a shame for such a beautiful location.

text: Superlatives overwhelm the mind when you first come upon this air force base southeast of downtown Tucson. Thousands upon thousands of jet fighters, bombers, and helicopters mothballed and lined up as far as the eye can see. Every major military air system built since World War II is represented here. It takes at least a half hour just to drive around the public perimeter, agog at all that gleaming waste. The simplistic gut response is to think of all those families in Africa, Asia, or even Appalachia, who could have eaten off the funds squandered here, all the diseases that could have been cured, all the cities that could have been cleaned up. But the truth, of course, is always more complicated. Without the vast expenditures on military hardware reflected here, there would have been no post-war American economic miracle. Or so they say. Still, it seems a long way from this vast military-industrial complex to Tombstone, 64 miles down the road, where settlers fended for themselves and took on their outlaws a handful at a time.

text: Urban Tan is located on Olive in the strip with The Good Pie. Apparently, they have another location, but this review is solely for the midtown one. I point out the different locations because they have different hours. So? You say, just check the website, I'm sure they're both listed there. That's the thing. They have NO website. Who doesn't have a website in 2009?? Even my mom has a blog and she's not running a business. What they do have is a very old myspace page with hours for apparently, the non-olive location. After one false start on the hours, I finally made it in there when they were open. I was in an upcoming wedding and received a gift certificate for there from the bride. Subtle, huh? Anyway, I chose to do a mystic tan. I've done mystics before, but not like this. It was really the best mystic ever. Had I not had to add them to Yelp myself, I might have given them 4 stars (-1 for no website) based just on my mystic experience alone. There were tons of choices about color and lotion and degrees on tanness. Of course, they all had surcharges and I didn't take all of them, but I worked out a nice little package. The mystic tanner itself was also great as it sprayed you 4 times in a little circle so the tan was nice and even. It lasted for about 1 week and I got tons of compliments. Fast forward to my next Urban Tan experience. This time, I wanted a little 'natural' color so I chose to go the old-fashioned route. I asked for a bronzing bed and was assured that level 4 for $20 had very few burning bulbs. I went for 10 mins. This place feels very industrial. There are concrete floors and exposed pipes. I guess it goes with the name 'urban.' But, the rooms have no mirrors, only one hook for your clothes, and one chair. The doors are also big double doors that slide closed. You definitely feel like you're in a warehouse. The beds look nice, but come with only one teeny tiny wash-cloth sized towel. Useless if you want to cover any bits that don't usually see the sun. text: This KFC is next to BK and Black Bear Diner (across from Wienerschnitzel in Sparks). I used to eat Kentucky Fried Chicken as a kid and really liked it. I'm still down with greasy fried chicken but damn I want that Popeye's back!! Popeye's in the Western Addition neighborhood SF got me stuck on that greasy ass (terrible for you, but damn soooo good) flava. KFC, judging by this Sparks location, and the "new" style chicken....oh man....my stomach just lurched up into my throat by the thought of it. I mainly went there because Jr. Thirst wanted to go. Sometimes eight-year-olds (he was @ the time anyway) can make surprisingly good calls on dining choices. umm not UURRP this time by the way. Holy God and Baby Jesus, dare I continue? There was some kind of "bonus deal" (more on this later) that involved a literal ass-load of chicken. Like a whole extra box o-chicken along with your regular 8 piece, or 10 piece, or whatnot. OK you got me pricewise. Gimme the usual sides of the biscuits and the cole slaw, and we're good. Biscuits are dry but taste OK, like always. That butter that comes in the nonrefrigerated packs is like chemical warfare material BTW. ICK! dip those mothers in the gravy or something, but don't use that warm, nonperishable butter substitute shit, whatever you do. Cole slaw--I freaking LOVE KFC cole slaw. Even after the upcoming (UURP) experience, I would still gladly eat any amount of KFC cole slaw. It's always the same with the sweetness and that fake mayo sauce or whatever it is. I wouldn't try to compare it to anybody's homemade stuff (or anything else fresh), but it's crunchy and juicy, and makes a great side. Plus, after the next (EURGHH) experience, cole slaw will probably be the only thing I'll ever eat at any KFC again. Period. Long story short = ate about four good-sized pieces of chicken. I eat a lot, so not a big deal for me usually. Also had a couple small portions of the sides, I hadn't eaten all day...should be just what I needed. I had eaten at this one before, actually I had taken it to go about three times, your typical fast food mediocrity, but pretty satisfying. Last time (which was probably late 2008 or so) was a very different matter. Before we even left the restaurant (20 minutes after the initial chicken ingestion) I started to feel dizzy and not right with the world. Let's see...I'm sober (at that moment) and with no major health issues, according to my doctor. The only thing that I can compare the sensation to: about 20 years ago, after dating a girl who was vegetarian, I had been vegetarian for about six months after giving red meat up for about a year beforehand. I visited my German grandma's house a day or two before Xmas, and she insisted on cooking sausage from the German deli, despite me saying I was only going to have the potato and vegetable sides. I ate about 2/3 of one veal-based, fatty sausage (which still tasted fresh and high-quality) and had to sit down. I felt dizzy and slightly nauseated, retired to the guest room and passed out for over two hours. To this day, I know that was my body not being used to producing the enzymes needed to break down meat (especially fatty meat). But now I eat meat. Lots of it. Almost every meal contains meat. And KFC still gave me that PHYSICALLY SICK feeling anyway. At the time they were trying to promote some kind of "no trans fat" fad thing, so they might have been using a synthetic, weird shortening to deep fry their chicken. Whatever the case, I had awful food-poisoning type symptoms (I'll spare the obvious details) for two days straight and felt like I was going to die. Which brings me to the "bonus" chicken. To steal a comparison that I heard years ago, getting "bonus" KFC chicken is like having a surgeon amputate a "bonus" limb when he goes in to remove a gangrenous infection. sooo, if you're slow and still don't get it, WHY THE LIVING HELL WOULD I WANT LIKE 8 PIECES OF CHICKEN WHEN FOUR MADE ME FEEL LIKE I WAS GONNA CRAP AND VOMIT OUT MY ENTIRE DIGESTIVE SYSTEM?? It's like they're trying to get rid of that toxic crap. I threw out all the chicken after getting home, but couldn't bring myself to dispose of the cole slaw. After eating some slaw the next day and not getting a bad reaction, I can say it was definitely the chicken that was to blame. EECHHH, I can barely watch a KFC commercial even now. And now they're promoting that supposedly heart-healthy "grilled" chicken. sorry KFC, some of us don't mind overly fatty foods, if they are done right, taste good, and don't make you sick. Your attempt at prolonging my life(with that "no trans fat" grease you fried the chicken parts in) made me want to slit my wrists with a rusty razor, rather than undergo more gastric agony. I can't bring myself to try any other chicken from y'all. Just give me a lifetime supply of cole slaw, and I suppose I can call it even.

Arranging two tables to accommodate four adults and three kids (all under age 4) took several staffers a few minutes, but they had fun shouting insults at each other and sharing tales of last night's adventures. The Landing has no high chairs, so we balanced the youngest baby on our laps. The food was poor overall. The gazpacho, (perfect for a hot day, right?) had grapes and canned pineapple in it. It was bizarre and inedible, but the server removed it from our tab. On the plus side, two of our friends enjoyed chicken wraps very much. The pear salad had a very heavy dressing. The kids' grilled cheese sandwiches were doughy and barely cooked. My one year old ate the beets and pear from my salad but wouldn't touch the sandwich. We asked for more iced tea and the server said, "I have to charge you for another bottle." I'm no restauranteur, but wouldn't it be cheaper to brew a big pot of iced tea than to stock bottles of the stuff? Service was slow and inaccurate, with the teenaged wait staff laughing and shouting at each other over diners' heads. They can't be blamed, really. We never saw a manager type appear, so they're probably just in need of supervision, training and a dress code. To top it all off, we were hit with an 18% gratuity because our party was more than six (we had seven.) We'd pay it without complaint if the service was good, but had trouble stomaching it considering that three of our diners are one, one and three years old! We ordered food for them, so I guess I can see it, but it was hard to fork it over when we were tempted to tip nada. There are several other cute places in New Hope. text: First, some caveats. I only go at lunch or jazz brunch, I'm very careful (including maintaining a healthy skepticism) about what I order, and I only go if I feel like relaxing and chatting with someone for an hour and a half or two. Your mileage may vary significantly if you deviate. I've been loving Commander's for almost a decade, and just had a great Samedi Gras experience. A duck confit and strawberry salad with toasted almonds, followed by the pecan crusted drum with crab, herbs, and surrounded by a pecan, corn and cream sauce, and finished off with a praline parfait was a great start to my day. The Mardi Gras Royaltini was festive, and good, but not quite my thing. I enjoyed a Swizzle much more--and it was surprisingly potent. There are going to be some exceptions, but the safest choices on the menu are (for an app) salads and (for your entree) gulf fish (pecan crusted or the heart healthy choice--they're both really good, and you can always keep from dousing your pecan crusted fish in the cream sauce, if you eat carefully). They can more often than not switch the fish they mention to you for something else you'd prefer--just ask. I like the soups too, but they're more variable--and don't even think about getting the gumbo if it's based on the "dark" roux--that one is atrocious, but the usual one is yummy. I wouldn't order a steak here, though a relative of mine who is a steak fan has never complained about his...I just think you're failing to benefit from comparative advantage if you go this route. I like it, but the coffee is not for everyone--there's a strong chicory element. I miss the pre-Katrina main dining room, and have shared some pics of the...I'm not sure how to describe it...new main dining room. There are stuffed birds perched on the walls, Beetlejuice-esque chandeliers, and two corner booths with backlighting, tassles, and anchor symbols. The service is very professional, sometimes old school, sometimes avant garde/zany/quirky depending on the server. They're usually great about doing anything reasonable you ask for and in a timely manner. They do get a little overwhelmed sometimes, so there are delays on occasion, but it's never been a serious issue for me. As mentioned up front, I come planning to relax and spend a lot of time, and if I see people are overwhelmed I try not to inhale my water or coffee or whatever (and give some lead time on my requests) so I don't end up waiting forever. I know that's not ideal, but some self-help goes a long way. Another random thought--the milk punch is disgusting. Don't go there. And if you're getting 25 cent martinis, I think you'd better go for the traditional one--I think I could have drunk 25 dollars in the other ones and not been buzzed.

I stole a friend's, and added the undressed lettuce to my sandwich. The sauce was homemade, which is great, but it lacked any real resemblance to the sloppy joe sauce of my youth, other than the fact that it was tomato based. I slathered it with hot sauce. The grilled vegetable sub ($7.95) Boyfriend ordered came on a long roll expertly cut by the cook like a hibachi chef or a teenager into food amputation, with the ends hacked off in one quick slam of the knife from above. This was probably the most entertaining thing to happen while we sat at the counter waiting for our food, since no one attempted to engage our group in any form of conversation whatsoever. text: A few months ago I had an incident at this Superfresh. They had a promotion going on and all the signage was very confusing, so I spoke with a customer service person to get a better understanding. I then spent an hour shopping and making very specific selections with the purpose of buying items that would maximize taking advantage of this promotion. But when I got to the checkout, it turned out that it had been explained to me all wrong. I was being given about 1/100th of what I had expected to receive out of this promotion. I asked to speak to a manager, and got bumped up and up and up to different people, all of them telling me there was nothing they could do. Ultimately I left behind my entire basket of groceries. I found everyone to be rude and, frankly, to not have a store honor the word of an employee is not only unfair, it's against the law. (Google "Implied Authority of Contract".) I ended up going VERY high up in the SuperFresh chain of command, talking to someone in their legal department who deals with their contests and promotions. I was ultimately mailed a package with what I was denied at the store (even though I didn't even buy the items.) I told this person that I would take a break from this store location and try again later. So after waiting half a year, I went back to this store yesterday. I shopped for 20 minutes. Because of a public transportation strike, the place was packed, and I waited in line for about 20 minutes. Then, while there were still 3 people in front of me, the checkout man pointed to the woman in front of me and said "Miss, you will be my last customer." I was flabbergasted. Trying to maintain my cool, I said "Excuse me? I was already in this line for 20 minutes! You can't just make me move to another line." The man, clearly NOT sorry or concerned with me, said "That's just how it is." "No, that's not acceptable," I replied. "We all understand that sometimes you have to close your line down, but you do so by telling NEWLY ARRIVED people that the line has been closed down. You don't make someone who was already waiting in the line move to another line with 15 people in it." Though I was not yelling or raising my voice, it became one of those situations where the people in line around me were rolling their eyes at me. That's kind of a shame, because I wonder how they would feel if they were in my situation. "Could you please point out the manager to me?" I said to the checkout person, who at this point would neither speak to me or make eye contact with me. So I wheeled myself over to customer service - a familiar area - and asked to speak to a manager. I explained the situation, and I also explained that I was abandoning the $100 in groceries I had intended to buy, and that this time, I was not ever coming back.

The cooks were still prepping and their waiter was off, so one of the cooks took my order. I decided to go for the jerk chicken with a side of "red peas and rice." While waiting for the food, I took a look around - island style decorations, bright colors, and music that ranged from bayou to reggae. I was a little surprised with the jerk chicken order - an entire half chicken: breast to thigh complete with wing and drumstick - and a few plantain fries with two wedges of lime. The red peas (red beans) and rice came out in an okay portion, too. I guess it should be a decent sized plate considering it costs $13.50 for the chicken w/ one side. The food looked great - unfortunately the taste didn't match up. My first bite of plantain fries left me feeling profound disappointment - there was absolutely no seasoning and they were stale instead of crispy. But that first bite set up the rest of my meal. Everything - the beans, rice, and chicken, was missing one key ingredient: SALT. Though the jerk chicken spices were decent, the lack of salt really turned me off. The breast portion was a bit overcooked and dry, but the thigh portion was just right. The spices were nice with a slow building heat to them, but without the salt it just tasted really bland. The same went for the beans and rice - I could taste some of what they were trying to do - a hint of herb here, some coconut flavoring there - but without some salt to kick everything up a notch, it all ended up feeling one note. I'm not much of a salt freak, but I had to add salt to EVERYTHING =/ Guess I had some high expectations for this place... maybe you can chalk it up to the restaurant just starting. Talking to the cook, he mentioned that the place had only been open for about three months. Maybe they just don't have their consistency down since it seems the other folks who tried this place liked it. From my experience, this place is pretty overpriced for underseasoned food. Sorry guys =(

Camille's also offers a variety of salads (my friend enjoyed the Bangkok Thai salad), hot and cold sandwiches, and flatbread pizzas. The flavor combinations are unique and quite refreshing when I think about how long I've been eating roast beef on Asiago bagels. Camille's also does catering, and I'll write a separate review for that when I've tried them for a work meeting. Oh no, NOTHING is wrong with Camille's just because it's a little empty. text: Overall, an above-average hotel with an awesome location. If you're coming from out-of-town on a touristy kick as I was, just stay here. It's walkable or cab-able or horse carriage-able to everywhere you want to go during the day, and within stumbling distance of everywhere you want to go at night. The staff here was pretty awesome, and the receptionist thought the picture on my driver's license of my 16-yr-old self was "adorable". Later on, we got shaving cream delivered to the room free of charge...and within of 5 minutes of the request. Nothing special, but it was simple and nice. The room was average, the TV was pretty nice. Nothing special of note there. The hotel has a large central atrium lobby which was hosting a Police Sheriffs of America (or something) convention. It's a good business event spot and the atrium almost passes off as an indoor-outdoor courtyard...with big comfy upholstered chairs. The location is great for walking to all the nearby pubs and restaurants in an older part of the city. Cobblestone wanderings drunk on Chimay (or anything else)....good times. The price for a Saturday wasn't too shabby either. I say, if you're going to do Philly, do it at the Sheraton.

text: If you're used to eating in strip malls, this place is for you. I don't know who is impressed by this place - I'm visiting from Seattle and have had better gumbo. My dining partner and I both got appetizers and entrees. My gumbo was cold, so I sent it back... and it came back lukewarm (at best)! I said I didn't want it, but 20 minutes later the manager brought it, obviously straight out of the microwave. Nice try, low class. The pocket bread appetizer was pretty good and reasonably priced, as well. I had the famous shrimp and grits which, while pretty good, were barely a notch above something you'd get at a run of the mill chain restaurant (but twice the price at NOLA). My companion got the fish of the day, which was Mahi Mahi and while she liked it, I thought it was nearly unpalatable. I suppose if you come here drunk and happy to be on vacation, then you can say you went to a "nice" restaurant. Otherwise, I was insulted at the size of our bill compared to the quality. Beware of the trendy factor here.
label: NEG

text: This isn't a restaurant. It's a kitchen in someone's home. That's the feel you get when you walk in. The ladies behind the counter gave me healthy amounts of samples when I asked about what things were so I can really taste and choose what I wanted. When I decided on the Catfish Po' Boy, rather than giving me the stuff that was on the heating tray, she waited until a new piping hot batch came out to stuff my po' boy. It was steamy with a very light crisp coating of batter. (see picture I posted). Well worth the wait. Unfortunately, I used my college level reading skills too late to realize that it was CASH ONLY. When I didn't have enough cash on hand to pay for my drink, the lady gave me a Coke, on the house. How nice are they. The place has very limited seating and I saw numerous accounts of people giving up their tables so that others can sit together as a group. I wish the world was more like this restaurant. It's 2 blocks away from the French Quarter on Camp, across the street from the La Quinta. It's not a tourist trap. This is the real thing when you're looking for a taste of New Orleans and true southern hospitality. They close at 2:30pm. Bring cash and a big appetite because their portions are more than generous. I only regret that I didn't have enough cash on hand to get the heaping plate of Red Rice & Beans and the Yam Fries.

text: Last week, we used Scoogi's for a luncheon following my grandfather's funeral. I can speak only to the banquet side of the restaurant, but we couldn't have been happier with their service and facilities. The food was also excellent. We had a buffet with a few options and everything was good. Standouts include the bread (OMG), salmon and cannoli. Following a somber morning, this was the perfect conclusion. It's bright, beautiful space, serving delicious comfort food with a friendly and unobtrusive staff. They also had a new big screen TV mounted on the wall that we used to present and video/slideshow. It was something that took a lot of effort and I really wanted to display it in a respectful, classy manner. I really anticipated rented some expensive equipment for the afternoon, but that wasn't necessary. This TV has a beautiful picture and very good sound. They even let us come by twice before to test everything out and they didn't impose any restrictions. I'd recommend Scoogi's for anyone looking for a classy, but casual, event.

text: I suppose this negative review is less specific to the Bridge than it is a commentary on movie going in the 21st Century. How I long for the days when cell phones didn't exist. text: As a Chinese, I am critical about Chinese cuisine. However, I do enjoy the Chinese food here. The sichuan food (a subcategory of Chinese food, featured by spicy) here is of high quality. They include almost all the famous sichuan cuisine I, as a Chinese but not from Sichuan province, could image. I may not be able to find better sichuan food in my hometown, which is not sichuan province. Besides, the inside setting of this restaurant is pretty good compared to most Chinese restaurants in the US, though the price is reasonable. As for the staff, it depends. I do enjoy the service by the young waiter, but I do not like the mid-aged waitress much. She seems to be busy all the time, and make you also feel in a hurry, which is not good for dining experience. Also, it is a little far away from downtown, but that's the trade-off.

text: One of my favorite things to do when in New Orleans is check out restaurants. The difference this time around was that I had my kids, so I wanted to find a place that they felt comfortable in (see Grand Isle). We stayed at the Westin near the river this time around, so I decided to ask the concierge about some places close by. She told me about an Italian Creole Place on Decatur and also about Olivier's. So we treked from the hotel on foot and ran into O's first (right across the street from the House of Blues. We met one of the owners who was "barking up" business outside and he was a consumate gentleman. We looked at the menu and while there wasnt any kid centric dishes, he assured me that they could accomodate a special order. Have you ever sat down at a place and it took more than a few minutes to get waited on, so you think its an omen for a bad experience and you know you should leave? If I had been by myself or with other adults, I would have encouraged it. My kids get a tad embarassed when dad is a hard ass (never rude mind you), so we decided to stay. Unfortunately, it was the wrong choice. With so many great restaurants in this town, you just hate to suffer through a mediocre experience. Let me summarize. Waiter was smarmy, unattentive and ill trained. Who ever taught you that it was ok to go around the table stacking dishes when picking them up. Ugh. The rabbit was flavorless as was the "oyster dressing" ($18.95), shrimp scampi was nothing more than grilled ($16.95) and even the open food pasta with fettucine and chicken was overun with vegetables, etc. Wine (good bottle selection) by the glass was ok but smallish and the dessert at $7.95 was certainly not prepared onsite and was average. I am all for family recipes but just like what Professor Colonel Sanders told the Waterboy....Mommas wrong again! What passed for fine dining here just didnt cut the roux. If you look at my 100 reviews, you know I dont give out two stars lightly, but this place was every bit deserving.

text: This place is amazing. A definite must when visiting New Orleans. The wood fired oysters were plump and juicy. Each oyster is covered with a spiced butter sauce that adds great flavor without overpowering the taste of the oyster. The osyters were so fresh and were imbued with a lightly smokey flavor from being in the wood fire oven. The fried alligator with chili garlic aioli was also very good. The alligator was not chewy at all. And the chili garlic aioli had that nice hint of heat without being overly spicy that your mouth is burning. The spicy grilled pork ribs with watermelon pickles was a hefty portion of very tasty meat with a hint of smokiness after being in the wood fire grill. The pickled watermelon provides a nice astringent crunch to offset the fatty sweetness of the ribs. Definitely coming back the next time I'm in NOLA.

text: The two statues of Thai dancers on either side of the entrance are sign #1 that this will be a good dining experience. A good Thai restaurant should be a full sensory explosion of Thai-ness, and Thai Bu Ree doesn't disappoint. I am greatly suspicious of minimalist-looking Thai restaurants, are they trying to fool people into thinking they are Japanese? The walls here are hung with beautiful wood carvings, and the unobtrusive background music is always traditional. Next up: the food. The food is a little of a mixed bag. The things they do well, they do *very* well, but the things they don't do well are really disappointing. For example, skip their Pad See Ew, trust me. The potato noodles also don't taste nearly as good as they sound. Oh, but the curries... They make a mean curry. In fact, they make at least half a dozen mean curries. And the really cool part is that they all taste different, it's not just the same sauce rehashed over and over with different meats and veggies. I don't know where they get fresh Thai basil in the depths of winter, but any of their dishes that are heavy on the basil are just rays of sunshine on a gloomy day. The service is often a little slow, but extremely polite. Now I'm craving Thai food. Just writing about it has made me want to go there again!
label: POS

text: Bottom line, it's a car wash. So if you care about paint swirls and fine scratches in your car's clear coat, stick to the traditional claybar/polish/wax method that you do in your garage. For those of you that either don't care too much about that, or, like me, have a car that's just not worth detailing, this place is great. It's cheap ($7 for a regular wash, $11 for the premium), they give your bumpers and windows a good scrubdown to get all those summer insects off before you enter, and there are no towel guys at the end that you might feel bad not tipping. The car comes out cleaner than in other auto-washes I've been to as well. I cant give it 5 stars cause it's an auto wash, but since it's a good one, I give it 4.

text: Nobody enjoys a good steak like I do... unfortunately, this was not one. Still a beautiful space, and with very good service, B&S is hyped as a retro steakhouse and certainly the menu reflects this, with a nod to yesteryear when a side dish could be comprised of equal parts shredded potatoes, sour cream, butter and salt. Let's face it, it's gonna taste good, even if I did feel the need to scan the room for my doctor before digging in. Just as unhealthy (and salty) was the Creamed Spinach - think Boston Market's version - with maybe a pinch of Tarragon? Not bad, but clearly nothing special. As for the main event, one of our party ordered the Porterhouse ($42 I believe) and we opted to share the Porterhouse for Two, at $73. We received exactly the same steak, the only difference being that ours had been pre-cut into many little pieces... perhaps to make it appear larger?! Retro theme is one thing, but I haven't needed my mommy to cut my meat for many years now, thanks. While tasty (grilled meat crusted in salt, of course it's tasty), I have never been served a Porterhouse that was as surrounded by grisle... and frankly for $73 I would have expected better. As for those tasty - if not very clever - side dishes, their prices were very much not retro, mostly in the $9 - $12 range, nothing unusual these days but in serving sizes for one, possibly two patrons at the most, absolutely not for the 'whole table' [of four] that our waiter had suggested. While not a bad meal, this is very much not a special meal. Perhaps we are old-fashioned, but I still expect a special meal when spending more than $100 a head. The restaurant will be a huge success for many years, as it has 'Starr' status, but if you are a true old-school carnivore, you might want to give up a bit of the ambience here and opt instead for Fogo de Chao instead, at half the price.
label: NEG

text: I'll admit that I really like going to the Bishop's Collar, which is my favorite bar within walking distance of my second home (the Fairmount neighborhood). While there can sometimes be a wait for a table and while it can get REALLY PACKED on the weekend nights, they do move through pretty quickly and it's not a huge deal to hang out at the bar until something opens up. The double gin and tonics are strong, and always made consistently: you know exactly how many to drink to straddle the line between pleasantly drunk and unpleasantly plastered. This summer they've also had the Arnold Palmer, which has become my favorite summer beverage and discovery: sweet tea infused vodka (oh. my. god.) and lemonade. They are fabulous, especially if you can manage to snag an outdoor table, enjoying the summer air and sipping on one of these. And although I'm not really a beer person, they have enough available that I can find something I like if I have to, and my more beer snobby friends never have problems either. However, secretly, I like the Bishop's Collar because they have perfect, cheap, unhealthy, fantastic, filling bar food. The plate of nachos is intimidating when sober, but after a night of drinking, sharing it with a friend hits the spot. Their wings are not gristly in the least, and the hot sauce, while not quite the same as a buffalo wing, is tangy and tasty. My favorite thing MAY be the chicken chipotle sandwich, with Old Bay fries, which is an absolute steal for $6, but it's hard to choose. Usually we just end up splitting nachos and wings, because it's hard to mess with a classic combination like that. But back to the Bishop's Collar: hits-the-spot food, great drinks, and a nice, low key evening to hang out with friends in the neighborhood.

text: Please pardon the delay in this review - my bike purchase date was actually in 2008 but I have found the degree of service, personal attention and courtesy to be just as effective now as then. I made the conscience decision to switch over from mountain bike to road bike, cold turkey. All reviews pointed to a select few bikes to try out and when I hopped on the Madone 5.1, I knew it was the bike for me. The Trek Store of Tampa was the - only - store to offer a military discount on both the bike and any accessories (all other shoppes I checked into would only offer a discount on accessories). One the bike was selected, the manager spent 40 minutes getting the bike and I dialed. I'm not sure if this is always included or because he was having a good day, but it was def. appreciated. They did not push needless accessories one, and several times suggest I try other less expensive options when it comes to helmets, computers, etc. I have walked into the shop for an 'express tune-up' and I am out the door in 15 minutes flat. Their mechanics are well trained and will expedite service if it is required. The staff remember your name and in my experience will always take the time to ensure you walk away from the store informed and comfortable with whatever it is you decided to, or not to purchase. Exceptional customer service, excellent inventory and reasonable prices make this Trek Store my personal 'go-to' choice for bikes in Tampa.

text: This store is the size of a large-ish supermarket, yet somehow I never find anything to buy. The clothes are arranged by color! This is the most useless method I've seen in any thrift store, by far. Who shops that way? What good is something which is the "right" color but 5 sizes too small or too big?! I am a dedicated thrifter, and am normally willing to spend hours combing the racks for a good find, but this is so illogical I just get irritated and leave. The book selection is no great shakes, scarcely any paperbacks for some reason. The shoes tend to be both poor quality and out of style. Not a bad variety of kitchen goods. They have a vastly inflated view of what obsolete computer stuff is worth ($10 for a 1996 Photoshop 4.0 manual? hee!) but that's pretty much a universal thrift store employee issue. The few bright spots are purses and bags (this is where the huge selection is great), blankets (ditto), and, strangely, exercise gear? I've never bought a used stationary bike or rowing machine, but this is where I'd go if I needed one, I guess. Worth a stop if you're driving right by it, but it's been years since I made a special trip to come here from Philly.
label: NEG

text: The Movie Studio has all of your typical mainstream movies available for rent, plus a huge selection of indie and foreign films. They even have a few racks of rentals set aside for their "alternative" movie collection (think a ton of independent Bill Murray movies). Because the Movie Studio is so huge, sometimes it can be a challenge to find a specific film. However, staff here are very nice here, and have always been happy to help when I can't find a flick I'm looking for. Last time I spent a good ten minutes searching for a Synecdoche, when a staff member helpfully pointed out that it was just one stack over. The best part? Free hot popcorn on the way out with your rental, or a giant bag of popcorn for only $3! My only critique is that The Movie Studio only gets in a few copies of each movie, including mainstream ones, so popular rentals are out of stock. So if you're looking for a newly-released flick, go early and check back often for copies!

text: This cozy, hoppin' South Philly cantina makes the BEST margaritas I've ever had. The menu here instigates the battle between my eyes & my stomach--I want to order way more than I can really handle, and so my only realistic option is to keep coming back here. Two visits in, I've had their amazing guacamole, several pitchers of margaritas on the rocks with salt, chips with green and red salsas, and burritos 2 ways: the verduras, and the shrimp; both loaded up with a la carte add-ons like jalapenos, sour cream, and guac... I prefer the shrimp burrito, but the verduras is quite good. This is one of many items on the vegan- and vegetarian-friendly menu. Their board specials vie for my attention, particularly the ceviches. Their desserts beckon, but I have not yet figured out how to get them in ma belly. Service is great; very attentive. The teamwork on the staff appears pretty tight. This is a hipster haven, but caters to a diverse crowd of all ages and types.

text: SORELY disappointing this time. We came here for lunch last week and although seated promptly, seemed to have been forgotten about. Straws should be considered an opt-out thing, not an opt-in. We shouldn't have to ASK you for a straw when you bring us our drinks. The drinking straw as we know it was patented in 1888 by Marvin Stone, and believe it or not, in the past 122 years, THEY'VE GOTTEN PRETTY FUCKING POPULAR! I'd NOW like to take the opportunity to apologize to the server for apparently ruining your afternoon. We are SO sorry that we asked for straws. We had no idea that it would so adversely affect your life and force you to roll your eyes at us. Was it a heavy flow day or something? If I wasn't trying to be nice (everyone is entitled to a bad day here and there), I promise I'd have made you fucking cry. And next time, I will. Oh wait, there's not going to BE a next time for this place. We ordered our food at the same time our straw-less drinks arrived. Then half an hour later, the server was still bustling around, actively trying to avoid eye contact. Presumably because she knew she'd fucked up? We finally got an answer about why our food's preparation had taken so long--she forgot to put it in. Whoops. It's customary at this point to offer the impatient customers a free appetizer. Then it's all reluctant apologies, excuses, and a begrudgingly free order of spring rolls. Oh, and don't forget to take advantage of their Yelp special. text: I have received better food and service from gas station gyro stands. The only asset Kalamata's offers to its patrons is a non-threatening strip mall environment for suburbanites wishing to declare "cultural awareness", by way of eating stale "middle eastern food" at a remarkably inflated price (gotta pay for that non-threatening atmosphere somehow). They will however attempt to provide you with a classic experience, by having a self-satisfied man hand mix you fresh salads in a dirty salad bowl, to resounding adequacy, as a front and center attraction. Give him three balls and he'll probably juggle too. OOOOOO Salad! The meal: Babaganouj: Small portion, certainly nothing worth being classified as an appetizer to share with another person, at most possibly a side dish, which should cost half of what was being charged, with one piece of covetous store bought stale pita bread. The babaganouj was a gray lifeless puree that looked, and tasted like it was made over a week ago. The overall bouquet embodied that of a typical ploy to substitute the flavor of eggplant by overwhelming it with garlic. I doubt they even make it from scratch, despite the ease of such a recipe. They did garnish it with one olive and a little oil while failing to provide cumin garnish to complete the dish. Shameful. Spinach Pie: It's a pita with spinach in it cooked, and they sprinkle a little bit of Feta over it and charge $4. Never mind, the true dish that requires light crispy, filo dough with spinach, and egg, prepared to perfection. The overall flavor was bitter, watery, and lifeless. Not Recommended. Gyros Sandwich: First of, Don't get the $9 dollar gyro plate it is a rip off, at best, if you have to, get the Gyro sandwich, throw it in the trash, and then go somewhere good to eat. The gyro meat is diced in an unconventional manner; probably to provide an eclectic spin on a basic over saturated dish. In reality dicing gyro meat was an attempt to put less of the most expensive ingredient into the overall sandwich, a brazen move but certainly one that cannot warrant its small portion size or price. I guess they have to look busy somehow. I asked for a Gyro with no Tomato only to receive a Gyro laden with Cucumber. NOT AN OPTION ON THE MENU, even more filler, and uncalled for. Restaurateur 101: Provide only what you advertise on your menu please! Some people are disgusted by the overwhelming flavor of Cucumbers. Plus, who is happy about a flat gyro. That's right completely flat. Not recommended. The salad tosser -"chef" did not like my basic issues with the food, and asked me to leave. I asked for what I ordered, remained and finished. After the experience my stomach was as if I just drank 2 cups of salad dressing, and fell sick. Bussing your own dishes is the name of the game, and try not to be disgusted by the three tiny trash cans that are overflowing with garbage right near the front door. Health Inspection Anyone? YUCK! A gourmet nightmare, strike that, a nightmare, and a disservice to anyone trying to promote the culture of the Middle East by way of cuisine. I will sum it up in one simple equation: Kalamatas + Middle Eastern Cuisine = Olive Garden + Italiano Cuisine.
label: NEG

text: Modesto is a great tapas bar that has been exceedingly lively and full of fun on all four of my visits. I've liked all of the tapas dishes that I've had, but due to food allergies there are a good number that I am unable to try. My favorites are mostly the hot tapas, and I highly recommend the fried lobster with sauce. The paella marinara is wonderful, and reminds me of my time in Southern France where Spanish food was a heavy influence on the local cuisine. text: My good friend and humanitarian extraordinare (Dana P with One Brick) has been down to New Orleans countless times...so, when my mother proposed a volunteer trip down here, my first email was to Dana to get the scoop... Some notes from the website: "You will literally help rebuild a family's home. This may include hanging insulation or sheetrock, mudding/spackling, sanding, texturing, priming, painting, laying floors, and/or hanging trim, doors and baseboard. If you have significant experience any of these areas or in framing, electric, plumbing and/or cabinetry, please inform the Volunteer Department prior to your arrival so that we can assign you to a specialty team." Another note, co-founder Liz McCartney has been named 2008 CNN Hero of the Year. A remarkable achievement... http://blog.nola.com/davewalker/2008/11/st_bernard_project_cofounder_l_1.html Ok, so my experience... Day 1 830am: report to St. Bernard Project HQ for a mini-orientation. Met with co-founder for a bit of background, motivational speech of sorts. It worked. We were ready to build! Notes: All 27,000 homes in St. Bernard Parish were leveled and deemed "uninhabitable" after Hurricane Katrina. The population went from 75,000 before HK, to 25,000 after. Many are still waiting for their homes to be rebuilt. This is nearly 5 years after the storm... 930am: report to site. The Duplessy home in a small subdivision a few miles from Camp Hope. We meet our site supervisor, Morgan, who is with Americorps. She is 18 years old, and knows more than the 4 of us combined. Truly inspiring, and dedicated. Not to mention fun and sweet :) The next 3 days: Drywall, mud, spackel, sand, sand, sand, sand, sand, wash stuff out, sand, sand, sand, sweep, play with the puppy across the street, sand, sand, sand, sand, eat at Rock and Carlo's, sand, sand, sand, mud, spackel, learn how to "speed finish" a floor, work on corners, sand, sand, sand. Yes, we sanded a lot. But damn, that house was SMOOOOOOOTH when we left! They really stress quality over quantity, as they rebuild these homes to last. Absolutely a 5-star experience. Fabulous organization from start to finish. Gracious, genuine, inspired, dedicated. I'm glad I could donate a little of my time...but honestly, there is still so much to do. I was literally amazed at the amount of empty homes. Empty. Abandoned. 5 years later and this is what it still looks like? It's incomprehendable, but absolutely true. 5 years. In one of the most well-developed countries in the world...it just blows my mind. You can't even believe it until you see it. Anyone want to go back? I'm game. Not only to you get to volunteer for such a worthy, cool cause...but you are mere miles from New Orleans, one of the most fun places to visit/hang out in the USA, in my opinion. Fun, leisure, volunteer work...a great mix, and awesome way to see a new place. I' still in awe of the work they've done...and continue to do. Definitely give it a thought if you are looking to volunteer in NOLA, and PM or email me if you've got any questions. I'm planning on going back.

text: When you live in the food snob capital of the USA, you have serious expectations when you dine out. My visit to Cochon in rebounding New Orleans, left me full, fat and happy! I hope it lasts forever so I can go back one day to be dined and delighted with pig parts and authentic southern cooking. The post-modern lodge style dining room amuses with porcine decor, sleek, utlilitarian picnic-style tables, benches and stools. A warehouse location and trendy bar crowd sets the scene. Complimentary bread has become so passez over the years, even those pencil thin breadsticks and wafer thin parmesan flatbread are so yawn that it's mighty refreshing when someone plops down a basket of WARM HOMEMADE POTATO ROLLS in front of you. Cochon makes a batch every 20 minutes and they contain real potato puree. The rolls and consideration for jaded-foodie palates gets 5 stars. Cochon does small plates and entrees so you can get your fill of local favorites and house specialties. Standouts from the Boucherie are fried boudin balls with pieces of pulled pork and deep flavor. My small plate of BBQ pork ribs came out cold though the sauce was tangy and sweet enough while I was looking for more smokiness. Fried pigs ears and rabbit livers I see more of a novelty for people like my dinner companion for whom having something fried and/or weird is a must for every fine dining experience. There's plenty of love for the local cuisine: My hen and adouille gumbo had a flavourful (and memorable) dark roux. Roasted Gulf redfish (a specialty of the chef) was picture perfect and it's flesh is melt in your mouth. A side of pecan-broccoli dressing was (surprise!) gratineed and rich. And, the eponymous Louisiana cochon was salty, moist and flavorful-"very enjoyable" said my wide-eyed companion. Of course, the fruit cobbler was a must, but sadly the only real disappointment of the night. The local strawberries were warm with a natural non-cloying sweetness but clashed with the somewhat doughy biscuits baked with a distracting (in a bad way) hint of ginger. My one suggestion for the dessert menu is to make a traditional lattice cobbler topping or biscuits without ginger. I loved everything else, this just made for an odd finish. Cochon was the culinary risk of my most recent trip to New Orleans. I had turned down Brigsten's and boycotted Besh. And, I was NOT disappointed. Chef Donald Link forced his way back into a broken city to get Cochon up and running. You can taste that passion in every cajun-style bite.

text: I fell in love with Ethiopian food during my stint in Oakland-Berkeley, and was utterly delighted to find that upon my return to St. Louis, an Ethiopian place had opened up in my old 'hood! Meskerem occupies a space on the south Grand strip that I always wished would house a restaurant. It's cozy but the two main dining areas make it more than big enough to handle large crowds and groups. This place is a godsend for veggie-leaning folks in the hunt for satisfying winter comfort food. The shiro wat (ground chickpeas with cumin and turmeric in berber sauce) was outstanding, bursting with spice, yet never so hot as to overpower the actual flavor. The whole white beans in awaze was filling yet felt utterly light. Gomen wat (steamed collard greens with pepper, ginger and garlic) has a pleasing, homey taste, kind of like your mom's cheesy spinach casserole, but if it was, you know, cheeseless and vaguely healthy. Really, the sheer variety and quality of the lentils and greens on offer in the vegetarian menu is a relief and welcome change of pace to most restaurants' token falalfel platter or portobello sandwich. Meaty meals don't disappoint, either. The chicken tibs had a slight berber kick to it, like a light stir fry. The big chunks of still-crisp onion were a big bonus. Beef dishes were, however, hit and miss. The tibs wat was hearty and flavorful, but the gomen besaega (beef in collard greens) was cold, thick, and vaguely tough. The injera (spongy, sorghum-based unleavened bread) wasn't quite as pillowy as I'd expect it to be, although it was jam packed with the bread's trademark sourdough bite. As always, the stew-soaked injera lining the serving pan was a highlight. It's like the muffin top of the Ethiopian food world -- the kind of little touch that feels like a treat, even though it's a part of every single meal. Both the meat and vegetarian combo platters are steals at ~$12, and are also great ways for first timers to dip their toes into the pool. The meat combo, in particular, might be the single best place for a wary diner to start. It comes with three beef dishes and two basic lentil stews, nothing threatening but all five full of the flavor and subtlety that are the hallmarks of the cuisine. Ethiopian food is normally served family style. If you're not particularly relishing the prospect of sharing a giant plate and eating with your hands, worry not -- it's a fun, ice-breaking experience. In fact, aside from maybe sushi joints or proper Chinese restaurants with big lazy susans in the middle of the tables, I can't think of a restaurant more suited to group outings and "get to knows". I'm beginning to believe that dinner at Meskerem would be the ultimate first-date litmus test. If you and your prospective mate can laugh over messy fingers, you've found a winner! Meskerem loses a few points for the astonishingly slow service on the night I visited, although I'm willing to chalk that up to simply being understaffed, even if it was a Saturday night. The waitstaff was nothing but friendly and apologetic for the delays, so I wouldn't expect slow to be the default level of service on any given night. Long story short -- Ethiopian food is one of those things that initially might make you go "huh? what's that?" It just doesn't quite compute for some reason; it didn't for me until someone made me try it. But give it a go -- the dining experience at Meskerem is welcoming and incredibly fun. Be prepared to be pleasantly surprised. And to become addicted.

text: When I first moved to St Louis I was surprised to find admission to the Zoo is FREE! Parking tip...come early to beat the traffic and park on the street for free. We went to the Zoo with the family while they were in town. I would have to say if you're going to go, you MUST visit the Sting Ray exhibit while it's here. It was one of the coolest experiences ever. I was expecting them to feel rubbery, but they actually felt soft like velveteen or a slippery mushroom. If your planning to spend the day at the zoo, the best deal you can get is the Zoo Safari pass for $10. It includes access to the Children's Zoo, unlimited Zooline Railroad, Conservation Carousel, Sea Lion Show and Wild Ride Motion Simulator. I always seem to learn something new when I visit the Zoo. Can't wait to go back.

text: If it was at all possible to give this place a negative review, I beg any willing administrator to do it, because this place definitely deserves it. First of all, I have definitely been to this D&B before, and no, I am not 21. But a couple of friends and I drop by one night to kill a couple of hours. And what do I find? A lady selectively carding people walking in. Apparently you had to be 21 to enter. Which definitely did not apply to the large crowd of African Americans walking in 2 minutes before us. Oh and I came here (to this exact location) before, never being carded. Well we argued with the manager for a couple of minutes on the basis of racial discrimination since apparently all African-Americans are over the age of 21, even if they look to be 15. They were exceptionally rude to all of us, saying nothing except that we should leave. (I'm still very upset about this, seeing as we were being perfectly reasonable). Well, we had a couple of coupons from somewhere and we figured we should at least charge them since we were here anyway (for later use at a different location). Apparently this was against the rules as well. Sooo... we couldn't go in, suddenly, because we weren't 21. And they didn't let us charge our cards, which really had nothing to do with the whole situation. Conclusion; This Dave and Buster's sucks. If you go, you support racial discrimination. There I said it. Oh, and its $11 for parking unless you are willing to walk 5-10minutes over (but even that's difficult because rare unless you come past 10pm).

text: I feel kinda weird going against the crowd on this one - but I really wasn't a huge fan. Granted, I've only been once - and if I go again, I will definitely update. We got here in the evening on the Saturday before St. Patrick's Day - which meant it was still packed with drunk people who had been drinking all day - no judgment there, I've done it :) - but it cleared out a little as those drunkies eventually had to stop drinking. Yes, it was pretty big - I guess the guy who asked if anyone had been out of the midwest missed all the patio areas? If you took all that away, yes, it would be small. They had a pretty good beer selection (including some Schlafly and O'Fallon) - but the Pale Ale my boyfriend go was STALE and definitely old. I ordered vodka tonic with their "premium" vodka - Smirnoff...for $9! Yes, it's an Irish pub, but what's with the lack of choices for liquor??? And $9, really? I expect a Grey Goose martini for that price - not a Smirnoff & tonic in a plastic cup. Overall, I just wasn't that impressed, and the crowd was kind of boring - maybe because they were all wasted, and I was definitely not. Meh - maybe I'll be back in the summer and grab some food. Til then - just a 2.

text: I have been meaning to write up 45 Tchoup for some time, as this is one of the best neighborhood bars in the Uptown area. text: If you're trying to decide on undergraduate or graduate school, I hate to break it to you, but Yelp is not the tool to be using. The campus is absolutely beautiful, so it's definitely worth parking and walking up to the main quad at least once. You'll also find the Kemper Art Museum here, too, which has been separately reviewed on Yelp. There are at least two bookstores where you can buy WUSTL and St. Louis apparel, and there are a lot of options for lunch, too: the food court in the Danforth University Center (DUC; the student union), a Subway, and Ibby's, a table service restaurant also in the DUC. text: If you've read my other reviews, you'll find a consistent theme, I truly enjoy the dairy goodness that is ice cream. Thus, I am happy to report a new find for all of the other ice cream fanatics out there in Central Florida. This Mom and Pop shop has oh-so-many flavors and concoctions to choose from! It almost made our heads spin. They home make their hard selection and you can tell. I sampled their banana pudding and it was heavenly. I ended up choosing a Marshmellow Caramel Sundae (for $3.20) and was extremely pleased with my choice. They do use quite a bit of whipped cream so if that's not on your list of favorites, you might want to ask for a reduced amount. Plus, the soft serve that composes their sundaes is low-fat so I didn't feel as bad enjoying every single bite. They also offer a generic version of DQ's Blizzard called the Hurricane. For $3.05 expect a ginormous portion of soft serve ice cream blended with almost every single candy, cookie, fruit and topping that you could imagine. I tasted the Peanut Butter Hurricane with vanilla soft serve and was astonished at the amount of Reese's Peanut Butter Cups I encountered in my 2 measly bites. Plus, to add excitement to the already glorious Hurricane, they drizzle just a smidge of Peanut Butter Sauce on top. They are big enough to share if you go on a fairly full stomach. Make sure to shake your piggy bank before going though, they only accept cash.

text: Wonk. I had high hopes for this place, but just because the decor is cute doesn't mean the food is good. Food is mediocre. - Yellowtail carpaccio: good, but the yuzu sauce was a touch too strong. Overpowered the fish. - Ahi pepper tuna: nothing spectacular. It was decent, but I wasn't falling all over myself. - Our trifecta of sushi (salmon, yellowtail, and toro) was disappointing, to say the least. The pieces were huge, such that we had to bite it in half (and I try to NEVER do this). The rice was so packed that it completely overtook the flavor of the fish. I guess that was sort of a good thing because the fish was not the freshest. BTW, the "toro" we got tasted and looked like regular tuna, but it was $10. Horrible mistake. We tried to give them the benefit of the doubt ("hey, maybe their rolls are better") and ordered the lobster mazy roll. OY. We didn't even finish it. It was mushy and fell apart when you took it off the plate. The gyoza was decent, but if you eff that up, you have some serious issues. Service was okay. Halfway through our meal, a group of gaggling girls came in celebrating someone's birthday. My husband and I wanted to burst out laughing when the first two told their group that they were excited because they ordered a California roll. Then our emotions quickly turned to horror when one of them said, "You're so loud you're almost black!" to another...there was a black girl right behind us, at another table near them. (O_o) Anyway, the price definitely did not justify. It was about $10 less than what we could have gotten at Vic or Sakeya, but I'd rather pay that extra $10 and get a truly decent meal.

text: The service was great, freaky fast. The food was was just okay, I would be cautious to say authentic or made fresh to-order. The atmosphere was colorful, contrast to the rest of the strip mall. The flavor was something I couldn't pin down, along with that orange color. it wasn't super spicy and had a little black bean taste to it. The food came out fast, freaky fast. It had that sad look of, "I've been ready all day." I don't know how to comment on the green rice or the green colored ranch salad dressing. Green is not the normal, or natural, color for either of those things. A table nearby ordered a couple margaritas, and I must say they were huge. Probably something that would have made my review better had I consumed a few first. I might have thought green rice and orange salsa were more fascinating under the influence, rather than strangely odd and unappetizing looking. text: Taking into consideration what Will said regarding Fu Manchu's acknowledgement of their inauthenticity, I will forego any judgement on that front. However, their food is not only terrible, its fucking terrible. My table ordered the all you can eat "tasting menu" because, well, I wanted to try everything. In the menu, it claims that you can order anything off the menu, and that there are "special" off menu treats that the cooks will make for you. We ordered about seven items off the menu, and every time the waiter came back, he asked us if we wanted to order anything else. Every time I told him that I wanted something "special," like the menu says. I wanted to be dazzled, with fresh ingredients and ingenious new ways of looking at Asian food, because, that's what the damn description says they'll do for me. And every time the waiter responded with, "okay, I'll tell the chefs." This happened four different times. I'd ask for something new and off the menu, and then he'd come back with something that was on the menu--it was driving me batshit insane. It would've been fine if the food was decent, but everything was crazy salty or sweet--I guarantee that place uses 10 gallons of hoisin sauce a night. I disliked Fu Manchu so much, that I've actually gone out of my way to tell my friends to tell their friends that its terrible. Its easily in the top five worst restaurants I've ever eaten at in my entire life, and just so you know, I've eaten at Applebee's, TGI Friday's, Ponderosa, Lion's Choice and Red Lobster. The only redeeming thing about my experience was a.) our waiter was excellent (aside from not understanding what I meant by saying "have the cooks make me something that isn't on your menu," and b.) some crazy Godzilla movie, which for some reason involved aliens, motorcycles and a baby Godzilla, was playing on the projection screen. Oh, and if I didn't mention before, this place sucks.

text: What a great little spot. As many times as I've driven down Route 70, never once did I notice this place... which is a shame for the owners. Their green tea ice cream with tempura bananas is a great dessert. The owners are always there and want to make sure you enjoy your dining experience. Beatles music always playing. Overall, I'd like to give this place 4 stars for being overpriced but it's just so good that I must give it 5 and just remind you that you may want to save it for special occasions. text: Yikes, I hate to give such a low rating, but....sushi lovers beware. We had the spicy tuna, salmon roll box lunch along with an eel bowl and what they called bulgogi (which normally is an unusually tender presentation of beef strips in a sort of teriyaki sauce, sometimes served with a kimchee on the side). Both the tuna and salmon roll were kinda chewy and not as moist as raw fish should be. The soup that came with the box lunch was extremely salty and overly and obviously peppery, like the pepper shaker fell in the pot. The grilled eel bowl was good, hard to screw that up. The bulgogi, I sent back because it was very chewy and just a big disappointment in flavor and no side of kimchee. I traded it in for shrimp tempura with vegetables. But tell me, is it a new trend for Japanese restaurants to take one shrimp, split it in half and sell it as a whole shrimp????? At any rate, with this being I think the worst review I've ever given a restaurant I will say some positive things. They were accomodating when I decided to send back the bulgogi, but they were not exactly overly gracious. The server was friendly, the restaurant nicely decorated. It's a steak restaurant as well and there's a Benihana-like side to the left as you come in with the grill table and chairs around for you to watch as your food is prepared. That I didn't try. But since I wasn't impressed with the sushi (the raw food) I won't go back.

text: I recently visited Kraftwork for my third time since their opening. I honestly feel bewildered by the negative reviews of the food. Everything I've eaten at this place has been good if not fantastic! Yes, the beer is great and the service is awesome, but it's the food that really shines for me. On my most recent visit I had an heirloom tomato salad that was dressed to perfection. If you thought you loved tomatoes before, this will take you to a new level. Plus, the short rib sandwich was flavorful, tender, just the right amount of spicy! I'm picky about my short ribs and this topped my list of faves. Finally, the vegetable board is nothing short of a work of art. With fresh seasonal veggies cooked to perfection and vegetarian "faux gras" and sesame paste (kinda like hummus?) with warm flatbread, the dish is not only incredibly tasty, but beautifully presented. Yes, the prices might be a little higher than what some are used to paying for "bar food," but this food is fresh, local, often organic, innovative and prepared with love. I'd gladly pay an extra couple bucks for that any day. The one down side is the noise level. Come here for eats and drinks, but don't expect to have an intimate conversation.
label: POS
