text: I have been to Boucherie twice, and neither time did it live up to the hype and positive feedback. One thing that particularly annoyed me was that both times I went, people in my party chose this restaurant specifically because of the online menu (food and cocktails), but when we got there, the menu had already changed. Sure, fine, I know this restaurant, and many others, change their menus, but if you're going to, you owe it to your customers to keep your online info UP TO DATE. Even if you change it that day. If you're going to use the Internet, keep up with it. So of course, both times I and others were disappointed before we even got our food. On my first visit, since the cocktail menu changed, I ordered a classic cocktail instead--a sidecar. The bartendar did not know how to make this, and actually suggested a type of brandy that one would never use in a sidecar. I have no bartending training but have been drinking this drink for years. A restaurant of this caliber should have a bartendar who knows how to make this kind of drink. The garlic aioli that was served with the boudin balls looked and tasted like it was plucked out of a No Name Brand store mayonnaise. My entree was served cold. And the Krispy Kreme bread pudding was dry and crusty, definitely nowhere near my expectation. Also, for my first visit, my companion got sick, so we had to reschedule our reservation. They had us down for 6:30, not 7:00 like we confirmed when we first called, so had we shown up for the initial reservation, we probably would have lost our table. On my second visit (to celebrate a promotion for a friend who chose this restaurant based on the online menu), the entree I had was good, and everyone was happy enough with their food. But those parmesan fries that people rave about? I thought they were just stupid. Regular fries dowsed in dry parmesan cheese. What is so special about that? We got the bacon brownie this time, and despite seeing bits of bacon, we could not taste it. Plus, the brownie itself looked and tasted like something you'd get at a school cafeteria, flat and just ok. I could buy two store mixes for the cost of that brownie, and they would have tasted better. And we did get the bread pudding again, which was just as crusty and dry as the first time. Finally, the cocktails on the second visit were just as bad. I ordered a drink with two sweet types of liquor, but could only taste bourbon. The other guests' drinks were also way too strong. I just wasn't impressed with this place and won't waste time going there again since there are so many other places with better food for the same price.

I've had real gumbo, and K-Paul's didn't deliver that, not even at nearly twice the price of other restaurants in the area, serving the exact same thing. Where normal gumbo is lighter in texture, with a rue-based sauce/gravy, K-Paul's on the other hand was soupy. I could have saved myself $8.50 by spending 50 cents on a can of Campbell's File Gumbo soup, because with it's beef soup type base, that's what it resembled to me. I was so disappointed. As a girl with a Gram from the south, who grew up eating delicious gumbo, K-Paul's version definitely didn't measure up. My husband had the shrimp po boy, and while it was ok, I wouldn't say it was anything spectacular, or anything you can't get at any number of restaurants in the French Quarter, cheaper and tastier than the sandwiches served at K-Paul's. Meh. The highlight of the meal was the onion rings. Sliced very thin, with a tasty batter, they were delicious. The line at K-Paul's is a bit ridiculous, too. When you walk in the door, a staff member hands you a paper menu listing lunch choices. You then take a seat, peruse the menu, then get in a LONG line to place your order. I stood there for about 25 minutes or so, waiting to place mine. It's a bit chaotic, as the staff taking your order are also responsible for making drinks at the bar. Seems like things would run better if they had a designated bartender and a designated order taker? Either way, the ordering process isn't pleasant, especially considering the food that results, which was mediocre as best. Finally, if you plan to dine here and enjoy a soda with your meal, please make other plans. They charge $2 for one can of soda. At a restaurant like this, which is supposed to be somewhat upscale, you'd think they'd offer at least a fountain drink with free refills, but not here. I won't be back. text: Buzz your 'coffee' woof. Monon's location and interior is nice if not a little on the weirder arrangement side. The staff is also very accommodating and friendly as well which is always a huge plus when you can talk shop with a barista when its not too busy. The real let down though is the coffee. Rather I should say espresso however since it comprises most coffee drinks as the main ingredient and I rarely drink drip coffee. My basis of judgement comes from a doppio shot of espresso I ordered there recently while I was in town and decided to check out the crowded Broad Ripple area. Upon receiving my shot(s) I was happy to see that a demitasse spoon was included. The look of the espresso however was very poor. The shot(s) were pulled semi normally, no real sense as being either lungo or ristretto. The problem was that the espresso was over extracted and burnt. Upon seeing the basic total lack of crema I knew something was wrong. It looked as if I had gotten a shot from Starbucks and sadly just about tasted like one too. The doppio was also way too hot I burnt my tongue slightly on the first sip. I also ordered a dirty chia latte. Hoping that the espresso shot would not offset the taste I was still thrown through another loop. This time the milk was steamed way too much. Being used to the pretty much standard microfoam used now to create latte art it was a shock to see dry foam. What was bad about it though was that it was uneven and way too sweet, something more expected to be seen from a cappuccino than a latte. In the end the dirty chia latte was way too sweet and the espresso was over extracted and burnt making it a huge let down. Since both the espresso and the steamed milk like in the chia are two major components of many coffee drinks it wouldn't really matter if they try to make things like a macchiato the traditional way because it would not be properly executed with the restraint and patience needed.

text: With only a few hours to kill in Santa Barbara, we decided to go straight to Stearns Wharf via State Street, which gave us a scenic tour of the local life. Not enough, but it gave us an idea. We even hit detour traffic because of the Farmer's Market that blocks off 400 to 500 State Street every Tuesday afternoon. Anyway, driving into Stearns Wharf got us excited especially since we saw the whole of it from our airplane window, as we began our descent into Santa Barbara Airport. At the end of State Street, you come into this rotunda where the Dolphin Fountain stands. I'd imagine it would be wonderful to walk the whole stretch of it but we had the car, sleeping kids and not a whole lot of time to spare. So we entered the Wharf, got our ticket and drove to the end of the wharf, where, surprisingly, parking was a breeze (pun intended). Maybe we were just lucky. They charge $2.00 an hour or a part thereof but it's 90 minutes free with merchant validation. We ate al fresco at the Santa Barbara Shellfish Company while enjoying the sights, sound and smell of everything around us. Indeed, the view of the beach, the town, and the mountains is spectacular. Then there's the activity of people from all walks of life in and around the wharf-- fishing, rowing, kite-surfing, sunbathing... But none of them were overwhelming. Yes, I do think their restaurants are overpriced and their stores are nothing special. But I appreciate that it's not too crowded nor too commercialized. It just is. If you're walking with little ones, take extra caution though. Parts of the wharf are just open, not fenced. Pelicans roam about the dock, maybe waiting for fishermen to get sloppy with their catch. And the wooded boards may cause a nasty splinter with a clumsy fall. Good thing I packed my trusty tweezers and sewing kit!

text: If I could, Patterson House would get 6 stars... I finally made it over last night to celebrate a friend's birthday. Service: The hostess took the time to scope out a seat at the bar for us as we were "first timers" and needed to get the full experience. Our bartender was fantastic. He was very honest in his recommendations and attentive without being overbearing. He even asked the birthday girl what kind of music she was in the mood for. His bartending skills were the star, though, as he paid extra attention to detail and ingredients (picking the perfect mint leaves, etc.) as he prepared our drinks. Drinks: I tried the Juliet & Romeo and the Pimm's cup. Both were heavenly...I really can't think of a better description. The drinks were served in chilled glass with uniquely shaped ice (my Pimm's cup had a long rectangle of ice that was the length of the glass and my friends whisky beverage had a big sphere of ice). In addition to the aesthetic quality, they did not melt as fast as regular ol' ice cubes so regardless of how long we spent sipping and savoring, we did not have to worry about our drinks becoming watery. Snacks: It's been said over and over and I'll say it again...the donuts! I don't even really care for donuts all that much and these were incredible. Value: Sure the drinks are $11...but for the quality/quantity, it is not a bad deal at all.

text: I went with four of my friends. We arrived at 4:00pm and were seated by a cheerful hostess. That's where the fun pretty much ends. After being seated, it was at least 8 minutes until we were even ASKED if we would like beverages. Water should always be brought to the table immediately. Nobody should have to sit around and wait for a drink order to be taken to get water, especially when everyone gets it by default. I don't care how busy a restaurant is. Three in our party ordered Strongbow cans and got them almost immediately. However, the other two members of the party ordered milkshakes. I have gone to plenty of diners and burger joints and never in my life have I had to wait so long for so little. Not only was the whipped cream on the top warm and starting to sag by the time we got our shakes, the bottom of the shake was completely liquid. That is simply unacceptable. The shake was $5, which doesn't seem unfair at all until you realize that unlike every other place that has ever served milkshakes since the dawn of time at a cheaper price, PYT doesn't give you the mixer in which the shake was created with bonus milkshake happiness. I understand that ice cream is expensive and all, but when one of your major selling points is milkshakes, you should live up to at least what your local corner diner can supply. The burgers were very delicious, albeit smaller than you'd expect or even make for yourself at home, and cooked to the proper temperature and with enough VERY fresh toppings to partially satisfy my hunger. However, I felt as though charging $1 for adding a tablespoon of hot peppers to the burger was a bit excessive and i almost missed seeing the two meager pieces of bacon on my burger. Then came the side item: kettle cooked chips. Like a pair of seasoned burger vets, two members of the party expected kettle cooked style hot potatoes or, at least, homemade kettle-cooked chips. What we got was prepackaged potato chips. I can see getting potato chips with a cold deli sandwich, but a burger NEEDS fries included on the side. It's not like it's more expensive to get potatoes in bulk than it is to get potato chips in bulk. The onion rings were advertised as some of the best, but they were pretty mediocre. The batter was delicious, but was often barely sticking to or properly coating the onions, so there were bits of burnt onion tainting the experience. They were also WAY too salty. After being spoiled rotten by Butcher & Singer's $5.95 lunch special and rapid fire service all summer and having made countless 'gourmet' burgers of my own in my life, I have to say that PYT doesn't really live up to all the hype going around about it. The service, while friendly, was too slow and the food, while tasty, wasn't really as filling. I am used to hyperbole and clever marketing when it comes to dance parties and club events, but that's the last thing I want when I am trying to get something good to eat. Now that I'm done reviewing, here are some suggestions. - Get a stand for the hostess. I know that sounds like a petty gripe, but it's pretty much standard fare for a restuarant so that people aren't wandering around trying to find someone to seat them. - Put all matching furniture outside. It's tacky when furniture is mismatched, especially when there are 3 different kinds of chairs at a table and only 2 of those chairs actually match the table. - Change your server assignment chart. Servers shouldn't have to run between the outdoor and indoor areas. Keep them to a section of the restaurant so that they can keep an eye on all of their tables at one time - Get your food and drinks out faster. It takes about 10 minutes to make a burger. 20 minutes is entirely too long for a burger of that size with no french fries. Add another bartender to the staff so that milkshakes don't come out with warm whipped cream and liquid at the bottom.
label: NEG

text: 1 star because I graced the building with my baptism. This is easily one of the most gorgeous buildings in the city. Stained glass abounds in the chapel and paintings abound in the Cathedral. The ceiling is studded with metalwork and the whole building is lined with alcoves, three-walled rooms dedicated to different sacred individuals and events. I'm going to stop describing it. I'm not arrogant enough to think that I can articulate the beauty here. Best time to visit is the middle of a weekday when it's empty. Come inside, let your eyes adjust to the darkness, and walk down the center aisle like you're the Pope. It's an experience. But no flash photography. That's not sacred. Despite the aesthetic wonders, Peter & Paul has one of the coldest, meanest, unfriendliest congregations in the city. Services here, especially those in the chapel, are awfully cold. I grew up mere blocks from this place. It was our family's parish & yet we never felt welcome. This is the heart of the diocese, which means that it is stuffed to the gills with visitors during Easter and Christmas. At all other times, there are much fewer bodies in the pews, and I wonder if the bodies that are there have any soul.

text: Do yourself a favor and go elsewhere. My sister and I took our Mom (who is legally blind) here for a trim, color & perm with Donna. It was a special treat for my Mom because she hardly goes out of the house since she is blind. When we came back to pick her up, we were horrified to see what was done to my Mom for $130.00. OK, I can't fault Donna for the Filipino-fro, since that is what my Mom wanted. But my Mom ended up with two-tone hair, and to add insult to injury, it was evident that no one even attempted to wipe off the dye on her skin, or brush off the little strands of hair from her face, neck and shoulders. I had to ask Donna once to brush the hair off, and then TWICE to wipe the dye off of my Mom's forehead, cheeks (yes, cheeks), and earlobes. After I helped my Mom get into my car, I noticed a ton of red dye behind her left ear. It was obvious that Donna did not even check or wipe once behind my Mom's ears. Had Donna bothered to check, she would have easily spotted the big gunk of red dye that is mucked up behind there. Seriously, she wouldn't have missed it. (My Mom's hair is cut really short.) I walked back into the salon and asked Donna if she typically sends her clients home with dye on their faces, necks, and ears. I told her about the dye behind the ears and asked her to clean it. Not only did Donna NOT apologize for not cleaning up, she had the audacity to cop an attitude and get snippy with me. She must have thought I am one of those quiet, demure, afraid-to-rock-the-boat little Asian flowers. Frankly, if she had just apologized at that point, you, dear reader, would not be reading this review here or on other user review sites. With the horrible economy and countless businesses failing, I can't fathom why service-oriented businesspeople would not strive to provide good service or take responsibility when they make a mistake (or three). There are other salons in the area and next time I will take our business elsewhere. PS: I am sitting next to my Mom on our couch while writing this review and just noticed how bad the haircut is. She has parts of her hair that are uneven, and areas that were supposed to have been shaved (behind the neck and behind the ears) but were not. There is also red dye INSIDE her RIGHT EAR! Jeebus, this almost makes me wonder who the blind person was in that salon this afternoon.

text: Coming from a family of picky New Yorkers and New Jersey folks, we're spoiled with delicious NY style pizza. We ordered a medium pie, first asking for Capicolla on our pizza, which the guy told us they were out of. We asked for prosciutto - they were out of that too. We opted for salami and Italian sausage. Add a small drink and a bottle of water, it was $21 bucks. I expect to pay a good amount for a high quality NYC pizza in Indianapolis, but, we felt like we were scammed when our fresh pizza arrive at the table and we realized that we got less than a few toppings for our money. There were probably two small pieces of salami (which tasted like a slightly glorified pepperoni ala Papa John's) and a few medium-small pieces of Italian sausage on each piece. I should have just ordered a cheese pizza, I would have had an equally as uneventful pizza experience. Even with great NY Style pizza, cheese can be a heavenly experience, but, here, it was boring and uneventful, and the money you pay for the lack of toppings was a joke. The staff had little to no personality, and they seemed more annoyed that we were there than anything else (we were the only customers, and it was game day and the middle of the afternoon). I'm disappointed by the quality and I have no intention on heading back to Bella's, cause there was nothing beautiful about the experience whatsoever. (Thank you...I'll be here all night.) I'd advise going down to Giorgio's on the circle for a better NY pizza experience.

I'm not sure if it's the bulgar, or what they've added to it, but it is ridiculously good. I quite often order a side of the tabbouleh and it eat it plain, sometimes adding some hot sauce to kick the flavor. But in and of itself, it is excellent. To me personally, the best tabbouleh I have ever had. Everything else seems good -- I have only tried the chicken, no beef/lamb. I typically get the greek salad (heavy on the tabbouleh), sometimes with chicken, sometimes not. The hummus (with oil & yes, more tabbouleh) is also good. Falafel was good, but nothing amazing. One of the things I enjoy most about this restaurant is the staff. The older guy who runs it seems grumpy most of the time, but he knows his stuff. Believe it's his wife running the cash register, she seems very nice. The hand-done chain stitched "GYROS" on their aprons is a thing of beauty. If you're nearby (or just on a really bad tabbouleh jones) give it a try.

A lot of people rave about the green tea frap at Starbucks, but it's got nothing on this! So delicious, and while I'm sure it wasn't healthy, it seemed less calorie ridden than it's counterpart. The focaccia also was delicious. I'm a fan of fresh baked goods. throw in some quality cheese, rosemary and tomatoes and I'm sold. It was perfect for something light. The atmosphere was nice, too. The outdoor seating always seemed to be packed the three days I was in the area. Inside the area by the fireplace was nice for those who wanted to grab a chair to watch tv, sit at the bar to navigate their laptops or grab a table to peruse the paper. The side room allowed for small meetings or conversations to take place without intruding much on those around them. Finally, the staff was friendly. It never ceases to amaze me how there are places where service with a smile seems dead. This is not one of them. text: I can't believe I've lived here for so long and hadn't been to the Parthenon until a couple of weeks ago. I've walked past it and sat outside it so many times. I have to say though, that I'm glad I waited because for the past fifteen years or so, the Parthenon has been undergoing renovations of various kinds. There was scaffolding all over the outside for many years, and during the 1990s, they were gilding the giant statue of Athena inside. I was pretty cheeky going in, and asked if they had a student discount. They do, it's half price, and not posted, so you have to ask, and you'll get in for $2.50 with a student ID. The bottom floor contains a gallery, which has some beautiful paintings, but not really any from renowned artists. There is also a small temporary exhibit space behind the main permanent gallery. What I loved best was the collection of photographs and memorabilia from the Nashville Centennial Exhibition. It really gives a sense of the era of great exhibits and shows the incredible lengths Nashville went to to celebrate its centennial. I don't remember anything quite as lavish for the bicentennial. The Parthenon is just one of the buildings from the exhibition, which spanned all of Centennial Park and much of the surrounding area. The exhibit is really informative about the planning and scope of the project and the photographs are truly amazing. The Athena statue is truly overwhelming in size and the captions tell you everything about the inspiration and making of it. You can spend a couple of hours here if you go through carefully and read all of the information available.

text: Had dinner here tonight with a friend who just moved into the neighborhood. There was a line out the door at Hook's across the street, but it turns out this place is better -- at least for sushi. The sign above the front door, which reads "the art of Asian cuisine" hints at the creativity of Sushi Rock's makizushi. For example, the Lollipop Roll (salmon and crab) comes wrapped in a thinly peeled cucumber rather than a traditional seaweed nori, and its fresh, clean texture is complemented nicely by a tart ponzu sauce. Another inventive item is the Sushi Rock Tuna (tuna, crab, asparagus), a rice-free roll that's lightly battered and tempura-fried in a pair of sauces. Speaking of sauces, they're a big part of what makes Sushi Rock's feel unique -- from the pineapple sauce on the Hawaiian to the spicy aioli on the grouper to the "dynamite action-packed cream sauce" on the 007. Everything we tried was fresh and flavorful, and the service was friendly and professional. Our only minor quibbles are that the place is REALLY dark -- I could barely read the menu -- and they were out of conch, but happily subbed in crab on our Island Volcano Roll. The only thing we tried from the regular dinner menu was a traditional gyoza appetizer, which was fine but not extraordinary. Nitpicking aside, I'll definitely be back. (2/4/2009)

text: Holy crap. Total splurge, but I loved every dollar and minute of it. I love trying new things, so tapas is always a good bet. We got: - Chorizo Pamplona. Mmm...I didn't care for the three little side things that came with it; give me straight chorizo (and okay, the bread too) and I'm good! - Aged manchego cheese with truffled lavender honey-- my husband actually ordered this, and I ended up LOVING it more than he did. I wanted to order another one but I figured I needed to try more on the menu. However, I didn't want it to end and was quite sad when it did. - Oysters with cava gratina and grapefruit espuma-- I'm not a fan of grapefruit at all, but this was amazing. Perfectly balanced shot of oyster on a spoon (comes with three). - Almejas con chorizo (clams and chorizo)-- can't get enough of chorizo, and add clams to it, and I'm in heaven! The broth was so good; I was sad the bread was gone, and I thought briefly of drinking it, but alas, more dishes were waiting... - Piquillos rellenos (crab-stuffed peppers)-- #^%#$%#^& two of my favorite things, rolled together, on a hot sizzling plate with some kind of sauce. I almost swooned; it was SO good. - Revuelto (shrimp & wild mushroom shirred eggs)-- this came with truffle toast, whose smell catapulted me right back to Yard House, which threw me back home in California. It was like my kind of comfort food with a twist. Awesome, awesome dish. - Amada's Empanada (spinach, manchego cheese, and artichoke)-- kind of like the one at Alma de Cuba, meaning it was freakin' good and I loved it. We ended the savory portion of our meal with the "Entrecute a la Catalana" (prime sirloin with catalan spinach, membrillo, and goat cheese). It was good, but was less shiny compared to the other dishes. If we had this earlier in our meal (say, one of the first dishes), it definitely would have stood out more. But because this was the last thing, my taste buds were on overload and the only thing that stood out was the goat cheese (which I don't particularly care for, btw). Dessert was the leche frita (fried vanilla cream, chocolate hazelnut sauce, and hazelnut ice cream). Perfect pairing; it wasn't too sweet. There was this fried thing that went on as garnish, and I really appreciated it, as it provided a bit of salt to balance the sweetness of the rest of the dish. Obviously, this is a crapload of food for only two people, but what can I say...my husband and I love good food and we were starving. ;) Next time, I'd like to try the chef's tasting menu. Aaaaand I'm so taking all my visiting friends to Amada! P.S. MAJOR bonus points for the bag hooks they have at the bar tables. It's little things like that make me happy.

text: ** NEVER GO THERE. TWICE THIS YEAR DR RIPPIE HARMED MY ANIMALS WITH VACCINES I SPECIFICALLY TOLD HIM NOT TO GIVE** Last fall I brought a young kitten with Cerebellar Hypoplasia to this vet for an infection. He was stray and had a serious calicivirus. Being in rescue for years I know that a CH kitten with an infection at this young age should have been allowed to heal first. I specifically told Dr. Rippie - DO NOT VACCINATE HIM I WILL BRING HIM BACK NEXT WEEK - three times. The kitten was coughing, had discharge and inflammation throughout his resp system, and a high fever. Dr Rippie stepped out of the room and came back a few minutes later with a syringe and gave my kitten the FVRCP vaccine despite my clear and repeated instructions not to. My kittens fever skyrocketed that night and his motor skills went out the window. He laid in a bed unable to move for 2 days and I had to take him to another vet for treatment. Recent a family emergency demanded that we board our puppy. She had already had the distemper, rabies, etc shots but needed a bordetella. I specified this and he gave her everything but. My puppy hallucinated and barked for a week straight. Google the neurological/psychological effects of having a puppy over vaccinated and it will show aggression and mental instability as a side effect. He's not even the worst this place has to offer. Thinking perhaps DDr. Dubin, one of the doctors, might be okay, I took a cat there. He is a bit of a quack and all too happy to do surgery unneccesarily. I took a polydactyl cat there who had standard poldactylysm ... one thumb on each hand, no real complicating factors... for a simple wound on her foot, far away from the thumb. The doctor said he would have to amputate the thumb to treat the wound. He also said he would amputate the extra digit from the other hand too, for no good reason. He said he always removes polydactyl thumbs. I took her for a second opinion and was told it was completely unneccessary and absolutely should not be done. After a round of CLAVAMOX, Noni is perfectly healthy and still has all her digits. This vet was very checked out, and talking in a dazed out voice the whole time he "examined" my pet.. which consisted of looking at the paws and making little noises. He never listened to her heart, checked her other vitals or did anything else you should do with an infection. He didn't even prescribe antibiotics, just pressured me to set up the surgery "in a week or so" ... leaving ample time for unmedicated infection to travel to her blood. The only person in this place who has a moment to spare or a friendly word is the receptionist. I don't know her name but she is very nice, and I thank her for her compassion toward both of my cats.

text: Sushi is an art! That means: A sushi chef should know how to craft his art , with the right ingredients and portions, and display with pride. Well, at Mochi - disappointedly it's a novice artist working to just sell the tiny-empty rolls. I love Japanese cuisine from traditional to very modern- flare, sashimi to sushi. Mochi is a very basic Asian -Vietnamese restaurant, which serves sushi, it's not a Japanese restaurant. With all do respect , calling Mochi a Japanese restaurant is a grave insult! There is nothing Japanese about the menu, it's very Americanized with the typical -fusion-meals like the all mighty Teriyaki bowls and Tempuras. We ordered 4 different rolls only to be disappointed with the content and portions for the price we paid. The taste- AHI was nowhere to be found, it was in such small portions that made me almost send it back, but I didn't. Another one of my favorite rolls= SPICY AHI, which was nowhere near the pepper, not enough fish, not enough flavor, I had to reluctantly ask for Sriracha on the side, even with the big lump of wasabi! The Wasabi was very MILD! Hamachi Kama, which is usually succulent and prized was brushed with teriyaki sauce, what a disgrace! Tempura roll- tiny shrimps didn't qualify for the roll itself. Miso soup tasted like the ones I buy in store, packeted. Nigiri- very SMALL and dry. We ordered one of the special rolls which had minute amount of nori and rice, and even smaller amount of ingredients! Anyhow, not so surprisingly, they have a Vietnamese menu as well. Maybe , they should just stick to calling MOCHI a VIETNAMESE restaurant and not a Japanese one!!! Although I shouldn't expect a lot from Midwestern sushi places , I was still a little disappointed with the Mochi sushi makers! They are doing the sushi experience Injustice! THE SERVICE: was slow, and kind of confusing. The server didn't seem to understand the menu ... maybe she was new, or ? I know nothing beats the real -deal in Hawaii , where Japanese food is #1.
label: NEG

text: I love lounges, mainly because unlike bars I never get kicked out of them. Even though Philly is cold and the people aren't as beautiful as in South Beach (hEllO, where I live), I like to visit Philly for its lounge scene. Tria exemplifies this. I have been to Tria many times in the past, but this review is about a recent visit. After an incredible dinner at Little Fish, I wanted cheese and wine. Ya, where else in Philly is as perfect for cheese & wine as Tria? Plus, I was on a date, which meant I wasn't paying, and my date was big enough to scare off all the people giving me attention. We stopped into the Tria near Rittenhouse Square. Please, the Gayborhood Tria is nice too, except late at night when there are call-trannys on the corner of Spruce and 12th. For real. Sometimes they start as early as midnight, which is just devestating when I'm trying to enjoy a nice glass of wine. The staff is lovely at Tria, all very 'scene.' You know, that Philly Urban Outfitters thing. They helped us to our table and my date ordered two glasses of dessert wine. I can't remember the names. hEllO, I drink to get drunk, not to collect a mental rolodex of wineries. And I was sooo impressed, because one of the glasses was out of stock, and the bartender graciously gave us a different type of dessert wine for free. When does that happen? Never in Miami, that's for sure. In addition, we ordered two cheeses, which came with bread, in a beautiful little display. I suggest the L'ami Du Chambertin. Don't worry about pronouncing it, the staff is chill and won't make you feel stupid. They didn't even hit on me while I was there, which surprised me, but then I remembered that they're all hipsters and seem to date within that scene. It's like... romantic segregation. Overall, my experience at Tria was superb. I will be back, whether Tria wants me or not. This has been a Review by Fulgencio

text: i wanted to see what all the fuss was about. here's this hot new restauarant that, a la dr. dog and not much else, is making a name for itself even outside of philly. well let's start at the beginning -- the host was, simply, a tiny douche of a man-ish thing. if you take all the negative aspects from the stereotype of the cosmopolitan gay dude, you get him. same thing if you take all bad from the archetypal bitchy hostess: unkind, unhelpful, unfriendly and uncalled for. he soured our birthday dinner from the start, unfortunately. i don't know if he's gotten a big head because the restaurant has some great press or if we were treated kind of second class because we were the only people under 25 not carrying plates. this is a problem i don't much run into in philly, but it truly pisses me off. however, our waitress was super, super enthusiastic about the food and the background of james. as great as that was to see, i didn't want an obviosuly pre-fab tale cooked up by the owners about what free spirits but serious foodies they are, having traveled here and there learning to eat this way and cook that way. just give me a sentence, tell me the customs and specials and let me soak the rest up. in any case, the food was yummy. the pasta in duck ragu was fab, with the pasta itself thin as a breath. the meat was great too, but nothing as impressive as, say, audrey calire's mushrooms. and the portions were quite large as well, everything was splitable, but there is a $2.50 spilt fee per plate. plus, there was an hour wait for our meals. all praise be to the man going 'round with the bread basket! none of the desserts looked impressive, so we left them in favor or some wine elsewhere. so, as good as the pasta was, and it was good, the place just did not give off a homey, welcoming vibe. maybe it's philly's lot to be nasty in its "we're not nyc or dc but rather stuck in the middle" insecurity. but i rarely experience such a crystallization of that like i did here. from the host-creature to the decor to the other diners -- who were the type you'd find at alfa, the type you don't want to know, the philly-yuppie plus.

text: I went to this place with my aunt several months ago, and the horrible experience I had has not yet left my memory - possibly because it was unforgettable. First of all, the seating outside is way too overpacked - I found myself negotiating out of the way as the staff/other patrons were walking by. I felt like I was playing a game of restaurant frogger, if there ever was one. Second of all, the service was WAY TOO SLOW! Maybe it was the live guitar music in the background, but the staff went about at a much too leisurely pace for the number of guests that were seated at the tables. We had to ask for extra chips and salsa 3 or 4 times before someone finally brought it over. It felt like we were pulling teeth! Thirdly - you might have guessed it, they got the order wrong. My aunt ordered a chicken fajita platter, but they brought her beef. When we pointed out the error, we told one of the employees who brought the waiter to our table. The waiter had the most arrogant attitude, we could tell that he was patronizing us. He abruptly said something to the effect of, "Ok, let me know the order so I don't bring you the wrong dish next time!" Sensing the bad attitude, my aunt started objecting to the overall bad service we'd been receiving, at which point, the waiter started escalating his tone of voice, and the back and forth continued until we asked for the manager, and he replied, "Ok, I am the manager, if you don't want the food, you can get up and leave....Okay, leave we're not serving you, we're not serving you!" Mortified by the loud argument, I sat there in my seat looking down at the table, too embarrassed to raise my eyes to meet those of anyone else sitting a few feet away. Now, my aunt is a very strong-willed individual and doesn't take flak from anybody, and being in the Santa Barbara food service business herself for over 20 years, began lecturing the manager about the poor service, how the customer should always be given the benefit of the doubt, and that it was basically unacceptable for him to behave in that manner. In what I could best describe as a match of verbal chicken, the manager, realizing his error and visibly shaken by the notion that the customer would stand up for her rights (and perhaps aware that this debacle could create some bad publicity), suddenly became conciliatory, with words like, "Ok, I don't want you to leave, let me go get your right order." At the end of the meal, he even offered to put the entire tab (about 50 dollars between two people) on the house, but we couldn't accept. Looking back on that meal, my impression is that while Carlitos may have been a quality restaurant at one time, the service has degraded after the management saw that they could bring in high revenue from the steady stream of tourists that walk down State St., wooed by the ambiance of outdoor seating and live music. If there's any lesson to be told, its that a restaurant is not just about the food or the location, its also about the people and the service. Keep that in mind on your next restaurant visit, or you might just end up in the middle of an unexpected verbal war with restauranteurs who don't know what that means.

text: After a number of enjoyable dining experiences at Ted's in the Atlanta area, I looked forward to our initial visit to this Ted's in Indy and extolled the virtues to friends who joined us for dinner on a Friday evening. I was surprised to discover the size of this location was a fraction of the size of the Atlanta locations I had frequented and I was taken aback at how crowded and stuffy this one felt upon entering and while waiting for our table. After a 30-min. wait for a table, we were seated and the waiter took our drink order. So far, so good. However, shortly thereafter, the evening began to quickly head downhill. After being advised the shrimp cocktail (unique Ted's offering with a wonderful sauce and one reason I had selected this restaurant that evening) had been removed from the menu, we scrambled and ordered salads instead. At that time, I inquired about the advertised prime rib of beef and after checking on it, the waiter assured me there was a nice very rare piece available. After receiving our salads, we placed our dinner orders (or at least attempted to). One gentleman in our group ordered the BBQ Bison Short Ribs and was told they had "run out". He then tried to order the Bison Pot Roast and once again was amazingly advised they had "run out". He then asked, "before continuing this game, what else don't you have that is on the menu"? The waiter responded that "everything else was available" and recommended the Bison Meatloaf. We joked about the third time being the charm and he wound up ordering something tertiary on his list. Subsequent drinks were very slow in arriving the remainder of the evening and this was surprising given the relative short distance from our table and the bar. About ten minutes after our entree orders had been placed, the waiter returned and apprised me that they had also run out of the prime rib- yes the same prime rib which I had inquired about earlier and was assured there was a piece meeting my desired specification of rare. Flummoxed, I went ahead and ordered the Crab Cakes as we all sat back and tried to make the best of this growing comedy of errors. As everyone else in my group dined on their food, I waited...and waited...and waited for my crab cakes. Approximately fifteen minutes after everyone else had received their food orders (and subsequently were nearly finished), my crab cakes arrived. The wait was certainly not worth it as they were incredibly dry and overall the taste of all the food on my plate was quite vapid. To the waiter's credit, he did not charge me for the entree, but a $20 credit could not come close to salvaging what had become a very disappointing experience. After finishing the meals, we sat around conversing for about 30 minutes and as a result were one of the last groups in the restaurant to leave. For some reason (normally we would have exited after finishing dinner), the manager decided to approach our table at that point and offered his apologies regarding our inability to enjoy a number of entrees from their already-limited menu. He mumbled something about "making things from scratch" in an effort to explain the mysterious lack of key entree items- no explanation was given relative to the slow service and other operational problems at his restaurant- and offered some credit for a future visit. He may have felt compelled to say something to us as we had yet to vacate but the true reason for his presence in our area was revealed a few seconds later as the group in the booth behind us had a number of complaints which he absorbed. The token gesture of $10 credit for each of us (that is, each of the couples) was typical of how this place is run and I only hope my travels take me to Atlanta or elsewhere as the only chance I would use this $10 credit is if I am at a Ted's in another city. Add Ted's Montana Grill - Indy Northwest location- to your boycott list. There are literally hundreds of other restaurants in town where you will actually receive fair value for your dining dollars and won't have to worry about a third of the entree offerings disappearing early in the evening.
label: NEG

text: Well, what can I say? Yelp let me down. I steered my group here based on the excellent reviews and we were uniformly disappointed. It wasn't horrible, but it certainly didn't live up to it's hype (or it's price!). We dined in the Bistro side, as we weren't wearing jackets, and there was a $4 surcharge for the three person band playing there (they were pretty good). The entree portions were quite small and they didn't come with any sides. The typical fish entree seemed to run approximately $29, but tack on $6 or $7 for a side salad and $7 or $8 for a vegetable side. Still, people were hungry after the meal. I myself got two of the baked oyster appetizers (at $10.95 each). They were pretty good, but the oysters were quite small and were covered with a lot of filler. The oysters were much, much smaller than the oyster shells they arrived baked in, leading to my speculation that perhaps the oysters did not actually originate from these larger shells. Luckily, the large shells provided a bigger substrate for increased filler, so at least I didn't starve. The oysters baked with the artichoke were the best of the bunch. The service was also stilted. Our main waitress seemed to have good intentions, but she seemed very new and unsure. She repeatedly had to go speak with her boss who contradicted what she had earlier told us. A trainee waitperson might be a little more acceptable at Olive Garden than at an "institution" where your group is plunking down close to $600 for a meal. Another disappointment was the Cafe Brulot (at about $6.75 per) after dinner coffee - which I read was quite excellent. Unfortunately, they would only make it if more than one person wanted it, and due to the lateness of the evening and the caffeine content, I was the only person that wanted any. The waitress said she thought that they could make it, but, again, the waiter boss made his showing to give his negation of the idea of a single order of Brulot. So, I will forever be unknowing as to the greatness of this coffee. But this incident perfectly captures my entire Arnaud's experience: again, for a party that nearly shelled out $600 and a dude that was willing to pay almost $7 for a cup of espresso, it would have been nice if allowances could have been made to accommodate my request for a solo order of Brulot. It was also one of her favorite places for a late night dinner when she was in college too. If you ever are in Tucson and have a hankerin' for some AMAZING Mexican food, you have to give Mi Nidito a try. I recommend going early or late because during normal dinner time, they are B-U-S-Y! It's not uncommon for there to be a 30-40 minute wait. But the wait is DEFINITELY worth it. The nice thing about Mi Nidito is that they are open until 2:00 am! I wish a few good restaurants in Phoenix would follow suit. My favorite is the #3 combination. It includes a taco, tamale, a cheese enchilada, and beans. The chips and salsa are great. The salsa can be a bit spicy, but they do have a mild warm tomato paste base for those who like a milder flavor, you just have to ask for it. I also like the rolled chicken tacos (basically big taquitos), which are really good too. The margaritas are great, although I'm usually the driver so I stick to iced tea. text: The wait at Stanley can be considerable, but the food is well worth the wait. I came for brunch and had Pecan Pie Ice Cream Malt, Egg Stanley, and Poor Boy Sliders. I would normally have a cocktail at brunch, but the shakes/malts looked far too tempting so I had to have one. I had a Pecan Pie Ice Cream Malt which was a pretty great way to start my meal. It was thick and had bits of malt. It could have been colder though as it got to room temperature much sooner then expected. Let's talk about the Eggs Stanley. It's essentially eggs benedict with fried oysters: english muffin, ham, fried oysters, poached eggs, and a hollandaise sauce. The oysters were crunchy and tender in the middle, eggs properly poached and the hollandaise was creamy. Decadent and rich I could only handle about 4 bites as there was other things to try. The Poor Boy Sliders consisted of a three mini sandwiches: fried oyster, korean BBQ and a club. Of the three the korean BBQ was the best. It was korean style beef with kimchee in french bread. Tangy, sweet and a little spicy it was a real winner. Sure a bit out of place in New Orleans but good food is good food. The fried oyster Poor Boy was pretty good as well with a slightly spicy remoulade sauce. The club was pretty basic and should be ignored when there are much better choices available. I read that others has poor service, but when I went it was pretty busy and I had good service. The only thing that was awkward was figuring out who exactly was my server. Once he introduced himself everything was peachy. I would certainly return to Stanley for another meal and if you haven't been I would certainly suggest stopping by.

text: Moving to Nashville in July opened up the position of ophthalmologist for me in my world. I had received the suggestion to check out SEE in Hillsboro Village for a possible replacement but when I visited SEE, I was rubbed the wrong way. The Pro's: The storefront is modern, bright, and attention is most certainly paid to the eye wear. In fact, trying on frames has to be the best part of getting glasses, even if it is just for reading purposes. I love the fact that each frame is unique to SEE and made in Europe generating that exclusive sort of feeling inside. The salespeople in the showroom demonstrated ambition and dedication to selling you some frames. The Con's: You must have a valid prescription within the last two years, which I do not. Also, I overheard the ophthalmologist is only in the store on Tuesday and Thursday so they suggest you visit a Walmart or Pearle Vision to have your eyes examined then "SEE" them for your frames. The cost of the frames was ridiculous! Everything I saw was in the upper $200.00's except for the $90.00 sunglass wall. Although they are in a convenient location and have some pretty frames, I do not think I'll be taking my business here to SEE.

text: My mom had dropped into town and I figured I would takd her out for lunch... looking on yelp I found this place and it sounded pretty cheap for thai. Had a little trouble finding the new location on 105 right beside sai woo. We went in and the staff was friendly along with everything being beautifully decorated. But when I first looked at the menu everything was regular thai priced (12-18) so I was a little disappointed offering to pay for lunch when it was expensive. We ordered the Shrimp and Pineapple with sweet mayo spring rolls for an appetizer ($12) A Yellow Curry with Potatoes and Chicken ($15) and lastly Pad Thai with chicken ($15). First thing she brought out were two tiny spring rolls on one plate, and my face instantly dropped until she said "vegetable spring rolls ON THE HOUSE!" Nothing makes my day more then free food. They were delicious. I'm not huge on veggie spring rolls usually but these were great, they came with a sweet sauce with cucumber. carrots and peanuts in it. Then the Pad Thai arrived, not the appetizer but I didn't mind I was ready to dig in. I was amazed by the size of the Pad Thai because everytime I go for Thai in Edmonton it's a measly portion meant for a 5 year old. Decorated with lettuce and an orange we devoured half of it before the curry came out. The currys taste was a bit disappointing, not as flavorful as some of the curries I have tried before. You could also see an oil layer on top which was a bit of a turn off but it was still decently sized and came with a portion of rice. LASTLY, the spring rolls finally came. I wasn't a huge fan of the sweet mayo mixed with the pineapple. It was just too sweet and rich for my tastebuds. Service was great my water was never empty and the waitresses were extremely nice and friendly. Overall it was a great experience ($44) and I would definitely return because we had TONS of leftovers. Oh yeah and..CASH ONLY !! Ps Sorry I don't know the actual names of the dishes they are way too weird to remember... I didn't write them down this time sorry !

text: The negative reviews suggest that there are some pretty consistent problems here, because I had a similar experience. So-so food, and poor, if friendly service. For the price, you can do a lot better in the neighborhood. I was there on a restaurant week Wednesday with four friends. We ordered a pretty large swath of the menu between us. The deal was that each diner gets two of the first two courses, followed by a main course and dessert. That's a lot of plates to carry, so I was unsurprised that everyone's first course did not arrive at once. After a few minutes, however, I was surprised that some of us had two dishes, while others had none. Sharing is nice and all, but people ordered what they wanted to eat. The second course was more of the same, except that instead of a five-minute wait for everybody to have at least one dish, it was at least ten minutes. You know what's more annoying than sitting without food while your friends either eat or let it get cold (we had the opportunity to try that both ways)? Having the waiters constantly show up to ask how you are doing, refill your water glass, or arrive with one plate and an elaborate description how good it is when two other people still need food. The main course arrived more or less at once, which for me was the best thing that could be said about it. My companions seemed to like their food. I had the rabbit risotto. It had bones in it. After the third bone in about six bites, I sent it back, which was a first for me. As far as the food goes, almost everything I ordered or tasted was a little soft on flavor. I liked the two feta appetizers and the flash-fried haloumi cheese. On the other hand, the aged manchengo cheese with white truffle honey was served with cold, stale bread, as were several other dishes (I understand saving some money, but why not toast it to cover what you're doing?). Aside from bones, the rabbit risotto had been overcooked into paste. I wish there was a good Greek restaurant in Philly but this isn't going to be it.

text: The decor is a mix between Las Vegas and NYC, and the food very average. I went there for dinner during restaurant week 2010. I ordered the stuffed pepper starter, which was flavorless - there was supposedly ham inside but all I tasted was crunchy bread crumbs and a little spiciness from the pepper. Next, I ordered the roasted chicken, which was cooked pretty well and did taste good, but the potato au gratin was too cheesy and overpowering. For dessert, I ordered the pumpkin spiced cake - the warmness was nice, but it should have been sweeter. My friend who ordered the tuna tartare said it was pretty bad, and another who ordered the salmon entree said it was okay as well. I tried a couple bites of the chocolate mousse which was really good. The bottle of Malbec we ordered was good too. I will say though that the service was great - this seems to be a consistent theme here in Philly. The decor is nice, but a tad over the top, but nice nonetheless if you are in the mood for that.
label: NEG

text: Miette is a really cool shop located on Magazine Street in the same block as Juan's and Aiden Gill. Miette has cool and trendy clothing and accessories. If your cool and trendy, or are just trying to be cool and trendy, this is the place for you. Some of the items I looked at had labels written in Korean. Apparently many of the items come from Korea and are for smaller statured women. I am a giant, and a dude, so none of the clothes are really geared towards me, but they did look cool. There were also some kid's onesies including my favorite one said Poo Dat. There is lots of jewelry and other cool items from local artists. Several light fixtures made from old Mardi Gras beads are also for sale. The owner was really cool and helpful and answered all of my questions. If you're in the market for some really cool clothing and your a small girl Miette is for you. If your not a girl there is still plenty of cool jewelry and other household items.
label: POS

text: No matter what your recipe calls for, you'll find it here. Fresh or dried, whole or ground, pure or mixed into tantalizing combinations, you can purchase anything from anise to Za'atar to flavor your food. You'll get a whiff of the wonders within just by walking by this little Italian Market store. And the prices are quite reasonable--often better than supermarkets and you get a higher quality product. A design book I was reading recommended installing open shelving in the kitchen, decorated with brightly colored packets of paprika (among other things). I had no idea why anyone would want to do this until I marched into Spice Corner to get paprika for a recipe and was confronted with not one variety but four. Who knew? And they were quite festive. Also, if you're a tea drinker you'll find plenty of variety in that department as well. I think they might carry coffee beans, too. I particularly love the ancient blue wooden carousel horse that sits outside the entrance, a plaintive note tacked to its pole: "ouch! my back hurts. please don't ride me. neigh - neigh - neigh." My dogs always try to pee on that poor arthritic steed. How embarrassing.
label: POS

text: When I was in Edmonton last week for a family reunion, my grandfather suggested the family meet for dinner at this restaurant for dinner. I called the restaurant from my cell phone before we left the hotel to ask for directions. I called three times -- the first two tries I was hung up on. Thinking that this must be a fluke, or simply my cell phone losing connection, I tried again. The third time, someone answered. I asked if he could please give me the restaurant's address. His response? (And this is verbatim ...) "No, why should I?" Feeling flustered, I asked if I had reached Zambelli's the restaurant and the man concurred. Now, feeling completely stunned, I asked him why he felt it was necessary to be so rude to a complete stranger who was simply asking for directions. His response was that because he could see that I was "calling from California" that he was justified in assuming that it was a mis-dialed number. This all leads me to wonder, (1) how on earth can a restaurant stay in business with such atrocious customer service, and (2) has this imbecile ever heard of cell phones? Unfortunately, because most of the family was already there, I still had to go to this place for dinner. The man at the front was clearly the person I had spoken to on the phone, and I he also appeared to be the owner (honestly, I can't imagine any other scenario by which a person like this would still be employed here). I confronted him about his poor behavior, and only after my insistence did he offer any sort of apology, and even then he only uttered the word "sorry" to make me leave him alone. Needless to say, while I refused to do anything that would ruin the dinner for my grandfather, I could not stomach the thought of eating any of the food here, so I can not comment on that. Our waitress did a fine job and seemed like a sweet girl -- I felt bad that she was working for such an awful person.
label: NEG

text: Normally I only review restaurants. This is my second departure from that rule. It's because if you love Hot Sauce WMD is your spot. The guy has his own line of sauces called Bobby Boulder which come in three heats across four flavors. Kelly is a tomato based sauce - which an extremely fresh start and a slow burn on the finish. Cleo is Carrot based - sweet and interesting flavor-wise. I'm really excited to try this on eggs... but I could see myself just drinking it from the bottle as well. Spike is a Jamaican jerk sauce - peppery and herby. It screams to be used on poultry and will probably be a feature ingredient in my 2010 rib recipe. Tony is mango based. Sweet - but not my favorite of the two. However - I think it wold be killer as a bar-b-que sauce. Need to taste it again when I get in that sort of a mood. The shop will also custom make sauces or labels for you - something I'll be looking forward to testing out in the spring. Non-WMD brands of hot and bbq sauces are also carried ranging from mild to "you-have-to-sign-a-waiver-it's-so-hot." (No - I mean literally... like he sells food additives...) Rob (the guy behind the counter when I was there) was extremely friendly and helpful - walking me through what he had and letting me try a bunch as well. Prices are mild for what you're getting - most prices around $5-6 a bottle. If heat's your thing - or you're serious about grilling - check this place out.
label: POS

text: Monday Night @ 7:30PM and the Grand Sierra has 300 of Choice Hotels International licensees and an additional 50 of Choice's professional hotel staff members there for a Regional convention. There were 5 in my party and another 13 in our other group. Plenty of others were in Briscola as well as Fin Fish and C.Palmer's Steak. I gave my name to the Hostess who said we could be seated in 10 minutes after they reset the table. Fine- we went to the lounge area where we sat for 25 minutes total, even after going up to the Hostess twice more to check on seating progress. The young hostesses were overheard commenting about how they didn't know there was a group of so many in the hotel(2 more in addition to ours) While in the lounge area, not once did a cocktail person come and ask if we wanted libations! We were seated at last and our waiter brought menus and wine list as well as explain about Briscola. We were watered and breaded and cocktails ordered although I was surprized that they only had Bombay Saphire,Tanquery and Beefeaters gins. The food presentations were artful and excellent and the quality of food ranked quite high in my book. Charlie Palmer and his mgmt. team took over this restaurant when GSR got rid of Dolce( previously reviewed by me). They have done a great job of redecorating the room and making it a pleasant, well lit and excellent addition to Reno's dining scene. Not an inexpensive spot, but well worth a visit and experience. I would say, however, that the final timing between dessert and final check being requested was too long. Also, just describing dessert items while holding the dessert menus in hand was a little complicated as we had no way to remember all the details- just give the menus to the patrons and explain items if there are questions. These comments are put forward in a constructive manner for a good restaurant to just improve a little bit. We will return.

text: I think the my fellow yelpers are being quite generous with their reviews for The Latest Dish. I have been here for food and drinks on several occassions and the experiences have ranged from OK to bad. The food is decent, I actually cannot say I ever got anything that was bad, but on the other hand I never got anything that was really that great or memorable. The menu is very approachable, with the usual suspects and proteins/flavors that can appeal to just about anyone. This can make for a boring dining experience, but when choosing a restaurant for a group its a safe bet. The cocktails are weak and small which loses big points in my book, but I do believe they have an extensive beer list. I personally do not drink beer so this does not benefit me. The service has usually been the biggest deal breaker on most occassions. Servers are usually slow and unattentive, and the bartender on a few occassions has been outright rude. Overall if you are going to dinner with a fussy eater or the family, The Latest Dish might be an OK idea because it is basic food that is appealling to the masses. But dont expect a life changing dining experience, actually don't expect much at all....
label: NEG

text: So, I went to Desi Chaat again this weekend to be even more pleasantly surprised (hence, why the one star upgrade.) 1. Friendliness - the guy behind the counter was super nice and really helpful in figuring out what I wanted. The co-owner (I'm assuming) was outside on his phone, yet, when I stepped into the restaurant he still greeted me with a smile and a hand. 2. Cleanliness - everything looked organized, neat, clean and just presented well 3. The food - I am really growing to like chaat. I got the samosa chaat this time. It had crisps at the bottom, chickpeas and potatoes on top of that, some mint leaves, and a few sauces including a yogurt and an onion-type chutney. It was extremely good although at points I had a hard time figuring out what exactly I was eating. I order VERY spicy and it was nice and spicy, but I still think that they could do more. 4. The price is right. It is very inexpensive and one container of the chaat with a mango lassi will cost under $9 and will feed two not very hungry people or one and a half hungry people.

text: A friend and I went to see a cover band last night, which I was skeptical of to begin with. If your place favors cover bands the service better be damn good. Regardless, the only thing enjoyable about this experience was the company I was with. The service was AWFUL! The decor meh and the food below average. I worked in the restaurant industry for over ten years and know that a simple smile goes a long way. Granted I learned this through trial and error, but that's beside the point. The token blonde bartender was freaking rude and didn't even have the decency to acknowledge her customers. I understand when you're busy there is little time for common courtesy, however, an "I'll be with you as soon as I can" can really do wonders for a tip. Not to mention, I peeped several staff members texting while working in the middle of a busy Friday night. So bad. We ordered a turkey burger with fries. The burger itself was bland and the fries were way under cooked. I mean c'mon! Can't even get the fries right??? I will say this though, the turnip soup (or whatever root veg it was) was pretty tasty. All in all, lame. I MIGHT go back for a second try if they have a decent happy hour.

I decided to get a burrito bowl with chicken, rice, beans, lettuce, pico de gallo, and guacamole. The guacamole was made prior to it's arrival at the restaurant; not fresh at all. Three strikes and this place is out.

The only thing I have had at Rippy's are the ribs, which were super tender and fall off the bone. The upstairs area is a great location for watching the tourists and homeless musicians. At times the service leaves a little to be desired, but because of the sheer popularity of the place, I really don't expect much better from them. Overall, check it out if you have not been there or if there is an event at the Sommet center.

text: **First my disclaimer. I'm not a serious golfer. I don't speak the lingo and don't even pretend to be a poser. People make fun of my old school clubs and I rarely stay even slightly sober on the course. That being said, I can at least hold my own on the course and know how to have a good time out there.** I don't visit Boise and immediately think 'Yeah, I'm in Boise, let's go play golf' because there are too many other fun things to do in that town. But I've played twice there over the years and both times were at Quail Hollow. I'll have to say this is one of my favorite courses I've ever played for the following reasons: 1) the staff is cool (except the guy who gave us shit for combining our two four-somes on the 18th hole - he was a tool) 2) the course is well laid out and fun to play with some really amazing scenery and views 3) it's not a tough course overall but there are some challenging holes 4) everything is clean and well maintained My only recommendation for the folks at Quail Hollow - get a bar!

text: As a hotel (just the physical place), this could easily be a three-star property -- maybe even four, but let's not get carried away Here's the deal: for our most recent stay, we were met with okay service at the desk but several hidden charges, i.e. parking, crappy breakfast, etc. Elevators are a nightmare -- as in, seriously frightening.... Then, trying to find the room, there is horrible signage to direct you to it (not to mention the hallways are a little ratty). Finally, the room: surprisingly not bad looking, if only they took care of it better. Apparently anything with a fan here is noisy: the bathroom light/fan AND the ptac unit -- not to mention all the noisy people coming and going past our door. Also, I don't trust that anything here is clean -- the coffeemaker certainly wasn't -- but I'm kind of weird about that anyway, so I can't really say that it's worse than other places, especially at this price point. Overall not a terrible experience, but I'd compare this place more with an Econolodge/Ramada than anything else. I really wish there was something a little nicer in the downtown area, besides Hotel Congress, which is in a totally different segment.
label: NEG

text: Usually I don't take notice of how a meal is plated/presented unless great care has gone into it, or extreme sloppiness. Unfortunately for Pizzicato, the presentation was a disaster. Although it is considered a grille, you would never know it by the way it is set up. We were greeted by the restuarant manager - a short very friendly Quebecois gentleman. He offered to take my jacket - something most restaurants won't do. Our table had a very classy arrangement with modern looking cutlery and placemat setting. Our server was prompt but very inviting and friendly. I ordered an orange juice and Carolina ordered a coffee. We were both impressed by the coffee. Not like someone came over and gave her a cup of coffee or gave a carafe of coffee a la Perkins or Denny's. It came in coffee press with brown sugar and warm milk on the side. Carolina said it reminded her of Italy or even in Mexico. To start we with given corn bread muffin to share with a side of butter. I ordered the Spanish Skillet and Carolina had the eggs benedict. They both came out with excellent presentations. It wasn't plastered all over the plate but rather they were separated by their own dishes. Carolina's "eggs benny" came with a side order of mashed potatoes. Both of our dishes came with a side order of fruit. What I found interesting was that the fruit dishes was solidified by what looked like a smidgen of mashed potatoes. An excellent idea to prevent plates from shifting. Next time Carolina is in town, we will definitely visit here for dinner. I would strongly suggest this place for a romantic evening. It is worth the 5 stars.

text: I've been a convert ever since i started shopping at wegmans in college (they have one in state college, pa, YAY!). So once i moved back to philly area i was disappointed there weren't any. So excited! Now, if you've never been you're thinking, "it's a grocery store, get a grip". Well you know what? Go to one, check it out and tell me it's like your usual market cuz it's NOT. Don't forget to get a wegmans card, like most other ones it's free and you get good deals. Some things are higher priced than others but their quality is always high. Faves? there are so many...but to name a few... *Tiramisu: so d*mn good. I just want to eat the whole thing and NOT share...comes in 2 sizes but beware...it's delicious with huge chocolate shavings. *Chocolate cake: they have small ones that look single sized but can easily be share amongst 2-4 people if you're nice and want to cut calories. It's super chocolaty delicious. *Cheese section: i am now in heaven. so many choices, so many imports...all so YUMMY. plus it's usually next to the olive bar (mmm) and they have pate too (double MMM) *Buttertop wheat bread: absolute favorite sandwich bread, they're sold out a lot of the time but if you can get yourself a loaf, do so. *Cheese bread: omg...bread that has cheese mixed/melted in. It's crusted with it and when you cut into it there's cheese everywhere. Toast this up and OMG. Cheesy bread heaven. *Wegman's Mango soda: different, not too sweet. And when on sale? 69 cents for a 2 liter bottle. *International section: choices for all different countries and pretty authentic ones too *Meat section: i love getting steak here. You can either get it from the counter or they have them vacuum packed. *Beer section: yup that's right. A market in PA that sells BEER! haha Lots of choices and the prices arent bad. You can grab a six pack or even single bottles depending on the brand. *Market Cafe: if you dont feel like cooking or are just hungry they have sushi, pizza, sandwiches, wings, chinese food, salad bar, soups, and all kinds of other goodies. The list goes on so i'll stop. But seriously. So awesome.

text: We were visiting friends in Oldsmar who had heard nice things about this place, so we decided to try it. The atmosphere is very warm - lots of dark wood and stone - and the service was attentive and friendly. We weren't as impressed with the food. We decided to share two appetizers. The cheddar-spinach dip was bland and the tortilla chips served with it tasted stale. The guacamole was prepared at the table, so we knew it was fresh, but it lacked zip, and the portion was too small for the $11.00 price tag. My husband ordered his flat iron grill medium-rare. The first one they served was well-done and the second one was practically raw. They finally got it right the third time. He enjoyed the sweet potato fries more than the steak. The glaze on my spit-roasted pork tasted like it had too much bourbon it, and it overpowered the flavor of the meat, but the sweet potato mash was delicious. One of our friends ordered chicken breast stuffed with spinach, goat cheese, artichokes, and sun-dried tomatoes and raved about it. Our other friend was very disappointed with his salmon, which he said was on the dry side. The server suggested we share a couple of orders of tumbleweeds, which are crispy onion straws served with a spicy dipping sauce. They weren't greasy and we all agreed they were excellent. We shared two desserts, fried banana caramel cheesecake, which wasn't as tasty as it sounded, served with vanilla ice cream, and apple-walnut pie, served with cinnamon ice cream, which was okay but nothing special. Our friends mentioned our disappointment to the people who recommended the place, and they said they had been here twice for lunch and enjoyed the burgers and wraps very much. We might try it for lunch the next time we're in the area, but based on our experience we would never make a special trip here.

The prices have gone up a lot in recent years. I understand what inflation is, but the fact is you're paying more money for less food. Rolls used to be larger and not so hurriedly constructed. All in all this place has an atmosphere like it just doesn't care anymore. The all you can eat special isn't even advertised on the menu anymore, but from what I hear, it's now $24. text: After much debate as to where to go for lunch, I overheard the word cajun and convinced my family that we should head there for lunch. There aren't many cajun restaurants in Boston after all, and this would be more fun than Italian or Mexican. From the moment I stepped inside the place, I noticed the New Orleans feel that it had. From the hanging balconies that hung from their ceiling to the Cafe du Monde-branded items, and the alligator head in the corner. It screamed cajun everywhere we looked but without looking tacky, weird or overdone. Instead it was a nice, fairly quaint atmosphere. We promptly ordered fried artichoke hearts to share as an appetizer and I got myself an order of seafood-free Jambalaya. I actually found out, after inquiring about it, that their lunch-menu Jambalaya is fish and seafood free, unlike their dinner one. Perfect, I obliged. As for drinks, I decided to get a traditional Cafe au Lait, which is coffee blended with some chicory and some milk. It came instants later and was great. Good depth of flavor and smooth as well. The artichoke hearts were quite tasty as was my jambalaya. The Jambalaya was spicy, not too rich and had bits and pieces of sausage in it. It was actually pretty good, much better than I expected. We thought about desert but weren't hungry at that point and decided to step out instead. The service was phenomenal and on top of their game and the prices were more than affordable. The place was clean, not too loud and well maintained. This was a great lunch and a place that I'd love to return to in the future when in the area.

text: Our office came here for our annual Christmas luncheon, which is usually a pretty nice affair. The person coordinating it had a 'good experience' at Terrace View, and I trust her opinion, so I was excited about eating here. Wrong. From the rickety tables and chairs to the concrete floors to the hey-you're-still-in-a-park (it's within Citygarden) 'industrial' restrooms to the waiter detritus everywhere, Terrace View isn't the most comfortable place to eat. I tried to ignore that and ordered an iced tea while staring at the interesting Adam & Eve sculpture in front of me. The lunch menu is pretty short--mostly sandwiches. The server enticed me with the promise of a cayenne-laced carrot soup, so I went for it and the oven-baked mushrooms with goat cheese. Sounds good, right? Wrong. The soup came out looking orange, smooth, and appetizing, but had three distinct flavors: raw carrot followed by watery heat followed by an unpleasant not-quite-sour aftertaste. I put my spoon down after I realized that I was actually forcing myself to eat it. The oven-roasted mushrooms weren't any better. What they call a 'small plate' was really just that: an anemic 5 tablespoons of sliced shiitakes, topped with a few dots of goat cheese. The cheese was warm; the mushrooms were cold. I left hungry. My co-workers ordered sandwiches and almost all of them had something 'off' about them: "The burger was good, BUT way overcooked." "My chicken sandwich was good, BUT the bun was kind of burned." "My eggplant sandwich isn't a sandwich--I need a fork!" The service was fine, but I feel bad for the Terrace View--this place has 'amateur hour, ready to fail' written all over it. Maybe I shouldn't feel bad. A good restaurant should have the opportunity to move into a location with so much potential.
label: NEG

text: N. To. The. O. First of all, why the flying hell is this place freezing on a goddamn blisteringly hot Florida afternoon? Homies, the world "moderation" needs to enter your vocabulary when it comes to you A/C. It was like I was entering the Arctic Tundra rather than a cavernous dining establishment in a Tampa neighborhood that I affectionately refer to as OAKLAND ON CRACK, or Ybor City. Ybor cannot be fixed. I should not pay more than $40 to eat ANYWHERE in this festering hellhole in which all establishments are wisely closing up shop and fleeing before Satan ascends and takes over. Ugh. So we came here, because the menu looks good and my boyfriend is something of a burger snob and he really wanted to try theirs. As we entered the restaurant, I felt like I was walking into a cave. It seems to me that this restaurant was trying for a fancy dynamic, but instead wound up with a great deal of wasted space that gives it a sort of desolate feel. Perhaps it's different when it is busy, but we arrived at 7:00 PM on a Thursday and the only people around were drunk dudes in suits at the bar. The booths are obnoxiously large, and for some reason just the 2 of us were seated at one. Our waiter was friendly enough, though he was definitely of the snobbish variety. Again, FOR WHY? I am eating in a freezing cold cave and some douchebag thought it would be a good idea to play Top 40 hits from 1995 as my dining music and you are SNOBBY? Ugh. I ordered the diver scallops for an appetizer. Which is essentially ceviche. And awful. This crap was not cooked in lime. This crap was thawed out and then thrown into a martini glass. Then they took out a squeeze bottle of lime juice and just drowned everything. I will be the first person to enthuse that lime is the new lemon, but PLEASE. I was puckered. My boyfriend ordered the Manhattan Clam Chowder. Being an absolute tomato-hater, I was surprised that he actually said it tasted decent. I took a few sips, and I had to concur. Wasn't terrible. Our entrees arrived before we were even halfway through our appetizers, which is always a bad sign to me. His burger hopes were immediately crushed. Soggy-city. Topped with Gruyere cheese and caramelized onions sounds wonderful, but it tasted like mush. A mushy sandwich is terrible. At the very least, the bun should have been toasted. My grilled salmon was decent, and tasted fresh. Unfortunately it was a bit dry, and I am still trying to figure out how one could screw up salmon. Especially when I am paying $20+ for it. Really, it's mystery that I may never solve. The vegetables were okay, too. But....ugh. Next time I'll just get takeout from Red Lobster because I hate to say it, but I think they do it better. I realize that, as a native of Tampa, I should be thrilled that folks are really trying to make this area a mecca of good eats. The problem I have is that they are going about it the absolute wrong way. Teatro is pretty much the embodiment of disillusionment. If it's good, I will pay tons of money for it. If it's mediocre and even marginally overpriced, you should stop serving it. Ugh.
