I don't know if it was just an off night, but my experience was NOTHING like those depicted in the other reviews. It was a Saturday night around 1am. We were a 7 top. The room we were in was about half full. Giving this place the benefit of the doubt, it must have been our waitress's first night, because it took 30 minutes to get our drinks and an hour to get our over-priced and over-cooked food. When my friend ordered a hefeweizen beer, the waitress looked at him like he had just ordered a glass of hamster pee. Ten minutes go by and she asks "What did you order again?" My friend replied in kind. Another five minutes pass and the waitress returns with the bartender in tow and this time the bartender asks what he ordered. Thank God she understood. Perhaps the waitress couldn't hear him clearly over the loud and terribly cliche 80's pop music. We looked over to the table next to us and noticed that the couple that was seated right after us had left with their drinks still pretty full. I guess they weren't as patient as we were. In the end, we should have folllowed their lead. Onto the food- We ordered every slider that was on the menu that night - Duck Confit, Smoked Trout, Falafal and Oyster. The Duck Confit was dry. Something as simple as a housemade aioli could have made this one a winner. The Smoked Trout was ok. The Falafal was pedestrian at best. The Oyster was probably the best one. It actually had some kick. However, all the buns were overbrowned/on the verge of being burnt. The fries were overcooked too. All in all a pretty poor effort. Regardless - $5 for 1 slider or 2 for $8?!?! Are you kidding me? What a racket. These guys must think they have a choke hold on the late night eats, so they have license to stick it to you. We also ordered the Chorizo Nachos. Way too light on the chorizo. Perhaps I wasn't drunk enough to appreciate them, but I thought they were not any better than nachos at a place like Houlihans. For something that sounds like it is exploding with flavor, it was pretty forgettable. As far as the quality of the food they put out - MAYBE I was there on an "off night." There was foreseeable potential that, perhaps with a better execution, could have been realized. But no matter how you cut it, all the food we had was way over-priced. Local hosts Nina Cardona and Anita Bugg report the news with smooth, practiced voices, and they provide local stories as well as national news. While Nashville's list of locally broadcast shows isn't extensive, it certainly provides the local flavor you'd expect from Music City. Among the local programs is Bluegrass Breakdown, which is hosted by Dave Higgs and features some pretty impressive bluegrass acts. The coleslaw tasted like it had been made fairly recently, since it had some crunch to it. However there was no zip to it(needed pepper or something else) and it wasn't creamy enough. It also irritated me that they served the coleslaw on TOP of my meat on the sandwich. I'm not sure if that was intentional or just a plating error. text: On my yearly crusade to the Big Easy I always come with a list of "must dos", this year a genuine absinthe experience was on my list and this place did not disappoint. We ducked out of the rain into the muggy and dank bar, the dim lights set the stage perfectly for our tasting. We plopped down at the bar and ordered 2 kinds of Absinthe. The bar tender was a complete joy and gave us the full experience. She talked all about the libation and its history and the proper way to serve and enjoy it. She poured ours over the sugar cube, to a match to the cube, and let it burn. The eerie blue flame was mesmerizing as we both let out a quiet, "oooo". Next she let little droplets of water fall through the melted sugar creating a swirl effect in the glass which is called "seeing the green fairy". She even put lights under our glasses so we could see it better. Finally we could taste. Mine was a bit sharper, the anise flavor was very apparent, my friends was much smoother and sweeter. Overall the adventure topped my list of favorite things to do in the city. It is such a nostalgic and unique thing to do, I highly reccomend paying a visit and seeing the green fairy for yourself!

text: Fast forward from my last update almost 6 months...a lot has changed in 6 months...WHAT is this white stuff on the ground?! Oh yeah, I moved from California (no snow) to Indianapolis (snow) :-) While I really do prefer to shop at the smaller, independent hardware stores, I was told that I needed to get driveway salt...and fast! As I got there at 7:00 a.m., there must have been about 20 employees milling about...then I realized they were having what appeared to be their daily rah-rah session :-) One very polite young man asked me if I needed any help (maybe he didn't want to attend the rah-rah session). I told him that I was new to dealing with the white stuff and asked him to suggest a product to use since I was getting conflicting information -- ice melt...or salt? He asked me some questions as to the type of surface that I was trying to clear (new or decorative cement, etc.) and explained that some products stain, and so forth. We discussed a few things and he directed me to the Prestone Driveway Heat. I looked at the huge bag with dismay and he suggested that I buy both the large bag and a smaller container and refill it as necessary. He also told me that between the 2, I should have enough for the entire winter. As I was checking out, he asked me if I needed anything else and suggested a few items. I then remembered that my daughter borrowed my ice scraper and said I needed a new one...he ran back to that section of the store and ran back with 2 options...the Cadillac of scrapers or the Kia of scrapers...since I usually park in the garage, the Kia would do :-) I still prefer the neighborhood independent hardware store, but I appreciate the convenience of the large warehouse store on occasion too.

We told our server and she brought us more, but they were only slightly better. I had the brisket enchiladas, and they were average at best. I ordered a side of black beans, which were kinda like mush. Didn't eat them. A few of my friends got various tapas and felt the same way. The food is not terrible, but I have no desire to go back. I also thought the prices were high for what you get. Agave does have a good bar. It's small and hard to get a drink if it's crowded, which it always is, but they have a great tequila selection. text: I went to MaryLinn's with my roommate after she got engaged. This was our first time looking at wedding dresses. I was horrified by how the sales ladies behaved and treated us. We walked in and there were four girls behind the desk, one of them on the phone (obviously personal call) and the other three chatting together. We stood there for several minutes until we finally interrupted the girl on the phone to tell her that we had an appointment. She told us to have a seat and we waited quite a while for someone to come over and speak with us. The first thing they said to us was that we couldn't take any pictures. They asked a few questions about the ceremony and budget, pointed out the different sections of the store, and told my friend to pick three dresses to try. She picked three, tried them on, and we were told to leave. We'd only been there a half hour and my friend really wanted to try on a few more. My friend was told she would need to make a second appointment if she wanted to try on more dresses. We hung around to look at more dresses on the racks, and by the time we left there were still no other customers in the store. I don't understand why they were rushing us out if they didn't have another appointment. We went back a second time and it went like this: "Hi, I have an appointment" "Ummm I don't see anything" "Well I called a few days ago and scheduled an appointment" "Well, ok I guess go pick out three dresses" "I liked the Alvina dress I tried on last time and I'd like to try that again" "Ok you can only pick two dresses then" Seriously? I don't know how this place is in business. I felt like they treated us with such rudeness because we're young, but after reading the rest of the reviews it seems this is just how they operate. I don't understand why someone would want to make such a big and important purchase in a place they're made to feel like a burden to the sales ladies.

text: Cochon provided an excellent lunch, but our server almost killed the meal. I'm very forgiving when it comes to waiters - I realize how difficult it can be. Our table shared the carrot cake (super huge!), blueberry cobbler (great crunch biscuit), and sherbert (very creamy). We enjoyed them all. text: This is the Westin's hotel restaurant and it can be accessed through both the hotel main lobby and through Liberty Mall. Obviously, there is never a wait for a table and you can go there for a relatively fast sit-down lunch. Service is typical for hotel restaurants, attentive, polite, thorough, with continuous refills on beverages, bread basket, etc. The dining room is spacious, clean, modern and quiet. Lunch menu is nothing impressive. A serious offering of salads, make your own salads, and chose your own protein, dressing, etc. along with a few carb-laden appetizers, soups and about 7 sandwich choices round off the offerings. Also typical of a hotel restaurant, menu is very expensive - most main ticket items start at $12 and up. Portions are Massive with a capital M. You could make three meals out of the salads alone. The side salad with your sandwich - could be a salad entrée on its own - so you get what you pay for. Lastly, typical of a mainstream hotel restaurant, the food is nothing to write home about. Ingredients are fresh, but the menu is nothing new and nothing you wouldn't be able to get at any other restaurant nearby for a fraction of the price and at half the size. This place is good for a business meeting lunch, where it's more about the business than the food. If you're staying at the Westin, I'd avoid this place and urge you to leave the confines of your hotel and meander out where there are a plethora of fantastic eateries at your fingertips.

text: Seems to be picking up on the Bistro wave, but La Minette is a great arrival...across from Beau Monde, that corner of 6th & Bainbridge is starting to look a wee bit Parisian. This place is so new you can still smell the paint drying in the tastefully decorated bathroom. A splash of red cushioned booths and bright yellow walls, the long narrow dining room was packed with couples and families enjoying a Friday night. Menu was a good spread of french bistro classics with a few stunners thrown in to boot. They sell carafes of wine, which a couple seated next to us was liberally helping themselves to; the guy was leaning over his date's plate a scooping up mouthfuls of potatoes off her chicken...it must've been that good. as you can tell from such detail, seating is tight. My wife ordered the Summer Tomato Tart; a small selection of tasty ripened beauties served on a flaky, buttery disc of pie-dough, it was a great dish. Accompanying it was a bit of greens laced with a tarragon vinaigrette. I had the Flammenkuche...which I found out later is THE dish of Alsace. Think of it as France's answer to pizza margarita; the caramelized onions and crispy pork lardons were served atop a flatbread laden with creme fraiche. I read another review of the place who complained about the mushiness of the dish, but it seems they corrected and served it up crispy. While good, I'd probably cut it up before serving...it was hard to eat with a knife & fork, so I eventually opted to go pizza fingers on it. Several other entrees looked good; I had my eye on the Lamb Shanks that were pouring out of the kitchen. We were stuffed though and went with dessert only, a Pot de Creme served with lightly sweetened whipped cream. The Pot de Creme had a mocha-like firm custard, not the chocolate bomb we were expecting, but very smooth...kind of like the after meal coffee in a cup.

text: well, I should have guessed I would walk away from this place slightly confused when it's called 'Water Ice' as opposed to??? So I wish this place luck (and apparently it doesn't need it, as there are multiple locations out there) - and for what I think they lack in for product that I dig, I did like that everyone working there seemed friendly enough. but I think I will be moving on to the gelato shop down the road

text: We scored a bonus night with 2 guides, Midian and Jennifer (or Julia? I'm sorry, I can't remember!). The guides know their stuff and tell the history of the people, places and ghosts of New Orleans with great panache. It's definitely not a scary tour, but I got a few goosebumps listening to the horrible acts former New Orleanians committed against each other. FYI - there is A LOT of walking, and it's not the slow, take your time to hear a story walking. It's fast paced to get from site to site, but while you walk, the guides aren't telling any stories, so you're not missing anything if you're a little bit behind. The only negative is that the guides had a LOT of stories to tell, but we could only visit so many places in 2 hours. I wish they offered a monster tour of 3-4 hours to get more stories in. Don't miss this tour if you're in New Orleans and like to get spooked!

text: I called Quarter Smith looking for antique or estate engagement rings and spoke with Ken. Since I don't live in the NOLA area, I asked about Quarter Smith's hours. Ken stated that his store is open from 7:30-2:30, Tues-Friday, but not on Saturdays. Since I wouldn't be able to get over there on a weekday, I asked if it would be possible to make a Saturday appointment. Ken laughed a little, as if this was a strange request, and said maybe, but that if I had an idea of what styles I was interested in, he would be happy to email pictures of any appropriate rings he had. I stated that I did know what I was looking for and described some styles to him. He asked me to send him an email with that information, anything else I could think of, and pictures of rings I liked from online or other stores. Since he seemed sincere, I went to the trouble of sending the email and pictures. He acknowledged my email, said he had some items that would interest me, and then I never hear from him again. ?!? I was in NOLA recently (having emailed Ken about a week before) so I stopped by his store and saw that it looked unused and nearly empty! When I got home, I checked the Quarter Smith website, which still appears well updated. However, the website states that the store is open from 9-4pm, Monday through Friday and Saturday by appointment. So what is the real story here? Beware this place, they will go out of their way to waste your time and are not at all interested in working around your schedule to serve you as a customer and make a sale. It's been at least a month and I've never heard from Quarter Smith.

text: Drinks here? Fine I'll tag along. Dinner? NO WAY! Looking for a place with good burgers in the CWE we decided to try Sub Zero since my mom wanted to go there anyway for drinks. They advertise "New American Burgers" on a neon sign out front, so we figured we would give them a try- turns out it was a bad idea. Not only were they really expensive ($11-$19), but they were just plain bad. I got the "breakfast burger"- I usually love the breakfast burger concept it's basically your normal cheeseburger with a fried egg on top. Theirs was gross. The meat tasted weird- not like rotten or anything, just bad seasoning. Would never order again. My husband got the cajun burger. First they cooked the shit out of it- it came out a bit more like a hockey puck rather than a burger- this was to pass as medium rare? He sent it back and received a more normal looking burger- but not til after the waitress came back with a message from the kitchen telling us it looked overcooked because of the cajun spices. Sorry, that excuse was not going to pass on this one, cajun spices don't account for the inside being cooked to powdery dryness. Anyway when he did get it back properly cooked he said it was waaaaaay salty. This is a guy who normally doesn't complain about anything at a restaurant- this was 2 complaints on one burger. He hated the burger, but liked the sweet potato fries. Mom had 2 sliders- 1 was a classic cheeseburger and the other was a veggie burger. She said the veggie burger was way better than the classic burger, but would still not order it again. We also got side salads with our burgers, those were pretty good. I loved their ranch dressing (I have a weird thing about ranch- I think they mostly suck, but when it's good it's sooo tasty good). Also my husband ordered an Unagi (eel) roll. He said it was alright- but in all fairness we did just move from Hawaii 6 months ago. It's going to be nearly impossible to get sushi in the midwest as good as it was there. Overall I'll never be eating here again- well maybe I'll try some other sushi but that's it. They do have about a billion different vodka drinks though, and for those I would go back. Atmosphere is a bit posh- very hipster vibe. Loud bass driven music on the speakers, dark lighting with blue neon all over the place. Not exactly my scene. Ice bar is pretty sweet though...

text: I have lived in South Jersey and worked in Phildelphia for the last 15 years. Prior to that it lived in NYC and rode the subway. So I have a slightly different perspective from people who compare it to SEPTA. In my view PATCO should have zero to few issues because it's only 1 line that end to end runs about 13 miles. How late can you be on average when the longest trip is scheduled for no more than 25 minutes. Having said that I find that this is a poorly run system. The cars are old which causes a lot of problems when the weather is bad. Many of the seats have lost all the cushioning and you sink down into a trough when you sit. Many cars leak when it rains rendering usually the seats toward either ends of the car unusable. In the winter in order to maintain the schedule they will run shorter trains at rush hour creating crowding issues and delays since everyone waiting for the end cars have to walk further up the platform. Off hours the schedules are unreliable at best especially on the overnight. More frequently then should be he case trains get cancelled without any notice or announcement. They very rarely communicate delays when they happen, they might apologize the next day via the barely decipherable public announcement system or a printed note left on the seats. The cars are not cleaned very frequently if at all while they are in service. They instituted the automated fare collection system called the Freedom Card. With that you can add specific denominations but not less than 20 dollars. They will not accept credit or debit cards to purchase individual ride tickets AND you get all your change in those heavy dollar coins. Try walking around with 18 dollars worth of dollar coins in your pocket. To add insult to injury they empty the fare vending machines during rush hour. You have people trying to get to work forced to use one machine while they service theonly other one in the station. I have had issues where the machines can't process credit or debit cards then you're stuck talking to someone on the customer service phones some of whom are nice others of which, not so much. They are OK if all you care about is getting from South Jersey to Philly in less than an hour. But there are far too many minor issues that are not addressed.

Do you have an IPA? Sure. But only on tap. Hm. So really, you don't have one. (and honestly, no printed beer list? Might want to add that to your cocktail menu, Tazia!) So we order our food. Only it turns out they gave us the wrong menus, so we can sort of get what we wanted, but with a few minor additions because apparently, we got next week's. Sea bass, crispy duck, sweet potatoes and green beans. Only the duck comes with green beans and the waitress didn't think to tell us that. She was nice, but maybe new on the job? text: I love pork. Perhaps it's because I am a native son of Iowa, the top US producer of pork. Perhaps it's because at the university I went to, we crowned a Pork Queen each Fall and for me pork has become a Freudian web of desire, excitement and a drive to be satiated. Whatever the reason, I crave succulent roasted pork. It is visceral and real. Unfortunately finding finger-licking, awe-inspiring roast pork in my neck of the woods is no easy task. Oh yeah there are abundant claims of mouth-watering porky deliciousness. But they are usually wishful-yet-empty boasts for pork that is dry and tasteless. Happily I have found a place nearby where I can reliably "get my pork on." Granted it is only available on Saturdays, "until it's gone," but hey it's a guaranteed fix. Saturdays Luigi and Giovanni's roast a pig and offer a roast pork sandwich that warms the core of my Iowa-born-and-bred heart! Yummmmm! Hot, drippy porky goodness.

text: This is quite possibly the worst cajun creole food on the planet. I can only say possibly because it's the worst I've ever had and I haven't been to every cajun restaurant in the world. But I'm pretty sure I could get away with making the claim of it being the worst period without catching too much flack. Where to start? I had some questions before ordering and the young lady (YL) behind the counter wouldn't let me finish a question before blurting out an answer to what she thought my question might be. YL: Are you ready to order? Me:I have some questions. Can you... YL: I can give you samples of stuff. Me: Thanks, but what I really would like to know is... YL: It's all on the board if you want to try it. Me: What is the... YL: blah blah blah blah blah I finally gave up. The chicken and mushroom etoufee tasted like someone had rushed to make milk gravy and accidentally spilled some rice in it. Imagine gravy made with too much flour and then undercooked. This is so far from a roux, that I thought we were at Bob Evans. The seafood gumbo looked and tasted like beef barley soup, complete with shredded beef and rice instead of barley. Still can't quite figure that one out. We sifted through it, looking for something that resembled seafood in the peppery beef broth and finally gave up. The jambalaya was watery, bland and had no cajun flavor characteristics. It was literally like someone made uncle Ben's rice and at the last minute said, "darn, we forgot the sausage and all that other jambalaya type stuff. Quick, throw some in it before you serve it." The crawfish casserole was...um...well, just read about the jambalaya above and replace "jambalaya" with "crawfish casserole". Shrimp Po'boy. It's supposed to be on a hard bun, not a soft one. The shrimp and the side of hush puppies had the same flavor. I'm assuming there is deepfry'omatic 3000 in the kitchen where everything goes in one end and comes out the other. It was about the only edible thing in our meal. Certainly the only thing we finished. Tea is out of the fountain, not brewed and tasted like a mud puddle. Long story short, it get's one star only because you can't give a place negative stars. For $7 less, we could have gone to Yats and had larger portions of the best cajun creole food outside of New Orleans. No offense to Mia, but this is not what cajun creole food is supposed to taste like. We really hoped this would be good, because it's so close to our home compared to Yats. We'll happily make the extra drive. I need to add this after the fact. i went to their website and looked at the menu. The pictures of the dishes are nothing like what was served to us. Extremely misleading to say the least. Edited on 6/27/08 to add the following: I'm not affiliated with any restaurant, let alone a competitor of mudbugs. My taste buds are just fine and able to differentiate between all kinds of flavors, textures and consistencies.. When I was there almost a year ago, both the food and service were horrible. Perhaps in the last 11 months they've gotten their act together. If so, kudos to them. They had a long way to go and it wouldn't have been easy. Judging by the other reviews, you'll either love the place or never go back a second time.
label: NEG

text: I suppose most people go to U.S. News and World Report, not Yelp.com, for information on colleges. But, for those of you who are reading, you might find this useful. I started my college career at U Arts as a jazz guitar major, and, if you want to be a jazz musician, there is no better place in Philadelphia to learn how. The guys who teach lessons and ensembles are some of the finest musicians and teachers in the country, and if nothing else, their genius forces you to recognize your own inadequacies, and to improve them. But, but, but --- the liberal arts classes were a joke. Granted, I suppose this is true of most art schools and conservatories of music; they find barely competent staff and pay them a minimum to deliver uninspiring lectures that few people care about, all so the school can be accredited. Sure, that's the way it goes. But, really, if you're paying to be in a class, and if you're being forced to spend your time there --- time you could be using to master your instrument --- then the school should at least provide you with a useful instructor. (Okay, one more caveat: the majority of art and music students are so wildly apathetic about learning to write and solve math problems that, even if U Arts brought in brilliant, inspiring scholars, only a small percentage of the student body would benefit. Or even care.) Okay, so where does that leave my opinion? When I went to college, I wanted to learn to be an awe-inspiring, history-making jazz guitarist; that's why I went to the school to begin with --- a school filled with people like me, whose primary purpose in life was their art. But I didn't know until I got there how much the "regular classes" meant to me, or how important it was for my personal/emotional growth to continue learning Statistics and Chemistry and Faulkner. At U Arts I felt like I was mastering a craft, but I wasn't acquiring the intellectual horsepower I would need to make real art --- that, at least, was my experience.

text: So, after a disappointing quasi-eating experience at El Rey (four thumbs down, giant middle finger up), we scrambled to find another Mexican food restaurant. After a quick look at Yelp, we hit the ATM and ran to Lolita. What a change. First of all, five stars for service. Their attentiveness was refreshing and amazing, and they treated ALL of their customers with the respect they deserved. We were seated immediately, with full waters all night. Also, five stars for the guac. Wow. We opted for the traditional, and I usually have to add salt. No salt necessary here. It was perfectly seasoned and well-made. It was also cool that it came with corn, plantain, and coconut chips. The food was good. It is definitely more imagined "Mexican" food. But with that being said, it was high quality and delicious. My wife opted for the pork, which was perfectly cooked, and I got the short ribs, which were pretty good. The food was served promptly and presented very well. Four stars because it is a cash only joint. The prices are high enough to warrant being able to use a card, especially if you are more than two people. It is also imagined Mexican food. It's really not a knock on Lolita, it's just not a place you go if you are craving folksy, old-fashioned Tex-Mex or Mexican food. Overall, a pleasant evening. Would go back to try the carne asada that everyone raves about, the guac, and the amazing service.

text: I was really excited when this place opened. Finally---an independent coffee shop that was conveniently located on my side of campus. No more raging guilt when I had to stop by Dunkin' Donuts or Starbucks because there was no other place to fetch coffee on University Ave. in the early morn. Oh, but how quickly my hopes were dashed. On my first visit, I waited in line for fifteen minutes. My simple order---buttered bagel and black coffee---had to be repeated three times because the girl kept ringing it up wrong. I was forgiving---after all, they had just opened. Then I got back to campus with my bag and found a bagel slathered with cream cheese. Um, was it really that hard? But again---forgiveness. So some friends and I skipped over before class one day to grab coffee. This time we were in line for 15 minutes, and then it took 10 minutes for our orders to come out---and no one got anything more than a coffee drink and a pastry. Plus, out of the six of us, one person's drink was missing the sugar and someone got a pastry they didn't order. That's a pretty crappy error rate. That peeved me, and I vowed never to return. But, a couple of weeks later, still somewhat squicky from the night previous, I was lured in by their chalkboard offer of a coffee and bagel for some cheap price. Despite my two bad encounters, I decided to go for it because there wasn't a line. I went inside and asked for the special, which was evidently beyond this girl's vocabulary. "On the chalkboard? The bagel and coffee?" She nodded and rang things up---but it totaled more than advertised. When I pointed out the discrepancy, she rolled her eyes and huffed, "It's like, *fifty cents.* What do you want me to do?" I was feeling too hungover to argue about the principle of the matter, so I just walked out. And that was the last time I ever set foot in that place. I hope it closes and gets replaced with something that isn't staffed with incompetents.

Love it! I also had the shrimp & grits once, and I had never had them before, but the dish was wonderfully balanced and delicious, unlike some of the other New Orleans restaurants that only heap on the salt and butter. Their bread pdding is a wonderful dessert as well. Again, very balanced with an even texture, with handmade ice cream piled on top. The only reason why this place has 4 stars instead of 5, though, is that the service is not great here. Wonderful, wonderful food, but they have some of the slowest service I have had here. They have all of these staffers and hostesses and waiters walking around the restaurant, which isn't too big, but they take a long time with everything!

text: What a complete and utter let down. I am so frustrated by my dining experience last night and I think it's partly my fault. I truly set my expectations too high and I left totally dissapointed. Before I delve into last night's total fail (which is a long doozy, I'd admit), here is what I expected of Philadelphia's supposedly "best restaurant": 1) Impeccable, involved and flawless service befitting a traditional upscale french restaurant 2) an educated and present sommelier 3) an exciting à-la-carte menu, specials and amuse-bouche 4) expertly executed food with beautiful presentations 5) fresh, excellent selections of beef, fish, shellfish, and bread 6) proper desert presentation and serving sizes Let me tell you, Le Bec Fin (which translates as the "Fine Nose" - [or literally 'beak'] for wine, food, etc) does not live up to the hype. Whatever Le Bec Fin was once known for, it no longer deserves the title. I've received far better food and service at a myriad of other places in the city. I've eaten far better French cuisine at Bistros elsewhere for a fraction of the price. Le Bec Fin failed on all six counts of my expectations. First, the service simply sucked. It was inexcusable. We were a party of five, reservation at 8:30 pm and aside from a party of 15 at the front of the house, the rest of the dining room was half empty and they had an ample staff working. The maitre'd was absent for most of the meal, and he was just plain awkward, disinterested and an amateur. Aside from the forced theatricality of placing napkins on diners' lap, the royal treatment ended there. He insisted on calling us madame and monsieur which was such a farce ( are we at a themed restaurant here? my family and I are French Canadian, and this man is no French speaker, he barely spoke english - so why bother?). Never offered the wine list until halfway through our appetizers and after we had to ask for one. The food runners/bread servers were awkward and ill-trained (kept dropping our bread on the floor, wrongly served us both our entrées and main courses - we had to tell them who got what) My parents ordered the esgargot as their entrées (yes, as their appetizer - I know I'm guilty of this too, using the word entrée as a main course rather than the first) and waited an eternity before the captain showed up to take off the lid off the cocottes. The sommelier was bored and robotic (perhaps, it's because we didn't order a $200 bottle of wine?) and after running out of our first two choices of wines, he didn't even bother to decant the wine he offered and poured sediment in three of our glasses. Moreover, beware of the wine list, all wines are priced up 200 to 300% - so choose wisely. Secondly, the food was just okay - I've had much better, but it was decent and the only thing that saved Le Bec Fin from getting only one star from me. I expected the small portions, I just didn't expect the food to be so average. Even from the beginning - it was a tell-tale sign: serving stale baguette bread with regular old butter - From the amuse-bouche (a grapefruit jelée? blah) to my entrée (foie gras, preparation and presentation both just so-so) and my plat principal (Japanese black bass - poorly cut piece of fish- with a 'yawn' yellow tomato-consomée) - nothing was memorable and nothing was worthy of the praise that Le Bec Fin seems to be getting from everyone and everywhere. What gave the evening a bit of a lift was the gorgeous desert cart with a plethora of offerings - each one appearing as delectable as the next. But the presentation (by the desert waiter?) was totally lackluster, jumbled and the portions served were truly miniscule. Teeny-tiny triangles dropped on white plates with no adornment, no frills - which was dissapointing except for the taste - rich, savoury and sinful - all of them. (not to mention that our coffees, espressos didn't even make a showing until after we had finished all our sweets) All in all, a terribly disorganized choreography of a meal - with dissonant notes throughout. Disjointed service and mediocre food. Sit down, Bec-Fin, I think your time here is done.

text: Salt-Lick! I think I satisfied my sodium intake for the year after dining here recently. I think my face is still puffy after I ingested their tortilla chips (salty), salsa verde, (saltier) and guac. (saltiest! - is that even word?) The rest of the menu isn't any better, or terribly exciting nor different than what the other local Mexican jaunts offer. What does make Jose Pistolas stand out from the crowd is that the place doesn't pride itself on margaritas or cocktails of the genre - but focuses on a good beer selection. That's always a smart move in this city of beer snobs and enthusiasts. But a decent beer list alone does not a great restaurant or bar make. In different iterations of restaurants past, I always found this little piece of real estate a challenge. The restaurant and bar area is always split in two. Very little bar space on the first floor, tiny bathrooms are far away located in the back past the emergency exit doors, a couple floors up. Also, though I hate places that try too hard to establish an atmosphere, I find Jose to completely lack one. Perhaps that is their intention, especially when you're located across that heinous Italian food chain (the name escapes) and just down the street from Applebees. Food isn't bad, but it definitely isn't good either. Offerings aren't any better than what you could make yourself or find at your local grocer. Big blah. What brings this restaurant's wattage down is their excessive use of salt, each time I've eaten here, I leave feeling like I've swam through the Dead Sea with my mouth gaping open. Also, the place is kind of expensive. After splitting chips+guac+salsa, getting a order of shrimp tacos + 3 happy hour beers (don't judge) with tip = $40? A little rich for my blood. When all is said and done, Jose is good for a quick stop for a beverage before a show on Broad Street when Good Dog is too packed. It's sort of a decent back-up option to watch a game when all the other places nearby are filled to capacity.

text: Cut to the chase: All in all, it was one of the best restaurants I've been to in Philly. Food: the flavors were very clean and everything was well seasoned. Price: On the pricey side, but not insane if you make your choices wisely. I got drinks ($20), while the bf got dinner ($60). Ch-ch-check it out, you'll be glad you did! __________________________________ Long, detailed story: I'm a fan of Alma de Cuba. We had a date night here not too long ago, and it was a wonderful experience. Got there around 8 PM without a reservation and the place was pretty packed. We checked our coats (free!) and went to the bar to pass the time. I got the white sangria ($9), which is exactly what I wanted at the moment. My bf got the 'Havana Old Fashioned' cocktail ($10), which to me, tasted like a blended cigar-- not my fave, but he liked it. The ambience is really nice-- the inside is COMPLETELY different from the outside, which looks kind of beat-up and lifeless. Inside, there is dim lighting with the glow of red light. The restaurant is split up into 3 levels, which I can imagine isn't fun for girls with heels (good thing I wore flats!). The bathrooms are also on the upper floors. However, the decor is quite stylish and clean-- much like Stephen Starr's other restaurants. The walls have pictures of cuban (?) people, which felt kind of odd to me, since it was like they had these poor looking people for decor, while we sat on our asses and ate... anyways, back to the story: We waited around 40 minuted before we were seated in the lounge for dinner. The garlicky bread balls they serve were soooo amazing. No words to describe it.. just addictively good. We started with the Kobe beef tacos ($12), which were 5 mini tacos with ground kobe and tomato. They were good, but not $12 good. I ordered the yellowtail ceviche ($14) which was about 8 small pieces of yellowtail marinated in a lime-citrus sauce. It was actually very delicious, but the portion was on the small side. My bf got the duck, which was def not what the description of the dish said it would be. However, it was very delicious-- the duck meat (6 small pieces) was extremely tender and seasoned perfectly served under creamy yucca, which was not overwhelming. The dish had small side of salad with some duck confit, which I liked. Again, the dish was on the smaller side. We also got a side of crispy plantains for the table, which tasted more like slightly crispy/slightly soggy bananas. I wanted to try the yucca fries with mojo sauce, but that will be for our next visit!

text: We went on a Monday, so no crayons, w/butcher paper, no lights in the backyard. But it wasn't crowded and we got our food quickly. Our server recommended the coconut shrimp, and I'm so glad we took his recommendation. They were fresh and delicious. The shrimp are delivered fresh every day and prepared on-site. No frozen coconut shrimp here! We ordered homemade ginger brew, which was thick and pulpy with fresh ginger. It was quite strong and spicy--not for the faint of heart. If you can't handle a lot of ginger, stick to the bottled ginger soda. For dinner, I got the escovish fish filet. It too was hot, peppery, and strong with vinegar. I hiccuped for a while after the first bite (spicy food does that to me), but it was great. I've has escoveitched fish before, but this was not as wet. Just different. The side dishes of Jamaican cabbage and rice & peas were so good! Coconut milk in the rice makes all the difference, I think. My friend got the jerk chicken (dark meat) which was also delicious. There was a lot of meat on that plate for a leg and thigh combo! The sauce was thick and tasty, sweet but spicy. We also shared some 'greens, greens, greens,' and I'm glad we did. Collards, spinach, and calaloo with coconut milk is a combination made in heaven. By the time we finished (yes, we ate it ALL) our generous portions of dinner, we had no room for dessert. Our server told us they bring the desserts in from Jamaica. They had lemon cake, rum cake, chocolate cake, and more. Next time I'll remember to bring half of my food home and save room for dessert.

text: My sister and I went to Caribou Cafe last night for dinner because she had received two gift certificates for free entrees there. Although the decor is quite nice and the wait staff seemed personable (our waitress was lovely), we were really disappointed in the quality of food and felt it was extremely overpriced for what it was. The wine list is decent, but again, too expensive for the quality. We started with the fennel, pear and almond soup which was actually quite good; unfortunately, the entrees were not. There are no vegetarian options at all (I knew this beforehand, but hey, free meal!), so I opted for the crab cakes. I really don't know how you can screw up crab cakes, but these were terrible. They were completely flavorless and I had to douse them with several lemon wedges to get any taste at all. The cakes weren't even properly breaded and were coated in this strange, thin, non-bread crust... it was odd. They were served with a very bland hollandaise sauce and some steamed spinach. I was very disappointed at the weak effort and high price ($27!) and have definitely made better ones at home for much less. Overall, a very boring dish. My sister ordered the special filet mignon, and was not thrilled about it. It was served with mashed potatoes and green beans. Although the steak was cooked perfectly and was very tender, she complained that the dish was very salty, and not worth the price. Again, we feel we could've had better if we'd made it at home. For dessert we split a creme brulee, which was decent, but nothing to scream about. I really wouldn't recommend coming here unless you are heartset on overpaying for an uncreative, tasteless meal.

text: I know Im a hater on brunch, but when Im on vacation and the largest to-do list for the day is "1. Get Drunk. 2. Rinse. 3. Repeat.", slugging down bloody marys is high on the must do list. Enter Farmicia. It's a sweet little place a couple blocks east of Independence Hall. They have a charming dining room, rusticly appointed, with a few outside tables and large french doors that invite a terrific breeze on a cool day. They also happen to have 1/2 priced "Barn Burners" where, for a mere $4.25, you get a terrific, spicy, full-of-horseradish-and-other-chunky-ingredients philly style Bloody Mary. The service can be slow while the place is in full swing, but the drinks hold off the demons. One Barn Burner in, Im impressed with the liquor, pissed off by the slower than I ought to have service. Two Barn Burners in, I get my appetizer - bagel bits with salmon. Smoked Salmon. And some sort of goopy cream cheese. Granted, not the wisest choice on a sensitive tummy, but I was desperate for food at this point and it looked the quickest thing on the menu. It arrived and I honestly ate the whole dish so quickly I cant remember the taste. I do remember however, that the Second Barn Burner was fantastic. Three Barn Buners and a perma-grin in, I get the Amish cheddar cheese grits and andoulie sausages. this came with bread. Which was much appreciated at this point. It was the perfect hangover remedy, and I almost recovered enough by the 3rd barn Burner to finish my meal, but alas...my eyes were bigger than my liquor tainted stomach, so I threw the white flag in. This did not however prevent me from ordering.... Barn Burner #4. Now things are getting ridiculous. And I am in such a good mood that it will be impossible for me to grant Farmicia anything less than a 4. Even if the meal's particulars are not particularly particular anymore. It's time to move on and learn me some US History down the street. Yes I enjoy getting drunk and going to historically significant sites. So shoot me.

text: Nice view and gorgeous space---check. Solid attentive service---check. Outstanding and inventive food worthy of the price tag---Hold it. I really really really wanted to have a great meal at Vin de Set. Sadly, it was not meant to be. Partially may have been because we went on a Sunday evening; perhaps the A team had the night off. We started with the steak tenderloin tartare with truffle oil and flatbread. It came out with nicely arranged radish sprouts and seeded flatbreads (bit of a skimpy supply of skinny thin points) over the tartare/truffle oil/??? mixture that was wrapped in a thinly sliced cucumber. The tartare looked like a dog's breakfast but fortunately tasted somewhat better. They were heavy handed with the truffle oil and the meat quality didn't wow me. It was only ok. Hubby liked this one more than I did. For entrees, I got the Steak and Frites, a reasonable test of a solid but not overly challenging french bistro dish, and my husband got the duck breast with fingerling potatoes and blueberry port reduction. First, for a place that sells itself as a french bistro, to me that entails some attractive presentation, classic knife skills demonstrated in the food, etc. Not the case here; there was no dish presented to us that I with my mediocre knife skills and lack of eye hand coordination could not have done myself at home. Furthermore, the lack of texture variation in the food was also notable. For fine dining, I not only expect great tasting food, but presentation also plays a role, and they didn't attend to this at all. For my dish, to their credit, it was actually cooked medium rare as asked; there are too few restaurants in Saint Louis who can actually correctly make a medium rare steak. It was not particularly flavorful however; I took about 3/4 of it home for my husband to have for lunch the next day. The fries were a huge disappointment. Unevenly cut, soggy undersalted fries. Not at all crispy and slightly cold. I, who am the queen of all carbs and the empress of french fries, only ate maybe 5 of them before I decided they were not worth the calories and did not take them home. The stuffed tomato with this dish was nice if a bit greasy and mushy; I didn't really taste the bacon that was supposedly in it. Some nicely crisped bacon or pancetta on top would have been great for taste and texture. My husband's duck was properly cooked as well. The potatoes were pretty average (except the undercooked one) and the "reduction" didn't seem very reduced---it tasted strongly of port with no blueberry to note and not much else. Nothing on the dessert menu tempted us, so we got a cheese plate which was tasty, though the cheese selection is somewhat limited. Love the fig spread, pickled onions and pickled brussel sprouts on this. They also had some nice wines by the glass, including a nice chenin blanc. For what we paid for this meal, I thought it was pretty disappointing. When the cheese plate is your sole highlight, there is a problem. Had I paid a third of what we paid, I still wouldn't have called it stellar food, but I would have not felt as cheated. We will likely try the food here in a less extensive meal again on a Friday to see if this evening was an anomaly, but this may end up being a bar and drinks only kind of place for us.
label: NEG

Most bridal salons ask for appointments, which makes sense. So after finding a dream dress in a magazine, I did some online research and found that the only local Melissa Sweet retailer was T&C. Viewing the storefront, I assumed it was not the first place I would've chosen to walk into, but I kept my mind open and set up an appointment. When I arrived, my friend/coordinator Mel was already there, pulling dresses from the racks. I was addressed by a sales clerk, who shook my hand and didn't offer her name. The clerk ("Sally", we'll call her) with whom I booked the appointment was currently with another bride. This lady ("Jane", we'll say) was going to "get me started". I was asked nothing about my wedding, budget or taste. Mel and I pulled about 6 dresses and asked for a fitting room, Mel being the one responsible for schlepping the dresses there, as "Jane" sped about the floor. I don't know how many espressos she had that day, but her energy and speedy speech made me dizzy and uncomfortable. "Jane" told Mel and I that any more dresses wouldn't fit on the dressing room hanger (???) and to go ahead and get started. We did, and after trying on all 6 dresses with no accommodation, I waited, half nude, in my dressing room for about 10 minutes expecting someone, like the "Sally" I made the appointment with to come and check on me. Nope. Mel got the other selected dresses and we proceeded on our own for the duration of my experience. Towards the end, "Sally" peeked in and said the other bride was a friend of hers that "just popped in." I guess she was more important than I was. :( After coming out of the dressing room for the first time, with one of the last dresses, my friend and I spied a sale rack, which was never pointed out to us. (Of course not!) We found 3 more dresses and as WE'RE pulling them to try on, "Sally" walks up and says, "Oh, you found some more you'd like to try? We ARE beginning to close..." ??? Seriously!?!? (I bet if you waited on me like you were supposed to, we'd be done by now!) That's just rude. You NEVER tell a customer "we're closing." Especially a bride, who's planning to spend a significant chunk of money on a very important garment. They weren't downright ugly to me, but I left Town & Country feeling low and stressed out. I definitely would NOT send any of my friends there for any reason. Find your wedding dress somewhere else!
label: NEG

text: I love to cook and go shopping for the ingredients so on my way back from Lansdowne I ventured into the Fresh Grocer at 56th & Chestnut. The prices here are great - when my order was rung up I was pleasantly surprised that I had spent $135 instead of $200. Their meat department is great - as close to an actual in-store butcher you can get without going to the Italian market. They have curried goat ready to hit your frying pan at home! Don't expect to find your fancy ingredients (ie: goat cheese) but if it is part of Southern or West Indian cuisine you should be good. The prepared food selection is piping hot and ready to devour. If you haven't been to this or the 40th Street location it is worth a trip in itself. There is a large parking lot and there is usually a hack out front if you need a ride.

text: I'm sure everyone is getting tired of hearing me go on and on about how record stores are becoming extinct and how great it is when you can still find a nice little shop that's not affiliated with some major chain... so I'll stop myself now. text: Is it cliche to complain about how some auto mechanic ripped you off? This place pissed me off so bad that I will take it to the grave with me. text: So where do I begin I came to Santa Barbara for my 2 year anniversary, and we were looking for a nice, new restaurant to experience in Santa Barbara, not a chain. Of course I go on YELP to look for some recommendations and I came across Holdren's. I am a big fan of steakhouses so when I found this I was really excited. We get there, but our table was not quite ready we waited almost half an hour, but when I saw all the food going by it looked really good and it smelled even better, but boy were we in for a nightmare. We decided to start off with the Spicy Crab and Artichoke Dip. What a mess it looked terrible not even appetizing and the cheese on top wasn't even melted and by far one of the worst appetizers I've ever had. We decided to send it back and get the ahi tuna tartare, which is absolutely delicious everywhere else I have it but here. The tuna didn't taste fresh and it was beyond salty. At this point we were ready to leave but we had already placed our entree orders. I had the 10 oz. filet mignon with a side of garlic mashed potatoes and clam chowder, which they ended up running out of and instead I got the tomato basil soup. The tomato-basil soup comes out and my boyfriend said," this tastes like a pasta sauce from a jar just warmed up," and it was room temperature. My filet comes out and its a mess. It tasted burnt and char-like and it was cold. My garlic mashed potatoes were also very cold and horrible. I was very disappointed. My poor boyfriend was craving a juicy kobe burger all week but instead he receives a charred, dry burger with no flavor. He also got a side of mac & cheese what a mess. KRAFT MAC & CHEESE is better then the crap that we received. Our server was mediocre at best. We will never come back here.

text: Big Stein's Deli is awesome. It's right on 4th Street and I always find myself craving something from there. I'm originally from NY, where we have the best delis. I'm not sure, but I think the owners might be from NY. And if they're not, they definitely understand the concept of what an NY deli should be. Plus, all their sandwiches have fun NYC-themed names. I brought a friend of mine from NY here when she came to visit and it definitely met her approval as well. There are a variety of sandwiches, wraps, soups, and salads on their menu. All delicious and all huge! Often, we'll get a sandwich, eat (maybe) half of it on the spot and save the rest for later. This especially applies to the Skyscraper Club, which is a monster. Any wrap or sandwich I have ever had from here has been great. I also happen to love their Broccoli and Cheddar soup. It's really really thick but creamy and cheesy and delicious. And their Greek salad is, of course, ginormous, but truly amazing with the option of having the potato salad right on top, which is a treat. The knishes were okay. It could be considered kind of pricey (compared to FL, not NY prices) but I would definitely say it's worth it.

text: Used to love this place but hadn't been since prior to their expansion. I had spoken very highly of it to friends from large metropolitan areas, claiming it was as good or better to their local joints so of course I had to prove it by taking them there when visiting recently. It's lost a lot of it's charm and quality. ugh. embarrassing. It wasn't awful, but certainly nothing to brag about. The decor, service, and quality of food. all mediocre. The usual AYCE crime of padding on extra rice so the flavor and texture balance was off and the presentation (which used to set it apart from other AYCE joints) has dramatically declined. The unique roll with the banana that is usually artfully arranged into a bursting blossom shape was sloppily piled on a platter and instead of being wrapped in a thin layer of banana, it just has mushy shards of banana haphazardly topping the roll. so disappointing. Even their cute tempura ice cream dessert got sloppy and ugly. :( Waitresses are nice and work hard, but cant keep to keep track of their tables and who has ordered and who hasn't, so you might get ignored for a while then bombarded with several girls checking up on you and bringing the wrong dishes. There also isnt a real hostess station or waiting area so you either get to stand awkwardly blocking the entrance crowding the nearby tables or wait outside, which sucks in the winter. I believe the owner is earnest and runs one of the better sushi places in Reno, but it's clear they are going through some growing pains. probably insignificant to many diners, but I also hate the new sign. It looks like a cheap liquor store signage. the kind that almost always has the word DISCOUNT in it. It does not make an appealing first impression and clashes with the color or theme of the interior.

text: FINALLY!!! (cue hallelujah music) I am soooo beyond in love everything about this place! The custard is AMAZING! I've tried the dulce de leche, uber creamy with just enough dulce de leche swirled into velvety rich custard and I've had the chocolate and vanilla, its yummy. It's been so long since we have had a great honest to goodness ice cream place with fabulous tasting food to boot!!! It just gets better, so the owner is from Wisconsin and not only can she make the best custard/frozen dessert in town plus the neighboring 8, she brought us Bratwursts and Curds. Both of which I had no clue what they were a week ago but now I'm a Bratwurst n' Curds Girl!! So what are they? Bratwursts are seriously good kickin sausage that comes in a great roll that isnt too soft or too hard. It's just right!!! The prices are phenomenal too unlike Whirled Peace. The whole vibe of Jake's just makes you feel good from the second you walk in. And then the curds, OH MY GOD!!!! I am a hot cheese nut, mozzarella sticks are in my Top Ten favorite foods, well these curds just took their place. They are Wisconsin cheddar cubes that get fried, they are the size of popcorn shrimp and you get a ton of them in a single order. I'm so excited that finally after years of not having a fantastic all around place to bop in and get an awesome meal, packed with down home goodness, you can't help but be happy. Oh! And, the colors they used to paint the walls inside, IN LOVE!!!! It's like a wollop of fabulous yum sprinkled with rainbow jimmies with a big old cherry on top that makes you instantly fall in love with the new guy in town, I HEART JAKE"S!!!!!!

text: There is almost nothing available at Harris Teeter that is not also available cheaper somewhere else. Their blatant markups are pretty disgusting. They occasionally mark down some about-to-expire-but-still-fine raw whole chickens, which are great if you immediately throw them in the freezer. I just bought two for $3.50 each, and one made a wonderful roaster. Produce might as well be gold-plated. I seldom touch it, because it is almost laughably expensive (e.g. $3.50 for a single red pepper), though the selection is great. text: Another on the must checkouts of Tucson, this place is located just down from the university. A small unassuming storefront made me almost miss finding the place altogether. Walking in, the aroma ensured me I had made the correct choice. Never having eaten guatamalen food before, I just picked some items at random off of the menu. The snack/appetizer came comprised of a corn pancake with cheese inside, topped with what looked like sauted onions and some other veggie I didn't recognize. I was hoping for more of a corn flavor but it was just a little bland, but maybe that's how this dish is supposed to be. I'll pass on it next time since the main dish was more than filling. The pork mole I ordered, on the other hand, was awesome. I figured a chocolate sauce could turn out really bad, or really good. Luckily it was the latter for me. Lightly sweet, the pork was fall-apart tender and was nicely complimented by the rice and black beans. I usually don't like my food swimming in sauce, but this time it was ok since I just mixed it into the rice and beans. For me, it would have been better if it were a little spicy, but that's just my preference. Check this place out. You won't be sorry.

text: Stayed here, as well as attended a friend's wedding, here this weekend. The wedding rate was $149/night and for that this is a 4 star hotel, but the usual rate is over $250 so in that case it's probably more like a 3 star hotel. The good: - Nice sized rooms with a separate living room area - Comfortable beds - A huge bathroom to primp myself for the wedding - Right in the middle of downtown Nashville, as well as across from the country music museum - Plenty of cabs always available even though Nashville isn't actually a cab friendly city - elevators that move at lightning speed - $13 breakfast buffet that I didn't try myself, but my fiance has mentioned what a great deal it was at least 10 times (it's the little things in life that excite him) The bad - unimpressive workout room - pretty gross indoor pool that you couldn't pay me to step foot in - they need to learn how to make a latte...I could hardly drink the one they made for me downstairs For those of you looking to plan a special event in Nashville I"d also recommend the grand ballroom- my friend had a beautiful wedding here last night! It's a simple, yet elegant ballroom...the type where any decorations will work. Would I return to the Hilton during my next trip to Nashville (if there ever is another trip to Nashville)? Yes, probably...but it would depend on the price. I would be happy staying here for under $200, but over that I'd seek shelter elsewhere.

All in all, it's not as bad as I describe, I guess, but when you get the bill, and wonder why you didn't just go to PF Changs for half the cost, it hurts more.
label: NEG

text: I got married in Lambertville a few months ago and was looking for a reasonable place to invite family and friends the night before the wedding to spend time with them and relax. After looking at a bunch of places online, we settled on Tortuga's Cocina. I spoke with the owner on the phone several times leading up to the event, and she was very anxious about the fact that we were a large party and where would she seat us on their busiest night. Frankly, if you decide to allow us to hold the event, that's not really my problem, but I talked it out with her. I wanted to have the dinner at 630, but she insisted that it be 530 p.m. and then tried to change it to 430 THE DAY BEFORE the dinner. I politely told her "no." We discussed the fact that my fiance's family was paying for the meal and we didn't want it to get too expensive, so she agreed to only offer wine and beer to the guests. text: I'm a doctoral student in Computer and Information Sciences finishing up my second year at Temple. I did my undergraduate degree in Computer Science from a small suburban school with a beautiful campus and very friendly professors who offered tons of opportunities. What I found at Temple was pretty much the opposite. I'll begin where most students do: at admissions. I was quickly accepted to Temple and quickly offered two fellowships, which were quite a pleasant surprise. Morevoer, the CIS department appeared to be bucking the computer graphics and cryptography trend I observed in other schools and doing bioinformatics research, which I had always had an interest in, so the research opportunities seemed promising. Once I accepted the offer, however, the school fell silent and would not respond to my emails or return my calls. I didn't even receive information on housing or registering for courses until I sent them *postal mail* threatening to enroll elsewhere if they didn't send me this information. Alas, it still arrived too late, and their screwup forced me into an off-campus apartment for my first year. Next, academics: As you'd expect, there are good professors and bad professors in the classroom. Some can teach, some can't; some are friendly, some aren't; some challenge you, some don't. It's when you begin interacting with them outside of the classroom (and as a graduate student, you do a lot of that) that you begin to notice the difference: Professors at my alma mater were rather laid back and tended to view the students as intellectual peers who just hadn't acquired the degree of knowledge that they had yet, but eventually would if they so desired. If they found an excellent student, they made sure to stimulate him sufficiently to learn and grow. As a result, they allowed students to define their own directions and routinely contacted students with opportunities for collaboration (actual two-sided collaboration!) and leadership. Probably because Temple is a large research institution, Temple's professors tend to view graduate students as employees and undergraduates as annoyances. The professors are all very busy cranking out publications (grad. students moreso) and appear to view teaching as a secondary duty. The academic system itself is rigid and (at the graduate level, anyway) assumes you are fully engaged with your research and have no time or proficiency outside your field, whether or not that is truly the case. Even attempting to audit classes outside of your major on your own dime is impossible - you could do this without matriculating for any degree, but not as a grad. student! Professors also seem more concerned with publishing papers than with novel research. Neither students' ideas nor solid research methods are given sufficient time. These years are critical ones in the development of any scientist, and Temple's system is not up to the task. As for the neighborhood, the campus is relatively safe, if a bit ugly. However, it really isn't safe to wander off-campus, ESPECIALLY AT NIGHT. It's a very run-down slummy area, right by the railroad tracks. On two occasions I was threatened. One of my professors was not so fortunate; he was first mugged and subsequently had his car stolen. While in my apartment (which was technically "off campus", but actually only two blocks from the student center), I had a wonderful view of an empty parking lot on my right and the railroad tracks on my left. Every so often people would start shouting things at night, making it difficult to sleep. On occasion I heard gunshots. Philadelphia being a city, parking is also an issue. Reserve a spot if you bring a car there. The Philadelphia mass transit system is vastly inferior to New York's, but I guess it'll get you where you want to go most of the time. You'll need to either drive or take mass transit to do anything off of campus, because there's nothing but the aforementioned slummy homes near the campus and you don't want to walk through that area. Student life? I can't comment; grad. students don't have lives :) I suppose Temple does have a few advantages: it's located in a city if you like that sort of thing, it's near Penn and Drexel, they have a very good medical school, and the curriculum is rather easy, even at the grad. level. If you take four grad. courses a semester and do a project over the summer, you can get a Master's degree in a year, which is very nice. Once you get into the swing of the research, a Ph. D. doesn't seem to be much harder. Of course, that means if you're looking for a challenge, look elsewhere. Update: I am now in my 4th year, having seen everything from repeated billing screwups and 2-year faculty vacations to an advisor who backtracked a month before an agreed-upon defense. My dissertation is complete. I am literally held here doing nothing. Every time I think the school can't get any worse, it surprises me. Do not attend if you value your education.

text: The story you are about to read is true. 5:31 pm. My partner, my wife and I head to the famous Jacques-Imo's for a taste of the local fare. It's a good thing we brought the GPS, without it and you have a better chance of finding a preacher on Bourbon Street. The restaurant is tucked away in the middle of a narrow street - parking is a game of chance even for early evening. Look for the traffic light mounted to the building with all three lights brightly shining. If you read other reviews, you will see that this is the best time to come. Plus it leaves the evening for a pub crawl through the Quarter. Jacques-Imo's is split between two buildings. Our host takes us back to the street and into the house next door. There is no wait and our server, Rebecca, is quick with our drinks. We find out that the writing on the front window which resembles an old time menu is for decoration only. The window says they have frog legs, but alas, that item is not available. The menu is divided into two sections, the items on the left are their consistent dishes that do not change. The right side shows their seasonal items. The selections are quite varied with items like rabbit on the menu. Our meals don't take long at all and the quality of the food is better than you would believe. I do have to say that I am an addict for bread pudding and when it comes time for desert - that's what I order. This, my friends, is the best bread pudding that I have ever tried. I would consider making a special trip to the Big Easy just for this dish alone. If you want a few tips, come early - this place deserves to be busy and you will wait if you are late. Expect authentic atmosphere and food, this ain't the Four Seasons! Finally, save room for the bread pudding - if not, order it anyway and send it to me.

text: this airport basically sucks. However, unfortunately, I do have to use it frequently, so it gets a couple of stars. Here is important info: If you are flying US AIR domestic (USA only), then you could be in Terminal C or F. Before you get to the airport, figure out which terminal you are flying out of. Next, if you are flying Southwest, know if you are in Terminal D or E. Knowing this info will help figuring out where you need to check bags, etc. getting from terminal to terminal inside the secure areas is tricky at PHL. You are better off just going to the correct terminal. You could walk from terminal to terminal on the roadside...but, it will be a long walk!! Parking in the airport is VERY expensive (short-term and long-term). So, if you are poor and have to drive, then use an off-site lot (8$ to 12$ per day) or the Economy lot. Food choices inside most terminals SUCK badly (except Terminal C). So, bring your own food if you want. Drinks, etc is very expensive, but you have no choice than to buy them here or not have a drink at all. Toilets can be hit or miss. Best used minimally. Flight delays are very common and are a rule with US AIR. Weather is often bad and low ceilings are common. The SEPTA train runs through each terminal and connects to downtown and other destinations. SEPTA rail costs $7 to downtown and $10 to Jenkintown. (one way). People (staff) are generally not friendly, since this is the northeast. You might luck out. Continental airlines usually have reasonably good staff. I fly this airline most of the time. There are not enough chairs for the number of people (especially in terminal D). This is not fun. Also, almost non-existent power outlets. There are some by the restrooms, if you want to sit close to the nasty smells. Overall, ok airport....this is going to be as good as it gets for Philadelphia. It wont be better until USAIR becomes bankrupt and stops flying. Then, we could get a different airline as a Philly hub which might improve facilities. Oh, Be VERY careful when exiting off of I-95 to the airport. Thanks to senseless road-designers, they made the airport exits as dangerous as they possibly can. Best to just take the train if you dont live here.

text: Arrggh! Bourdain! I feel like you have thrown me under the bus... Anthony Bourdain is my culinary god and I value his opinion because he calls a spade a spade and will let me know when the food is bad. He has sorely let me down. (I guess that is what I get for worshipping false idols.) Simply, I have always been leery of Emeril Lagasse; thinking him the typical "celebrity chef." More flash than substance... Not till I watched Bourdain's episode on New Orleans where he "came around" did I decide to give Emeril a shot. I feel that Anthony owes me money. As for the food, it was okay. Nothing more, nothing less. If not for the Gumbo Shop, it would have been the worst gumbo I would have eaten in New Orleans. It is hard to pin down exactly what makes Emeril's "bad." Maybe it is the expectation of a great meal to get nothing more than mediocre. And then to pay the price for that meal is almost criminal. I honestly can not understand why people like his food. We even ordered his "signature dishes" and were disappointed. Our friend, a souffle fan like I am for bread pudding, took one bite of the signature chocolate souffle and spit it out. I think that is the problem. Emeril keeps raking in the $$$ because of silly gimmicks on TV that bring people into his restaurants. But after people have tried his food, they are too embarrassed to call him out. (This may be because the service is excellent and it is hard to yell at a guy doing a great job serving you.) So, I feel that I was suckered. But not so much from Emeril Lagasse who I rightly pegged as a fraud, but Anthony Bourdain, who led me astray...

text: Went to Joanie's last night; I hadn't been there in years but nothing seems to have changed. We sat downstairs (I was with a smoker friend) and it was definitely smoky and kind of loud with the obvious regulars at the bar. I was hating the '80s music overhead, but I know that's being picky. It's really unfortunate that the non-smoking section is upstairs. We witnessed someone with a walking disability having to be helped slowly down the stairs by two friends, which seemed ridiculous. On to the pie. We opted for the double crust, for a change of pace. It did come out looking like a big pie with the crust on top. The Joanie's veggie was literally crammed with fresh vegs (bonus ponts for summer squash and spinach) which spilled out when you took a slice, and not overloaded with cheese, so it was manageable without being messy. The bottom crust also held up without getting soggy. A great pie, to be sure! They also have a limited but decent beer selection, not relying on just A-B products.

text: We all were really disappointed with the meal. There were some redeeming things about it, but not enough to ever go back. We ordered a few apps - we got hummus, spanikopita and tahdeg, all were fine but uninspired. The tahdeg was the only one that was even interesting. Then we each got different things for dinner - lamb, chicken, shrimp, and filet were ordered. All had good flavors, but the beef and lamb were dry and overcooked. They never asked how we like our meat done and it came out medium well, when we prefer medium rare. They served the same rice with all our meals, and it isn't very good. It would be fine if I were over a friend's house, but in a restaurant I expect a little more than the side rice you could get at a Gyro stand. Lastly, the most annoying problem of the night was our service. One person at our table had an allergy to tomatoes. We asked that none of the apps have tomatoes on them and her entree should also not have tomatoes. Of course, the first hummus came out - chopped tomatoes all over it... then the spanikopita with tomato on the side... then her main entree with grilled tomatoes mixed in with her veggies. This really upset us. Our waitress didn't even seem to care that she and the kitchen continued to get it wrong. To sum up - even without the lousy service, this was a mediocre meal at best.

text: First the good - the fried scallops at happy hour are absolutely scrumptious - fresh and crispy -the best I've had outside of New England. Well cocktails are a good size and well priced. Nice nautical atmosphere. (Don't bother with the Happy Hour shrimp and scallop scampi - a cheesy, messy blob of fish drowning in gooey white sauce. Hard to believe these two items came out of the same kitchen.) The "bad" - came back last Friday for dinner. Honestly, it was embarrassing, and I felt bad for the tourists who probably thought they were going to have a lovely dinner in SB. In the past I have brought out-of-town guests here, and we all thought the crab cakes were outstanding, and everyone liked their dinners. THIS time, however, I was glad it was just the two of us "locals": I ordered their drink "special" of the night - some kind of peach concoction "from the farmers market" the menu stated, expecting something Bellini-like. Instead I was given a clear cocktail with all these chunks of hard, unripe peach floating around in it. The flavor was okay so I didn't send it back, but really - it looked ridiculous, did NOT have the fresh peach taste it should have had, and never should have gone out that way. My Halibut, one of the more expensive items on the menu at about $22.95 was unseasoned and although fresh enough, relatively tasteless. And sitting on a bed of overcooked, oily spinach I could not gag down. The potato "pancake" seemed like another afterthought - a way to use up leftover mashed potatoes by sticking them in a fryer. Again, little if any seasoning or flavor. The sourdough bread might have been good had it not been stone COLD. I noticed a bread drawer by the back door - why don't they use it? My husbands shrimp scampi was an amateur attempt at best - it was swimming (drowning) in a casserole of butter, broth, who knows what? - about 2 cups of liquid that rendered the fish soggy and disappointing. His vodka gimlet was half the size of the one he'd had at happy hour, and of course almost double the price. I understand the pricing but shouldn't the glass size remain constant? What a waste of $75 bucks. We do not have plans to return, except perhaps for those Happy Hour scallops. It is hard to believe these folks are opening another restaurant without "fixing" this one first.

text: Everyone knows that the meat is excellent here, but if you're not a huge steak-eater (which I'm not) the salad bar is more than a meal. I've come here before and done the full meat deal, but for someone like me (a petite girl who isn't into steak enough to eat her money's worth), the salad bar at half the price ($25) is totally worth it. I'm not a vegetarian, but I looooooove veggies and Fogo has some of the best, along with small meats, cheeses and breads to round out the meal. Probably the best salad bar I've ever experienced. Asparagus stalks as thick as your thumb, hearts of palm that melt in your mouth, thinly sliced prosciutto, the freshest of fresh salmon, and a giant wheel of perfectly aged Parmesan that you want to dive head first into and just start gnawing. Plus a variety of salads (chicken, mushroom, caesar), fresh baked bread, and all the typical salad ingredients. Everything is amazingly fresh with servers constantly bringing out new and replacement dishes. I doubt anything sits there for even an hour. And the service was no less stellar for me, the salad bar patron. Fogo is truly a topnotch establishment. Bonus - they brought out a complementary slice of chocolaty fudgey mousse cake for my bf's bday. That's not so special in and of itself, but we didn't even tell them it was his bday... they noticed a birthday card on the table, asked who's it was, and promptly brought out the cake. Bravo! I always applaud cake.
