There was nothing about it that suggested a Napa Valley resturant. The server made a good effort, but our drinks took longer than necessary to arrive and the wine list was limited to one small page, with whites, reds, and other varietals listed on the same page . When I ordered butter for the bread, there was a 10-minute wait, then it arrived on a plate looking like a lump had been chopped off the edge of the block, and with 3 little shaved pieces (not curls) on the side. I ordered the ahi tuna entree - it was unattractively served on a bed of quite lukewarm quinoa and a side of limp, unappealing sliced cucumbers which had almost no taste. The tuna was rare as ordered, but covered by an unattractive crust that made it difficult to cut. My mother initially ordered the ravioli but asked that another vegetable be substituted for the spinach which she cannot eat for medical reasons. The server was at first reluctant to accommodate this request, then dismissed it by saying "I don't know what we would have to substitute." My guests had the tagliatelle pizza, which was dumped into a shallow bowl with no attempt at presentation; it was also lukewarm. This definitely a third-rate restaurant to which I will not be returning.

But cue the much needed remodeling, and you now have a seriously amazing Indian BYOB to enjoy that's not too far away from concert central Fishtown. As you can tell from some of the reviews some people aren't down with the changed results, and while I can understand why, so long as I can sit down to some saag paneer and a bottle of wine before the next show the Deli books at Johnny Brenda's, I freaking LOVE it! I knew that when I was looking for something spicy to fill me up during an insanely cold day. And when I saw the three peppers next to the Kadai Chicken to gauge it's spice, I considered myself a serious contender. I'm someone who recklessly puts Siracha on just about anything (I only really draw the line at ice cream). But holy hell did some of those bites turn up the heat in my mouth like no other entree has to date. I finished up every bite that came out of the decorative bowl though, with just a little bit of help from the water that our servers were spot on with pouring, and the complimentary crispy naan appetizer that they hooked up. While I might keep it lightly spiced with their full on veggie options next round, I fully intend to be back!

text: I am in complete awe of the Magic Gardens. I have seen it from the outside during my previous visits to Philadelphia and finally went through during my most recent visit. I am so happy I did! The weather was beautiful and sunny, which certainly made the experience more enjoyable, but really, this place is so uniquely beautiful on its own, that it's hard to imagine it not being wondrous even if it were raining. I could have easily spent hours or days taking everything in--the level of detail and the fact that practically everything is covered in mosaic, make this the case. I really can't get over the incredible and magical space Isaiah Zagar and others have created. Visitors are invited to take everything in, look anywhere, take pictures of anything, and touch whatever they want. This type of art--the type where the only rule is that there really are no rules, is probably my favorite. I would highly recommend visiting the Magic Gardens.
label: POS

text: In the middle of the week (read not many tourists), we took the Mom-in-law on a little tourist excursion to Old Town New Castle. Walking the cobbled streets of DE.'s oldest surviving town in the DE. Valley (we are talking 1651), makes one a bit thirsty and in need of a bite to eat. Jessop's Tavern seemed to fit the bill. I am telling you, you no longer have to wander around wondering where would be a good place to drink and eat. This is a piece of history with good food and great drinks; a real colonial dining experience. The interior is dark and small, with antiques and pewter plate service. The husband had fish and chips and claimed they deserved their #1 rating and the M-i-L and I had the daily colonial chowder with crab and corn, it was wonderful and you could almost imagine it being cooked in a cast iron crock over a fire. We finished with Martha's daily Colonial cobbler which was peachy keen. And most of all the cocktails, this is a pub so you would hope the bartender knows what he is doing, after all this place has been open for ~360 years. And yes he does know what he is doing...the husband and I had their drawn pints and the M-i-L a cosmo which made her giggle. This was a perfect dining experience.

text: Although the location is fantastic for a grad student who will live his life in the lab or the library and the price includes all utilities, this graduate student housing is, in the end, very disappointing. 1. For what you get, the prices are higher than the already expensive Santa Barbara market despite being purportedly affordable housing designed for graduate students. The rents continue to increase despite falling prices in the SB market. An additional 5 min bike saves me $200/month with much more space. 2. Although being in close quarters to many other graduate students, the community is incredibly sterile. 3. The bedrooms are cramped, as are the kitchens. 4. It seems that the RAs are encouraged to act as a police force, more concerned about policing residents than helping. 5. Although the fields in back seem nice and convenient, they are filled on the weekends with screaming soccer parents and their children. This eliminates the possibility of a quiet Saturday morning's sleep. 6. The mail service is very slow. 7. Most of my friends feel like they are being patronized as if they are undergraduates. That said, there are actually a large number of undergrads living here because it cannot be filled with enough graduate students. 8. Similar amenities in undergraduate living spaces are not present here. There is no fitness room or pool. 9. The policies governing family graduate student housing are far more lenient than those in this housing for single students. If you're a new graduate student looking for housing, I would seriously consider other options. Although it is convenient to sign up for this housing before you get to UCSB, it is neither ideal nor cost effective.
label: NEG

Mark was able to replace the floorboards while he was working on the flange and now there is no more fear of the toilet falling though the floor AND no more leaks coming though downstairs. text: This Provence location is a good Hillsboro Village brunch alternative to the Pancake Pantry and Fido. Their coffee is a little pricey (about $1.85 for a regular), but it's exceptionally tasty, and comes in a quaint porcelain cup. We ordered an avocado, sprouts, and mango chutney sandwich that was really fresh, but I didn't like the sweetness of the chutney mixed with the other ingredients. The bread was that perfect combination of crusty outside and chewy and moist inside. My friend and I also shared a chocolate-filled croissant, which disappeared fast. In addition to sandwiches, Provence offers loaves of bread, gourmet cheeses, cake, breakfast pastries, and soup. Provence is clean and airy inside. It kind of reminds me of a classier European version of Bread & Company. They have a few tables out front where you can watch every single person who walks by Book Man/Book Woman stop to browse the discount books, and then walk away empty-handed. The only problem with Provence is that if you're hungry, it can get expensive. The sandwich alone cost almost $7, and sides and drinks all come separately. So for a sandwich, a bag of chips, a cookie, and a drink, you'll probably end up paying around $12.

text: This restaurant was a huge disappointment for me. I was in the city for one night on business and picked 3 restaurants - couldn't find the other 2 and this was my 3rd choice. I will not be going back on a future trip. The restaurant was empty, except for one large party. The staff at the door were friendly and helpful, however one of the kitchen staff actually challenged me about a food allergy after I made a special request. The server talked a lot about their 'specialties' - which were 'sustainable fish' (in conversation later, I figured out that he didn't even know what sustainable meant), homemade items, and fresh ingredients. I didn't experience any of the above. I wasn't sure what to order (the menu does look enticing - with many choices), so I ordered a cup of italian wedding soup while I thought about my meal. It was the WORST soup I have ever had. It is NOT italian wedding soup. The ingredients are prepared separately and then thrown together when ordered. The broth is like a brine - I only had a few sips and I swelled up the next day. There were no beans, only flavorless meatballs and uncooked spinach floating in the brine. I finally decided on a pizza because they insisted seafood was their specialty and I love shrimp on a pizza. So I asked for the 5 cheese pizza, which is described as a white pie with 5 different cheeses (no tomato sauce). I asked them to leave off the gorgonzola and add on shrimp. They got the shrimp right...that was about it. I basically got a cheese pizza....tomato sauce and all. All the cheeses are mixed together so you cannot appreciate the flavors of the different cheeses. As I was taking my pizza in a box to go, I asked the server "you're sure this doesn't have tomato sauce, right" and he says "of course - our 5 cheese pizza never has tomato sauce". Wish I had opened the box right there and saved myself the trouble of throwing it away in my hotel room. Finally, I'll mention my flat sparkling water. While I waited on my pizza I sat at the bar and had a glass of 'sparkling' water. Don't order Pellegrino here - they don't even know what it is. When I asked for a glass, they offered me the wine list. LOL. So then I asked for sparkling water and got a very old bottle of not-so-bubbly water. And when the server asked me if I wanted to take the rest with me, I told him 'no thanks, it was flat anyway' and he didn't offer to do anything about it. The only reason this restaurant is getting 2 stars instead of 1 is that the bread was amazing. But I highly doubt it's made in house!

text: I am told that this part of Nashville, just north of downtown, is an up-and-coming area in which people are coming in and renovating many of the structures. This little restaurant on the corner is a real charmer with a nice menu. I had a business lunch here yesterday and thoroughly enjoyed it. The iced tea is laced with orange and cinammon - just enough to give it a nice, unique flavor. I started with chicken and anduille sausage soup and had a pasta dish topped with artichokes, chorizo, sundried tomatoes, grilled chicken in olive oil - absolutely delicious. The entree also came with a small salad. The salad ingredients were fresh and the balsamic vinagrette dressing was very good. The service was attentive without being pesky and the staff overall was quite friendly. This is a nice place, off the beaten path, and definitely worth a visit.

text: I had my first visit to Foot Finesse after hearing about it from several friends. While I found the foot soak, foot & leg massage extremely relaxing, the rest of my massage was rough and pain-enducing. It felt like my neck was being kneaded like a ball of bread dough, which led to visible broken blood vessels in my neck two days after my visit. I would hardly compare a visit to Foot Finesse to an actual massage, by a professional massage therapist. It seems like they go through the same process from client to client, never varying to meet specific client needs. They don't ask if you have any injuries, any problem areas or how you like your pressure. Honestly, this place kind of scares me. I certainly wasn't convinced that the massage therapist working on me knew anything about anatomy, as they applied excessive pressure directly to my knees and spine. Their website says their staff are licensed and certified massage therapists, but currently, in Indiana, there is no licensing for massage therapists. (There will be next year.) Yes, it's cheap and relaxing (at some points), but unprofessional (as far as massages go) and lacking the education and knowledge that keep massages safe and beneficial.

But to present yourself as a place that is kind of hippiesh and earth friendly, it doesn't settle well with me that it wasn't mentioned when three of us ordered this that one would have been more than enough. text: We went here for an early dinner on a Saturday evening. There was street side seating and regular seating. The lady looking after the street side seating was looking grumpy, pissed off and uninterested. When we asked her if we should wait to be seated or seat ourselves, she replied very curtly. We should have turned back here because I never tolerate bad service at restaurants. -1 star They have a weird waiter service inside. Apparently two waiters tag team and look after a bunch of tables instead of one. That being said, one of the two waiters looking after us was not very friendly and did not like to spend much time at the table talking to the customers. The food - bread was complimentary and delicious. Some interesting cocktails but expensive at $9 a pop. The same costs $5 if you are seated street side. The Basil strawberry mash cocktail we ordered was nothing out of the ordinary. Actually the waiter warned us many people find in string but this thing we got was horribly light. Like soda water and some touch of vodka. -1 star Light plates (appetizers) were ok. We had a crab cheesecake. Delicious but the portion is way too small at $9. The entree selection was very limited. One chicken (Rotisserie), two steak (burger and steak), one shrimp, three fish. That is it. The pecan crusted catfish was very good. The breading and sauce are very heavy tough. Cat fish was very fresh. The andy (Andoulie) crusted fish was not so good. They used some sort of white fish. The texture was very spongy and buttery than being firm. It was not very good. -1 star The sauce accompanying the fish was delicious but very heavy. Overall experience is very spotty. Unless you look like a big spender, you probably wont get attention. Being a tourist trap, we cannot expect a decent service in the first place. The place has an air of being pretentious. In a nut shell, Aim for the street side seating Skip the cocktails unless they are at $5 Dont go with very high expectations. The food will be a hit or a miss.

text: I started this review about three months ago... My children and I had a late lunch/early dinner there recently, my son had been asking to go there based on a suggestion from a classmate and I finally gave in... First off, we were greeted by the nice girls at the front and promptly seated in a booth. A server approached us and took our beverage order, came back quickly with them and suggested we try an appetizer, we had our minds set on the flaming Feta, but she said the Flaming Saganaki was much better, so we decided to go with her recommendation. When Saganaki came they did a big show of it, which would have been nice if the servers could at least fake a smile instead of showing what a torture it actually is to put cheese on fire while yelling OPA! every ten minutes. But their tortured faces weren't as bad as the actual flavor of the cheese, it was the most disgusting thing I have ever tried and I am a cheese lover, I stand in the cheese aisle at any decent supermarket and drool whenever I can. So this dish was a big disappointment. We ate most of the pita, which was delicious, and left the majority of the cheese untouched. When the server came and asked us if we didn't like the cheese, I said we didn't, she offered to "exchange" it for another appetizer, but we decide to just wait for our entree's. She OFFERED to bring us some more pitas, and because my kids liked them so much I said yes, we got about 5 on a plate. Our entree's came, my son had an all meat calzone that he enjoyed a lot, daughter had some pizza since she isn't a very adventurous eater, and I ordered a greek salad with deep fried calamari. Pizza was crappy( I know it's not an italian restaurant), calzone pretty good according to my son, but my greek salad left A LOT to be desired, there was about 4 oz of calamari in it, feta was very scarce and there was a piece of what looked like a fish bone in my salad, luckily the bone hurt my gum while I was chewing, so I didn't swallow it. Now, standard procedure in most restaurants, when a situation like this arises is to, 1. Find out what is wrong 2. Apologize 3. Fix the problem. Not in this case, the waitress just said that she didn't know what it was and that if I WANTED to, she could have the kitchen make me another salad. My appetite was long gone now, so I just pushed my plate aside and said I didn't really want anything else, plate wasn't removed, a few minutes later a manager came by the table and asked how everything was. At this point I was very offended, you don't go to a table that just found a piece of fish bone or whatever they want to call the foreign object found in my food and ask how everything is! You go and address the problem, acknowledge the situation and fix it. I said nothing, the best thing to do in this cases at least to me is to just pay the bill and leave. And the bill I got, I was charged for the pita that was offered to me, charged for the nasty cheese that I didn't eat, charged for the salad that had foreign objects (see how I love this word) in it, I could have made a big deal about it, could have demanded at least the pita was taken off, but I just paid and decided that what was going to be take off is this restaurant of my places to visit list.

text: It's your final day in Philly before you fly back to London and it's the middle of summer and steaming. You need to cool down but you want to make the most of your time. What do you do? You could do a lot worse than to visit the Franklin Institute. There are so many interesting and varied exhibits, with plenty for the whole family. There are shows of different types, including IMAX and simulators. There are fun competitions and do-it-yourself experiments as well as a great shop with puzzles, games and memorabilia. You could spend the whole day here or just walk around half of it and come back at a later date. There are all sorts of packages of shows and exhibits available, making it fun and educational for everyone. P.S. One thing. If you go to the shark show expecting blood and guts, you'll be disappointed. But you might just fall in love with a whale shark. P.P.S. There's nothing at all wrong with falling in love with a whale shark.

It has definitely added a LOT more tables and seats and it's just classically decorated. They also added two super nice conference rooms that can be reserved for your group meetings. And you can't beat the outdoor seatings during a cool fall night. See pics. You will be amazed. Also, as I began to spend more time here, I've ordered their pastries, sandwiches, and salads and I fell for the place more and more. My current fav: Bella Bella salad. It has fresh greens with fresh diced tomatoes and sliced portobello mushrooms. AND it has big chunks of mozzarella cheese with freshly sliced salamis. It just doesn't get better than this. text: I've been to Noshville 3 times now and every time has been a disappointment. We ordered the regular club on sourdough and a french dip. The club showed up stacked high with what looked like a pound of turkey. The sandwich was dry (they don't put mayo on it for some unknown reason) and the turkey completely overpowered the sandwich, couldn't even tell there were 3 pieces of bacon on. The sourdough tasted like something you could buy at a grocery store. It's pretty difficult to mess up a club, but they have managed to at Noshville. The french dip was stacked high with unseasoned roast beef, large mushy chunks of onion, and greasy flavorless cheese all on a soggy grocery store roll. The aus jus tasted like water, completely bland and a wasted opportunity to save the crapwich. The fries were extremely greasy and soggy. The highlight of the meal was the colesaw which was crisp and had the right amount of mayo and celery seeds. We both left feeling ill and bothered for wasting nearly $25 for 2 mediocre sandwiches. Will not give Noshville another try.

text: valley green inn is blessed with a beautiful location but comes up a bit short on food and service. my girlfriend and i decided to ride our bikes up the river to vgi for lunch this saturday. and while the weather and the view from the porch were great, the lunch itself turned out to be merely mediocre. we ordered a course of soup and some sandwiches. the soup arrived in a timely manner, but my choice, the du-jour lentil soup, garnished with prosciutto and asiago, had a poor texture (gritty) and tasted heavily of bacon. what does it take to pass a soup through a chinois? our other soup was the everyday french onion which seemed to be topped, generously, with mozzarella cheese, but was otherwise good. if we were a bit underwhelmed by the soup, the sandwiches didn't improve on things. the individual elements of my girlfriend's grilled salmon club were fresh and tasty, but the sandwich was overloaded with, in her words, "blah bread." minus one slice of the chiabata, it was actually very nice, but as served, no. i really wanted to like the catfish po boy. it had a nice coleslaw topping and looked good on my plate. but again, the bread overwhelmed the fillings and to add to its troubled existence, the catfish itself was, well, a bit fishy and bland. i wasn't that impressed with their side of iceberg, red cabbage, and carrot salad. this is the kind of salad you get from a bag at the supermarket finally there were the yam fries. while they are tasty, the preparation and presentation on this offering is problematic. the fries are of a shoestring cut and served in a big bird's nest, which makes them almost impossible to pick up or eat without making a mess. and why they served them with ketchup is beyond either of us. we weren't up for dessert when our server returned. the service itself was good, but not very hospitable. plates were bused in a timely manner, but in a perfunctory fashion, and glasses were refilled with water, but not iced tea (nor was iced tea even offered again). a woman behind us complained about an undercooked piece of food to her server, who dismissively agreed to get the manager for her. the manager was civil, and certainly didn't contradict her in any way, but was not exceptionally gracious in hearing her complaint either. go if you're stuck in the park on a nice day. otherwise, skip it, or just go to the ice cream stand on the side of the building.

text: Stay Away!! Price Is Too Good To Be True!! The price seemed too good to be true, I should have trusted my gut. I reserved a car with Payless in Tampa at the last minute, so I didn't do my research on the company ahead of time. I'm writing this review because of the high pressure, scare tactics used by the staff and my suspicions of "fine print" scams that motivated me to walk out without the car. When I get to the counter at the off-site location a mile from the airport not indicated when I reserved, the guy seemed nice enough. He went through the company insurance options--seemed like the usual schtick that I always decline. He insisted that I needed it because my insurance company wouldn't cover everything, specifically the rental cost while the car was being repaired if I was in an accident. He insisted that because Florida was a no fault state I need their insurance (I lived in Florida for 6 years...I know the deal.) We went back and forth and finally he gave in that I didn't want the insurance and then says, "So I'll charge your credit card $200 since you declined the insurance." To which I replied, "But I'll get it back, right?" His answer, "Well, only if you fulfill all the terms and conditions of the contract and the car is in the condition you received it in." Something about the way he said it, how he carefully worded that statement seemed very shady and made me feel uncomfortable. Of course he was ready with a chart to compare to other rental company's deposit scales. I've rented cars many times including in Florida and foreign countries and there was something not right about this whole situation. The scare tactics, the hard sell, the fine print. I left without renting a car - unfortunately I reserved it through expedia so I had already paid for the car...better to have peace of mind than get scammed by some cut rate shady rental company. That is when I read reviews and saw that overwhelmingly other people had similar experiences.
label: NEG

text: Being Cajun myself, hailing from Lafayette, LA, it was a no-brainer for a friend of mine to bring me here recently to try the food. I'm no professional food critic of course but like almost all non-Cajun 'Cajun' restaurants, (i.e. those outside of Acadiana, Louisiana) High Street misses the mark on extremely flavorful Cajun cuisine. I don't blame them however; I found the food to be a great substitute for the real thing. Portions are generous and they have Cajun favorites such as chicken, crawfish or shrimp etouffe', though the crawfish were a bit tough and no doubt Chinese crawfish. (there is a distinct difference between domestic/Louisiana-grown crawfish tail meat and its Chinese counterpart; the domestic generally tasting fresher, less tough and less like its been frozen for a long period of time). On a very quiet Saturday night in West Chester, this place was hopping, a testament to the owner and his choice of opening a Cajun restaurant in the most yankee of locations. The ambiance was okay though the place is a bit crowded, an obvious attempt is made to get as many folks into the main dining area as possible with the result giving the feel of a cafeteria setting as opposed to a quaint, boutique cafe. High marks for the food, good marks for the service and a bit lower on the atmosphere and feel. I'd definitely recommend it if you're in the mood for Cajun-esque food; but please, try to visit south Louisiana at least once in your life for the real thing!

text: My boyfriend brought me here for dinner on a romantic getaway to Santa Barbara for our anniversary. Bella Vista is located inside the Four Seasons Biltmore directly opposite the beautiful Pacific Ocean. We had reservations at 5:30p.m. in order to view the sunset, but unfortunately it was a cold day and the sun decided not to come out (bastard!). We were seated at a table for 2 right next to one of the two fireplaces which was lovely. Our server was friendly, quick, and efficient. I ordered a glass of Pinot Grigio ($12) and my boyfriend ordered a glass of Syrah ($14). We were brought a basket of bread after our server took our order. We decided to pass on appetizers since nothing was really jumping off the page. We ordered the following: Grilled Halibut ($26)- This was in the section of the menu entitled "From The Grill". You are able to pick the type of fish/meat you would like along with two sides and choice of sauce. I picked garlic sautéed spinach, truffle whipped potatoes and a lemon caper butter sauce for my fish. The fish was amazing and the lemon butter sauce went perfectly with it. Main Lobster ($38)- Served with Cavatelli Gratin, Spring Onions and Micro Baby Vegetables. My boyfriend ordered this and said the lobster was wonderful but wasn't a fan of the Cavatelli Gratin. I ended up sharing my truffle whipped potatoes with him. Dark Chocolate Soufflé ($14)- Served with a side of Vanilla Crème Anglaise and Raspberry Coulis. The soufflé takes 20 minutes to prepare, however ours took about 30. They were very nice about the added wait time and gave us a plate of petite fours in the meantime. The soufflé was perfect. It was light and airy yet oh so decadent and chocolaty. In honor of our anniversary they also gave us another complimentary plate of petite fours with "Happy Anniversary" written in chocolate and two candles. I thought that was very sweet. English Breakfast Tea ($7)- A nice pairing with the Chocolate Soufflé and a great way to end the meal. Our total bill after tax and tip came out to $147. The overall experience at Bella Vista was right in the name- Bella! Beautiful! If it's nice outside I would definitely recommend requesting a table near the window for a great view of the ocean at sunset. If it's a little cooler out I would certainly ask to sit next to the fireplace- if you're on a date it's quite romantic. We'll definitely be back!

text: I researched this restaurant for a graduation dinner in June 2009. Found the restaurant on Yelp among many others. We pick this place because it can accommodate a large group (patio only), decent menu choices and they accepted reservations whereas other restaurants in this area with a decent rating did not. Regardless, we booked in April and our reservation time was 8:30 p.m. (restaurant close at 9 p.m.). I had communicated with the event coordinator to call me ahead if there was a cancellation. She came through and called me an hour before our reserved time and said our table would be ready at 8 p.m.; needless to say, our table was not ready and we waited an additional 15 minutes after our original 8:30 time. It's all good, the important thing was she did call me. Location location location: The restaurant is located right off a public beach. The restaurant is not facing west, so no sunset while you're enjoying your cocktail. But nice views of the beach and ocean. There's nothing here but the restaurant and public beach. Service and Food: When we finally sat down, we were all tired and I'm sure the staff were too, but there were really attentive and accommodating. The hostess were helpful....moving the umbrella...getting extra chairs. The food was pretty good (thank you yelpers!). Fresh, a little salty for some, nice portions, entrees include soup or salad. What a deal, most seafood restaurant charge you extra for soup or salad. I had the cioppino and it's was yummy with large prawns, crab claw, fish, mussels, clams and scallops. Everyone enjoyed their food, thank goodness especially after the long wait. We didn't have dessert, it was just too late. Their honeycomb mojito and the acai martini was good. Bar access from patio or restaurant. Bathroom was clean (it's the one room kind). Patio had heat lamps and surrounded by glass. I gave it a four star with the combination of ambiance, location service and food; if not for the location, 3.5 stars! Would I come back if I'm in the area....maybe...I'll try their small plates next time!

text: To be honest, I don't really understand self-described "burger lovers." I mean, I love a cheeseburger as much as the next person, but 90% of them taste the same/similar; the only thing you can really mess up is overcooking them (which I know, sadly, is easy for some places to do). The few burgers that are outstanding, are outstanding because they're totally different from a normal burger, ergo making me a "unorthodox burger lover." Wait, that doesn't sound right. Anyway, I find The Fatted Calf to be ridiculous. How quaint, you're housed in a German inspired craftsman-ish building in the middle of corporate Clayton! And you serve burgers, how proletarian! It reminds me of celebrities that go to In-N-Out on first dates, its ironic charm. "I have all this money and fame, but I'm going to take you somewhere cheap to show you how cool and grounded I am!" To be fair, the burgers are solid and cooked perfectly. To be truthful, its expensive as hell. Burger, fries, mushrooms and a drink cost $22. American. That is redonkulous. The serving size of fries and mushrooms is a joke, especially at that price, and it boggles my mind that this place costs more than Peter Luger--like 30% more. How can you, a "modest" burger cafeteria in St. Louis, Missouri, cost 30% more than the most famed steakhouse in the five boroughs? I understand that $22 isn't a lot of money, but it is if you just want a burger, and that's all it is--a burger. FC makes a good burger, but so do a lot of other places in St. Louis for a lot less money. Save yourself some time and skip it. Unless you're Elisha Cuthbert, and you want to show me how Hollywood hasn't changed you. No, its cool baby, I believe you.

The sauce is so sweet and has no herbs whatsoever which is then ladled over this doughy "crust" and then they add the "toppings" which are then concealed by the cheese. We had ordered two extra large pizzas with 4 toppings, which was their promotional special. Each half had different ingredients and we had to lift the cheese to see what was what since we had added extra cheese. Hello, is any sausage, green pepper and onion down there? Each pizza comes with a container of garlic butter sauce and I thought, what the hell and dumped it all over the pizzas, what a greasy mess. We were not happy campers with our pizzas. HOWEVER! The dough became a crust, the garlic butter had sunk through and the garlic shouted out to us and we both agreed it was so much better. A plus is that you can build your own pizza and order and pay for it on line. Hubby had the wings, 10 wings which can be plain or sauced in different ways and he said they were not very good. text: There are two Esau's Diners in and around the Santa Barbara area. One 10 miles south of SB, in Carp, and this one right downtown in Santa Barbara--recently risen from the proverbial ashes. Formerly the downtown Esau's was located on lower State street . It has now, after a year's absence, moved up a few blocks, and across one to Chapala, directly across from Paseo Nuevo. In its former location Esau's was everything you expected. A diehard surfer diner, primed for big breakfasts, and thanks to the UCSB crowd, open till late at night too. Noisy, busy, rough around the edges, but always fun, fast, and satisfying. Sadly, none of that seems to ring true in its new locale up on Chapala. It's been open for at least three months now, but we could easily have mistaken our recent foray there as if it was opening night. Long lines, inept waiting list helpers, and a front of the house crew who all seemed to be on their first ever food service shift. The service wasn't so much bad, as essentially non-existent. Nobody was nasty or offensive. Just simply not there. Even when someone did show up at the table, they were still not really there. Eyes glazed over, and clearly not interested in... well anything it seemed. Since we had however waited 45 minutes to get a table, once seated (akwardly) we opted to stay and order some lunch. (Breakfast time had since well passed). A Patty Melt and a Rueben Melt, one with fries, the other with rings. Food did arrive within a somewhat reasonable timeframe, but there was no love at all. Items were clearly tossed onto the plate, and thrown off the line as fast as possible. The sandwiches were edible, the fries well cooked, and the rings unfrozen. We ate, we paid, we tipped, and we will never return. This is not the Esau's we came to know and love when we first moved to SB 7 years ago. And it pains me to now know, that that Esau's down on State street will forever be nothing more than a pleasant memory.

text: I discovered Chadwick's on restaurant.com and one glance at their kids' menu determined that we HAD to check it out. My husband and I went last week to try it out, figuring that if we liked it, it could become a regular place to take the kids, with food they would actually eat, and at reasonable prices! Pulling up we were impressed with the building, the golf course location, and the decor. The restaurant was almost empty, with one small table, and one larger family gathering of about 10-12 as the only other customers at the time. We decided we would try the sampler, but with seasoned fries rather than portabello fries. Note that the portabello fries on their own are $7 and the seasoned fries are $4. Our waitress told her that there was no way they could replace them, and that she could ask, but it would be pointless. Ok, either you know for sure that it's not a possibility, or you don't know and you ask, without making it seem like it's wasting your time. So we decided to try the "asian" chicken wraps. There were no drinks on the menu, but considering we walked past a bar on the way in, "Do you serve alcohol?" seemed like a legitimate question. She seemed shocked that we were asking, and then said that they didn't have a drink list, so what kind of drinks did we want? We asked what wines they had, and she came back from the bar with the names written down. We ordered the Riesling and Pinot Grigio and when she brought them back, she said she had no idea which was which. My husband got the Cowboy cut Prime Rib, described as being lightly seasoned with steak sauce, and served on top of fizzled onions. We knew there might be trouble when she asked how well he wanted his prime rib done... I went with the top sirloin steak, medium well. Neither one of us noticed that she didn't give us the choice between baked potato, fries, or mashed, as was listed on the menu. One of the other waiters brought our appetizer. On first glance, I was super excited. They had the typical choices...chicken, shredded carrots and cucumber... and they had what they called lo mein noodles, wonton strips, and three sauces. Then we dug in. The lettuce was small spring mix type lettuce, not typical iceberg, and it wasn't crisp enough to be able to hold anything inside of it. The lo mein noodles were spaghetti with no flavor, the wonton strips were stale, and the three sauces were an italian type vinagrette, a duck sauce, and something of barbecue consistency that tasted like a black jellybean. Our entrees arrived and Jason's prime rib had grill marks on it. Contrary to what we both thought "fizzled onions" would be (sauteed onion slices), they are actually the crispy onions from a can that you put in green bean casserole, and the whole thing was drenched in a less-spicy A-1 knockoff steak sauce. My steak looked alright, but tasted like liver. We both got baked potatoes. I got butter and sour cream. Jason got neither. At least our steamed vegetables were good (and like an old folks' home dining room, they are all you smell as soon as you walk in the door.) Halfway through we ordered another glass of wine each. She brought it to is explaining that she found out how to tell the difference... that Pinot is almost clear, and Riesling is darker.... Ummmmm not most ones that I've tried but ok. The confusing part being that neither one of the glasses tasted quite the same as our first. We chalked it up to being a little wine buzzed and having traumatized taste buds, but when we got the bill, we realized that they had given us four completely different (and differently priced) glasses of wine. But hey, at least we had shirtless rednecks rebuilding engines on the Speed channel to watch on the big screen TVs on the walls...

text: On February 29th of 2008 I organized a small group of friends of mine to to be charged an enormous amount of money for possibly the worst dining experience of Chinatowns history! Woo Hoo! Someone sent me a link to what sounded like the dinner of a lifetime: Join Chef Poon for a traditional 10-course Chinese New Year Banquet featuring dishes from 8 nations. It sure wasn't difficult to convince some friends to join me since the menu sounded absolutely wonderful. When we arrived at 1010 Arch street in Chinatown we found ourselves ascending a flight of dirty carpeted stairs that rewarded us with what looked like a wood-panelled storage room turned into emergency shelter/Chinese banquet room. You see, there was an abundance of personal items and restaurant supplies such as old chairs, lamps and boxes of Christmas decorations piled up along the front part of the 2nd floor space. There was no pretentious covering this stuff up. No, it was there it was flavor! The tables set up for our party and the other groups of victims were actually stainless steel work bench tables you might see in an industrial kitchen. But of course these were covered with white table covers that were bleached, and yet still stained, so often they were holy. Folding chairs were covered with images of Chef Poon, which would be creepy if not for the striking resemblance and level of class that one would see at Buddakan. Steven Starr, eat your hear out. Also, my group being fortunate, we were placed at the much sought after tables with the best views. We were actually in the space deemed "the kitchen" The equipment and sinks were only a mere 5 feet from our table! Nonetheless the mood was one of anticipation. If the place was THIS humble, imagine how great the food must be! So we began with ordering a round of drinks. We had a choice of generic Chinese beer or a glass of cheep box wine for a bargain $6. We had no idea what was in store for us. The meal was over in less than 40 minutes and perhaps that's a good thing. I wish you were there.... Oh.. let me walk you through it! No, no, it will be my pleasure to share this! The first 2 "courses" were some mouthful-sized appetizer tastes that were actually pretty decent though tiny. (Try and read the following as if you're training for the speed reading championships.) These first courses were brought out at a leisurely pace of one per every... oh let's say 2.5 minutes. It's a good thing though, since each of us had such supermarket-sample-sized portions we often were able to consume each before the next part of the feast arrived creating a sense of pride and accomplishment. Honestly, there's no finer dining atmosphere better than that of a pie eating contest and this was damn close to it. So, as each dish was delivered to our work-bench table we found ourselves slowing down. It was similar to when a child discovers something that causes pain and is reluctant try it again. Larger dishes to be shared were brought out and and presentation occurred all at once so it really started feeling like a feast. The presentation of some seemed aesthetically pleasing, while others were a bit scary. Mostly though the seafood was fishy. The Bass was greasy and the salmon tasted old, like "honey we should've thrown this out a week ago" old. The Fried rice dish was sweet and unpleasant while perhaps the lowest point of the meal was the Lobster dish. A large dish of linguine was covered by pieces of lobster broken to hard chunks still in their shell. They were delivered with no tools to crack the shells or retrieve the lobster meat. Digging with a fork seemed useless but in a way I was glad the lobster was till in it's impenetrable shell; it protected it from being contaminated by the tangy-sour and glowingly artificial red BBQ sauce which stung the eye as much as the tongue. And being Chinatown, we certainly were treated to our well deserved happy ending. The sumptuous dessert consisted of a half-inch square of still mostly frozen cheescake/cookie pierced with a toothpick which held the single white grape on. MMMmmmmhmmm. And then, the generosity flowed when Chef Poons staff rushed out to clank onto our table a half glass of Cook's sparkling wine. So in the end we each paid $54 per person (in Chinatown!) for what we all agreed was our worst culinary experience to date. *Please note, the delay of this review is partially because this event predated my Yelp awareness and I had tried to suppress these memories. Forgetting is hard though since lately when my friends and I experience unpleasant meals or find ourselves greatly ripped off, we say we've been "Pooned". It's become a handy verb.

text: An agreeable, occasionally bizarre bazaar, Booth's Corner has been around for a number of decades, but I've only recently started exploring it's depths. This is the wrong way to go, though. Do not be wary of the beaming ruddy women who look like extras from Big Love. Don't stamp your feet with impatience when you are stuck behind a lumbering mass of humanity (or a battalion of strollers) trying to navigate the corridors. This is all part of the experience that has become my treasured Saturday tradition. Rather than try to form a decent informative paragraph, let me just list off the top of my head the various goods & services you can purchase here until my hands cramp: Raw goat's milk, spices galore, jewelry, cheese curds, knives & swords, homemade ice cream (pumpkin, YUM), used books, herbs, socks, vinyl records, a hair cut, discount shoes, all manners (and matters) of fruits and vegetables, "mystical gifts", name brand perfumes; flour, unbleached & bleached; second hand vacuums, dvds, VHS tapes sorted by actor/actress (heavy on the Tom Cruise, Jodie Foster and Adam Sandler selection) cupcakes, fresh fish, a pet dog, frumpy clothes, hewn furniture, more polished-looking furniture, "legal services"; you can possibly purchase a home by stopping at the Century 21 outpost, luncheon meats, an 8-track player, chocolates, coffee, farm-fresh fowl, specialty sausages, an infinite number of prepared foods, flowers, those holiday flags your neighbor adorescandlesnutsbreadspastriesfreshsqueezedorange juiceeggnogmyfingersarecrrraaammmppping... Then of course there are the restaurants that dot the market, upwards of ten or so. I haven't been to any other than Cajun Kate's, but, uh, they exist. Carry cash, some stands take CCs but others don't. There's an ATM in Booth's Corner though, have no fear. Generally speaking, the items to purchase here are less expensive than their non-Booth's Corner counterparts, but always appraise a price with the keener of your two eyes. Not always is a bargain to be had. Um, parking sucks but you'll deal. They're open only Fridays & Saturdays, so waves of people come and go en masse. Wear your grimiest clothes and your most relaxed, accepting attitude and have a blast. (Insert one last plug for Cajun Kate's here)

text: This is my 4th or 5th time going to Bar Ferdinand and it was just as awesome as always. I was there with a bunch of friends from The Restaurant School (TRS) for our friend Ann's visit back to Philly. This is one of her favorite places too. We also got our favorite waitress! I wish I knew her name cause I would give her mad props. I think every time I've had her, its been in a large group, and she handles us so well. On to the food! Everyone was sharing their dishes at the table, but I remember the one's April and I had the best. I got the carrot and ginger soup that was on special and it was wonderful. Very delicate flavor, silky and just delicious. I saw that they had a new sandwich, Pato Ahumado, that was a duck slider. It was the tastiest of all the sandwiches and I've tried them all. We both got the Datiles con Tocino which are dates, bacon, and cream cheese in a puff pastry. These are April's favorites. April also had their Salmon special for the night, which was house cured and presented on a Himalayan salt block. The salmon was stuffed with some sort of micro greens. It was good but some bites were a little too salty for me. She also got the Pork Belly and Monkfish Skewers, Pixin con Panceta. This is another dish I have had before and like. The pork belly they use is like 80% fat and just melts in your mouth while going so well with the monkfish. Our whole table ordered the Paella, which was not as good as I remember from my first visit there. It was good, but I just remember it being so much better. I guess the first time I had it was also the first time I had Paella too. Finally for dessert we finally tried their Churros con Chocolate, which we have been wanting to try every time we go but wind up going with something else. I guess our instincts were right, cause they were just ok. The chocolate dipping sauce was excellent, very rich and thick, but the churros just didn't do it for me. I guess I just prefer the Mexican style more.

text: The Bleeding Deacon is a dark, smoky, S. City neighborhood bar with music related decor and lots of bald headed, facial haired, pierced individuals running around (think Royale, CBGB's, etc.). The service is friendly. They have a jukebox with an eclectic selection of tunes, or you might hear everything from Red Hot Chili Peppers to Cheap Trix via iPod. They also have Wi-fi, multi player LAN games and a small patio out back. The menu is definitely a step up for pub grub. Lots of comfort food with a modern twist. Very reasonably priced. The entrees average $10 and most every thing else is less than that. The value is very good. And while bacon is a menu staple (even on the dessert menu), they also cater to vegetarians. Sweet potatoes are a staple too (mashed and salsa - yum!). A couple of negatives... the place is smoky, the chicken with mac & cheese entree is sounds great but fails to deliver any taste and the 20% gratuity for parties of 6 or more is a joke. Mandatory gratuity for small groups (less than 10) is quickly becoming a St. Louis standard and is ridiculous. I understand with large groups but let's get this straight people. GRATUITY IS OPTIONAL and not enforceable under law (unless it is agreed upon and in a contract, such as a restaurant discount program or a catering contract). In addition, PAY YOUR PEOPLE. It's not our job! Amount of tip is for me to decide based on the service provided. There is nothing wrong with suggesting a tip, but adding it is another thing. Overall, I think the Bleeding Deacon is a great find because of the affordable, bar food that is homemade and tasty. I've had better comfort food in a bar for less, but it's a great value, which gets them almost 4 stars. If it was smoke free, it would be four stars without a doubt.

The receptionist was busy checking out other clients and talking with someone she appeared to be friends with, so it took a minute to get me checked in. I wasn't really warmly greeted and the receptionist went right back to talking to her friend rather than welcoming me, a new client. I was on time for my waxing appointment, and the waxer was running behind, but no one bothered to tell me, or even check in to see how I was doing during my wait or apologize for not running on schedule. No one asked me to take a seat or offered me any coffee or water from their refreshment area until a random stylist came up to me after I had been waiting for about 10 minutes already. When my waxer came out, she was visibly flustered because she was running behind. I kind of felt bad for her. Granted, I was using a Groupon for waxing services so I'm sure that's why she was so busy. She was very nice throughout the whole appointment. She led me into the waxing room, which was nice looking and private. She had me take off my shoes and pants with her in the room, which I thought was a little strange. When I have gotten waxed before I was given a few minutes of privacy to do this. She had me leave may panties on to wax as well. I guess some people do it that way, but again, I had always had my knickers off before when having this service. Then came the reason I won't return: She used the same metal spatula to apply all my wax and was "double dipping" in the wax pot. If I wasn't in such a rush to get this done for a special occasion and I hadn't bought the groupon already, I would have ended the appointment. That is extremely unhygenic. Now I get to spend the next week or so praying that I don't get a skin infection or anything. I was also bruised just a bit, but not much. My waxer also told me her last 2 appointments directly before me were also for bikini services, so all I was thinking the whole time was "ew" and "man, I hope those other 2 girls showered as thoroughly as I did before their appointments." I can't speak for their other salon services, but for what they charge for a wax, to be treated the way I was and for the waxing to be unhygenic like that I feel ripped off. I'll probably call and complain about the 'double dipping,' because that just shouldn't EVER happen. The only reason this place gets 2 stars is because it did look nice, the waiting area was comfortable, and my waxer was very sweet and friendly. EDIT: I called the salon and expressed my concerns about the waxing method. My waxer called me back promptly and informed me that they use NuFree waxing product, which is 'self sanitizing,' allowing them to use one spatula per client (I did forget to mention a new, clean spatula was used on me). I did look it up online and was able to find a scientific published study that seems to back up this claim. Still, based on my other experiences there, I don't know that I would go back.

text: Sixteen years ago I adopted the best dog in the whole world. Found in cage number 11, he barked and smiled and barked some more and it was love at first sight. But, the SPCA did not want to let me adopt him. I was young, I rented an apartment, I did not have a property deed. It is understandable to want to ensure that a pet will have a good home. And perhaps promises of undying love and devotion are not enough to warrant the transfer of a dog from a shelter to a stranger. But they made me jump through many hoops: copies of my lease; wanting to talk to my landlord (before cell phones made this possible at the times they were open.) And, they were not very nice. Rude, dismissive, too busy to be bothered, annoyed. Three times I visited hoping to adopt him. And next to me were homeowners (this seemed to be the key) looking at a dog. They clearly stated, "If he doesn't work out we can just bring him back." It was unbelievable that these people, elderly but possessing a property deed, were able to be so brazen about their lack of commitment and still allowed to adopt the dog. Well, the short side of the story is that I did what all young girls are tempted to do when they feel mistreated. I called my father. I am not sure what he did, or who he talked to, but on the fourth day and fourth attempt to adopt Kota, I was granted the privilege of taking him home. We have been together ever since. And I am very thankful to my father for his mysterious assistance. Just recently, 16 years later, I found a dog running lose, trailing his leash behind him in Media. Of course, I grabbed him before he ran into traffic on State Street and proceeded to ask everyone I saw if they knew the dog. Then Sam and I spent several hours going from place to place, pet store, emergency vet, etc. to see if anyone knew where he lived, if he had a micro chip, etc. The Del. Co. SPCA was our last choice. Funny, that ideally it should have been our first choice. But the sentiment was consistent at each place we visited. Perhaps better to keep the dog for a few days and post signs than to drop him off there... In the end we had no choice. We walked into the SPCA and were completely ignored as the staff talked amongst themselves commenting on a recent client...negatively in front of other clients. They seemed disorganized and annoyed (still!) And there Sam and I stood wtih a little dog in our arms...waiting...waiting. Finally we had to be rude to get someone's attention. (What did they think we wanted standing there with this dog anyway?) There is a happy ending. Someone realized she had taken a "Lost Dog" call for the dog we had found. The owners were called and we volunteered to drive the dog home. He never had to be checked into or checked out of the SPCA. It would have been hard to leave him there. If people love animals and want to work with them, I would hope that they would like people who also loved animals and are trying to help them. But it seemed there is no protocol to dealing with people, or communicating, or being helpful. A place to adopt animals should be much friendlier, perhaps cleaner, perhaps more organized.

text: For many years, my family and I, 1st generation Vietnamese immigrants, have been coming to Pho Tau Bay. We loved the food, the warmth, and the way it brought Vietnamese immigrants together over a hot bowl of pho. Over the past few years, however, PTB has lost its genuine Vietnamese charm, prioritizing American approval over Vietnamese solidarity. The past few times I have been to PTB have been extremely disappointing. When I try to speak Vietnamese to people on the staff (the ones that are obviously Vietnamese), they curtly respond in English. One waitress won't even acknowledge me when I place my order in Vietnamese. But to their American clientele, they are courteous and attentive. The servers I've had come to my table twice--once to take my order and once to bring the food. No refills, no courtesy check-ups, nothing. People remark about how cheap PTB is, but if you compare their portion sizes to other Vietnamese restaurants in the New Orleans area, it's not that great of a deal. The pho bowls are small and they give you more broth than anything else. If you look closely, you'll notice that very few Vietnamese people eat here these days. It's because all of them have noticed the same thing I have: we are no longer wanted here. Realizing this, I will no longer eat at PTB, but instead at its Westbank rivals, Tan Dinh or Pho Hoa, or the lesser-known restaurants in New Orleans East, Dong Phuong, Pho Bang, & Ba Mien, where most of the waitstaff still speak to me in my native tongue. Please don't get me wrong, I'm not discrediting the food at PTB. The dishes are delicious. It's why I've been going there since I was 8, why I referred it to so many of my American friends, why I still decided to give it the benefit of the doubt despite feeling unwanted there, why I gave it two stars instead of one. But I'm Vietnamese. When I eat a bowl of bun bo hue or some goi cuon, I want to feel like I'm home. And that place is no longer with Pho Tau Bay.

text: Everything I had read or heard about this place was true and more. We were there last Friday for dinner. The menu is hand written on a 20 by 30 chalkboard that the server brings to your table and then proceeds to explain every single entree being offered that evening (there were about 6 appetizers and 10-12 entrees but I did not really count). This exercise in itself was quite enjoyable. We ordered the ravialo truffes ($16) as the appetizer. For main course I chose the canard (duck in honey and lavender sauce, $25) and my husband chose the boeuf bourgignon ($25). The kitchen is visible from the eating area and you can actually watch the chef prepare the meal and even hear him humming a tune now and then. Quite charming. The appetizer arrived quite promptly - 6 pieces of ravioli in butter sauce, accompanied by a good amount of bread "for dipping in the butter sauce". The first bite was all I needed to be convinced that we had found our new "special" place. OMG. It was an orchestra of delicate flavors in my mouth. The truffles, the cheese, the aged balsamic in the butter sauce... it was perfect. The duck was very tender and the sauce was.... divine. My favorite was the sweet potato tart (tart is my name for it, the chef might not agree) that was the side. My husband's choice had exceeded his expectation, he said. I am not a big fan of French haute cuisine but this was country-style - bolder, heartier and much to my liking. By 7:00 pm, they had one duck and one filet available. But in some ways perhaps that is Le Coq Rouge's strong point. We will definitely go back any chance we get.

text: Truly a disgrace. I've been going to Tujaque's with my wife for over 15 years and have witnessed its steady, disappointing decline. It was one of the first venerable "Old New Orleans" restaurants I ever experienced. And I loved it. The set menu food was tasty, succulent and somehow original even though the menu had not changed in decades. I liked the attentive waitstaff and maitre'd who had apparently worked there since he was young. The place was always packed. I went there often enough that it felt like home. No longer. We returned to Tujagues about a month ago for the first time in over two years and, man, were we ever unhappy. The beef brisket, which was once the best possible way to start a meal, was rubbery, salty and bland. The waiter, a feckless girl, offered seconds. We declined. The shrimp remoulade arrived as a runny, sloppy mess. It was salty and the tiny shrimp were tough little bastards. I ate the lettuce because I was hungry. Same for the bread. I barely remember the soup except to say that my wife didn't touch her's. The real disaster started when the entrees came out. There were four choices: beef, shrimp, chicken and fish. We passed on the beef since the brisket was so bad. It didn't matter. Everything was alternately salty, overcooked, undercooked (that red stuff in the chicken was not gravy...gross), bland, slimy or, generally, unappetizing. We ended up trying everything because we had to send it all back. Some kind of dessert with "rum sauce". It was bland and salty. I don't think there was any rum in it. I don't know what happened to the Tujague's we loved. Maybe there's a new chef who never ate at the restaurant in it's heyday. Maybe he doesn't understand the history. Maybe the owners are now too old to appreciate good New Orleans food (too much salt, butter, love, etc.) Worse, maybe they are content to let the money roll in from all the tourists and assorted suckers who wind up wasting their time and money here. Whatever the reason, it doesn't matter. Tujague's is a disgrace and this was the worse meal I've suffered through in the past decade. It's all pretty depressing as the restaurant was once one of the jewels of our dining scene. I guess it's true what they say. You really can't go home again. R.I.P. Tujaque's. I don't know when you died, but it's a real bummer that you were replaced by Zombie Tujaque's.

The sub/zep roll is fresh and works perfectly with the roast pork/peppers; not too much pull on the bread to make the sub/zep messy and not too soft to cause the juiciness of the pork/peppers/cheese to leak through the bread. Make sure to add provolone to the mix and you have one great sandwich that you know you are going to make at home any day of the week. Also order some delicious homemade pierogies (I hade the cheese/potato) to bring home with you. They were frozen but are homemade. I placed them in salted boiling water for about 6 minutes (dont overcook them or they will fall apart in the boliing water) and then fried them in melted butter for about 2 minutes per side until they were lightly browned. They were awesome! I travel through Pa/NJ/NY/CT weekly and always seeking all types of on the go excellent bneighborhood mom/pop food (especially subs/zeps/wedges/hoagies). Wasko's is a definite stop back for excellent roast pork/peppers/cheese zeps/subs whenever I am in the Phoenixville area!

text: To preface this review: This is the first review that I have written and given 1 star. Came here on a Friday night with my boyfriend and his parents, his father being a trained chef and food distributor. This place leaves something to be desired... We sat at the sushi bar and all 4 of us requested the all you can eat sushi ($25pp). We also ordered a very large bottle of sake ($60) which was beautifully presented in a gold ice bucket. After sitting at the bar for about 15 minutes and receiving not even a glance from the sushi chefs, we asked our waitress how we order. She wasn't sure but handed us some ala-cart sheets to fill in. So we marked some orders on the sheets and handed it to the chef who then looked very surprised and still had not made any eye contact. We asked for some edamame as we were starving and still waiting to even place an order. The edamame was served in a very small dish, was cold and overcooked, and the waitress only brought 2 orders for the 4 people and no dishes to put our shells on. The sushi started to slowly come out, some coming from the chefs at the sushi bar and some mysteriously being walked out from the chefs in the kitchen - maybe they have an extra hidden sushi bar in the back? I have an allergy to fish roe (go figure - as sushi is one of my most favorite foods!) and always alert the chefs and ask that no fish roe be included on certain rolls that I eat. I rarely ever have a problem with this request and I eat sushi on a weekly basis. As expected, they ignored the request and almost every roll came out with some lingering fish roe from the last roll made. Needless to say, I could not eat anything that came out. Additionally, the raw sushi rolls were served on very warm plates - yuck! To make matters worse, the waitress didn't come back to offer us any plates to share sushi and didn't remove the pile of plates that was stacking up or clear the edamame dishes. The final straw was when rolls started coming out that literally looked like giant rice balls with one tiny slice of fish that could barely even be seen hidden within all the rice. We decided this was not worth eating and called over the manager/owner who was most apologetic but that still didn't make the food any better. We showed him the warm plates, the giant rolls of rice, the poor cuts of fish and the gristle that was left on several slices. We informed him that we eat sushi in reno weekly at a variety of places and this was perhaps the worst sushi meal we have had yet. He provided us with a 50% discount as we told him we were no longer interested in eating any more then we already had. Sadly, we all left hungry and unsatisfied. All in all, the sake was excellent and beautifully presented. But that was about the only enjoyable part of our meal at rim. Maybe once they work out some kinks, this place will be worth trying again. For now, leave this place to the tourists who are looking for a mediocre at best meal while staying at the GSR.

text: I really wanted to like OTS. I've heard good things from people so I went there for dinner today for the first time with two girlfriends. I was really unimpressed. It took probably 20 minutes to get our burgers and another few for the wedges. I didn't think the potato wedges were good at all; they were really bland. I was expecting some seasoning or something but they were just fried and served with green onions and a bit of crumbled bleu cheese on top. My friend and I asked for our burgers well done and they came out very pink. By that time I was so hungry that I just ate it, but anywhere else I probably would have sent it back to be cooked longer. My friend's medium well burger was really really pink. I got the mushroom burger and the mushroom and swiss cheese topping was very good. It was served with a ranch sauce which was good but too runny, it slid straight off the burger. The burger was also really small. The menu said it was 1/3 pound, but it seemed much smaller. If you want waiter service this is one of the few places in IV you can go, and it's not terrible. I didn't have a bad experience, just was unimpressed. text: When my sister who's also my Maid Of Honor told me we would be going wine tasting in Santa Barbara for my bachelorette weekend I was overjoyed! We instantly went on Yelp and started hunting for the most cost effective wine tour company with great reviews. We landed at Captain Jacks. My sister called up Jack (who's apparently much easier to get ahold of when you're paying), she booked the tour for nine and we were on our way! The van picked us up at our hotel and to our surprise there was only room for 8, meaning only 8 seatbelts. Yet Captain Jack gladly took our payment for 9 girls. We get to our first winery and everything was fine and dandy, we all pile in the car to head to the second winery when my sister and I received the scariest phone call of our lives. Our parents had been in a rollover accident and they're both being rushed to the hospital. We immediatelyreturned to the hotel where they were the epitome of class and compassion and only charged us for cleaning fee for that day and refunded our money for the night. The driver from Captain Jacks was also very understanding and told us not to worry, that as long as we explained our situation we should get some sort of refund. Days later my sister called Captain Jack and explained the situation. He merely offers a $175 gift certificate for a future visit. My biggest question is why on earth would we return to an establishment who's unwilling to work with it's customers during a time of tragedy. In complete disbelief I asked my fiancé to talk to Captain Jack. He spoke to someone named Andrew who brought up Disneyland as an example. He stated that if we were to visit Disneyland and hadan emergency and had to leave, they wouldn't refund our money. He dismissed the example as a pathetic attempt to make a comparison with no validity. He then asked to speak to Captain Jack but Andrew told him he had left for the day. My Fiance called the following day 4 times with no luck getting a hold of Jack. When my Fiance spoke to Andrew again he explained that any refund would've been accepted and appreciated. I'm dissapointed that a business with zero ethics can still be in business. Please make sure your family is safe and sound in a bubble before giving this company your money because you will be left high and dry in the case of an emergency.

text: Nothing completes a fulfilling dining experience more than a great view of the traffic on 22nd Street... Yep, I am naturally projecting a bit facetiousness upon you about the "ambiance" of Maico. All kidding aside for just a second, the dining experience at Maico is decidedly unsophisticated. Indeed, I was quite drawn to the rustic feel of the place: there is no indoor dining per se. One reviewer characterized this situation thusly: "Maico: eat with flies." They do, however, have plenty of tables and chairs in a patio area. And when I say patio, I mean the patio of a former home. So on top of having to eat al fresco, you literally have to order at what used to be a window. Seriously, take a second from being enraptured by this review to look at the nearest window on your home, apartment, or other dwelling and imagine it without any sort of glass. Then look around your living space and kitchen and imagine it converted to one big cooking area devoted to making Mexican food. Finally, picture that food being produced being pretty damn good. Now snap back to reality and continue with my review. Like you, I'm sure, when I first heard of Maico, I was like "WTF, what the hell is Maico?" I had passed by the place several times with interest barely registering. Then I heard that the dude from Travel Channel's Bizarre Food paid a visit to the place a while back. He apparently sampled the birria, or goat stew. A few weeks ago, I happened to drive by the place on my way to a friend's. I was hungry and decided to make a spontaneous stop. In all honesty, I've only been here once and ordered just three tacos. Like any good, self-respecting taqueria, the carne asada was seasoned well, cooked properly, had fresh condiments including salsa with a nice bite, and tasty flour tortillas. I also had one aforementioned birria taco. That, too, was made properly. You could tell that it took hours to cook, as the goat was very tender and effused with spices and chili. The three tacos were washed down with the required Mexican soda. I caught glimpses of dishes from other patrons, and it all appeared tasty, so I will make plans in the future to try some non-taco items. The food there undoubtedly was good. Judging from my wise-cracking comments earlier about the ambiance of Maico, I truly don't have a problem with eating outdoors. In fact, I would say that the majority of places in town that serve the best tacos don't have indoor seating. In fact, tacos in Mexico are quintessentially a street food made and eaten on the street with the flies and whatnot. Though I don't think many streets in Mexico matches the beauty, character or liveliness of our little 22nd Street.

text: I don't know why I do this to myself. I really don't. It's not like there aren't other sub-par chain alternatives out there. I could have done TGI Fridays. Just as repulsive, but a little closer to my house. I could have done The Olive Garden. Again, just as repulsive, but with a little more care taken in the final product. But this meal wasn't for me. It was for two friends whom I hadn't seen in several years. They like the joint and I was just kind of tagging along. I obliged happily, perused the on-line menu before hand, and figured I'd make the best of it. Ruby Tuesday's has gotten a fair amount of press of late for the apparent "upscaling" of its menu. Well you can take the girl out of the trailer, but you can't take the trailer out of the girl. It doesn't matter how much lobster you put into something as homey and mac & cheese. If some basic cooking fundamentals aren't there, then it's still cardboard a la cheese. But I digress. My friends and I gathered on a Saturday night and expected a crowd. Well, perhaps Ruby Tuesday's just ain't the hip thing anymore; the restaurant was only about a quarter full. My friends and I were seated in a too-small booth. Since none of us is terribly large, we think this may have been a two-person booth. We were greeted promptly by a very kind and cheerful young waitress who took our drink orders. We perused the menu and placed our order when she returned. She took our appetizer and main entree orders at the same time. I'm normally reluctant to do this because -- as would be confirmed later -- I find restaurants often rush out the mains after serving the apps just minutes before -- a HUGE no-no in my mind. We each ordered the salad bar with our meals and decided to head up. Honestly, this was the best part of the meal. The vegetables weren't perfect, but they were discernible foodstuffs. And, it was actually a pretty tasty salad. We each agreed this was our favorite part. The waitress brought our appetizer -- guacamole -- and I gave it one look and knew it wasn't going to be good. There were big chunks of all sorts of stuff in there. Tomato, jalapeno, onion. This was definitely not a "normal" guacamole. Also not normal was the excessive amount of heat provided by the jalapenos. The avocado had little -- if any -- flavor and I almost wonder how Ruby Tuesday's prepares this dish and if it's even real avocado. The presentation was messy, as well. Sorry, but serving something goopy like guacamole in a lettuce leaf is unacceptable. A good deep bowl is what's called for when it comes to guac! The chips and accompanying salsa were no good, as well. The salsa, in particular, lacked flavor and a good bit of salt. Disappointingly, a few minutes after receiving the guac, our entrees arrived. Simply put: How annoying! Ugh...but whatever. This meal wasn't designed to impress. For my main, I ordered the turkey burger minis. Instead of fries, I opted for a side of broccoli. What a disappointment. The burgers were lifeless and flavorless. I swear the only reason I didn't put down the burgers was because my body required a good amount of protein after a workout an hour earlier. I literally needed to shove those burgers down my throat so I would get the protein I so richly needed. The broccoli I substituted wasn't necessarily bad -- it's just it looked a mess! There were about five tiny florets scattered messily around the plate as if no one in the kitchen had taken any care with presentation. My friend ordered the 7-oz. sirloin medium well. It looked like it came out medium. She also ordered the mashed potatoes and broccoli. After one bite of the potatoes, she could eat no more. I tasted them and something was definitely off. Almost like they poured a whole canister of MSG in them -- there was definitely a taste about them. My other friend ordered some wings and mashed cauliflower. The mashed cauliflower went uneaten after one bite; the wings were greedily devoured. Unimpressed, we decided against ordering dessert; we went out into the mall and walked a bit to the nearby gelato stand in the food court and had a decent bowl of that Italian delicacy. Can't say I'll ever be returning to a Ruby Tuesday's. The generic, uninspired Americana cuisine they're serving doesn't make me proud to be an American at all!

text: The Hotel Provincial is an excellent guest house on the quiet side of the French Quarter (closer toward Esplanade). But even if a haunted hotel doesn't top your list of places to stay, the Provincial is worth looking into. Amenities include 2 pools, free continental breakfast, valet (at $18 per day, which isn't bad for the Quarter). Guest rooms are quite beautiful. If you prefer a quiet room, request one that is not located facing the main courtyard, where the sounds of guests (who can sometimes get loud by the pool) really bounce of the walls. During your stay, ask the front desk about nightly walking tours of haunted New Orleans; they are fun and totally worth the price! Croissant D'or (on Ursulines between Chartres and Royal), located just around the corner from the hotel is the perfect spot to grab a delicious and reasonably priced morning coffee.

Bottom Line: The only reason I could see someone going here is if you're in Northern Liberties and you want to eat between the hours of 3 and 4 am. text: My boyfriend and I wanted to go to the opening of BBP in Philly last Tuesday night, but with 4 young kids between us we decided to wait. Thank God we did. Folks are commenting on how there was only one cashier working - I made the same comment to my boyfriend when we got in the door to which he pointed out that if they moved the line along any quicker by adding another cashier there'd be no seats. And there were seats available which at first was surprising given the number of people in line and the relatively small size of the place. We sat right down at the counter. It is worth mentioning that the wait staff was super friendly and accommodating...be interesting to see if that lasts past the first week. Anyway, on to the food...I had the LA Burger and I fretted over this decision the entire hour I was in line because there were so many good ones to chose from. Turns out it was probably one of the best burgers I've ever had. It doesn't come with any sauce on it and I never even thought to put ketchup and mustard (my normal burger combo) on it because the flavor of the burger was just so damn good I didn't want to mask it with anything else. My boyfriend had the Ceasar burger which was the April burger of the month. We taste tested each others burger. He said mine was better than his. He was right. But, the pepper flavor on his burger was super delish. I agree with some other reviewers that the fries left a litte something to be desired. We got the sweet potatoe fries and the regular fries. Sweet potatoes were probably the best I've had, but I'm not gaga over sweet potatoe fries so I was more interested in the regular fries. They were a litte disappointing because they really weren't seasoned. No salt, no spices, nada. The dipping sauce was tasty and I was thankful to have it to dip my unsalted, unspiced fries. I actually dipped my fries in all of the sauces at the counter and loved them as well - especially the Chipotle Ketchup. We also split the Vanilla Caramel Bourbon shake. Wow, that was a good shake. Try the shake. I want the pistachio one next time - no alcohol, but I love pistachio ice cream. Bottom line on BBP - you've got to go. They hype on a Food Network star opening a burger chain will not let you down. Bobby knows how to make a great burger and uses the best quality meat to do it.
